en: Reference system: NyS_ = Nyāyasūtra;
NySBh_ = Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya.
When there is the comprehension of an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that means of valid cognition is effective because it possesses the capacity for purposeful action.
Without a means of valid cognition, there is no comprehension of an object;
and without the comprehension of an object, there is no capacity for purposeful action.

Indeed, having apprehended an object through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), this knower either desires to acquire it or desires to avoid it. The exertion of one thus impelled by the desire to acquire or avoid is called "activity" (pravṛtti). Furthermore, its efficacy consists in its connection with the result.
One who exerts effort, desiring to obtain a certain object or wishing to abandon it, either attains that object or abandons it.
An "object" (artha), moreover, is happiness and the cause of happiness.
This object of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is incalculable.
Because the varieties of living beings are innumerable.

And when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is purposeful, the knower (pramātṛ), the object of knowledge (prameya), and the act of knowing (pramiti) become purposeful as well. Why? Because if any one of these is absent, the purpose cannot be accomplished.

In this context, he who, impelled by the desire to acquire or the desire to avoid, engages in activity is the knower (*pramātṛ*). That by which he correctly cognizes—that is, knows—the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And that object which is correctly cognized is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
That which is known is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
What, then, is reality?
It is the existence of that which exists and the non-existence of that which does not exist.

That which is apprehended as "existent" is reality (*tattva*) when it is grasped as it truly is and without error; and that which is apprehended as "non-existent" is reality when it is grasped as it truly is and without error.
But how, then, is the latter apprehended through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Because it is not perceived in the same manner as that which is being perceived, like a lamp.
For example, when an object visible by means of a lamp is being perceived, that which is not grasped there—just like the lamp—is present;
if it were to exist, it would be cognized just like this [visible object], but because of the absence of cognition, it does not exist.
Thus, in this way, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which reveals what exists, also reveals what does not exist.
Now, that which exists will indeed be taught as arranged in sixteen categories.
Of these various existing things—

NyS 1.1.1: From the knowledge of the true nature of the means of valid cognition, the objects of valid cognition, doubt, purpose, example, tenet, member [of a syllogism], reasoning, ascertainment, discussion, sophistry, cavil, fallacies of the reason, quibbling, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat, there is the attainment of the supreme good.
In this exposition, the analysis [of the compound] follows the literal wording:
it is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of "and" (*ca*).
In the phrase "the reality (*tattva*) of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth," the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śaiṣikī* sixth case).
The two genitive cases in "knowledge of reality" (*tattvasya jñānam*) and "the attainment of the supreme good" (*niḥśreyasasyādhigamaḥ*) denote the object of the action.
These are all the existing categories [of objects].
The teaching here is for the purpose of providing non-erroneous knowledge of them.
Thus, this meaning of the system (tantra) should be understood as presented without omission.
Indeed, from the true knowledge of the objects of cognition—beginning with the self—comes the attainment of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). And that [attainment] is restated by the subsequent sūtra:

"That which is to be abandoned, the cause of its production, the absolute abandonment of it, and the means for that [abandonment]—these four categories of objects must be correctly understood; having understood them, one attains the supreme good."

In that regard, the separate mention of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the others is purposeless, for doubt and the rest are included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*) as the case may be, and do not exist apart from them.
This is true;
however, these four sciences (*vidyā*), having distinct systems, are taught for the benefit of living beings, and of these—

This fourth [branch] is Ānvīkṣikī, the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). Its distinct categories (*padārtha*) are doubt and the others. Without the separate mention of these, it would be merely the science of the inner self (*adhyātmavidyā*).
Just as in the case of the Upaniṣads,
it is therefore established as a separate system by means of categories such as doubt and the rest;
for therein one does not proceed toward an object that has neither been perceived nor determined.
What then? [It concerns] a matter that is doubted.
And so it has been said:
"Ascertainment (nirṇaya) is the determination of a matter after having deliberated through the pro and the con."
*vimarśa* is doubt;
the thesis (*pakṣa*) and counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) constitute the operation of reasoning (*nyāyapravṛtti*).
Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of an object; it is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
On the other hand, doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that lacks such determination, consisting merely of an inquiry into an object as "what might this be?
Although it is included within the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), it is mentioned separately for this purpose.
"Artha" means purpose; that by which one is impelled to act is the "prayojana" (motive),
for it is desiring to obtain or avoid some object that one undertakes an action.
By this [Self], all living beings, all actions, and all sciences are pervaded; and upon it as its basis, the principle (nyāya) operates. What, then, is this principle?
The examination of objects by means of the instruments of valid knowledge—
namely, inference based upon perception and scripture—
is *sānvīkṣā*.
*Anvīkṣā* is the subsequent investigation (*anvīkṣaṇa*) of an object that has been perceived through perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*).
That which proceeds by means of this is *ānvīkṣikī*, the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*), namely the treatise on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*).
Furthermore, any inference that contradicts perception and scripture is a fallacy of logic (*nyāyābhāsa*).
Among these, debate (*vāda*) and sophistry (*jalpa*) have their specific purposes;
however, cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) is now examined. One who proceeds by means of cavil is a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).

If, when questioned about his purpose, he provides an account, then that becomes his position (*pakṣa*) and that becomes his tenet (*siddhānta*), whereby he abandons the status of a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).
But if he does not provide an account, he falls into the position that he is neither a worldly person nor an investigator.
Furthermore, if he states that the purpose is to make known the refutation of the opposing position,
this too is exactly the same;
for it is one who makes [something] known.
That which knows, that by which one makes known, that which is made known, and that which understands this— [all these are the same].
In that case, he abandons his status as a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*).
On the other hand, if he does not accept [the thesis], then his statement— that the purpose is to make known the refutation of the opponent's position— becomes meaningless.
And a collection of statements devoid of a thesis is *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).
If it accepts its own subject matter, that becomes its position (*pakṣa*) which must be established;
but if it does not accept it, it becomes a mere incoherent babble, devoid of meaning.
Thus, the state of being mere cavil is excluded.
Now, the example:
an object within the range of direct perception is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In this regard, the view of worldly investigators is not contradicted;
and that [view] is an object of cognition (prameya),
as well as its separate mention.
Inference and scripture have that [direct perception] as their basis;
when it exists, inference and scripture exist, and when it does not exist, they do not exist.
The application of logic is based upon that;
and by means of contradiction with an example, the refutation of the opponent's position must be stated,
while by means of the resolution of an example, one's own position must be established.
A nihilist who accepts an illustrative example abandons his nihilism;
if he does not accept it, by what means could he refute his opponent? Furthermore, it is possible to state [the argument] using a clearly defined illustrative example.
"An example is an instance which, through similarity with the subject (*sādhya*), possesses the property of that [subject]; this is the *udāharaṇa*.
(NS 1.1.36) "Or, by the reverse of that, it is the opposite.
(NS 1.1.37) Thus, a matter that is being accepted as "this exists" is a tenet (*siddhānta*).
And that [object] is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
Its separate mention is because debates (*vāda*), disputations (*jalpa*), and destructive criticisms (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed when there are various types of established tenets (*siddhāntabheda*).
"Not otherwise":
when the establishment of the matter to be proven is completed within a certain collection of words,
its five members— namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth— are called "members" (*avayava*) in relation to that collection.
Among these, the collection of means of valid cognition consists of:
scripture is the proposition (pratijñā),
and the reason (hetu) is inference (anumāna).
The example is perception; the application is comparison;
and the conclusion is the demonstration of the capacity [of the reason] when all [the members] converge upon a single object.
And the establishment of reality is based upon that.
And these members, being specific types of verbal expression, are included within the objects of knowledge (prameya); they are stated separately for this purpose.
Thus, reasoning (tarka) is not included among the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
It is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
rather, it serves as an auxiliary to the means of valid cognition for the sake of attaining knowledge of reality. An example of this is as follows:
Is this birth produced by a fabricated cause, or by one that is unfabricated, or is it accidental?
Thus, when the true nature of an object is unknown, reasoning proceeds by means of the application of causes: "If [birth] is brought about by a produced cause,
then through the cessation of that cause, this cessation of birth is logically established."
If, on the other hand, it is due to a non-artificial cause, then because the cessation of that cause would be impossible, the cessation of birth is untenable.
Or if it were accidental, [the same fault would apply].
Therefore, since that which is being extinguished by chance will not be extinguished again, no cause for cessation is logically possible;
thus, there would be no termination of birth. Regarding this subject of reasoning, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) operate to show that birth has karma as its cause.

They are assisted by reasoning (*tarka*). And because it provides a classification of the objects of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), reasoning serves as a means for that knowledge of reality.

Thus, although this reasoning—which has become such as described—is already included within the objects of cognition (*prameya*), it is mentioned separately for the purpose of being employed, together with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in debate (*vāda*) for the sake of establishing a point or for refutation.

Certainty is the knowledge of reality, which is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Discussion (*vāda*) culminates in that [certainty]. For the sake of its preservation, there exist debate (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*).
These two, reasoning and ascertainment, sustain the course of worldly life.
This ascertainment, being included within the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), is mentioned separately for this specific purpose.

Indeed, *vāda* (debate) is a collection of sentences consisting of various speakers, which establishes a proof for each respective point and concludes with the determination of one of the two positions; it is mentioned separately for the sake of illustration, because through what is thus illustrated, practical discourse leads to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Its two specific types, *jalpa* (contentious debate) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), have been stated to be for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality.

The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are enumerated separately from the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because they are to be pointed out in formal debate (*vāda*); however, in contentious discussion (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), all points of defeat are applicable.

The separate teaching of *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna* is for the purpose of illustration. Once these have been illustrated, one should avoid them in one's own speech and subject them to critical inquiry (*paryanuyoga*) in the speech of an opponent.
Regarding *jāti*, however, when it is employed by an opponent, its refutation is easily achieved.
And its application is easy to master oneself.
Thus, this Ānvīkṣikī, when analyzed through its categories such as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth,
is the lamp of all sciences and the means for the accomplishment of all actions.
She is proclaimed in the enumeration of knowledge as the support of all phenomena. Thus [it is said].
This knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasādhigama*) are to be understood according to their respective sciences.
Here, however, in this science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*), the knowledge of the self and so forth is the knowledge of reality.
Now, does that supreme good indeed occur immediately after the knowledge of reality?
It is said: "No; what then? [The answer is:

"From the knowledge of reality—NyS 1.1.2: upon the successive disappearance of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the non-existence of each preceding one, which is liberation."
In that regard, false knowledge of many kinds exists concerning the objects of cognition, beginning with the self and ending with liberation:
first, [the notion] "it does not exist" with respect to the self;
and [the notion] "the self" with respect to what is not the self.
perceiving suffering as happiness, the impermanent as permanent, and that which offers no protection as a protection;
In what is fearful, [he perceives] fearlessness; in what is loathsome, [he perceives] the desirable; in what is to be abandoned, [he perceives] that which is not to be rejected.
Regarding activity, [one holds that] there is no action and no fruit of action;
regarding defects, [one holds that] this cyclic existence is not caused by defects.
"In the state after death, there is no creature, nor a living soul, nor a being, nor a self that could depart and come into existence again;
birth is without cause, and the cessation of birth is without cause."
That rebirth has a beginning and is endless;
that being occasional, rebirth is caused by karma;
and that rebirth is without a self, consisting in the cessation and reconnection of the continuum of body, sense organs, intellect, and sensations.
Liberation (apavarga), indeed, is the cessation of all activity and the dissociation from everything;
since much that is auspicious is lost upon liberation, how could a wise person find pleasure in this liberation, which is the annihilation of all happiness and a state of insentience?
From this false knowledge arise attachment toward agreeable objects and aversion toward disagreeable ones.
Under the influence of attachment and aversion, there occur defects such as envy, malice, pride, and greed.
Impelled by the defects (doṣas) and acting through the body, one indeed practices violence, theft, and forbidden sexual intercourse;
through speech, falsehood, harshness, calumny, and incoherent talk;
and through the mind, malice toward others, covetousness for the property of others, and atheism.
This evil-natured activity leads to unrighteousness.
Now, as for the auspicious [action]: by means of the body, it consists of giving, protection, and service to others;
by means of speech, truthfulness, what is beneficial, what is pleasant, and the recitation of sacred texts;
and by means of the mind, compassion, lack of greed, and faith.
This is for the sake of *dharma*.
Here, *dharma* and *adharma*, which are the means for engaging in activity (*pravṛtti*), are expressed by the word "activity" (*pravṛtti*),
just as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) have food as their means.
"Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings.
This very activity is the cause of birth, whether it be contemptible or honored.
Birth, moreover, is the manifestation of a specific grouping of the body, the sense-faculties, the intellect, and sensations.
When that exists, there is suffering;
furthermore, that [suffering] is to be experienced as disagreeable, being affliction, pain, and torment.
These factors, beginning with false knowledge and ending with suffering, proceeding without interruption, constitute *saṃsāra*.
But when false knowledge departs due to the knowledge of reality, then the defects caused by false knowledge depart;
upon the departure of the defects, purposeful activity departs.
With the cessation of activity, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, suffering ceases;
and with the cessation of suffering, there is ultimate liberation, which is the supreme good.
Knowledge of reality, indeed, is explained as the opposite of false knowledge:
first, with regard to the self, it is "it exists"; and with regard to the non-self, it is "it is non-self."
In this way, it should be understood according to their respective objects that [the world] is suffering, impermanent, unprotected, fearful, loathsome, and to be abandoned.
Regarding [the truth of] origination: "Karma exists; the fruit of karma exists.
Regarding [the truth of] defects: "This saṃsāra is caused by defects."
Regarding the state after death (pretyabhāva), there is indeed a living being— a soul, a person, or a self— which departs and comes into existence again after departing;
thus, birth has a cause, and the cessation of birth has a cause.
"Transmigration is beginningless and ends with liberation"; thus,
transmigration, being occasional,
has activity as its cause.
Being endowed with a self (*sātmaka*), it proceeds through the severance and reconnection of the continuum of body, sense-faculties, cognition, and sensation.
As for liberation (*apavarga*): indeed, this liberation is the cessation of all [bondage], the tranquility resulting from the dissociation from everything.

Since much that is painful, terrible, and evil is being destroyed, how could a wise person not find favor with liberation (apavarga)—the eradication of all suffering and the cessation of the experience of all suffering?
It is just as food mixed with honey and poison is unfit to be consumed;
likewise, pleasure that is accompanied by suffering is unfit to be accepted. //2//
The operation of this treatise is threefold: enumeration (uddeśa), definition (lakṇa), and critical examination (parīkṣā).

Among these, enumeration is the naming of a mere category of objects by means of its designation. Definition is the property that excludes everything other than the true nature of that which has been enumerated.
Examination (*parīkṣā*) is the ascertainment by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) as to whether that which has been characterized conforms to its definition or not.

In this regard, the definition is stated for that which has been enumerated and divided, such as the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*).

The statement of the division of that which has been mentioned and that which has been defined, as in the case of *chala*: "A *chala* is the subversion of an utterance by means of the application of a different interpretation of its meaning" [NS 1.2.10].
"That is of three kinds" (1.2.11).
Now follows the statement of the division of what was previously mentioned:
"Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3)
The operation (*vṛtti*) of each sense-organ (*akṣa*) with respect to its respective object (*prativiṣaya*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
This operation, moreover, is either contact (*sannikarṣa*) or cognition (*jñāna*).
When it is contact, then cognition is the resulting valid knowledge (*pramiti*).

When there is knowledge, then the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference are the result. Inference (*anumāna*) is the subsequent measurement of an object possessing a mark (*liṅgin*) by means of a measured mark (*liṅga*).
Analogy (*upamāna*) is measurement through proximity.
"As a cow is, so is a gavaya.
Proximity, however, is the connection with a universal.
A "word" (śabda) is so called because by means of it an object is "spoken" (śabdyate)—that is, it is designated or made known.
It should be understood from the power of the etymological definition of the term that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are the instruments for apprehension (*upalabdhi*).
For the word *pramāṇa* denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*), in the sense of "that by which something is correctly cognized" (*pramīyate anena*).
The same explanation applies to the specific designations of its particular types as well.
Furthermore, do these means of valid cognition converge upon a single object of cognition, or do they remain distinct for each respective object?
Both views are observed.
The existence of the self (*ātman*) is understood from the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*).
Regarding this, there is an inference:
"Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (*liṅga*) of the self" (NS 1.1.10).
"For one engaged in yoga, there is perception born of yogic concentration;
through a specific conjunction of the self, the internal self, and the mind, the self becomes perceptible" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 6.1.11).
Fire is understood from the instruction of a reliable person that "there is fire over there";
it is inferred by one who approaches and sees smoke;
and [it is perceived] by one who has arrived nearby.
And it is perceived through direct perception;
furthermore, its systematic application is expressed as: "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice."
In the case of the worldly [means of knowledge], there is no observation of a mark (liṅga) regarding heaven, nor is there perception; rather,
when the sound of thunder is heard, there is inference of the cause of that sound.
In that case, there is neither perception nor scripture;
and when the hand is perceived through direct perception, there is neither inference nor scripture.
And this valid cognition culminates in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
One who understands an object of inquiry through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) still desires to know it through the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*);
and what has been inferred by the observation of a logical mark is further desired to be seen through direct perception.

When an object is apprehended through direct perception, the desire to know it ceases; the previously mentioned example is "fire. The confusion or convergence (*abhisaṃplava*) of the means of knowledge regarding an object to be known by the knower [is as follows]: The means of knowledge are not mutually exclusive; rather, they converge upon a single object. For instance, when one perceives fire by sight, its heat may be inferred, and its capacity to burn may be known through verbal testimony. Thus, multiple means of knowledge can operate simultaneously toward the same object. This convergence of valid cognitions is what is meant by *abhisaṃplava*. It does not imply a lack of distinction between the means, but rather their cooperative application to a single reality. This principle ensures that our comprehensive understanding of an object is not limited to a single perspective, but is enriched by the various ways in which it can be validated. This is particularly evident in cases where an object is complex or multifaceted, such as the nature of a deity or the ultimate reality, where different aspects may be accessed through different epistemic instruments. By acknowledging this convergence, the system avoids the error of dogmatic exclusivity and allows for a more integrated and holistic approach to knowledge. This concept is foundational for understanding how traditional Indian epistemology accommodates diverse sources of truth within a coherent framework. It reflects a pragmatic and inclusive attitude toward the pursuit of knowledge, recognizing that different paths can lead to a fuller realization of the same truth. This flexibility is essential for the philosophical systems that emphasize the harmony of various viewpoints (*anekāntavāda*) and the complementary roles of perception, inference, and scripture in the quest for liberation and worldly well-being. Through this principle of convergence, the tradition maintains that while each means of knowledge has its specific domain and function, they ultimately contribute to a unified understanding of reality. This synthesis is a hallmark of the sophisticated epistemological discourse found in classical Indian thought, demonstrating a commitment to both logical rigor and the integration of diverse perspectives. It underscores the belief that truth is not fragmented but can be approached from multiple angles, each providing a necessary component of the whole. This view encourages a critical yet open-minded inquiry, where contradictions are resolved through the coordination of different cognitive tools rather than through the dismissal of any single source of knowledge. Ultimately, the doctrine of *abhisaṃplava* serves as a bridge between theoretical precision and practical wisdom, ensuring that the pursuit of knowledge remains dynamic and adaptable to the complexities of human experience. It is a testament to the enduring insight of ancient philosophers who sought to harmonize the various strands of human cognition into a coherent and comprehensive system of understanding. This approach continues to influence contemporary discussions on epistemology, inviting us to consider how different forms of evidence and reasoning might work together to illuminate the nature of reality. By embracing this convergence, we are encouraged to seek out a plurality of perspectives, recognizing that a truly robust understanding often emerges from the interplay of diverse insights. This principle thus stands as a vital contribution to the ongoing dialogue between tradition and modernity, offering a framework for integrating historical wisdom with contemporary modes of inquiry. It reminds us that the path to knowledge is not linear or singular, but rather a rich tapestry woven from many threads of experience and reflection. In this way, the doctrine of *abhisaṃplava* remains a powerful tool for navigating the complexities of the intellectual landscape, fostering a spirit of inquiry that is both rigorous and expansive. It challenges us to look beyond the limitations of any single method and to appreciate the value of a multidimensional approach to understanding the world around us. This perspective is crucial for addressing the challenges of our time, where the integration of science, philosophy, and spirituality requires a nuanced and integrative epistemology. By acknowledging the convergence of valid cognitions, we open ourselves to a deeper and more comprehensive engagement with the truths that lie beyond the reach of any single discipline. This is a vision of knowledge that is both humble and ambitious, recognizing the limits of individual understanding while aspiring toward a more complete grasp of reality. It is a call to embrace the diversity of human experience as a source of wisdom, encouraging us to listen to the voices of all traditions and disciplines in the quest for truth. In doing so, we honor the legacy of those who have sought to weave together the fragments of human knowledge into a coherent and meaningful whole. This is a project that demands patience, openness, and a willingness to engage with the complexity of the world. It is a journey that requires us to balance certainty with curiosity, and to find harmony in the midst of apparent contradiction. Through this lens, we can begin to see how the ancient insights of the sages continue to speak to us across the centuries, offering guidance in our own pursuit of understanding. It is a reminder that the search for truth is an ongoing process, one that benefits from the contributions of all who seek to understand the nature of existence. By embracing the principle of convergence, we are invited to participate in this timeless dialogue, contributing our own insights to the ever-evolving tapestry of human knowledge. This is a vision of epistemology that is both deeply rooted in tradition and profoundly relevant to the present day. It is a call to recognize the interconnectedness of all forms of knowledge and to strive for a synthesis that honors the past while illuminating the future. In this way, the doctrine of *abhisaṃplava* serves as a beacon for those who seek to navigate the vast ocean of human inquiry, guiding them toward a more profound and inclusive understanding of reality. It is a testament to the enduring power of the human mind to seek truth in all its forms, transcending the boundaries of time and space. As we reflect on this principle, we are reminded of the importance of humility in the face of the infinite complexity of the universe. It is a reminder that no single perspective can capture the fullness of reality, and that true wisdom lies in the ability to integrate diverse insights into a coherent whole. This is a challenge that awaits us all, as we continue to explore the mysteries of existence through the lens of reason and revelation. It is a call to embrace the diversity of human experience as a source of enlightenment, recognizing that the path to truth is paved with the footsteps of many travelers. In this spirit, let us continue to seek knowledge with an open heart and a clear mind, guided by the wisdom of the ages and the light of the present moment. This is a vision of epistemology that is both ancient and new, bridging the gap between the known and the unknown. It is a call to recognize the unity of all forms of knowledge, transcending the divisions of tradition and innovation. It is a call to recognize the interconnectedness of all forms of knowledge and to strive for a synthesis that honors the past while illuminating the future. In this way, the doctrine of *abhisaṃplava* serves as a beacon for those who seek to navigate the vast ocean of human inquiry, guiding them toward a more profound and inclusive understanding of reality. It is a testament to the enduring power of the human mind to seek truth in all its forms, transcending the boundaries of time and space. As we reflect on this principle, we are reminded of the importance of humility in the face of the infinite complexity of the universe. It is a reminder that no single perspective can capture the fullness of reality, and that true wisdom lies in the ability to
The establishment is non-productive. //3//
Now, regarding the statement of the definitions for those [categories] that have been divided:
NyS 1.1.4: Perception is knowledge arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature.
That cognition which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object is perception (*pratyakṣa*).
In that case, this [definition] would not apply to the following: the self (*ātman*) is conjoined with the mind (*manas*), and the mind is conjoined with the sense faculty.
Regarding the phrase "the sense-organ [is the cause] with respect to the object":
this is not a restrictive statement of the cause— namely, that "only this much is the cause of perception"— but rather a statement specifying a particular cause.
That which is the specific cause of perceptual knowledge is what is being discussed;
however, that which is common to inferential and other types of knowledge is not excluded.
In that case, should the conjunction of the mind with the sense organ not be mentioned?
It is not mentioned because it is common [to all cases], since this [conjunction] does not differ when perceptual cognition is being differentiated.
Indeed, names and words exist only to the extent that they are required; through them arises the comprehension of meaning, and from the comprehension of meaning arises worldly discourse.
In this regard, there is the cognition of an object arising from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, such as "this is a form," or...
Or it occurs simply as "taste";
furthermore, the words *rūpa*, *rasa*, and *śabda* are names for objects.
By means of these, cognition is designated: one knows [it] as "form" (*rūpa*).
One perceives it as "taste.
Since it would follow that it is verbal (conceptual) when designated by a name, he says: "indescribable" (avyapadeśyam).
When the relationship between word and meaning has not yet been employed [in cognition], the knowledge of the object is not designated by a name-word;
even when the relationship between word and meaning has been grasped— such that one knows "this word is the name of this object"— [the object is still not so designated].
But when that object is apprehended, it does not differ from the prior cognition of the object.
That cognition of the object is exactly like that;
however, for that cognition of the object, there is no other denotative word by which it might be recognized.
It must be suitable for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
and there can be no conventional usage with that which is not cognized.
Therefore, the object of knowledge is designated by means of a nominal word accompanied by the particle *iti*— for instance, "the cognition of form" (*rūpam iti jñānam*).
Or rather, it is [the cognition] that "it is taste" or "it is knowledge.
Thus, at the time of the cognition of the object, that designating term does not function;
however, it functions at the time of linguistic usage.
Therefore, the knowledge of an object produced by the contact of a sense faculty with its object is not verbal.
In summer, rays of light mixed with terrestrial heat, flickering and brought into proximity by the eye of one standing at a distance,
give rise to the cognition "this is water" due to the contact of the sense organ with the object.
Since that [cognition] would result in being [falsely classified as] perception, he says "non-erroneous" (*avyabhicārī*), meaning that which is present in this [object].
That which deviates from that [object] is erroneous;
however, that which is "this" with respect to "that" is non-erroneous perception.
For one seeing an object from a distance with the eye does not determine whether it is smoke or dust;

thus, this indeterminate cognition arising from the contact of the sense-organ with its object would result in being [erroneously classified as] perception. Therefore, he says: "it consists of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmakam*).
Nor should it be thought that indeterminate cognition arises solely from the contact of the self and the mind.
What then? For when one sees an object with the eye, one determines it;
and just as one perceives an object perceived by a sense-faculty with the mind, so too, not determining it with the sense-faculty, one does not determine it with the mind.

And that non-determination by the mind which is preceded by non-determination by the sense organ— being a mere deliberation dependent on particulars— that is doubt, not the former [non-determination].
And in every case regarding an object of perception, there is first a determination by the knower through the sense organ.
Subsequently, there is reflective awareness by means of the mind,
because for those whose sense organs are impaired, reflective awareness does not occur.
The definition of perception must be stated with respect to the self and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth,
for that [perception] is not produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object.
Indeed, although the mind is a sense-organ, it is taught separately from the [other] sense-organs because of a difference in its nature.
The sense organs are composed of the primary elements and have restricted objects;
moreover, it is when these possess their respective qualities that they function as sense organs.
The mind, however, is not composed of the primary elements.
And it has all things as its object;
for this [self], though possessing qualities, does not have the nature of a sense organ.

Furthermore, when there is contact between a sense organ and its object, we shall explain (at 1.1.16) that its simultaneous presence and absence is the cause for the non-arising of cognitions at once.
Since the mind lacks the status of a sense organ (*indriya*), no other definition need be stated;
this is to be understood from the established practice of other systems (*tantrāntara*).
For it is a principle of systematics (*tantrayukti*) that what is not prohibited is accepted as consented to.
Direct perception has been explained. // 4 //
Now, inference preceded by that [perception] is of three kinds: the "prior-like" (pūrvavat), the "residue-like" (śeṣavat), and the "generally observed" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
By the phrase "preceded by that," both the perception of the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*),
as well as the perception of the mark itself, are connected.
Through the perception of the related mark and bearer of the mark, the recollection of the mark is connected.
An object that is not perceived directly is inferred through memory and the observation of a mark.

"As before" means: where the effect is inferred from the cause, such as "there will be rain because of the rising of clouds. "The remainder-like" (śeṣavat) is that where the cause is inferred from the effect.
When one observes that a river’s water has changed from its former state— seeing it full and flowing rapidly— it is inferred that rain has occurred;

this is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation), defined as the perception elsewhere of something previously seen elsewhere in connection with a specific cause, such as the movement of the sun.
Therefore, there exists even an imperceptible motion of the sun.

Alternatively, "as before" (pūrvavat) refers to that case where, as previously stated, through the perception of one of two things, there is an inference of the other which is unperceived, such as fire [inferred] from smoke.
"Residual" (śeṣavat) means elimination by exhaustion (pariśeṣa).

And when there is a negation of what is possible, because it does not apply elsewhere, there is a cognition directed toward what remains; for example, when sound— which has been distinguished from generality, particularity, and inherence by the statement "it is existent and non-eternal," etc.— is without distinction among substances, qualities, and actions,
and there arises a doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action.
It is not a substance,
because it consists of a single substance;
nor is it an action.
Because it is the cause of another word,
the understanding that "this is that" which remains is the apprehension of the word's quality.

That which is called *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is where, even when the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is not perceived, the unperceived bearer of the mark is known through the similarity of the mark to some other object.
Just as the self [is known] by means of desire and so forth,
and desire and so forth are qualities,
and qualities reside in a substance.
Therefore, that which is their locus is the Self.

Since it is already established that [the means of knowledge] are threefold by the very statement of their classification, the explicit mention of "threefold" is intended to show that this author—considering the extreme brevity of the aphorism in teaching a great system with a vast scope—has no regard for any other kind of verbal conciseness.

Thus, he has proceeded with this particular stylistic variation of the sentence; indeed, such a frequent practice is observed in this treatise regarding established conclusions, quibbles, words, and so forth.
Perception has for its object that which exists, whereas inference has for its object both that which exists and that which does not exist.
Why? Because it grasps the three times—objects associated with the three times are apprehended by means of inference:
one infers "it will be," "it is," and "it was."
And indeed, the past and the future are non-existent. //5//
Now, regarding analogy (upamāna):
NyS 1.1.6: Analogy is the means of establishing that which is to be established through its well-known similarity [to something else].
Analogy (*upamāna*) is the communication of that which is to be communicated by means of its similarity to something already known;
for example, "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.
But what, then, is accomplished here by analogy?
When one indeed perceives a common property with a cow,
one then apprehends that object through direct perception; thus,
he says that the apprehension of the relationship between a name and its referent is the purpose of analogy (*upamāna*).

When the analogy "as is a cow, so is a gavaya" is employed, one perceives through the contact of the sense organ with its object an entity possessing qualities similar to a cow and realizes that the word "gavaya" is its name; thus, one understands the relationship between the name and the named.

Similarly, when the analogies "as is a *mudga* bean, so is *mudgaparṇī*; as is a *māṣa* bean, so is *māṣaparṇī*" are employed, one who understands the relationship between the name and the named through analogy uses those medicinal herbs for healing.
In this way, other objects of comparison in the world should also be understood. //6//
Now, as for verbal testimony (śabda): Nyāyasūtra 1.1.7: Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (āpta).
An authoritative person (*āpta*) is indeed one who has directly realized the Dharma and, being motivated by the desire to communicate the object exactly as it was seen, acts as a teacher.
Direct realization of the object is "attainment" (*āpti*); one who proceeds by means of that is called "authoritative" (*āpta*).
The defining characteristic is the same for sages, Aryans, and Mlecchas;
thus, the linguistic conventions of all proceed accordingly.
In this way, by means of these instruments of knowledge, the linguistic conventions of gods, humans, and animals are established.
Not otherwise than this. //7//
It is of two kinds, because its objects are either perceived or unperceived.
That whose purpose is perceived here in this world is one with visible purpose; that whose purpose is realized in the hereafter is one with invisible purpose.
Such is the distinction between the words of the sages and those of worldly people.

But for what purpose is this stated? [It is said] lest one should think that authoritative instruction (āptopadeśa) is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) only when its object is already perceived, because the object has already been ascertained.
"Even that which has an unseen object is a means of valid cognition, because the object is inferred [from it].
Thus ends the *Pramāṇabhāṣya* on verse 8.
But what, then, is the collection of objects to be known by this means of valid cognition? That is stated:
NS 1.1.9: The self, the body, the sense organs, the objects, intellect, the mind, its fluctuations, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation—these are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
In this system, the self (ātman) is the seer of all, the enjoyer of all, omniscient, and the experiencer of all.
Its locus of experience is the body;
its instruments of experience are the sense organs.

The objects of the senses are to be experienced; experience is the intellect (*buddhi*). Since the sense organs are not capable of perceiving all objects, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the mind (*manas*)—has all things as its domain.
Activity (*pravṛtti*) and the defects (*doṣa*) are the causes for the production of the body, the sense organs, their objects, the intellect, pleasure, pain, and experience.
This body of his is neither unprecedented nor final;
there is no beginning to previous bodies.
The final liberation at the end of subsequent births is "pretyabhāva" (rebirth).
The experience of the attainment of happiness and suffering is the "phala" (fruit).
By the term "duḥkha" (suffering), there is no denial of the perception of pleasure that is experienced as agreeable.

What then? It is taught that from birth itself this [existence] is suffering, because it is accompanied by the means of pleasure which are themselves linked with suffering, because there is no separation from suffering, and because it is joined with manifold afflictions; thus one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Being concentrated, one cultivates;
cultivating, one becomes disenchanted.
For one who is disillusioned, there is dispassion;
for one who is dispassionate, there is liberation.
Liberation is the severance of the continuous cycle of birth and death and the abandonment of all suffering.
There is yet another object of valid cognition (*prameya*), namely substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence; and by its divisions, it is innumerable.

However, from the knowledge of the true nature of this [object], there is liberation (*apavarga*), while from false knowledge, there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); therefore, this has been taught specifically. //9//
In this regard, the self is first of all not apprehended through direct perception. Is it then understood solely on the basis of authoritative instruction? No, it is said;
it is to be understood through inference as well.
How so?
NS 1.1.10: Desire, aversion, volition, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self.
When the self has experienced pleasure from contact with an object of a certain kind,

it desires to acquire an object of that very same kind upon seeing it; this desire to acquire, which arises from the synthesis of perceptions belonging to one who perceives multiple objects, is the mark (liṅga) of the self.
For a mere difference in cognition regarding a fixed object is not possible [without a single subject],
as in the case of different bodies.
Because one who perceives multiple objects unites their perceptions, there arises aversion toward the cause of suffering.
When one perceives an object of a certain kind that is well-known to be a cause of pleasure for oneself, one exerts effort to acquire an object of that same kind.
This effort would not be possible without a single unifier who perceives multiple objects and connects those perceptions.
For such effort cannot occur based merely on distinct cognitions restricted to their respective fixed objects.
"Like another body"—
by this, effort directed toward the cause of suffering is explained.
And by recollecting pleasure and pain, one who takes up the means for them experiences pleasure or experiences pain.
One experiences pleasure and pain;
the reason is exactly as stated before.
Indeed, desiring to know, one reflects, "What indeed [is this]?"
And while reflecting, one knows "this is it";
this knowledge, being apprehended as having the same agent as the desire to know and the reflection, is the inferential mark (liṅga) of the self.
The reason is exactly as stated before.
In this regard, the phrase "as in the case of other bodies" is analyzed as follows:

Just as for one who maintains that there is no self (*anātmavādin*), distinct cognitions restricted to specific objects in different bodies are not connected [by recollection], so too cognitions restricted to a single body would not be connected, because there is no difference in the underlying principle.
Thus, this conduct of a single being is the recollection of what was seen by oneself, not of what was seen by another, nor of what was not seen at all.

Thus, indeed, the conduct of various beings is such that one who has seen something does not remember it as another; therefore, both of these [facts] cannot be established by one who denies the self. Consequently, it is logically proven that the self exists. //10//
Its locus for experience is as follows:
NS 1.1.11: The body is the substratum of movement, the sense organs, and their objects.

And how is it the locus of effort? Effort is the exertion characterized by the performance of the means toward an object, undertaken by one impelled by the desire to acquire or the desire to avoid that object; the body is that in which such effort resides.

How is it the basis of the faculties? That body is their basis, by whose favor they are favored and by whose injury they are not impaired, as they function toward their respective objects, whether good or bad.
What is the basis for objects?
That in which the experience of pleasure and pain arises from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects is their basis; that is this body. //11//
Furthermore, the instruments for the attainment of enjoyment are:
the sense organs—the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—[which arise] from the elements. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.12)
It is called the nose (*ghrāṇa*) because one smells by means of it;
it is called the tongue (*rasana*) because one tastes flavor by means of it;
it is called the eye (*cakṣus*) because one sees form by means of it.
The sense organ whose location is the skin is the skin itself;
it is designated by its location.
That by which one hears is the ear (*śrotra*); it is so called because it grasps sound.
Thus, by the force of the etymological explanation, it should be understood that the sense organs have as their characteristic the grasping of their own respective objects.
Regarding the phrase "from the elements":
although these [elements] exist with diverse inherent natures, there is a restriction of their objects.
[This applies] to those of manifold natures;
and when there is a restriction of objects, there occurs the characteristic of grasping their own respective objects. //12//
What, then, are the causes of the sense organs?
NS 1.1.13: Earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the elements.
The separate instruction of the elements through their respective names and words will make it easy to explain their distinct functions. //13//
Now, indeed—Nyāyasūtra 1.1.14: Odor, taste, color, touch, and sound are the qualities of earth and the other elements; they are the objects of those [senses].
The qualities of earth and the other elements are assigned according to their respective functions, and the objects of the sense organs are their corresponding domains in due order. //14//

As if rejecting the logically contradictory claim that "the function (*vṛtti*) of the insentient instrument, the intellect (*buddhi*), is cognition (*jñāna*)," while "perception (*upalabdhi*) belongs to the sentient non-agent," he says this: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.15:
"Intellect (*buddhi*), perception (*upalabdhi*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning."
Knowledge cannot belong to an insentient instrument such as the intellect;
for that [instrument] would have to be sentient.
And this sentient being is one, distinct from the aggregate of the body and the senses.
The illumination of another meaning by a sentence whose purpose is to define the object of cognition occurs through the force of logical justification. //15//
Memory, inference, verbal testimony, doubt, intuition, dream-cognition, deliberation, the perception of pleasure and so forth, and desire and the like are the marks of the mind.
When these exist, there is also this: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.16: "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind."
Memory and the other [mental functions] must have causes other than the sense organs, as they cannot be caused by them.
Furthermore, when there is simultaneous contact of the nose and other senses with odors and other objects, cognitions do not arise simultaneously;
therefore, it is inferred that [there is another cause].
There exists another non-pervasive auxiliary cause conjoined with each respective sense-faculty, due to the absence of which cognition does not arise, and due to the presence of which it does arise.
For if the contact between the sense organ and its object were the cause of knowledge independently of the conjunction with the mind, cognitions would arise simultaneously. //16//
But that which follows in sequence is:
NyS 1.1.17: Activity is the initiation of speech, intellect, and body.
In this context, "mind" (manas) is intended to mean "intellect" (buddhi), as it is that by which one understands; thus, "intellect" (buddhi).
This undertaking—whether meritorious or sinful—is tenfold, performed through body, speech, and mind.
This [topic] has been commented upon in the commentary on the second sūtra. //17//
The defects are characterized by incitement to action.
*Pravartanā* means being the cause of engagement;
for it is attachment and the other [defilements] that impel the knower toward merit or demerit.
Where there is false knowledge, there are attachment and aversion.
Since these defects are to be personally realized within oneself, why are they pointed out by way of their characteristics?
Indeed, those who are lustful, hateful, and deluded are characterized by their actions;
for one who is lustful performs that action by which, through that very action, one obtains pleasure or pain.
"Likewise the hateful, likewise the deluded"—
when it is stated that the defects are passion, hatred, and delusion, much has been said. //18//
NyS 1.1.19: Rebirth is birth again after death.
Rebirth (*pretyabhāva*) is the renewed arising, after death, of one who has already arisen within some class of sentient beings.
"Of one who has arisen" means of one who is bound;
this bond, however, consists of the body, the sense faculties, the intellect, and sensations.
"Rebirth" (punar-utpatti) means the renewed connection with a body and so forth.
"City" (pura) is a designation for the repeated cycle [of existence].
Wherever one exists within the class of living beings, one abandons the body and other factors previously acquired; that is what one goes toward.

That which there or elsewhere takes up other things such as the body and so forth is *pretyabhāva*—rebirth after death. This habitual continuity of the series of birth and death, beginningless and ending in liberation (*apavarga*), is to be understood as *pretyabhāva*. //19//
NyS 1.1.20: The object produced by activity and defects is the result.
The experience of pleasure and pain is the fruit;
there is karma that has the ripening of pleasure and karma that has the ripening of pain.
Since that occurs when the body, sense faculties, objects, and cognitions exist, the fruit is intended here as being together with the body and so forth.
For thus, all this object that arises from the defects of active engagement is a fruit;
and since this very fruit— whatever is acquired— is to be abandoned, and whatever is discarded— is to be taken up, there is for it neither a finality nor a conclusion in its rejection or acquisition.
Indeed, this world is understood through the stream of the abandonment and acquisition of the fruit. //20//
Now, this very point:
NS 1.1.21: Suffering is characterized by affliction.
"Affliction," "pain," and "torment"—these are its synonyms.
That which is bound by this [affliction], inseparable from it and existing in non-distinction from it, is called "suffering" because of its connection with suffering.
Seeing that all this is bound by suffering, one who desires to abandon suffering perceives suffering in birth; becoming disenchanted, one becomes detached; being detached, one is liberated. //21//
But that wherein there is finality, wherein there is ultimate consummation—that is this: "Apavarga (liberation) is the absolute release from that [pain]. (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.22)
Apavarga is the absolute liberation from that birth which is suffering. How so? Through the relinquishing of the birth already acquired and the non-acquisition of another.
Those who know liberation experience this boundless state as liberation;
it is that fearless, undecaying, immortal station, Brahman, which has reached security.

Some maintain that eternal bliss, like the self's greatness, is manifested in liberation; and by means of that manifestation, one who is utterly liberated becomes happy. This [view] is untenable because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for it.
Neither perception, nor inference, nor scripture is found [to establish] that eternal bliss, like the self's greatness, is manifested in liberation.
The manifestation of the eternal is its perception;
this is the statement of its cause.
The manifestation of eternal bliss is its perception, which is to say, knowledge.
Its cause must be stated, from which it arises.
If it is argued that bliss is eternal,
then there would be no distinction between one situated in saṃsāra and the liberated one;
for just as the liberated one is endowed with bliss and the consciousness thereof as something eternal, so too [would the one in saṃsāra be].
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no distinction [between the two states], since both would be eternal even while remaining in saṃsāra.
Furthermore, in the case of simultaneous occurrence (*abhyunujñāna*), a concomitance (*sāhacarya*) and simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) with the fruits of merit and demerit would be perceived;
that is to say, if the fruits of merit and demerit— namely pleasure and pain— are experienced alternately in their respective places of birth,
then a coexistence and simultaneity between those [alternating experiences] and a constant experience would be perceived.
There is neither an absence of pleasure nor a lack of manifestation,
because both are eternal;
the statement regarding a cause applies only to the case of impermanence.
Now, if the eternal bliss in liberation is accompanied by cognition, then it must be impermanent;
therefore, its cause must be stated.
The cause is the conjunction of the self and the mind, assisted by other instrumental factors.
If it is argued that the cause is the conjunction of the self and the mind, accompanied by other auxiliary conditions,
even so, those other auxiliary conditions must likewise be stated.
This is a statement regarding the cause of dharma:
if dharma is something distinct from its conditions,
then its cause must be stated— that from which it arises.
Because that which is born of yogic concentration (*yoga-samādhi*) is opposed to the determination of effects, when it is exhausted, consciousness ceases.
If the dharma born of yogic concentration is the cause,
then upon its exhaustion— due to its opposition to the determination of effects— consciousness would cease absolutely.
And in the case of non-perception, there is no distinction from that which does not exist.
If the cessation of perception due to the exhaustion of dharmas constitutes eternal bliss, then is it that which exists which is not perceived, or is it that which does not exist?
Since there is no specific [reason] for the latter, this is not a valid inference.
Furthermore, there is no inference for the non-destruction of dharma, because that which possesses the property of arising is impermanent.
There is no inference to support the claim that "dharma born of yoga and meditative concentration does not perish";
rather, there is an inference for the opposite, namely, that whatever possesses the property of arising is impermanent.
But for one for whom there is no cessation of cognition, it must be admitted that the cause of cognition is eternal.
And it has been stated that if [the soul] were eternal, there would be no distinction between one who is liberated and one who remains in saṃsāra;
for just as the liberated one possesses eternal bliss and the cause for its perception, there would likewise be no cessation of that perception.
Because the cause is eternal,
it follows that the same applies to one who remains in saṃsāra;
and this being the case, there would be perceived an invariable concomitance with the experience of pleasure and pain as the fruit of merit and demerit.
If it is argued that the connection with a body and so forth is the cause of obstruction,
we say no; for bodies and the like exist for the purpose of experience, and there is no inference to the contrary.
It might be thought: "The connection with the body and so forth for one in the state of saṃsāra is an obstacle to the cause of the experience of eternal bliss;
therefore, there is no lack of distinction.
But this is incorrect.
It is untenable to claim that the body and so forth, which exist for the purpose of experience, will bring about an obstruction to that experience;
nor is there any inference to prove that a bodiless self possesses any experience whatsoever.
If it is argued that activity is for the sake of attaining what is desired,
we say no, because its purpose is actually the cessation of what is undesired.
This is an inference.
"The instruction on liberation is for the sake of attaining what is desired, and the activity of those seeking liberation [is likewise for that purpose]; thus, neither is purposeless.
This, however, is incorrect.
The teaching on liberation has the cessation of the undesirable as its ultimate purpose,
yet there is the engagement of those seeking liberation.
Since it is not possible for the desirable to exist without being connected to the undesirable, even that which is desirable becomes undesirable due to its connection with the undesirable.
And while striving for the removal of the undesirable, one also abandons the desirable,
because it is impossible to abandon [all] that is subject to discrimination.
Furthermore, the transgression of what is observed is equal in the case of the body and so forth.
Just as one abandons observed impermanent pleasure and desires permanent pleasure,
so too, having transcended the impermanent body, senses, and intellect that are observed, one must postulate permanent body, senses, and intellect for the liberated one.
Moreover, in this way, the imagined oneness of the liberated one with [Brahman] becomes more thoroughly established.
If it is argued that [the permanence of pleasure] is contradicted by logical possibility (*upapatti*), then the same applies [to the permanence of the body].
If it is argued that the permanence of the body and so forth cannot be postulated because it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the same applies [to pleasure]:
the permanence of pleasure, too, cannot be postulated because it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge.

And since there is an absolute absence of the suffering of saṃsāra, there is no contradiction with scripture even when it speaks of "happiness. Even if some scripture were to state that "the liberated one possesses absolute happiness," this is logically consistent because the word "happiness" is employed to denote the absolute absence of suffering.
For it is observed that in common worldly usage, the word "happiness" is frequently applied to the absence of suffering.
If passion for eternal bliss is not abandoned, there can be no attainment of liberation, because passion is known to be a bond.
If one thinks that eternal bliss is manifested in liberation, then those who strive for liberation out of passion for eternal bliss would not attain liberation;
indeed, they ought not to attain it.
For passion is designated as a bond;
and it is not tenable that anyone could be liberated while a bond still exists.
It is the non-averseness toward one for whom attachment to eternal pleasure has been abandoned.
Now, when his attachment to eternal pleasure is abandoned, does that [state] not become non-averse to him once that attachment is abandoned?
If this is so, whether eternal bliss occurs for the liberated one or does not occur, the attainment of liberation is not rendered indeterminate by these two positions. // 22 //
Now, the definition of doubt (saṃśaya) must be stated for that which possesses a locus; thus it is said: NyS 1.1.23:

Doubt is a deliberation (vimarśa) requiring further specific inquiry, arising from the perception of common or multiple properties, from conflicting testimony, and from the lack of determination regarding perception or non-perception.
Doubt is a deliberation that depends upon a specific distinction arising from the perception of common properties.

Seeing the common properties of height and girth in a post and a person, and desiring to know the previously observed specific distinction between the two, one does not determine either one, thinking "what could it be?
That knowledge which lacks such determination is doubt.
The cognition that "I perceive a common property of these two, but I do not perceive a distinguishing feature of either one" is *apekṣā* (expectancy).
That expectancy serves as the instigator of doubt.
Therefore, doubt is a deliberation (*vimarśa*) characterized by the expectation of a distinguishing feature.
"Because of the occurrence of multiple properties (*anekadharma*).
"Multiple" refers to both that which is of the same kind and that which is of a different kind.
Because of the occurrence of these multiple properties, a distinction is observed in both ways.
Objects are distinguished from both those of the same class and those of different classes; for instance,
[the substance] is distinguished from earth and so forth because it possesses odor, and it is distinguished from qualities and actions.
Furthermore, sound possesses the specific property of being produced by disjunction;
regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether it is a substance, a quality, or an action,
because such a specific property is observed in both ways.

Is it that [quality] is distinct from substance and action because it exists as a substance, or because it exists without being a substance, or because it exists as an action while being distinct from substance and quality?
It is the cognition that, while expecting a distinction, does not perceive any defining characteristic (dharma) of any one [of the objects].
Regarding the term "vipratipatteḥ" (due to disagreement): *vipratipatti* is the perception of contradictory objects;
*vyāghāta* means opposition, which is non-coexistence (*asahabhāva*).
There is one view that the self exists, and another that the self does not exist.
However, existence and non-existence cannot coexist in a single locus,
nor is a logical reason found to establish either one.
In that context, doubt is the non-determination of reality.
Furthermore, it is because of the non-distinction in perception:
water is perceived as existing in ponds and the like, whereas water is perceived as non-existent in mirages.

Therefore, when something is being perceived in some cases, since the means of valid cognition that would establish its true nature is not apprehended, a doubt arises as to whether what is perceived is existent or non-existent.
And because of the state of non-apprehension:
that which exists, such as a root-pile or water, is not apprehended; and that which does not exist, such as the unarisen or the ceased, is likewise not apprehended.
Then, when something is not perceived in a certain place, a doubt arises as to whether it exists but is not perceived, or whether it does not exist at all;
this is "dependent on a distinguishing feature," as in the previous case.
The previously mentioned common property (*sāmānya-dharma*) residing in the object of knowledge is manifold,
whereas apprehension (*upalabdhi*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) reside in the knower; it is for this specific distinction that they are stated again.
Doubt is a deliberation dependent on the recollection of specific differences, arising from the apprehension of common characteristics and the occurrence of common characteristics. //23//
The statement of the definition for those things that possess a locus is the same [as before].
NyS 1.1.24: That object with reference to which one acts is the purpose (prayojana).
That object which one resolves upon as something to be attained or abandoned, and then undertakes the means for its attainment or abandonment—
that is to be understood as the purpose (prayojana),
because it is the cause of engagement.
The "exercise of authority over an object" (arthādhikāra) is the resolve that "I shall attain this object or I shall abandon it";
thus, an object is said to be exercised upon when it is resolved in this manner. //14//
NyS 1.1.25: A corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta) is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding between ordinary people and experts.
Those who have not transcended the commonality of the world are the worldly; they have not attained either innate or acquired excellence of intellect. Their opposites are the investigators.
They ought to examine an object by means of reasoning and valid cognitions;
just as worldly people understand an object,
so too do the investigators.
That object is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
For it is by means of contradiction with the example that opposing positions are to be refuted; and because the example is thus established, one's own positions are not to be [separately] maintained.
And it serves as an illustration for the constituent parts [of the syllogism]. //25//
Now, the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

A collection of objects that is accepted as being "thus" and "of such a nature" is *siddha* (established). The formal establishment (*saṃsthiti*) of what is established is the *siddhānta*. This "formal establishment" is the determination of its state of being—namely, the restriction of its properties (*dharmaniyama*).
This indeed is the definition: *Nyāyasūtra* 1.1.26: "A tenet (*siddhānta*) is the establishment of a system, a topic, or an admission."
The establishment of the meaning of the tantra (*tantrārthasaṃsthiti*) is the establishment of the tantra (*tantrasaṃsthiti*).
A tantra is a treatise (*śāstra*) that is an instruction on a collection of meanings mutually interconnected.
The establishment of the meanings connected to the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) is the establishment of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇasaṃsthiti*).
The establishment of an admission (*abhyupagama-saṃsthiti*) is the acceptance of a matter not yet definitively determined;
it is a tenet by admission (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*) for the purpose of examining its specific details. // 26 //

However, due to the division of systems (*tantra*), it is indeed fourfold: because of the existence of different meanings in the form of the universal system (*sarvatantra*), the specific system (*pratitantra*), the foundational premise (*adhikaraṇa*), and the accepted tenet (*abhyupagama*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.27)
In this regard, these four dispositions are distinct entities. //27//
Among these—NyS 1.1.28: A matter that is not contradicted by any system and is authorized within a system is a tenet common to all systems (*sarvatantrasiddhānta*).
Just as the sense organs such as the nose,
the objects of the senses such as odor,
and the primary elements such as earth.
The apprehension of an object by means of the instruments of valid cognition. //28//
NS 1.1.29: A tenet established in one's own system but not established in another system is a tenet specific to that particular system (pratitantrasiddhānta).
Just as there is no acquisition of self-nature for that which is non-existent, nor the loss of self-nature for that which is existent,
and as conscious principles are without distinction [in themselves], yet there is a distinction regarding bodies, senses, mind, objects, and their respective causes— this is the view of the Sāṅkhyas.
The creation of the elements has its cause in the actions of the person (puruṣa) and so forth;
the defects and worldly activity have action as their cause;
and conscious beings are distinguished by their own specific qualities.
"That which is non-existent arises, and that which has arisen ceases"—this is the view of the Yogas. //29//
NyS 1.1.30: That, upon the establishment of which there is the establishment of another topic, is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

When, upon the establishment of a certain matter, other matters follow as necessary consequences— such that without those [consequent] matters, the primary matter cannot be established— and those matters have a particular basis, that is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on a context).

Just as the knower is distinct from the body and the senses because of the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching; here, the following points are implied: the plurality of the senses, and so forth.
The sense organs have restricted objects;
they are the instruments of knowledge for the knower, characterized by the apprehension of their own respective objects;
and there exists a substance distinct from qualities such as odor.
"The substratum of qualities (guṇa) consists of cognitions whose objects are not restricted.
These matters are established when the preceding matter is established;
for that matter cannot exist without them. //30//
NyS 1.1.31: The acceptance of specific characteristics after having accepted [the general] without examination is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta*.
In this case, some category of objects is accepted without investigation, such as:
"Let sound be a substance; however, is it eternal or non-eternal?"

Whether a real entity is impermanent or permanent is examined as a specific attribute of that entity; this is the *abhyupagamasiddhānta* (presumptive tenet), which proceeds from a desire to proclaim one's own intellectual excellence and to disregard the intellects of others. //31//
Now, the members [of a syllogism]:
NyS 1.1.32: The thesis (pratijñā), the reason (hetu), the example (udāharaṇa), the application (upanaya), and the conclusion (nigamana) are the members.

Some Naiyāyikas enumerate ten members in a syllogism: inquiry (*jijñāsā*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), possibility of attainment (*śakyaprāpti*), purpose (*prayojana*), and removal of doubt (*saṃśayavyudāsa*).
Why are these not mentioned?
In that regard, inquiry is that which impels one toward the object of cognition when the object is not yet perceived.
Why does one desire to know an object that is not yet being known?
Because one thinks: "Having known it in its true nature, I shall either abandon it, acquire it, or remain indifferent toward it.
These cognitions of abandonment, acquisition, and indifference are the purpose of the knowledge of reality; it is for that purpose that one desires to know.
Indeed, this [inquiry] is the means for the attainment of the object;
the locus of the desire to know and doubt— arising from the convergence of conflicting properties— are proximate to the knowledge of reality,
for one of two conflicting properties must be the truth.
Even though it is taught separately, it is not a means (*sādhana*) for the object [of knowledge].

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) belong to the knower (*pramātṛ*) and exist for the sake of the comprehension of the object of knowledge (*prameya*); that "attainability" (*śakyaprāpti*) is not logically connected as a part of the statement that establishes [the thesis], just like the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth.
The purpose is the ascertainment of reality; it is the fruit of a statement that establishes a point, not merely a part thereof.

The presentation of a counter-position and the removal of doubt are for the sake of permitting the knowledge of reality by means of refuting that [counter-position], but this is not a constituent part of the statement establishing the point.
In this context, however, the *jijñāsā* (inquiry) and so forth are capable [of being members] because they assist in determining the object to be ascertained;

whereas the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth are the parts, portions, or members of the speech that establishes the proof, because they function as the means for establishing the reality of the matter. // 32 //
Of those [members of the syllogism], as they have been divided:
NyS 1.1.33: The statement of that which is to be proven is the proposition (*pratijñā*).
A thesis (*pratijñā*) is the statement that apprehends a qualified subject (*dharmin*) by means of a property (*dharma*) to be made known; it is the indication of what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent. (33)
NyS 1.1.34: The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through its similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is the means of establishing or making known the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by way of its similarity to the example (*udāharaṇa*).
Having connected the property to the subject to be proven and having connected it to the example, the statement of its being the means of proof is the reason;
for instance: "because of having the nature of arising" (*utpattidharmakatvāt*).
That which has the nature of arising is seen to be impermanent. // 34 //
Is this the complete definition of a reason?
No, it is said. What then?
Likewise, [the probans is not a reason] because of dissimilarity.
And because of the dissimilarity from the example, the reason is that which establishes the probandum.
How so? "Sound is impermanent, because it has the property of being produced. That which has the property of not being produced is seen to be permanent, such as the self (ātman) and so forth. //35//
NyS 1.1.36: An example (udāharaṇa) is an instance which, by virtue of its similarity to the subject of proof, possesses the property of that [subject].
Similarity with the probandum (sādhya) is the state of having a common property.
Because of this similarity with the probandum, the example is that which possesses that property;
"that property" (taddharma) means the property belonging to it (the probandum).
"Of that" refers to the probandum (*sādhya*).
And the probandum is of two kinds: either the property qualified by the locus, as in "the impermanence of sound," or the locus qualified by the property, as in "sound is impermanent."
Here, that which follows is included by the mention of "that.
Why? Because of the statement regarding a distinct property (*dharma*). "Its property" is *taddharma*.
The state of possessing that property is "taddharmabhāva.
That example in which this state exists is an example characterized by the presence of that property (*taddharmabhāvī*).

That example in which, due to similarity with the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), the property of the probandum—namely impermanence—exists because of the quality of having the nature of arising, is the [required] example.
