Due to similarity with the probandum (sādhya), because it possesses the property of being subject to origination, it comes to possess that property; this is intended as the example (udāharaṇa).
For instance, substances such as a cooking pot, which possess the property of origination, are seen to be impermanent.
In this regard, that which arises is subject to the nature of arising;
and having come into being, it ceases to be— it relinquishes its own self and is extinguished— and thus it is impermanent.
Thus, the property of having the nature of arising is the probans (*sādhana*), and impermanence is the probandum (*sādhya*).
This relationship between two properties—one as the probandum and the other as the probans—is established and perceived through similarity (*sādharmya*).
Perceiving that [relationship] in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one infers it in the case of sound as well.
"Sound is also impermanent because it possesses the property of being produced, like a cooking pot and so forth.
By means of this, the relationship of probandum and probans between two properties is illustrated; thus, it is called an "example" (*udāharaṇa*). //36//
Or, by the reversal of that, it is the opposite.

The term "example" (*udāharaṇa*) refers to the "illustrative instance" (*dṛṣṭānta*), as is the subject under discussion. An illustrative instance is an example characterized by dissimilarity from the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*) and which does not possess the property of that [probandum].
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; that which is eternal, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, does not have the property of being produced."

This example of the self (*ātman*) and so forth is [cited] by way of dissimilarity with the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*); because it possesses the property of non-arising (*anutpattidharmakatva*), that property of the probandum—which is impermanence (*anityatva*)—does not exist in it.

Perceiving here in the example of the self and so forth that impermanence does not exist due to the absence of the property of arising, one infers the opposite in the case of sound: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of arising."

An example (*udāharaṇa*) is an instance where, because of its similarity to the probandum (*sādhya*), the property of the [subject] exists in that which is stated with a reason based on similarity (*sādharmya*). An example is an instance where, because of its dissimilarity to the probandum, the property of that [subject] does not exist in that which is stated with a reason based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

In the former case of the example, one perceives those two properties as being in the relationship of probandum and probans; one then infers that the relationship of probandum and probans exists between those two [properties] in the probandum as well.

In the latter example, one observes that when one of two properties is absent, the other is absent; one then infers in the subject (*sādhya*) that because one of those two is present, the other is present.
This [inference] is not possible in the case of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*); therefore, fallacious reasons are non-reasons.
Thus, this capacity of the reason and the example is extremely subtle, difficult to comprehend, and to be understood only by those who appear as true scholars. //37//
The application (upanaya) is the subsumption of the subject of proof (sādhya), based on the example, as "so it is" or "not so it is."
"Dependent on the example," "governed by the example," and "under the sway of the example" [are used here].
"Sway" (*vaśa*) means capacity (*sāmarthya*).
In an example that possesses similarity with the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), it is observed that substances such as a cooking pot, which possess the property of arising, are impermanent.

And thus, in the case of the statement "sound has the property of being produced," the fact that sound, which is the probandum (*sādhya*), possesses the property of being produced is summarized [in the application].
Furthermore, in the example characterized by dissimilarity to the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*), it is observed that substances such as the self (*ātman*) are non-produced and eternal;
yet sound is not like that, for it does not possess the property of being non-produced.
By the negation of the application of the property of non-arising, the property of having the nature of arising is applied. This twofold application arises from the twofold illustration;
furthermore, "application" (upasaṃhāra) should be understood as that by which something is applied. //38//
Furthermore, regarding the two kinds of reasons, the two kinds of examples, and the duality of the conclusion, it is the same:
"The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason (*hetu*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.39)

Whether the example is stated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), the conclusion is drawn accordingly, such as: "Therefore, because it has the property of being produced, sound is impermanent. This is the *nigamana* (conclusion).
It is called *nigamana* because by means of it the proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), and application (*upanaya*) are brought together (*nigamyante*) into one;
that is, they are confirmed (*samarthyante*) and connected (*saṃbadhyante*).
In that regard, first, regarding the reason stated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), the statement is as follows:
"Sound is impermanent" is the proposition (*pratijñā*); "because it possesses the property of being produced" (*utpattidharmakatvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).

A pot and other such substances, which possess the property of arising, are impermanent: this is the example (*udāharaṇa*). Likewise, sound possesses the property of arising: this is the application (*upanaya*).
Therefore, because it possesses the property of arising, sound is impermanent: this is the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Even when stated by way of dissimilarity:
"Sound is impermanent, because it possesses the property of being produced."
Substances such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, which possess the property of non-arising, are observed to be eternal;
however, sound is not likewise of a non-arising nature.
What then? It possesses the property of arising.
Therefore, because it possesses the property of origination, sound is impermanent.
And in a sentence, which is a collection of members, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establish the object by coming together through mutual connection.
First, regarding their occurrence:
the thesis (*pratijñā*) has sound as its object.
Because authoritative instruction is corroborated by perception and inference, and because independence is impossible for one who is not a seer (*ṛṣi*);
inference is the means [of proof],
since comprehension occurs through seeing [the relationship] in the example (*udāharaṇa*).
This has been explained in the illustrative commentary (*udāharaṇa-bhāṣya*).
An illustration concerns an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because the unperceived is established by means of the perceived.
The application (upanaya) is the illustration (upamāna),
because it concludes with "so it is";
and when there is a negation of the property of the illustration with "and not so," it is established as a conclusion of the opposite property.
The conclusion (nigamana) is the demonstration of the capacity of all [the members of the syllogism] for the comprehension of a single object.
There is also a mutual interdependence: if the proposition (*pratijñā*) were non-existent, the reason (*hetu*) and the other members would not function, as they would lack a support.
If the reason were non-existent, for what would the status of being a means of proof (*sādhanabhāva*) be demonstrated?
And in regard to the example and the probandum (*sādhya*), for whom would there be a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*)?
And by reference to what would there be a restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) as the conclusion (nigamana)?
In the absence of an example (udāharaṇa), by means of what similarity or dissimilarity could the proof of the probandum be undertaken?
Or by virtue of whose similarity would the application (upasaṃhāra) proceed?
Furthermore, without the application (upanaya), the probative property, not being applied to the subject to be proven (sādhya), would not establish the object.

And in the absence of the conclusion (nigamana), for whom would there be the demonstration—by way of "it is so"—of the application of the proposition (pratijñā) and the other members toward a single purpose, their connection having remained unmanifest?
Now, the meaning of the individual components:
the purpose of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the establishment of the connection between the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and its locus (*dharmin*).
The purpose of the reason (*hetu*) is the statement of the probative nature of the property to be proven—whether it be similar to or contrary to the example (*udāharaṇa*).
The purpose of the example (*udāharaṇa*) is to demonstrate the relationship of probandum and probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between two properties in a single instance.
The purpose of the application (*upanaya*) is to establish the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the property serving as the probans with the property that is the probandum.

The purpose of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is to preclude the possibility of the opposite consequence regarding the probandum, once the relationship of probandum and probans between the two properties residing in the example has been established.

And when this purity of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*udāharaṇa*) is established, the proliferation of futile rejoinders (*jāti*) and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) resulting from the various ways of counter-arguing by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) does not occur.

For indeed, the proponent of the futile rejoinder (*jātivādī*) counters only after failing to establish the relationship between the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*) within the example.

But here, when the relationship between the two properties as the proven and the prover is established and the instance residing in the example is grasped, it is the proving property that is adopted as the reason (*hetu*), and not mere similarity.
Nor [is it] merely for the sake of the dharma. //39//
Since reasoning (*tarka*) must be defined hereafter, the following is stated:

NyS 1.1.40: Reasoning is the deliberation (*ūha*) regarding an object whose true nature is unknown, for the purpose of attaining knowledge of its true nature, based on the logical possibility of the reasons.
When the true nature of an object is not yet understood, a desire to know arises first, in the form: "May I come to know this object.
Then, regarding the object thus desired to be known, one deliberates by distinguishing between two contradictory properties:
"Is it indeed thus, or is it not thus?"

When two doctrines are being deliberated upon, one accepts the one for which a justification by means of a cause is established— thinking, "In this case, a cause, a means of valid cognition, and a reason are possible"—
on the grounds that "this may be so because of the establishment of a cause, but the other is not."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
the inquiry is "one should know in reality that very knower who knows the object to be known."
The inquiry is whether it is of a nature subject to arising or of a nature not subject to arising.
When an object whose true nature is unknown is being investigated, one accords approval to whichever property for which a justification can be established.
If this [self] is of a nature that does not arise, then it would be the knower who experiences the fruit of its own performed karma;

furthermore, there would be cyclic existence and liberation, such that suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge constitute a sequence where each preceding one is the cause of each succeeding one, and upon the removal of each succeeding one, the one immediately prior to it ceases to exist, resulting in liberation.
Furthermore, if the knower were subject to arising, these two [the doer and the experiencer] would not exist.
For once the knower has arisen, he is indeed connected with the body, the sense faculties, objects, cognitions, and feelings; thus, this fruit of his own action does not belong to him.
Moreover, having come into being, he ceases to be.
For that [self], which is either non-existent or ceased, there can be no experience of the fruit of its own performed karma;
thus, in this way, there would be an absolute absence of one [self] being joined with multiple bodies or being separated from a body—
wherein he perceives the cause to be untenable.
He does not assent to that;
this reasoning characterized in such a way is called *ūha* (investigation) or *tarka* (speculative reasoning).
But how is it that this [reasoning] has the purpose of knowing reality, yet is not itself the knowledge of reality?
Because it does not provide a definitive determination.
It merely permits one particular phenomenon through the application of a logical reason.
But one does not yet apprehend, resolve, or determine that "this is exactly so.

How is it for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)? Because, following upon *ūha*—which is characterized by the admission of the object of the knowledge of reality, having been cultivated and rendered clear—the knowledge of reality arises through the power of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, it is said to be "for the sake of the knowledge of reality."
Thus, this reasoning (tarka), by connecting the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and thereby being permitted by those very means, is declared to be accompanied by the pramāṇas in debate.

Regarding the phrase "in respect of an object whose true nature is unknown": its *tattva* (true nature) is that state of being as it actually is; it is non-perversion, its being according to reality (*yāthātathya*). //40//
And regarding this subject of deliberation (tarka):
NyS 1.1.41: Determination of the truth through the examination of a thesis and its counter-thesis is ascertainment (nirṇaya).
Establishment is proof, and refutation is censure.
These two— proof and censure— relying upon a position and its counter-position, proceeding in an intertwined succession, are called "position and counter-position."
The cessation of one of these two and the persistence of the other is unavoidable, as it is necessarily bound to occur.
That which persists is the ascertainment of the object; this is *nirṇaya* (certainty).

This determination of the meaning through a thesis and a counter-thesis is not possible; for one person establishes the proposed meaning by means of a reason and rescues it when it is refuted, while for the second person, the establishing reason is refuted and his own refuting reason is rescued. Thus, the first person desists.
When that [doubt] has ceased, that which remains is the ascertainment of the object; this is *nirṇaya* (certainty).
He states that the determination of the meaning occurs through both [reasons] alone.
By what logic?
Through the possibility of one and the impossibility of the second.

These two—possibility and impossibility—cause doubt to cease simultaneously when both are possible; however, when neither is possible, doubt does not cease. "Having deliberated" (*vimṛśya*) means having performed the act of deliberation (*vimarśa*).
Thus, this deliberation (*vimarśa*) is employed because it brings about the operation of logic (*nyāya*) by illuminating the thesis and the counter-thesis.
Furthermore, this [deliberation] is to be understood as occurring between two contradictory properties residing in a single locus (*dharmī*).
However, where two contradictory properties residing in a common locus (*dharmisāmānya*) are both possible through their respective reasons (*hetu*), there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Because the existence of an object in such a manner is established through its cause;

just as in the statement of a definition, "a substance possesses action," that substance for which a connection with action is possible by way of its cause is "possessing action," while that for which it is not possible is "actionless."
And there is a temporal distinction between two mutually contradictory properties residing in a single substratum which do not exist simultaneously,
as for example: that very same substance is "possessing action" when joined with action,
yet it is "actionless" when the action has not yet arisen or has already ceased.
Furthermore, this is not a restrictive rule that determination (*nirṇaya*) consists solely in the ascertainment of an object through the consideration of a proponent's and an opponent's positions;
rather, indeed, there is determination as the ascertainment of an object arising from perception produced by the contact of a sense organ with its object.
However, in the case of an object under investigation, determination is the ascertainment of the object after having considered the proponent's and the opponent's positions.
In the treatise and in debate, [the inquiry] is excluded from deliberation. //41//
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
There are three types of discourse:
debate (*vāda*), wrangling (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*).
Of these—

NyS 1.2.1: Debate (vāda) is the taking up of a position and its counter-position, employing means of valid cognition and reasoning for proof and refutation, not contradicting established tenets, and consisting of the five members [of a syllogism].
Two contradictory properties residing in the same substratum constitute a thesis (*pakṣa*) and a counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) because they stand in opposition,
such as "the self exists" and "the self does not exist.
Even if they are contradictory, two properties residing in different substrata do not constitute a thesis and a counter-thesis.
For example: "The self is eternal; cognition is impermanent.
*Parigraha* is the formal establishment of an assertion.

This debate (vāda) consists of the adoption of a position and its counter-position. Its qualification is that it employs means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and reasoning (tarka) for both proof and refutation;
that is, it employs means of valid cognition and reasoning as proof, and employs means of valid cognition and reasoning as refutation.

In this [treatise], proof and refutation are carried out by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). Proof (*sādhana*) is establishment (*sthāpanā*); refutation (*upālambha*) is opposition (*pratiṣedha*).
These two—the proof and the refutation—are intertwined and connected for both sides as long as one has ceased and the other remains established;
for the refutation belongs to that which has ceased, while the proof belongs to that which remains established.

Because points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are employed in *jalpa* (disputational debate), they are prohibited in *vāda* (truth-seeking discussion). To permit certain [points] while prohibiting others, it is stated that [the reason] must not contradict the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Thus, in *vāda*, the point of defeat known as the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*)—defined as that which, having accepted an established tenet, contradicts it—is permitted.

The phrase "endowed with five members" is intended to permit these two cases: that which is deficient by even one member is "deficient," and that which has an excess of either the reason (*hetu*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is "excessive."

Regarding the inclusion of the members (*avayava*) within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), the separate mention of "means of valid cognition" and "reasoning" is for the purpose of making known their mutual connection in the establishment [of a proof] and the apprehension [of a counter-argument].
Otherwise, if both sides were to proceed solely by means of a probative reason (*sthāpanāhetu*), it would simply be a debate (*vāda*).
Furthermore, it is observed that the means of valid cognition establish an object even without a formal connection to the members of a syllogism.
By this [definition] as well, he makes it known that proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*) occur in debate (*vāda*).

From the statement, "Discussion (*jalpa*) is the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the purpose of proof and refutation," one should not understand that discussion is merely a state of being defeated; rather, discussion is precisely the employment of quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat for the purpose of proof and refutation.

The separate mention of "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) and "reasoning" (tarka) is for the purpose that one should not understand [the term *vāda*] as referring solely to that which consists of the establishment [of one's own position] and the refutation [of the opponent's position] by means of pramāṇas and tarkas. //1//

NyS 1.2.2: Debate (*jalpa*) is the establishing of a proof and the refutation of an opponent's position, characterized by the employment of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), as previously described.
"Endowed with what has been stated" means:

the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis characterized by the employment of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), not contradicting established tenets (*siddhānta*), and consisting of the five members [of a syllogism]. "The employment of means of proof and refutation through quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)" means: the application of these as instruments for establishing and refuting.
Jalpa is defined as that [debate] in which both proof and refutation are carried out by means of the six types of fallacies and the points of defeat.
Indeed, the establishment of any object by means of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is not possible;

for in both their general and specific definitions, it is heard that their purpose is solely refutation: "Quibble (*chala*) is the subversion of an argument through the fabrication of an alternative meaning," and "Futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is a counter-argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)."
"Misapprehension and non-apprehension are points of defeat. This applies to the specific definitions as well, each according to its own case;
and one should not understand this [definition] as being intended solely for the purpose of negation, since it establishes the meaning [of the term].
Even when it is stated that "jalpa is a debate characterized by the employment of fallacies, quibbles, and points of defeat, and consisting of mere cavil," this [definition] is understood.

The role of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is subsidiary to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in establishing and refuting [positions], because their purpose is the protection of one's own position;
they do not possess the status of independent means of proof.

That which is the establishment of an object by means of the *pramāṇas*, in that regard, quibbles, futile rejoinders, and points of defeat have no subsidiary role, since their function is merely protective.
For when these are employed, they protect one's own position by refuting the opposing position.

Thus it has been said: "Wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of reality, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds.

And when this censure of the counter-position is carried out by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), these [fallacies], being employed, become auxiliary factors by preventing the refutation [of that censure].

Thus, in the context of debate (*jalpa*), there is the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and the other [fallacies] as subordinate members (*aṅga*), but they do not possess the status of independent means of proof (*sādhana*).
In the context of censure (*upālambha*), however, they also possess independence. // 2 //
That [vitaṇḍā] is a destructive criticism (vitaṇḍā) that lacks the establishment of a counter-position.
That speech becomes cavil (*vitaṇḍā*). By what qualification?
It is deficient in the establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣasthāpanā*).

Regarding those two contradictory properties in grammatical apposition which were called "the thesis and the counter-thesis," the caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) does not establish either one of them; rather, he proceeds solely by means of negating the opponent's position.

Well then, let that [negation] be the *vitaṇḍā* as being devoid of a counter-position (*pratipakṣahīna*). Indeed, that statement characterized by the negation of another's position is the caviller's own position (*pakṣa*).
But since he does not establish any thesis by asserting some object to be proven, let it remain exactly as it was originally stated. //3//
Because they lack the defining characteristics of a reason, these are non-reasons; yet, due to their similarity to reasons, they appear as if they were reasons.
These are:
the erratic, the contradictory, the one that is equivalent to the point at issue, the one that is identical with the probandum, and the mistimed—these are the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
Among those—Nyāyasūtra 1.2.5: The inconclusive [reason] is that which deviates.
Deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is non-occurrence in one [of the two alternatives]. That which exists together with deviation is "deviant" (*savyabhicāra*).
An example: "Sound is eternal because it is intangible."
A jar possessing touch is seen to be impermanent;
sound, however, does not possess touch in that way.
Therefore, because it lacks touch, sound is eternal.

In the example, the two properties— possessing tangibility and impermanence— are not grasped as being in the relationship of the probandum and the probans, since it is held that "an atom possesses tangibility and is eternal.

Furthermore, regarding the example of the self (*ātman*) and so forth, where the reason is said to be the means of proving the probandum through similarity with the instance (*udāharaṇasādharmya*), the reason "because of the absence of tangibility" deviates from eternity.
Furthermore, cognition is both intangible and impermanent.

Thus, because there is a deviation in both types of examples, the relationship between the probandum and the probans does not exist; therefore, due to the absence of the defining characteristic, it is not a valid reason (*ahetu*).
Permanence is one extreme; impermanence is another extreme. That which exists in one extreme is "exclusive" (aikāntika); by contrast, that which does not is "non-exclusive" (anaikāntika).
Because it pervades both extremes. // 5 //
NS 1.2.6: Having accepted a tenet, that which contradicts it is the "contradictory" (viruddha) [reason].
"That which obstructs it" means that which is contradictory to it;
that is, it contradicts the accepted tenet.
For example: "This modification departs from its manifestation, because of the negation of permanence."
A modification that is eternal is not tenable;
furthermore, even when a modification has departed, it still exists because its destruction is denied.
Thus, this reason—"because of the denial of eternality"—contradicts one's own established doctrine, namely, that "even when a modification has departed from its manifestation, it still exists."
How so? Manifestation is the acquisition of selfhood;
the means [of its cessation] is falling away.
If there were a modification that had fallen away from the acquisition of selfhood, [it would not exist].
The negation of permanence is not tenable;
for that which exists as a modification even after it has departed from its manifestation is indeed what constitutes permanence.
The negation of permanence is established by the fact that modification deviates from its own acquisition of being.
That which deviates from its own acquisition of being is seen to be impermanent;
that which exists does not deviate from its own acquisition of being.
Existence (*astitva*) and non-deprivation of self-acquisition (*ātmalābhāpracyuti*)—these two properties are contradictory and cannot coexist.
Thus, this very reason, by relying upon a certain tenet (*siddhānta*), contradicts that very same tenet. // 6 //

NyS 1.2.7: That for which there is deliberation regarding the subject matter is called *prakaraṇasama* (the "equal-to-the-issue") when it is adduced for the purpose of reaching a definitive conclusion.
A *prakaraṇa* (dilemma) consists of two sides, a proponent and an opponent, both of which remain unestablished due to doubt.
The investigation of that [dilemma]—the scrutiny beginning from doubt and continuing until before a conclusion—is *jijñāsā* (the desire to know).

When this [investigation], having been undertaken for the sake of a conclusion, fails to reach a resolution because of the equality of both sides, it does not transcend the dilemma; such is the *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by the dilemma), which is incapable of leading to a conclusion.

The demonstration, however, is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because its permanent properties are not perceived"; for that which does not possess perceived permanent properties is seen to be impermanent, such as a pot and the like.

When a property similar to that of the subject (*yantra-samāna-dharma*) is adduced as a reason (*hetu*) and becomes a cause for doubt, that is "equal to doubt" (*saṃśaya-sama*), which is indeed nothing other than the "inconclusive" (*savyabhicāra*).

However, when there is a requirement for further deliberation regarding the specific characteristics of the two sides and no perception of a distinguishing feature between them, that initiates the "point of controversy" (*prakaraṇa*).
Just as the property of permanence is not perceived in sound, so too is the property of impermanence.

This non-perception of a specific characteristic in either case gives rise to an inquiry into the matter (*prakaraṇacintā*). Why? Because the inquiry ceases only upon the establishment of the opposite.
If the property of permanence were perceived in sound,
there would be no context;
or if the property of impermanence were perceived, [there would likewise be no context].
Even so, the discussion would be brought to a halt;
this reason, by setting both sides in motion, is not capable of leading to a determination of either one. // 7 //
NS 1.2.8: That which is not distinct from the probandum, being itself something yet to be proven, is "equal to the probandum" (sādhyasama).
"Substance is shadow" is the thesis (*sādhya*);
"because it possesses motion" is the reason (*hetu*).
[The reason] is "equal to the thesis" (*sādhyasama*) because it is not distinct from the thesis, since it itself must be proven.
This too must be explained as being unestablished, like that which is yet to be proven.

First, this is the point to be proven: does the shadow move just like the person, or is it rather that as the obscuring substance moves, a continuous absence of light is perceived due to the succession of obstructions?
Indeed, as the substance moves, whatever portion of light is obscured by it, its continuous absence alone is perceived.
Obstruction, however, is the negation of attainment. //8//
NyS 1.2.9: That which is stated when the time [for its application] has passed is the "mistimed" (kālātīta).
That whose portion of the meaning is stated after the [proper] time has elapsed is "stated at a time that has passed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and is called "one whose time has expired" (*kālātīta*).
An illustration: "Sound is eternal because it is manifested by conjunction, like color.
Color, which exists prior to and after its manifestation, is manifested by the conjunction of a lamp and a jar.
Likewise, sound, though already existing, is manifested by the conjunction of a drum and a stick,
or by the conjunction of wood and an axe;
therefore, the argument that "sound is eternal because it is manifested by conjunction" is not a valid reason, as it is stated at a time when its application has passed.
The manifestation of the manifested color does not exceed the time of the conjunction that manifests it.
When there is conjunction with a lamp, the perception of color occurs; when the conjunction has ceased, the color is no longer perceived.
But when the conjunction of the axe and the wood has ceased, the sound is heard at a distance at the time of disjunction;
this is the manifestation of the sound.
Since it persists beyond the time of conjunction, it does not have conjunction as its cause.
Why? Because in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of an effect.
Thus, due to the absence of similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*), this reason is not a valid proof; it is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Furthermore, stating the members [of the syllogism] in reverse order is not the meaning of the Sūtra.
Why?
Because whatever has a semantic connection with something belongs to that thing, even if it is situated at a distance;
for among things that are semantically unrelated, mere contiguity is no cause [for a syntactic connection].

From this statement, it follows that even when stated in reverse order, the reason—whether by similarity to the example (*udāharaṇasādharmya*) or by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—does not abandon the definition of a reason (*hetulakṣaṇa*) as the means of proving the probandum (*sādhyasādhana*). Since it does not abandon the definition of a reason, it does not become a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Furthermore, "stating the members [of a syllogism] in reverse order" has already been declared as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) under the category of "speaking out of turn" (*aprāptakāla*).
Since this very same thing is being stated again here, it is not the intended meaning of the Sūtra. //9//
Now, regarding quibble (*chala*): Nyāyasūtra 1.2.10 states: "Quibble is the subversion of a statement by means of the fabrication of an alternative meaning."
Quibble cannot be illustrated with respect to a general definition; however, examples [of it] exist within its specific divisions. // 10 //
And the classification [is as follows]: NS 1.2.11: That [quibble] is of three kinds—quibble regarding speech, quibble regarding a general term, and quibble regarding metaphorical usage.
Among these—Nyāyasūtra 1.2.12: Quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is the imagining of another meaning than that intended by the speaker when the meaning expressed is non-specific.
The usage "this young brahmin is a *navakambala*" [is explained as follows]:
here, the speaker's intention is that "he has a new blanket" (*navaḥ kambalo 'sya*).
However, there is a distinction in the analytical statement (*vigraha*), but not in the compound (*samāsa*).

In this regard, the quibbler (chalavādī), disregarding the speaker’s intention, imagines another meaning not intended by him—namely, that "he has nine blankets" (*nava kambalā asya*) was what was said—and having so imagined it, he refutes it on the grounds of impossibility, saying: "He has only one blanket; how could he have nine?"
Thus, this is "verbal quibble" (vākchala), which occurs when the cause for the application of a word is its general sense.
The rebuttal to this is as follows: when a general term has multiple meanings, a specific statement is required for the assumption of denoting one particular meaning.
In the expression "navakambala," there is the denotation of multiple meanings: either "one who possesses nine blankets" (navaḥ kambalo 'syeti), or [the other possible interpretation].
And regarding the expression "he has nine blankets": when this [compound] is employed, the conceptualization that "he has nine blankets" which was stated by you is not possible.
In this assumption of denoting either one [of the two], a distinction must be stated,
because it is through a distinction that a specific meaning is recognized among various meanings, such that "this meaning is denoted by this [word].
And yet, that distinction does not exist.
Therefore, this is merely a false accusation.
And the establishment in the world of the relationship between word and meaning is the application of a fixed rule regarding the signifier and the signified:
"this is the meaning of this signifier. This is common to general terms; it is specific to particular terms.
These words are employed in their meanings only when they have been used previously,
not when they have never been used before;
and such usage is for the purpose of conveying the understanding of the meaning.
And linguistic usage proceeds from the cognition of meaning.
In that case, when a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, there is a restriction on the use of a general term by virtue of its inherent capacity. For example:
"Lead the goat to the village."
Words such as "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*) or "bring" (*āhara*), though they are general terms, are employed for specific components of the referent;
by virtue of their functional capacity, they operate where a practical purpose can be accomplished, not with respect to the general meaning itself.
Because the teaching of [the literal] action is impossible;
thus, this general term "navakambala" applies to that meaning which is possible, namely, "one who has a new blanket" (navaḥ kambalo 'syeti).
It does not apply where it is impossible for him to possess nine blankets;
thus, this censure of another's statement through the postulation of an untenable meaning is not applicable to you. // 12 //
NyS 1.2.13: Quibble regarding the general (*sāmānyacchala*) is the imagining of an impossible meaning due to the application of an overly broad sense to a possible meaning.

When it is said, "Oh, this Brahmin is indeed endowed with learning and conduct," someone says, "It is possible for a Brahmin to possess the perfection of learning and conduct. To refute this statement, one employs a conceptualization of an impossible meaning through a shift in the sense of the words: "If the perfection of learning and conduct is possible in a Brahmin, then surely it would also be possible in a *vrātya*, for a *vrātya* is also a Brahmin."
Let that [Brahminhood] also be endowed with knowledge and conduct;
however, when one attains or even exceeds the intended object, that is "excessive generality" (*atisāmānya*).
For example, Brahminhood sometimes attains and sometimes exceeds the perfection of knowledge and conduct.
The quibble based on a common characteristic (*sāmānyacchalam*) is a quibble concerning a general mark (*sāmānyanimitta*).

The rebuttal to this is as follows: this is merely a restatement of the subject matter of a statement whose specific cause was not intended to be expressed, because the sentence is for the purpose of praise;
therefore, the construction of an unreal meaning here is untenable.
Just as when one says, "Rice grows in this field," the production of the seed is neither excluded nor intended to be expressed;
rather, it is the field, as the locus of activity, that is being praised.
This is a description of the field; it does not mean that rice-grains are not produced there. Although the production of rice from the seed exists, it was not intended to be expressed.
Thus, since the perfection of knowledge and conduct occurs in a Brāhmaṇa, being a Brāhmaṇa is the locus of that perfection, not its cause;
nor is a cause intended to be expressed here. Rather, this is a restatement of the subject for the sake of praising the sentence.

Since being a Brahmin is the efficient cause for prosperity, by praising the object [of the injunction] through the statement, the production of the result from its cause is not denied. Thus, this being the case, it is not tenable to claim that there is a subversion of the verbal injunction by imagining an unreal meaning. // 13 //
NyS 1.2.14: When there is an instruction based on a distinction of properties, the negation of the actual existence of the object is quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*).

The property of a designation is its application according to the actual object. A variation of properties is the application elsewhere of what was seen in another context. In the exposition of that, it is the "exposition of the variation of properties."
Just as in the expression "the beds are crying," the negation occurs precisely because of the existence of the actual referent— namely, that the persons situated on the beds are crying,
but the beds themselves are not crying.
What, then, is the arising of a conceptualization of meaning here?

It is the imagining of a meaning other than that intended when something was employed in one way; it is the imagining of primacy where there is figurative usage—that which has figurative application as its object is "quibble regarding figurative usage" (*upacāra-chala*).

Metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) by virtue of such causes as association and so forth; metaphorical designation is the expression of something as being that [which it is not] when it does not possess the nature of that thing.
Here is the summary: When usage is established, the affirmation or negation of the meaning of a word according to the speaker’s intention is not a matter of arbitrary whim.
In common worldly practice, the use of both primary words and secondary (metaphorical) words is established.
Since usage is established, the meaning of a word—whether affirmed or negated—must follow the speaker’s intention and not be subject to personal caprice.
If the speaker employs the primary word,
then there is either an affirmation or a negation of things as they truly are, not according to his own whim;
or else, is it [employed] as a subordinate term?
In that case, it pertains to that which has become subordinate.

However, where a speaker employs a word as a subordinate element while intending it to be the primary element, and another person objects, that objection is merely based on his own whim; it does not constitute a valid critique of the other. // 14 //
NyS 1.2.15: Figurative quibble is indeed just verbal quibble, because there is no distinction between them.

The quibble regarding figurative usage (*upacāra-chala*) does not differ from the quibble regarding verbal expression (*vāk-chala*), because there is no distinction in both cases involving the postulation of a different meaning;
for here too, the word denoting a quality refers to that which possesses the quality.
Having assumed that the word *pradhāna* has the sense of "abiding," it is refuted. // 15 //
No, because that [word] has a different meaning.
Quibble regarding usage (*upacāracchala*) is not merely quibble regarding speech (*vākchalameva*), because its negation of the existence of a thing's meaning constitutes a different kind of meaning.
Why? Because it involves the postulation of a different meaning;
for the postulation of a different meaning is indeed distinct [from quibble regarding speech].
The negation of the existence of another object. // 16 //
Or, if there were no distinction, it would follow that all cases of quibble (chala) would be one and the same, simply because they share some similarity with one another.
Having permitted duality for the fallacy (*chala*), triplicity is prohibited on account of some common characteristic (*sādharmya*).
Just as this reason prohibits triplicity, so too does it prohibit the duality that was previously permitted.
For since some degree of similarity exists, [the universal] does not cease; likewise, the triad-ness will also not cease. // 17 //
From here on—NyS 1.2.18: A *jāti* (futile rejoinder) is an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
For when a reason has been employed, the objection that arises is a *jāti* (futile rejoinder).
And that objection consists of a counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*), a censure (*upālambha*), or a refutation (*pratiṣedha*) based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
For example, the counter-argument by way of dissimilarity to the instance against the definition: "The reason is that which proves the probandum through similarity to the instance."

Likewise, "the reason is that which establishes the probandum through dissimilarity with the example" is countered by [the argument] based on similarity with the example; a point arising from such an opposing state is called a *jāti* (futile rejoinder). // 17 //
NyS 1.2.19: Misconception and lack of comprehension are points of defeat.
Misconduct (*vipratipatti*) is either a perverted or a contemptible practice. One who practices misconduct incurs defeat;
indeed, a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the attainment of defeat.
Non-comprehension, however, is the failure to initiate action even regarding a subject that ought to be undertaken;
it either does not refute what has been established by another,
or it does not resolve the refutation [of one's own position].
And because they do not form a compound, these alone are not points of defeat. // 19 //

But is there no difference between *jāti* (futile rejoinder) and *nigrahasthāna* (point of defeat), as there is between a *dṛṣṭānta* (example) [and other members of a syllogism], or is there a difference, as there is between the *siddhāntas* (established tenets)? To this, he says:
"Due to their various subdivisions, there is a multiplicity of *jātis* and *nigrahasthānas*. (NyS 1.2.20)

The multiplicity of *jātis* (futile rejoinders) arises from the various ways of opposing [an argument] through similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Furthermore, the multiplicity of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) arises from the various ways of misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*). "Vikalpa" means manifold conceptualization.
Or, "conception" (*kalpa*) is manifold conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

Among those, non-reproduction [of an opponent's argument], ignorance, lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), distraction, admission of the opponent's position (*matānujñā*), and overlooking what ought to be questioned—these constitute "non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*) as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
The rest, however, constitute "miscomprehension" (*vipratipatti*).

These categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), have been enumerated; they have been defined according to their enumeration, and they will now be examined according to their definitions. Thus, it should be understood that the operation of this treatise is threefold. // 20 //
The second daily lesson of the first chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
And this first chapter is completed.
[Salutations to] Śrī Śrīnivāsa Svāmin and Śrī Vināyaka Svāmin.
Goddess Śrī Sarasvatī. Oṃ.
Now, in the Nyāyabhāṣya with its commentary (Ṭīkā), the first Āhnika of the second Adhyāya begins.

Hereafter follows the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the other categories. And that [examination]—as stated in the sūtra "Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the object after deliberation through the thesis and the counter-thesis" (1.1.41)—is first examined as deliberation (*vimarśa*) itself.
NyS 2.1.1: Doubt does not arise from the ascertainment of common or multiple properties, nor from the ascertainment of one of the two properties.
Doubt arises from the ascertainment of a common property (*sāmānyadharma*), not from the mere presence of that property;
or else, if one perceives "I perceive a common property of these two," there would be no doubt upon grasping both the property and the substratum (*dharmin*);

or else, doubt regarding a substratum that is a distinct entity is untenable as a result of the ascertainment of a common property—never indeed does an ascertainment of color, which is a distinct entity, give rise to doubt regarding touch, which is a distinct entity.
Regarding the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*):

alternatively, doubt—as a cognition of non-determination—cannot logically arise from determination (*adhyavasāya*), that is, from the ascertainment of an object, because there is no similarity between cause and effect.
By this, the [opposing view] that "it arises from the determination of multiple attributes" (*anekadharmādhyavasāyāt*) is also explained away.
Furthermore, doubt does not arise from the ascertainment of either one of the two properties; for in that case, there would simply be a definitive determination of one or the other. // 1 //
NyS 2.1.2: And because of misconception, lack of consensus, and dogmatic adherence.
Doubt does not arise merely from conflicting testimony or merely from a lack of consensus;
rather, doubt arises for one who perceives conflicting testimony,
and likewise in the case of a lack of consensus.
Alternatively, one might ask: "How can there be doubt based on the perception that some think 'the self exists' while others think 'the self does not exist'?
In this way, since perception is unsettled and non-perception is also unsettled, once they have been determined through such a distinction, doubt is not tenable. // 2 //
And because there is agreement even in the face of disagreement.

That which you consider to be a disagreement (*vipratipatti*) serving as a cause for doubt is actually an agreement (*saṃpratipatti*); for it concerns the presence of opposing properties in two subjects.
In that case, if doubt arises from disagreement, it would instead arise from agreement itself. // 3 //
And because non-determination is determined within a self that is itself undetermined.
There is no doubt:
if this lack of stability (avyavasthā) were itself established within the self,
then the doubt is untenable, because that which is established cannot be a lack of stability.

Now, if non-determination does not reside in a self that is undetermined, then, because there is no identity [between them], non-determination does not occur; thus, there is an absence of doubt. // 4 //
Likewise, there would be perpetual doubt, because of the constant occurrence of those [contradictory] properties.

By that same reasoning through which you consider doubt to arise from the perception of common characteristics (*sāmānyadharma*), an infinite regress of doubt (*atyantasaṃśaya*) would necessarily follow—because there is no cessation of the perception of common characteristics, there is no cessation of doubt. For this subject (*dharmin*) under investigation is not perceived as lacking those [common] characteristics; rather, it is always perceived as possessing them. (5)
A brief rebuttal of this elaborate refutation:

NyS 2.1.6: Precisely from the aforementioned determination, when there is dependence upon its specific qualities, doubt arises; thus there is neither an absence of doubt nor an endless succession of doubts.
It would follow that neither the non-arising nor the non-cessation of doubt occurs; how so?
As for the claim that "the ascertainment of a common property (*samānadharmādhyavasāya*) is the cause of doubt, not the mere common property itself"—this is indeed true.
Why, then, is it not stated in this way?

Thus, because of the statement "dependent on a particularity" (*viśeṣāpekṣī*), that [doubt] is established. Dependence on a particularity means a desire for it (*ākāṅkṣā*); and that [desire] is fulfilled when a particularity is not perceived.
Nor has it been stated [in the definition] that "[it is] dependent on a common property" (*samānadharmāpekṣaḥ*).
And if this [object] were imperceptible, how could there be no desire for a common property?
By this implication, it is indicated that [the definition] is "from the determination of a common property" (*samānadharmādhyavasāyāt*).

Or, because of the statement of the logical justification (*upapatti*), it is said to be "from the occurrence of a common property" (*samānadharmopapatteḥ*). And there is no occurrence of a common property other than the cognition of its existence;
for a common property whose existence is not perceived becomes, as it were, like something non-existent.

Alternatively, by the word *vaṣiya* (the indicator), there is the designation of the indicated (*vaṣayiṇaḥ*) cognition. Just as in common usage, when it is said, "Fire is inferred by means of smoke," it is understood that "fire is inferred by the perception of smoke. How so? For one infers fire after having seen the smoke, not when it has not been seen. Yet, the word "perception" (*darśana*) is not heard in the sentence [itself].
And yet, the sentence's capacity to convey meaning is admitted; therefore, we conclude that by the word *vaṣiya*, the indicated is meant.

The cognizer accepts the expression of the condition (*pratyaya*). Likewise here too, by the word "common property" (*samānadharmā*), he expresses the ascertainment of a common property. As it was said:
"'I perceive a property common to these two'—in the apprehension of the property and the property-bearer, there is no doubt.

This refers to an object previously perceived: "As long as I have seen these two objects before, I now perceive a common property between them, but I do not perceive a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣa*). [He thinks: "How indeed might I see a distinguishing feature, by which I might determine one or the other?"
Nor does this [doubt] cease merely upon the apprehension of the property-bearer (dharmin) when a common property is perceived.

As for what was said—that there is no doubt elsewhere than from the determination of something else as being another object—that would have been so only if one were to maintain that the mere determination of something else as another object is the cause of doubt.
Furthermore, as for the argument that there is an absence of similarity between cause and effect:

The correspondence between cause and effect consists in the presence or absence of the effect depending on the presence or absence of the cause; that which arises from the arising of something, and which does not arise from the non-arising of something else—that is the cause, and the other is the effect. This correspondence exists both in the cause of doubt and in the doubt itself.
By this, the refutation that [doubt] arises from the determination of multiple properties (*anekadharmādhyavasāya*) is answered.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that doubt does not arise from "contradiction" (*vipratipatti*) and "lack of determination" (*avyavasthā*)—
it is because one perceives two opposing claims of separate disputants and does not perceive, nor does one know, the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) by which one might ascertain one or the other.

"What distinction could there be by which I might determine one or the other?"— this doubt, born from conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*), cannot be removed by mere agreement or disagreement with that testimony.
It should be understood that the same applies to doubt produced by the lack of a settled determination regarding perception and non-perception (*upalabdhyanupalabdhy-avyavasthā*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement: “And because there is agreement despite disagreement,” the meaning of the term *vipratipatti* (disagreement) is the ascertainment of that [meaning] which depends upon specific qualities; this is a cause of doubt, and its cessation does not occur through a different designation.
The meaning of the term *vipratipatti* is two conflicting discourses concerning the same locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the ascertainment of that [meaning] is likewise [a cause of doubt].

The cause of doubt depends upon specific distinctions; and when this [term] is applied as a synonym for the word *saṃpratipatti*, its status as a cause of doubt does not cease. Therefore, this [objection] is merely a delusion of the unrefined intellect.
As for the further point: “Because non-determination is established within itself, it is therefore non-determined.”

Since the object that serves as the cause of doubt has not been refuted, and since non-determination (*avyavasthā*) is admitted [as a cause], the postulation of another term based on a different reason is redundant.
This refers to the postulation of another term: "Non-determination is indeed not non-determination, because it is established within the nature of non-determination.

It is not denied that these two—perception and non-perception—have existence and non-existence as their respective objects, nor that they do not serve as causes of doubt when a specific distinction is required.
To the extent that non-determination is established within the self, to that same extent it does not abandon the self; for by that much, non-determination is admitted.
Thus, even though this conceptualization of another term is being formulated, it does not establish a different object.
As for the further point: "Likewise, there would be absolute doubt, because of the continuous occurrence of its properties."
Doubt does not arise from the common properties and so forth alone;
rather, it arises from the ascertainment of those objects accompanied by the recollection of their specific differences. Therefore, there is no infinite regress of doubt.
As for the claim that "doubt does not occur because of the ascertainment of one of the two properties," that is not tenable—doubt is a deliberation that depends upon the specific differences.

Because of the statement "it is a doubt. Furthermore, a specific property (*viśeṣa*) is a characteristic of one or the other [of the two alternatives]; as long as that [object] is not being determined, the requirement for a specific property cannot arise. // 6 //
Where there is doubt, there is this successive application of further questions.
Wherever in a treatise or in a debate there is an investigation preceded by doubt, in each such case, once the doubt has been countered by an opponent, a resolution must be stated;
therefore, because it pervades all investigations, doubt is examined first. // 7 //

Now, the examination of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇaparīkṣā): NyS 2.1.8: Perception and the other [means of cognition] lack validity, because they cannot be established in relation to the three periods of time.

Perception and the other means of valid cognition lack validity, because they are not established in the three times, as it is impossible for them to exist prior to, posterior to, or simultaneously with [the object]. // 8 //
Now follows the analysis of the meaning of the general statement:
"For, since the means of valid cognition have already been established, perception does not arise from the contact of the sense organ with its object. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.9)
If the cognition whose object is odor and so forth is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then is the establishment of the odor and so forth prior or posterior [to that cognition]?
This [cognition] does not arise from the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with the odor and so forth. // 9 //
If [the means of valid cognition] are established subsequently, there is no establishment of the objects of cognition from the means of valid cognition.
In the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by what could an object being cognized be established as an object of cognition (*prameya*)?
Indeed, it is only when an object is cognized by a means of valid cognition that it is established as an object of cognition.
NyS 2.1.11: If [cognitions] were established as simultaneous, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence of cognitions, because each cognition is restricted to its own respective object.

If the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*) exist simultaneously, then even so, cognitions restricted to their respective objects would arise simultaneously regarding sense-objects such as odor and the rest; thus, because cognitions are restricted to their respective objects, there would be an absence of sequential occurrence for these cognitions regarding objects. Or [if you argue that] these cognitions occur sequentially regarding objects...

Their occurrence [simultaneously] is impossible because they function sequentially; furthermore, there is a contradiction with the sūtra: "The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.26).
Moreover, this entire scope concerning the existence of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge is untenable.
Therefore, it is not possible for perception and the other means of knowledge to possess the status of valid cognition. // 11 //

The definition of this [perception] is as follows: because there is no fixed rule regarding the priority, posteriority, or simultaneity of the cause of perception and the object perceived, it is described according to how it is observed. In some cases, the cause of perception comes first and the object of perception later, as in the case of the light of the sun.

In some cases, for things that are arising, the object of apprehension exists first and the cause of apprehension later, as a lamp is for objects already situated; in other cases, the cause of apprehension and the object of apprehension exist simultaneously, as in the perception of fire by means of smoke.
Furthermore, the cause of apprehension is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the object of apprehension is the object of cognition (*prameya*).

Thus, since the temporal relation between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—whether prior, posterior, or simultaneous—is not fixed, one must speak by making a distinction according to how the matter is observed;

in that case, an absolute negation is untenable, for the negation was stated by way of a general distinction. Because the designation [of "means" and "object"] is connected to all three times, such a designation is appropriate. As for this further point: "If the means of knowledge is established later, the object of knowledge is not established—for an object is an object only when it is being measured by a means of knowledge."
"It is known as the object of cognition" (*prameya*);

for this designation "means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the cause is its being the instrument of apprehension. Its connection with the three times—namely, "it has produced apprehension," "it produces apprehension," and "it will produce apprehension"—is due to the connection with the three times of the cause of the designation; thus, because of that connection with the three times, the designation is likewise [applicable] in those ways.

That by which an object is measured (pramita), is being measured (pramīyate), or will be measured (pramāsyate) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That which has been measured, is being measured, or will be measured is the object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
This being so, everything follows: "In this [object], there will be apprehension through a cause," "this object will be cognized," and "this is the object of cognition.

Furthermore, if the occurrence [of cognition] across the three times were not admitted, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible. For one who does not admit this, such transactions as "Bring the cook; he will cook" or "Bring the reaper; he will reap" would be untenable.

“The non-validity of perception and the other means of knowledge [follows] from their non-establishment in the three times” (NS 2.1.8)—such statements constitute the negation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, one must ask: what is being done by you through this negation?
Is the existence [of the means of knowledge] being precluded?
Now, if it is intended that non-existence is being made known, does that mean existence is being negated? If existence were negated,
then since existence does indeed exist, the refutation of perception and the other means of knowledge would be untenable.

If, on the other hand, non-existence is being made known, then the negation falls under the definition of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—because the non-occurrence of a means of valid cognition is itself a cause for apprehension. // 11 //
And what follows from this?
[Nyāyasūtra 2.1.12: Because it is not established in the three times, the refutation is untenable.
The analysis of this [objection] is as follows: if the negation is established first, then since the object to be negated does not exist, what is being negated by it?
If it is established later, there is no establishment of the negation because of the absence of the object to be negated.
If they are established simultaneously, the negation is useless because it would imply the admission of the existence of the object to be negated.
And since a statement characterized by negation is untenable, it is established that perception and the other means of valid cognition are authoritative. // 12 //
And because all means of valid cognition are denied, the denial itself is untenable.

How so? If an example is adduced for this reason—"because [the means of knowledge] are not established in the three times"—then the capacity of the meaning of the reason to prove its conclusion must be demonstrated in the example. Yet, in that case, there would be no invalidity of perception and the other means of knowledge;
or, if there is indeed invalidity of perception and the others?

Even if an example were adduced, it would not establish the point. Thus, this reason (*hetu*) is a non-reason (*ahetu*), being contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), according to the rule: "That which, having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), contradicts it, is the contradictory (*viruddha*) [reason] (NS 1.2.6).

For its tenet is the meaning of the statement, and that meaning of the statement is: "Perception and the other means of knowledge do not establish the object. Furthermore, this adducing of the members of the syllogism is for the sake of establishing the object. Or, if it is not adduced?
The refutation—that "an example has no probative force when the meaning of the reason is not demonstrated"—is untenable, because the status of that [example] as a reason is unestablished. // 13 //
Or, if that [scripture] is authoritative, there is no sublation of all means of valid cognition.
If, in your own statement characterized by negation, you admit the validity of those means of knowledge such as perception which rely on the [five] members [of a syllogism],

then it follows that the validity of those relying on the members must also apply to the statements of others— since there is no distinction between them. And thus, not all means of knowledge would be negated.

Regarding the term "vipratiṣedhaḥ," the prefix *vi-* is used here in the sense of agreement (*saṃpratipatti*) and not in the sense of contradiction (*vyāghāta*), because there is no such meaning [in this context]. // 14 //

And there is no refutation [of the means of knowledge] across the three times, because their establishment occurs through words, just as the establishment of a musical instrument occurs through its sound.
For what purpose, then, is this stated?

It is for the sake of providing a further basis for what was previously said: "Because there is no fixed rule regarding the prior, posterior, or simultaneous occurrence of the cause of apprehension and the object of apprehension, the distinction between them is stated according to how they are observed. This [present statement] is made so that the origin of that [previous point] may be understood from this context.
Indeed, this farmer, seeing that there is no fixed rule, rejects the prohibition by means of a fixed rule, stating: "The prohibition of the three times is improper.
In this regard, he cites one mode [of proof]: "Like the establishment of the musical instrument from the sound.
Just as a pre-existing musical instrument is inferred from a sound established later, the musical instrument is the probandum (*sādhya*) and the sound is the probans (*sādhana*).

And the word "ca" (and) [indicates that the following applies]. For when a musical instrument has disappeared, there is an inference from its sound—such as "the lute is being played" or "the flute is being blown"—whereby one recognizes the specific instrument through the specific sound. Likewise, an object of perception already established beforehand is recognized by means of a cause of perception established afterwards. Furthermore, because this is intended as an illustration, the examples for the remaining two modes of proof should be understood as stated previously.
But why is that which was previously stated not repeated here as a justification?
In any case, this matter must be elucidated; whether it is elucidated here or there, there is no difference.

Furthermore, the designations "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) function through mutual inclusion—by virtue of the basis for those designations. The basis for the designation is...

The means of apprehension (*upalabdhi-sādhana*) is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of apprehension (*upalabdhi-viṣaya*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Furthermore, when the object of apprehension in a certain instance serves as the means of apprehension, then the terms "instrument of knowledge" and "object of knowledge" are used to denote a single underlying reality. // 15 //
To illuminate this point, it is said:
"And [the cognition] is an object of knowledge, like the validity of a scale" (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.16).

The balance (*tulā*) is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), being the instrument for the cognition of weight and measure. The object of that cognition, such as gold or other heavy substances, is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Furthermore, when another balance is established by means of gold or the like, then in the apprehension of that second balance, the gold and so forth are the means of knowledge and the second balance is the object of knowledge.

In this way, the meaning of the entire system (*tantra*) should be understood as indicated without omission: first, the self (*ātman*) is enumerated among the objects of knowledge because it is the object of perception; yet, because of its independence in the act of perception, it is the knower (*pramātṛ*).

Intellect (*buddhi*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is the instrument for apprehension; it is the object of cognition (*prameya*) because it is the objective domain of apprehension; and it is the resulting cognition (*pramiti*) because both [the state of being an instrument and the state of being an object] are absent [in that respect]. In this way, the application of these designations should be understood as occurring with respect to specific functions. Thus, verbal terms denoting causal factors (*kāraka*) function through overlapping application based on their respective conditions. For example: "The tree stands" (*vṛkṣastiṣṭhati*), where it is the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its independence (*svātantrya*) in its own maintenance;

"He sees the tree" (*vṛkṣaṃ paśyati*), where it is the object (*karman*) because it is desired to be reached by the act of seeing; and "He makes known the moon by means of the tree" (*vṛkṣeṇa candramasaṃ jñāpayati*).

Because that which makes known is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), it is the instrument (*karaṇa*). In the expression "he sprinkles water for the tree" (*vṛkṣāyodakam āsiñcati*), since he aims at the tree by means of the water being sprinkled, it is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). In the expression "a leaf falls from the tree" (*vṛkṣāt parṇaṃ patati*), according to the rule "that which is fixed in its departure is the ablative" (*dhruvam apāye 'pādānam*), it is the ablative (*apādāna*). In the expression "birds are in the tree" (*vṛkṣe vayāṃsi santi*), according to the rule "the support is the locus" (*ādhāro 'dhikaraṇam*), it is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

This being the case, neither the substance alone nor the action alone is the *kāraka*. What then? The *kāraka* is that which is the means for accomplishing an action (*kriyāsādhana*) and is connected with a specific action. That which is the means for accomplishing an action and is independent (*svatantra*) is the agent (*kartṛ*). It is neither the substance alone nor the action alone.
That which is most desired to be reached by the action is the object (*karman*). It is neither the substance alone nor the action alone.
The same applies to the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) and the other [kārakas].

Thus, the grammatical description of the *kārakas* is established not merely by logical possibility, but likewise by their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). This description of the *kārakas* is neither based on the substance alone nor on the action alone; rather, it is based on that which accomplishes the action as being connected with a specific action.
This term *kāparaka* [is used for] both "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of knowledge" (*prameya*), and it cannot abandon the characteristic of being a causal factor (*kāraka*).

Indeed, sir, there is a convergence of causal terms based on their respective causes: the means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth are so called because they are the causes of apprehension;
and the object of knowledge is so called because it is the objective domain of apprehension.

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), such as perception and the rest, are also objects of experience; for specific distinctions are grasped in the form: "I perceive by means of perception," "I perceive by means of inference," "I perceive by means of comparison," "I perceive by means of scripture"; and likewise, "My knowledge is perceptual," "My knowledge is inferential," "My knowledge is comparative," "My knowledge is scriptural."

Furthermore, when made known by way of their definitions, they are specifically understood through such [formulations] as: "knowledge produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object," and so forth. // 16 //

Is this apprehension, which has perception and the other means of knowledge as its objects, derived from another means of valid cognition? Or is it without a means of valid cognition—that is, without a proof?
And what is the distinction here?
NyS 2.1.17: Since [the existence of] means of valid cognition is established by means of valid cognition, it follows that there must be an infinite regress of further means of valid cognition.

If perception and the other means of valid cognition are apprehended by a means of valid cognition, then there must be another means of valid cognition by which they are apprehended; thus, the existence of yet another means of valid cognition follows, leading to an infinite regress. He states this infinite regress: "that too by another, and that too by another.
And an infinite regress cannot be admitted, because it is untenable. // 17 //
Or rather, from the cessation of that [doubt], there is the establishment of the objects of knowledge, just as there is the establishment of the means of knowledge.

If another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is set aside when there is perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, then another means of knowledge will likewise be set aside even upon the perception of the Self (*ātman*), since there is no distinction [between the two cases]. And in this way, there would be the total abolition of all means of knowledge. // 18 //
Therefore, he says:
"Not so, because its establishment is like the establishment of the light of a lamp" (NyS 2.1.19).

Just as the light of a lamp is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the perception of visible objects because it is an auxiliary factor of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and that light is itself apprehended by another direct perception—namely, through the contact of the eye—with the cause of the perception being inferred from the fact that the perception occurs when the lamp is present and does not occur when it is absent; so too, one understands it through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*), such as: "You should take up a lamp in the darkness."
Thus, the apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge occurs through perception and the others themselves, according to how they are observed.

First, the sense organs are inferred solely by their grasping of their respective objects. Objects are apprehended through direct perception. The contacts between the sense organs and their objects, however, are inferred by the mark (liṅga) of obstruction. And the cognition produced by the contact of the sense organ and the object arises from a specific conjunction of the self and the mind, as well as from its inherence in the self.
It is apprehended like pleasure and so forth. In this way, the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be explained by way of differentiation.

And just as the light of a lamp, being itself visible, becomes the cause for the perception of other visible objects and thereby acquires the status of "visible perception," so too a certain class of objects (*arthajāta*), being themselves objects of cognition (*prameya*), acquire the status of "means of valid cognition" and "object of cognition" because they are the causes of their own apprehension.

This apprehension of perception and the other means of knowledge, according to their respective appearances, occurs through perception and the others themselves; it does not arise from another means of knowledge, nor is it without a means of proof, as there can be no establishment [of knowledge] without a means of proof.
If it is argued that there is no apprehension of that [object] by that very [means], we say no;
for there is no difference in the object because the definition is common.

It is incorrect to say that perception and the other means of knowledge are apprehended only by perception and the others respectively, since it is observed that one thing is indeed apprehended by another.

No—because there is a commonality of definition regarding the distinction of objects; for by the definition of perception, many objects are subsumed, and therein, the apprehension of one by another occurs, so there is no fault.
This is likewise the case with inference and the other means of knowledge, just as by water drawn up from a source, that which remains in the reservoir is apprehended.
And because the knower and the mind are observed [together]:
"I am happy" and "I am suffering"—by that very knower, the grasping of that [mind] itself is seen.
"The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of the mind."
And thus, by that very mind, an inference of that very [mind] is observed:
namely, the non-difference of the knower and the known, and the non-difference of the grasping and the grasped.
If it is argued that there is a difference in the cause here [in the case of the self], that is the same [as our position].
For one who knows does not know the self without another cause; nor is the mind grasped by the mind without another cause—this is the same in both cases.
