In the case of the statement that "perception and the other means of knowledge apprehend perception and the other means of knowledge," here too, no difference in meaning is apprehended.
Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be anything that is not an object of perception and the other means of knowledge.

If there were some category of objects that was not an object of perception and the rest—something that could not be grasped by perception and so forth—one might employ another means of knowledge to grasp it; however, that is not possible, because everything, both existent and non-existent, is an object of perception and the others exactly as they are observed.

However, some take up an example that is not supported by a reason (*hetu*) and, in the absence of a qualifying reason (*viśeṣahetu*), employ it to prove their thesis: "Just as the light of a lamp is perceived without the light of another lamp, so too are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) perceived without another means of valid cognition. But this [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because in some cases cessation is observed, while in other cases non-cessation is observed.

Just as this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is employed for the sake of establishing the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because cessation is observed, so too should it be employed for the sake of establishing the object of cognition (*prameya*), since there is no distinction in the reason.

Just as the light of a lamp is employed for the sake of establishing the object of cognition when perceiving the form of a pot or similar objects, so too should it be employed for the sake of establishing the means of valid cognition, because there is an absence of any distinguishing reason.
Thus, this example, being accepted for one side without the inclusion of a distinguishing reason, is not accepted for the opposing side; therefore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Furthermore, since there is an example in only one of the two positions, the argument is inconclusive (anekānta), because there is no specific reason [to favor one over the other].
When there is the inclusion of a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*), there is no refutation because of the permission for the application [of the reason] to one side.

For a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) that is grasped by a specific reason cannot be prevented from being applied to one of the two positions; and this being so, the refutation "it is inconclusive" (*anekānta*) does not occur.
[Objection: If perception and the other means of knowledge are apprehended by perception and the others themselves, would there not be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)?
No; for the occurrence of linguistic usage is established through the apprehension of consciousness, objects, and causes—such as:
"I apprehend an object through perception," "I apprehend an object through inference," "I apprehend an object through comparison," or "I apprehend an object through scripture";
likewise, "my cognition is perceptual," "my cognition is inferential," "my cognition is comparative," or "my cognition is scriptural."

"Knowledge" (jñāna) refers to one who perceives both the object of consciousness and the cause of consciousness; for such a person, worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)—which has as its purpose the attainment of dharma, artha, pleasure, and liberation, as well as the avoidance of their opposites—is rendered possible. This very activity is accomplished by that much alone.
There exists no further activity to be established through an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), such that being impelled by it, one would incur an infinite regress. // 19 //
Having examined the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general, they are now examined in detail. Regarding this:
NyS 2.1.20: "The definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is untenable because it is stated incompletely."
For the contact between the self and the mind has not been mentioned as a separate cause;

moreover, a quality produced by conjunction cannot arise in a substance that is not conjoined. Since the arising of cognition is observed, the contact between the self and the mind is a cause. Furthermore, if the contact between the sense organ and the object were the cause of cognition without depending on the contact with the mind, cognitions would arise simultaneously; therefore, the contact with the mind is also a cause. // 20 //
This very sūtra has been commented upon previously:
NyS 2.1.21: "In the absence of contact between the self and the mind, there is no production of perception."
Just as perception does not arise in the absence of contact between the sense organ and its object, it does not arise in the absence of contact between the self and the mind;
and since the production of knowledge is observed when there is contact between the sense organ and its object, they declare [this contact] to be a causal factor. // 21 //
NyS 2.1.22: By this same reasoning, the same undesirable consequence applies to direction, space, time, and ether as well.
Since cognition occurs when space and the other [factors] exist, they too are causes. Even though they are not causes, cognition arises because the proximity of space and the others is unavoidable.

Even when space and the others are not causes for the arising of cognition, cognition must still occur when space and the others are present; for it is impossible to avoid the proximity of space and the others.
In that regard, the statement of the reason regarding their being causes is: "For this reason, space and the others are causes of cognition."
In that case, the contact between the self and the mind must also be added as a separate category.
In this regard, it is said:
"Because the self has cognition as its mark, there is no failure to include it [within the definition]. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.23)
Knowledge is the mark of the self, because it is its quality. Furthermore, there is no production of a quality born of conjunction in a substance that is not conjoined [with another]. // 23 //
And because non-simultaneity is its mark, [the existence of] the mind [is established].
The term "non-restriction" (anavarodha) carries over [from the previous sūtra].

When it is stated [in NS 1.1.16], "The non-simultaneous production of cognitions is the mark of the mind," it is established that the contact between the sense organ and its object, which depends upon the contact with the mind, is the cause of cognition. // 24 //
And because the contact between the sense organ and the object is the cause of perception, it is mentioned by its own specific term.

The cause for perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony is the contact between the self and the mind; however, for perception alone, it is the contact between the sense organ and the object. Because these are not identical, the specific mention of that [contact] is made. Furthermore, this is because for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted, the cause [of perception] is the contact between the sense organ and the object.
The apprehension [of objects] belongs to the contact between the sense-faculties and their objects, not to the contact between the self and the mind.
For indeed, at one time this person, having directed his attention toward the time of awakening while asleep, awakens by virtue of that directed attention;

however, when intense sound and touch serve as the cause of awakening, then it occurs for one who was not [previously] asleep, due to the cause of the contact between the sense-faculties and their objects.

In that case, the knowledge of awakening arises; here, the predominance belongs neither to the knower nor to the contact with the mind. What then? It is the predominance of the contact between the sense organ and the object—for the self, desiring to know, does not at that time impel the mind through effort. Indeed, on one occasion, when this person’s mind is distracted by another object and, by the force of volition, desires to know yet another object, he joins the sense organ with the mind impelled by effort, and [perceives] that other object.

But when knowledge indeed arises for one who is free from volition and free from the desire to know, due to the encounter with external objects by means of an attentive mind, then the contact between the sense organ and the object is predominant; for in this case, he does not, being desirous of knowing, impel the mind through effort.

And because of its predominance, the contact between the sense organ and the object must be mentioned [as the cause of perception], whereas the contact between the self and the mind is not, due to its subordinate status. // 26 //
And there is another reason for their predominance: [Nyāyasūtra 2.1.27] "And by means of these, there is the designation of specific types of knowledge."
The specific types of cognition are designated by means of those sense faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*artha*). How so?

[One says: "one smells with the nose," "one sees with the eye," "one tastes with the tongue"; or, "nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), tongue-consciousness (*rasanavijñāna*)," and "consciousness of odor (*gandhavijñāna*), consciousness of visible form (*rūpavijñāna*), consciousness of taste (*rasavijñāna*)."

And thus, because cognition arises in five ways due to the specific distinctions between the sense organs and their objects, the contact between the sense organ and its object possesses primacy. // 27 //
As it has been stated: "The mention of the contact between the sense-organ and its object [is] the intended effect, not that of the contact between the self and the mind. Why?
Because for those whose minds are asleep or distracted, the contact between the sense-organ and the object is the cause of cognition. This [argument]—NyS_2.1.28:
is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.

If, first of all, the causality of the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃnikarṣa*) for the production of cognition is not admitted in any case, then the sūtra "The non-arising of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of the mind" (NS 1.1.26) would be contradicted. In that case, the contact of the sense-faculty with its object would not require the contact of the mind; and if the contact of the mind were not required, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous arising of cognitions.

Now, if it is proposed that the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃnikarṣa*) is the cause of all cognitions so that there may be no contradiction, then this remains exactly as before: "Because the contact between the self and the mind is the cause of cognition, its apprehension must be performed. (28)
NyS 2.1.29: It is not so, because of the intensity of a particular object.

There is no contradiction; for the fact that the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃnikarṣa*) is a cause of cognition is not subject to deviation. However, the primacy of the contact between the sense organ and its object (*indriya-artha-saṃnikarṣa*) is maintained—since, due to the intensity of a particular object, the arising of cognition occurs at times even for those whose minds are asleep or distracted. A "particular object" refers to a specific sense-object; its "intensity" consists of its forcefulness and clarity.

And that [cognition] occurs when there is intensity in a particular object, having the contact between sense-organ and object as its domain, not the contact between the self and the mind; therefore, the contact between sense-organ and object is primary.

Even in the absence of focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) and intention (*saṃkalpa*), the cognition that arises from the contact between sense-organ and object for those who are asleep or whose minds are distracted has the conjunction with the mind as its cause;
thus, the cause of action in the mind is the very same spiritual quality (*ātmaguṇa*)—the effort (*prayatna*) born of desire—that impels the mind, just as it does in the case of the knower.

There exists another quality (*guṇāntara*) in everything that brings about activity and is produced by defects (*doṣa*), by which impelled the mind becomes connected with a sense-organ. For, when the mind is not impelled by that [quality], there is an absence of conjunction; consequently, since cognition does not arise, its capacity for all objects (*sarvārthatā*) ceases. Furthermore, this other quality must be admitted to function as the efficient cause (*kāraka*) of substances, qualities, and actions; otherwise, [the production of effects] from the four kinds of atoms would be impossible.

Since there would be no possibility of any cause for action other than the subtle elements, the minds, and [the self], it would follow as a logical consequence that bodies, sense organs, and objects could never arise. // 29 //
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.30: Perception is inference, because an object is apprehended through the perception of one part of it.

That cognition which arises from the contact of the sense-faculties with their objects, such as "this is a tree," is indeed said to be perception; however, that is actually nothing but inference. Why?
Because the apprehension of the tree occurs through the grasping of a single part.
One perceives the tree by grasping its front portion, yet a single part is not the tree.
In this regard, it is exactly like how one, having perceived smoke, infers fire; that [inference] is of such a nature.
But do you consider the object to be inferred to be something other than the single part being perceived?
[If so,] in the case where [the whole] is a collection of parts, it would be the other parts; and in the case where a substance is produced, it would be both those parts and the whole.

First, regarding the position that [the whole] is a collection of parts: there would be no cognition of a "tree" from the perception of only one part; for a tree cannot be perceived when other parts are not being perceived, just like the single part that is being perceived.

Now, if it is argued that the cognition of a "tree" arises there through the synthesis of the whole by means of inferring the other parts from the perception of one part, then in that case, the cognition of a "tree" ought not to be considered inference at all.

Under the view that a distinct substance arises [as a whole], the composite (avayavin) is not inferable—because that which is connected to only one part is not perceived, and if it were perceived, there would be no distinction [between the perceived and the unperceived], and thus no absence of being inferable;
therefore, the cognition of a tree is not an inference. // 30 //

Relying on the apprehension of a single part, it is established that perception is a form of inference; and this is because [perception] apprehends not only that much, but as much as is present. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.31)
Inference is not perception; why?
Because it is apprehended by perception itself.
That which is relied upon as the grasping of a single part is an apprehension by means of perception.
Furthermore, there is no perception that is without an object; as long as a collection of objects exists, that which is admitted to have them as its objects serves to establish it as perception.
What, then, could be other than that collection of objects?
It would be either a whole (*avayavin*) or an aggregate (*samudāya*).
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish that the apprehension of a single location constitutes inference, because of the absence of a logical reason (hetu).
Furthermore, there is no possibility of perception being classified as inference; for inference is preceded by perception (*tatpūrvakatvāt*).

Inference is preceded by perception: for one who has perceived through direct observation that fire and smoke are related, an inference regarding fire arises from the perception of smoke. This includes both the perception of the related sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*), as well as the apprehension of the perception of the sign alone.
Without this [perception], there is no operation of inference; yet this is not itself inference, because it arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object.
Furthermore, inference does not occur through the contact of the sense-organ with the object to be inferred (the *anumeya*).
Thus, one must rely upon this great distinction between the definitions of perception and inference. // 31 //
Nor is there perception of only one part [of an object] because of the real existence of the whole.
And it is not merely the perception of one part; what then?
It is both the perception of one part and the perception of the whole (avayavin) which coexists with it. Why? Because of the actual existence of the whole.
For there exists this whole (avayavin) which is distinct from its parts;
since it occupies the same location as its parts and has reached the conditions for perception, its non-perception when one part is perceived is logically untenable.
If it is argued that [the whole] is not grasped in its entirety, we say no; for there exists no part other than the causes [that compose it].

Nor are the parts themselves grasped in their entirety, because one part is obstructed by another part. Thus, the whole is not grasped in its entirety, meaning that it is not fully realized within the parts being perceived.
Thus, this perception of only one part remains unrefuted.

Indeed, "the whole" exists only when there is no remainder; "not the whole" exists when a remainder persists. And this [distinction] exists with respect to the many parts—because there is apprehension when there is no obstruction, and non-apprehension when there is obstruction.
Now, my friend, being questioned, please explain: regarding the whole that is being perceived, what do you consider to be unperceived?
[The opponent argues: "By means of which there would be the perception of one part [of the whole]; for its parts do not exist as something other than their constituent causes;
therefore, in that case, the existence [of the whole] as residing in its parts is not tenable."

This is its function: that which is perceived through the contact of the sense organs with the parts is perceived together with those parts; that which is not perceived due to the intervention [of other parts] is not perceived together with those parts.
Nor is there any distinction created by this.
Furthermore, would the "collection" (samudāya) be the tree, or would it be the entirety [of the collection]?
Or is it the attainment of that [tree]?
In either case, there is an absence of apprehension.
Would it then follow that a "tree" is a collection consisting of the entirety of roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and so forth?
Or is it the attainment of those who assemble?
In either case, the apprehension of a tree as a composite whole is not tenable.

First of all, because one part is obstructed by another part, the apprehension of the whole is not possible; nor is the apprehension of that which is in contact possible, since those things with which there is contact are not themselves apprehended.

Thus, this cognition of a "tree," which is invariably accompanied by the apprehension of only a single part, is accounted for as arising from the production of a distinct substance, and not from the mere collection [of parts]. // 32 //
NyS 2.1.33: Because it is the object of proof, there is doubt regarding the whole.
The argument "because of the existence of the whole" (avayavisadbhāvāt) is not a valid reason, because it is itself the very point to be proven (sādhyatvāt).
To begin with, this remains to be proven: that a substance distinct from its causes is produced. This has not yet been established.
This being the case, there is merely a misconception, and from that misconception arises doubt regarding the whole (avayavin). // 33 //
NyS 2.1.34: There would be no perception of anything at all, because the whole (avayavin) is not established.
If the whole does not exist,
the perception of everything is not possible.
What is that "everything"?
Substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence. How so?
First of all, the state of atoms as a substance does not become an object of perception, because atoms are beyond the senses. Another substance...

Furthermore, there is no whole (*avayavin*) that exists as an object of perception. These objects of perception—substance (*dravya*) and so forth—are apprehended; they would not be apprehended if they lacked a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet they are indeed apprehended, as in: "This pot is dark, singular, large, conjoined, moving, and made of clay.
Moreover, these properties such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth do exist. Therefore, because everything is thus perceived, we see that there exists a whole which is a distinct substance. // 34 //
And because of the possibility of holding and drawing [the body].
Regarding the claim that the composite (avayavin) is a distinct entity:

holding and pulling are produced by cohesion (saṃgraha). Cohesion is a distinct quality (guṇāntara) associated with conjunction, caused by moisture and fluidity; it exists in an unbaked jar through the conjunction of water, and in a baked jar through the conjunction of fire.
If, however, they were produced by the parts themselves,
they would be perceived even in heaps of dust and the like;
and if no new substance were produced, they would not exist even in grass, stones, wood, and so forth, when held together by lac.

Now, one who rejects the whole (*avayavin*) while asserting that "let there be no loss of perception" and claiming that a collection of atoms (*aṇusañcaya*) is the object of vision—how should he be questioned?
He should be interrogated regarding the object of the cognition "this is a single substance":
is the unitary cognition (*ekabuddhi*) directed toward an undivided object?
"Ah, do they have distinct objects? If it is argued that "they have a non-distinct object," then the existence of the whole (avayavin) is established because another entity [the whole] is admitted.
If it is argued that [the cognition] has various objects as its domain, then the perception of a single [entity] among distinct things is untenable;
for a contradictory cognition—that there is "one" in what is "many"—is not observed. // 35 //
If it is argued that the perception [of atoms] is like that of an army or a forest,
we say no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.

Just as the cognition "one" arises with respect to the components of an army or the components of a forest when their distinctness is not perceived from a distance, so too the cognition "one" arises with respect to atoms when they are accumulated and their distinctness is not perceived.
Just as there is a non-perception of the distinctness of the components of an army or a forest from afar due to a specific cause, [so it is here].

Just as there is no apprehension of the genus "palāśa" or "khadira" apart from the individual trees being perceived, and just as there is no apprehension of motion apart from the movements being perceived; so too, when a collection of objects is perceived, because their separateness is not perceived, the cognition "one" occurs only in a figurative sense. It does not, however, apply to atoms whose separateness is being perceived, because their separateness is not perceived in relation to their causes.
The notion of "oneness" is figurative—because atoms are beyond the senses.
This very point is being examined: does the notion of oneness have an accumulation of atoms as its object, or not?

Thus, it is not correct to say that an army, a forest, and so forth are merely collections of atoms and that they cannot serve as examples when being examined— because they themselves are what remains to be proven (sādhya).
If it is argued that this is observed, we say no—because the investigation of its object is logically possible.

(Sūtra 14) Even if one should think: "This perception of 'one' is observed because the distinctness of the individual parts of an army or a forest is not apprehended; and what is observed cannot be rejected."
But that is not so; for the examination of its object is possible.

It is precisely this object of perception that is being examined—namely, this cognition "one" which is observed—is it examined as having a distinct substance as its object, or rather as having an accumulation of atoms as its object?
Thus, in this case, the perception does not establish either [of the two alternatives].

Furthermore, because the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) of atoms is not perceived when they exist in a manifold state, there is the apprehension of them as "one" through non-differentiation; this is a cognition of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃstaditi-pratyaya*), just as one might perceive a man in a post.
What follows from this? Since a cognition of something as what it is not depends upon a primary object (*pradhāna*), the primary object must be established.

In the cognition "a man in a post," what is the primary factor? It is that cognition of a man which exists with respect to an actual man; because, when that [cognition] exists, one perceives the commonality (*sāmānya*) of "man" and thus thinks, "This is a man in a post. Similarly, in the case of diverse things, the cognition "one" can only occur when there is a perception of a commonality. And since no such primary factor is perceived in all cases, it is not tenable. Therefore, this cognition of non-difference applies only to that which is actually non-different.
"One" means: "a single [thing]."

If it is argued that the cognition of non-difference regarding the objects of the various sense-faculties is due to *pradhāna* (the primal cause), we say no; because there is no specific reason [for this], the analogy is not established.

(Sūtra 15) Regarding the non-different objects of the ear and other faculties, such as sound and so forth, the single cognition [of them] is due to *pradhāna*, according to the principle that "there is a single cognition with respect to the manifold."
This being the case, the employment of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) is not established, because there is no specific reason [to choose one over the other]:
Is the single cognition regarding atoms when they are accumulated a cognition of "that" in what is "not-that," like the cognition of a person in a post?
Or is it a cognition of "that" in that very thing because the object exists in such a way, as in the case where a sound is said to be "one" because the sound is a single entity?
Without the inclusion of a specific reason, two examples lead to doubt;
therefore, "fragrance and so forth" is not a valid example for the claim that "fragrance and so forth are merely aggregates like a jar.
In this same manner, one should also challenge the notions of dimension, conjunction, motion, and specific universals, as the same logical consequence applies to them as well.

The notion of oneness in that [object] is the specific cause for the cognition "this is that"—namely, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition "large" (Sūtra 16).
The two cognitions—"This is one" and "This is large"—have the same object and are coreferential; therefore, it is understood that what is large is that which is one.
If it is argued that the cognition of "large" is merely the apprehension of an excellence in the collection of atoms?
Thus, this perception of "large" with respect to atoms, which are not large, is a cognition of something as what it is not (*atasmiṃstaditipratyaya*).

What follows from this? Since a cognition of something as what it is not depends upon a primary [object], the existence of that primary object must be established; therefore, the cognition of "large" must necessarily occur with respect to something that is actually large.
If you argue that the existence of the primary object is established because of the determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*) that "the sound is small" and "the sound is large"?
No; the perception of mildness or intensity occurs because there is no determination of its magnitude, as in the case of a substance.

(Sūtra 17) The perception that "the sound is minute, small, or mild" and the perception that "the sound is great, clear, or intense"—why do these occur? Because there is no determination of its magnitude. For one who determines "this sound is great" does not determine "it is this much," unlike [one who perceives] jujube, myrobalan, or wood-apple fruits.
And the apprehension "these two are conjoined" consists in grasping a conjunction that has a common substratum for its two relata.
If it is argued that two aggregates are the substratum of conjunction (saṃyoga), [we ask]:
what is this "aggregate" (samudāya)? Is it the reaching together (prāpti) of many things?

If it is argued that a collection is simply the multiple attainments (*prāpti*) of a single [entity], then there would be no perception of attainment, because attainment is dependent upon [the entity] attained. [Objection:
"These two things are conjoined"—in this case, two separate attainments are not perceived as being conjoined.
If it is argued that "a multitude" (*anekasamūha*) is the "gift" (*sudāya*), we say no; for there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with duality.

When there is the apprehension, "these two objects are conjoined," the conjunction is not apprehended as residing in a multitude of many things, nor is there an apprehension of two atoms (*aṇu*). Therefore, [the substratum of duality] must be large (*mahat*).
The location of conjunction is in a substance.

If it is argued that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is not a distinct entity, but rather proximity (*pratyāsatti*) culminating in resistance (*pratīghātāvasāna*), we say no; for conjunction has a distinct cause.

(Sūtra 6.2.21) Conjunction is the cause of sound, color-form, and so forth, as well as motion (*spanda*). Furthermore, the causality of conjunction with respect to sound, color-form, and motion is not perceived apart from the production of a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*) between two substances; therefore, it is a distinct quality.
And the object of a cognition [of relation] is either a distinct entity or the negation of that [entity].

(22) If, in the case of the cognitions "the teacher wears earrings" and "the student does not wear earrings," a distinct entity is not the object, then the negation of a distinct entity must be the object; in that case, there is a statement of that which is being negated. (23)
Regarding the phrase "in a conjoined substance," that distinct object which is observed elsewhere and is here negated must be stated;
[it is] not based on atoms, because [the object] is perceived as residing in two large [substances].

There is no denial of a specific genus (jāti-viśeṣa) which has as its mark the persistence of the cognition [of that genus]. Or, if it were denied, the establishment of the cognition would be untenable. Because that which is in a different substratum is not manifested, there must be a statement regarding the substratum. (Sūtra 24) If it is argued that the object is the state of atoms being aggregated?
This is a statement concerning the capacity of what has been attained and what has not yet been attained.

(25) Is the specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) residing in that [atom] perceived when the state of atomic aggregation (*aṇu-samavasthāna*) has not yet been attained, or is it perceived once it has been attained?

If it is argued that perception occurs through contact, then there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving even the state of atoms situated at a distance; for when atoms are situated at a distance, the specific universal residing in them should be perceived.
If it is argued that perception occurs only through contact?
If it is argued that there is no manifestation when the middle and the far parts are not reached,
and that manifestation occurs only to the extent that [the object] is reached—

then it follows that the substratum is only that much, namely the portion of the atoms' aggregation wherein a specific universal (*jāti*) is perceived upon reaching it. In that case, while a single aggregate is being cognized...
[This would occur] when there is a difference in the object.

(26) And this being the case, that collection of atoms which is perceived as a "tree" would be perceived as a plurality of trees; for wherever a portion of the collection of atoms is grasped as being a tree, each of those would be a tree.

Therefore, because the specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) is manifested with respect to a distinct entity consisting of the state of atoms aggregated together, the whole (*avayavin*) is an entity distinct [from its parts]. (36)
Direct perception is that which has been examined.
Now inference is examined:
"Inference is not a means of valid knowledge because it is subject to error due to obstruction, destruction, and similarity. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.37)
"Invalid" means that it does not establish the object even once.

For example, when a river is full due to being dammed, one might then falsely infer, "It has rained upstream. Likewise, the movement of ant eggs occurs even due to damage to their nests, and yet one might [then falsely infer] "It will rain..."
The false inference "there is rain" occurs even when a person imitates the cry of a peacock; in that case too, it is a false inference due to the similarity of the sound. // 37 //
[The definition of a fallacy] does not apply to cases of fear of a part, similarity, and so forth, because these are distinct entities.
This is not a case of error in inference; rather, this is merely a misconception of inference where there is no actual inference.
How so? That which is undistinguished cannot serve as a valid logical mark (*liṅga*).
For rainwater is indeed distinguished from previous water by its greater velocity, the carrying away of more foam, fruit, leaves, wood, and so forth.
Perceiving the river to be full, one infers that "it has rained upstream," and not merely from the rise in water level;
when there is a migration of eggs by a swarm of ants, one infers that "rain will come," and not from the movement of just a few.
The claim that "this is not the cry of a peacock, this is a sound similar to it" is a false inference due to the failure to discern the specific characteristics [of the sound].
However, for one who perceives a specific sound as the specific cry of a peacock, the specific object being perceived serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), just as in the case of snakes and the like.

This, then, is a fault of the inferrer, not of inference itself, that he seeks to understand the object to be inferred through the perception of a non-specific object when there exists a specific object [to serve as the mark]. // 38 //

Inference has as its object the three periods of time—this was stated because it grasps the three times—and in this regard: Nyāyasūtra 2.1.39: There is no present [action], because for one who is falling, there is the occurrence of the past and the future times of falling.

When a fruit has fallen from its stalk and is approaching the ground, that portion above it is the path already traversed (*patita-adhvā*), and the time associated with that is the "time already traversed" (*patitakāla*).
That which is below is the path yet to be traversed (*patitavya-adhvā*), and the time associated with that is the "time yet to be traversed" (*patitavyakāla*).
A third path does not exist here where one could grasp a "present time" (*vartamāna-kāla*) in the sense of "it is falling. Therefore, present time does not exist. // 39 //
NyS 2.1.40: There is likewise the non-existence of those two [past and future], because they depend upon the present.
Time is not manifested by the path;
rather, it is manifested by action.
When the action of falling has ceased, that time is called "the time of having fallen."
When that time for falling arises,

it is the present time when an action existing in a substance is perceived; and if one does not perceive this falling as existing in the substance, with respect to what would one predicate its cessation or its state of being about to arise?
The action that has occurred is expressed as "the time has fallen," and the action yet to arise is expressed as "the time is to fall";
in both of these times, the substance is devoid of action.
"Spreading downwards" is connected to an action;
thus, the present time grasps this relationship between the action and the substance. If it did not exist, the other two times, which depend upon it, would not exist either. // 40 //
The establishment of the past and the future through mutual dependence is not possible.

If the past and the future were established in mutual dependence upon one another, we might accept the annihilation of the present. However, the establishment of the future does not depend on the past, nor does the establishment of the past depend on the future.
By what reasoning?
In what sense is it past? How is the establishment of the future dependent upon the past? And in what sense is it future?
This cannot be explained.
"This is an indeterminable [question] regarding the loss of the present.

And as for what one might think—that just as the establishment of short and long, high ground and low ground, and shadow and light occurs through mutual dependence, so it is with the past and the future—that is not tenable, because there is no specific reason [for such a distinction]. Furthermore, just as in the case of the example, a counter-example would also follow: just as...

Visible form and touch, as well as odor and taste, are not established in dependence upon one another; likewise, the past and the future are not established in dependence upon one another. Thus, for nothing whatsoever is there establishment through mutual dependence, because in the absence of one, the other is absent, resulting in the absence of both.
If the establishment of one is dependent upon the other, then what is the dependence of that other? If the establishment of that other is dependent upon the first?
Now, what would one depend upon?
Thus, in the absence of one, the other would not be established; consequently, the non-existence of both would follow.
Furthermore, this present time is manifested by the actual existence of objects—as in "the substance exists," "the quality exists," and "the action exists. (41)
And for one who does not admit this [present], there would be no apprehension of anything at all, because perception would be impossible in the absence of the present. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.42)
Perception is that which arises from the contact of a sense faculty with its object. And what is non-existent does not come into contact with a sense faculty;
nor is this [object] existent.
If one admits that anything exists [only] in the present, then perception—its cause, its object, and its resulting cognition—would all be untenable.

Since perception would be untenable, inference and verbal testimony, which are preceded by it, would also be untenable. If all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were thus abolished, there could be no apprehension of anything at all.
Furthermore, time is perceived in two ways: in some cases, it is manifested by the existence of an object, as in "the substance exists."

Thus [it is said]. In some cases, it is manifested by a continuum of actions (*kriyā-saṃtāna*), as in "he cooks" or "he cuts. A continuum of actions (*kriyā-saṃtāna*) and the repetition of an action (*kriyā-abhyāsa*) both consist of various kinds of actions directed toward a single purpose;
and an example of various kinds of actions toward a single purpose is "he cooks" (*pacati*).

Placing the pot on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, bringing the fuel near, kindling the fire, stirring with the ladle, draining the scum, and taking it down—these constitute the repetition of the action. As for the statement "he cuts," it refers to the repetition of the act: one is said to "cut" when, repeatedly raising the axe and bringing it down upon the wood.

And that which is being cooked and being cut is "being acted upon" (*kriyamāṇa*); while that is being acted upon—[Nyāyasūtra 2.1.43: "But because both the state of having been done and the state of being to be done are possible, there is apprehension in both ways."

The continuum of action that has not yet begun but is intended to be performed is the future time, as in "he will cook" (*apakṣyati*). The cessation of the continuum of action upon the completion of its purpose is the past time, as in "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*). The continuum of action that has already begun is the present time, as in "he cooks" (*pacati*). In this regard, that which has ceased is "the state of having been done" (*kṛtatā*); that which is intended to be performed is "the state of being to be done" (*kartavyatā*); and that which is currently existing is "the state of being in the process of being done" (*kriyamāṇatā*).
Thus, the collection of the three times situated within the continuum of action—expressed as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "it is cooked" (*pacyate*)—is grasped by the designation of the present;

for here it is the non-interruption of the continuum of action that is enjoined, not its commencement or its cessation. This very [continuum] is grasped as the present in two ways: as separated from and as not separated from the past and the future. It is manifested by duration (*sthiti*).
"Substance exists"—this [expression] denotes the non-interruption of a series of actions and is associated with the three times, as in "he cooks" or "he cuts.
Furthermore, other various forms of expression denoting that [substance] should be inferred in common usage through the intention to speak of proximity and so forth, such as "the chariot";
therefore, present time exists. // 43 //
(Now, the examination of analogy:
NyS 2.1.44: Analogy is not established because of similarity that is absolute, general, or partial.
Comparison is not established through absolute similarity—for it is not the case that "just as a cow, so a cow.
Nor is comparison established through general similarity—for it is not the case that "just as an ox, so a buffalo.
Nor is comparison established through partial similarity—for nothing is compared with everything in every respect. // 44 //
Since comparison is established through well-known similarity, the aforementioned defects do not apply.

Comparison does not function by relying on the entirety, the majority, or the smallness of similarity; rather, it functions by relying on the relationship between the probandum and the probans based on a well-known similarity. And where this [relationship] exists, comparison cannot be refuted; therefore, the aforementioned fault is not tenable. //45//
In that case, let analogy be inference—because the unperceived is established through the perceived. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.46)

"Just as the apprehension of the imperceptible fire by means of the perceptible smoke is inference, so too is the apprehension of the imperceptible gavaya by means of the perceptible cow; thus, this [comparison] does not differ from inference.
To this he replies: "In what way does it differ?"—by what reasoning?
NyS 2.1.47: We do not see the purpose of comparison as a means of valid cognition when the gavaya is not perceived through direct perception.

For when this person, having employed the analogy, sees an object similar to a cow while looking at a cow, he then arrives at the determination of the conventional designation "this is a *gavaya*"; yet this is not inference.
Furthermore, analogy is for the sake of another—for it is performed by means of a well-known object of comparison for the benefit of one for whom the object to be compared is unknown.
If it is argued that analogy is for the sake of another?
No—because there is independent determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Indeed, sir, there is independent determination, such as "as is a cow, so is a *gavaya*.
It is not [mere] non-determination.

However, that [comparison] is not an analogy (*upamāna*), for it is defined as: “Analogy is the means of establishing what is to be established through well-known similarity” (NS 1.1.6). And for one to whom the object of comparison (*upameya*) is already well-known, the relationship of "means of establishment" and "that which is to be established" does not exist. // 47 //
Moreover:
"It is not the same, because comparison is established through the application of the word 'so' (tathā). (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.48)
Thus, comparison (upamāna) is established through the application of a common property in the form "so it is," and not inference (anumāna); and this is the distinction between these two.
(Now, the examination of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition:
NyS 2.1.49: Verbal testimony is inference, because an object [known through it] is not perceived [directly] and is therefore inferable.
Verbal testimony is inference, not a separate means of valid cognition. Why?
Because the object of verbal testimony is inferable.
How is it inferable?
Because it is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

just as an unperceived object possessing a mark (*liṅgin*) is later inferred by means of a known mark (*liṅga*), so too an unperceived object is later inferred by means of a known word. Thus, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is inference.
Furthermore, verbal testimony is inference for the following reason:—
NyS_2.1.50: Because perception does not function in two ways [simultaneously].

When there is the occurrence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), apprehension (*upalabdhi*) functions in two ways: for in inference it functions in one way, and in comparison (*upamāna*) it functions in another; this has been explained.
However, the apprehension of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and inference functions in a non-dual way; just as it operates in inference, so too does it in verbal testimony.
Because there is no difference [between them], verbal testimony is [in effect] inference. // 50 //
And because of the connection.
The phrase "verbal testimony is inference" carries over [from the previous sūtra].

When the relationship between a word and its object is established, the apprehension of the object occurs upon the perception of the word; this is just as, when the relationship between a mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is recognized, the apprehension of the possessor of the mark occurs upon the perception of the mark. // 51 //
As for the claim that "the object is what is to be inferred," that is not so;
for the comprehension of the object from the word occurs through the power of the instruction of a reliable person (āpta).

Regarding non-perceptible objects such as heaven, the Apsarases, the Northern Kurus, the seven continents, the ocean, and the arrangement of the world, cognition does not arise from the mere word; rather, conviction arises from the thought, "This word was spoken by a trustworthy person. This is because there is no conviction when the opposite is the case. However, this is not inference. As for that which—
Regarding the statement, “Because apprehension functions in two ways” (2-1-50):

this very point constitutes the difference in the operation of apprehension between verbal testimony and inference; therefore, when that distinction exists, the [opponent's] reason—namely, "because there is no distinction"—is not a valid reason.
Furthermore, as for the argument, “And because of the connection” (2-1-51),...

There is indeed a relationship between word and meaning that is admitted, and there is one that is denied. The specific meaning of a sentence characterized by the genitive case, such as "this belongs to that," is admitted; however, the relationship between word and meaning characterized by actual contact (*prāpti*) is denied. Why? Because it is not perceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First of all, there is no perception of the contact between word and meaning through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*); for the sense organ by which the word is grasped has already passed beyond the domain of [contact with] its object.
The object is not perceived,
yet there exists an object that has become a supersensuous domain; furthermore,
when two things are grasped by the same sense organ, their contact is perceived.

And if the relation between word and meaning were grasped as having the characteristic of "attainment" (prāpti), then either the meaning would be located near the word, or the word would be located near the meaning, or both would be present in both places. (52)
Now, furthermore:
because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is an absence of connection.
The meaning is also that [the word] lacks a place of articulation (*sthāna*) and a manner of formation (*karaṇa*).
Nor is this [meaning] perceived even through inference—that the object is in the vicinity of the word.

Even on this view, that the object is in the vicinity of the word which is to be uttered by means of the places of articulation and manners of formation located in the mouth, it would follow that when the words "food" (*anna*), "fire" (*agni*), and "sword" (*asi*) are uttered, the acts of filling, burning, and cutting would be perceived; yet they are not so perceived.
Because it is not perceived, the relationship characterized by "reaching" (prāpti) cannot be inferred.
Regarding the phrase "the word [is] at a distance from the object": there is no utterance because of the impossibility of the *sthāna* (articulatory place) and *karaṇa* (articulatory organ).

The *sthānas* are the throat and so forth; the *karaṇa* is a specific effort (*prayatnaviśeṣa*). Since these are impossible for something located at a distance from the object, [no sound is produced].
And because both [possibilities] are negated, it is neither;
therefore, the object is not apprehended by means of the word. // 53 //
NyS 2.1.54: There is no refutation [of our position] because of the established usage of words and their meanings.

Because we observe the systematic determination of the word, the object, and the cognition, it is inferred that there exists a relationship between the word and its object which serves as the cause of this determination.
For if there were no such relationship, it would follow that any word could produce a cognition of any object whatsoever; therefore, the existence of the relationship is not refuted. // 54 //
On this point, the [author's] position is as follows:
"No, because the comprehension of the meaning of a word is based on convention. (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.55)

The determination of the relationship between word and meaning is not caused by an inherent connection. What then? It is caused by convention (*samaya*), as we have stated: "The relationship between word and meaning is the specific object of a sentence qualified by the genitive case, such that 'this belongs to this'; we have called that convention. But what, then, is this convention?
The application of the rule governing the relationship between signifier and signified—namely, that "this collection of objects is the denotation of this word"—is the necessary constraint;
when that [constraint] is applied, the comprehension of the object arises from the word.
For in the absence of such a constraint, even upon hearing the word, there would be no comprehension.
Furthermore, this [connection] is unavoidable even for one who maintains the doctrine of a real relation (*saṃbandhavādin*).
Moreover, because ordinary people employ [words],
and because grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the formal exposition of speech characterized by words for the sake of maintaining linguistic convention (*samaya*), [the connection is necessary].
A sentence is characterized by speech which has meaning as its characteristic;
a sentence is a collection of words when there is a completion of the sense.
Thus, even though the relationship between word and meaning is characterized by attainment (*prāpti*), it does not serve as a cause for inference, even for one who relies upon that meaning. // 55 //
And because there is no restriction regarding specific classes [of beings].

The comprehension of the meaning of a word is conventional, not inherent; for among sages, Aryans, and Mlecchas, the employment of words proceeds according to their desire for the purpose of conveying meaning.
If the capacity of a word to convey meaning were inherent, such freedom of usage would not be possible;
just as the quality of luminous light being the cause of the cognition of form does not deviate from its specific nature. // 56 //
NyS 2.1.57: Its lack of authority [as a means of valid cognition] is due to the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and tautology.
In the context of the repeated performance of the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice and other such rites,
the venerable seer restricts the application [of the injunction] specifically to the particular word "tasya" (his).
Why is it that the status of the word as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is not possible?

Because of the defect of falsehood—regarding the *Putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice, it is said: "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi. Yet, when the sacrifice has been completed, the birth of a son is not seen; because a statement whose purpose is perceptible is false, it is understood that even a statement whose purpose is imperceptible—such as "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra"—is false. Furthermore, because of the defect of contradicting what has been enjoined—regarding the fire-oblation, it is enjoined: "It should be offered after sunrise," "it should be offered before sunrise," and "it should be offered at the time of twilight."

Having prescribed that "one must offer," he subsequently contradicts what was so prescribed: "A dark horse devours the offering of him who offers after sunrise; a brindled horse devours the offering of him who offers before sunrise; indeed, both a dark and a brindled horse devour the offering of him who offers at the time when the stars have vanished but the sun has not yet risen."
Furthermore, one of the two [contradictory statements] must be false due to internal contradiction (*vyāghāta*).

And there is the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*): when repetition is enjoined—such as in the rule, “He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times”—the fault of redundancy occurs. And that which is redundant is the speech of a careless person. Therefore, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because of the faults of falsehood, contradiction, and redundancy. // 57 //
It is not so, because of a deficiency in the action, the agent, or the instrument.
There is no fault of falsehood in the *putrakāmeṣṭi* sacrifice; why?
Because of the deficiency in the ritual action, the agent, and the means.
For it is by means of this sacrifice that the parents, when united, procreate a son.

The sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), the means (*sādhana*). The parents are the agents (*kartārau*). Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the action (*karman*). From the conjunction of these three qualities, the birth of a son occurs; from their deficiency (*vaiguṇya*), the opposite results.
First, regarding the sacrifice as the basis, the deficiency of action consists in a failure of effort (*samīhābhreṣa*);
the deficiency of the agent consists in an ignorant performer and one of evil conduct (*kapūyācaraṇa*).

Deficiency in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) consists of the sacrificial oblation being unrefined or defiled; the mantras being deficient or excessive, or lacking in proper accent and phoneme; and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being ill-acquired, insufficient, or censurable. Furthermore, deficiency in the action (*karman*) based on the participants consists of improper application;
deficiency in the agent (*kartṛ*) consists of injury to the womb and damage to the seed.

Deficiency in the means (*sādhanavaiguṇya*) has been stated in the context of the desired [result]. In the world, there is the injunctive sentence: "One desiring fire should rub two pieces of wood. In that case, deficiency in the action (*karmavaiguṇya*) is incorrect rubbing;
deficiency in the agent (*kartṛvaiguṇya*) is negligence regarding wisdom and effort; and deficiency in the means (*sādhanavaiguṇya*) is wood that is damp or hollow.

Thus, since the fruit is not produced therein, there is no fault of falsehood; for the production of the fruit is observed through the application of specific qualities, and this does not differ from worldly practice—as in the injunction: "One desiring a son should sacrifice with the Putreṣṭi. // 58 //
Because, having admitted [the opponent's position], one states a fault regarding the difference in time.
The phrase "there is no contradiction regarding the offering" (*na vyāghāto havane*) is understood to carry over.

When one violates the accepted time for the offering and offers at another time, this violation of the accepted time is called a fault: "A dark [dog] devours your oblation if you offer after sunrise. This is a statement of censure regarding a failure in the ritual procedure (*vidhibhreṣe*). // 59 //
And because the justification for restatement is established.

"The fault of tautology [is avoided] by means of repetition"—this is the subject under discussion. Repetition that is purposeless is tautology; repetition that possesses meaning is restatement (anuvāda).
This repetition which [occurs here]—

The restatement, “He recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times,” is appropriate because it serves a purpose; for by this triple recitation, the *sāmidhenī* verses reach the number fifteen, and thus there is a mantra addressed to the fire: “With this thunderbolt of speech consisting of fifteen [verses], I strike down my rival—him who hates us and whom we hate.”
The mantra speaks of the thunderbolt of the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; that [thunderbolt] would not exist without repetition. // 60 //
And because the division of sentences is understood through the inclusion of the term "meaning" (artha).
Verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition, just as it is in the world.
And the classification of Brahmana statements is threefold—NyS 2.1.62: because of their application as injunctive, explanatory, and reiterative statements.
Indeed, the words of the Brahmins are classified into three types: injunctive statements (vidhi), explanatory statements (arthavāda), and restatements (anuvāda). // 62 //
In this regard—Nyāyasūtra 2.1.63: A positive injunction (vidhi) is that which prescribes.

That sentence which is prescriptive and impelling is an injunction (*vidhi*); an injunction, moreover, is either a mandate (*niyoga*) or a permission (*anujñā*), as for example: "One who desires heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice," and so forth. (63)
Praise, censure, the deeds of others, and ancient legends constitute *arthavāda* (explanatory or corroborative statements).

The praise characterized by a statement of the fruit of the injunction is *stuti* (eulogy), intended for the purpose of generating conviction—namely, that one should have faith in what is being praised—and it is also an incitement, since one proceeds upon hearing the result:

“The gods, indeed, were all-conquering; they conquered everything for the sake of attaining everything and for the sake of winning everything; by this [rite], one attains everything and wins everything.”

And so forth. Discourse on undesirable results is a form of censure intended for avoidance—based on the principle that "one should not practice what is censured. For example: "This Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first of sacrifices; he who performs another sacrifice without having first performed this one falls into a pit."
"This very person here either grows old or dies," and so forth;
a statement concerning a contradictory injunction performed by another agent is a *parakṛti*.

"Having offered the oblation, they first baste the omentum, and then the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus indeed baste the speckled butter first, asserting: 'The speckled butter is the breaths of Agni; [it is] the Stoma,' and so forth. A rule handed down by tradition and practiced through custom is called a *purākalpa* (ancient precedent)."

Therefore, by means of this [verse], the Brāhmaṇas praised the Bahiṣpavamāna Sāman with the Stoma, beginning with: "O Source, let us extend the sacrifice," and so forth. How are *parakṛti* (the action of another) and *purākalpa* (ancient history) [considered] explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)?
It is called an *arthavāda* because, through its connection with sentences of praise or censure, it illuminates some matter that serves as the basis for an injunction. // 64 //
NyS 2.1.65: Anuvāda (reiteration) is the restatement of that which has been enjoined by a prescriptive rule (vidhi).
Reiteration consists both of the restatement of an injunction and the restatement of what has been enjoined.
The former is a restatement of words (*śabdānuvāda*), while the latter is a restatement of meaning (*arthānuvāda*); just as repetition is of two kinds, so too is reiteration.
But for what purpose is that which has already been enjoined restated?
It is for the sake of providing a governing context (*adhikāra*).
With reference to what has been enjoined, either praise or censure is made known, or something supplementary to the injunction (*vidhiśeṣa*) is stated.
Furthermore, even that which has a meaning immediately following an injunction may be a restatement (*anuvāda*); in this way, other cases should also be inferred.

In common worldly usage as well, there are three types of sentences: an injunction (*vidhi*), an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and a restatement (*anuvāda*). For example, "One should cook rice" is an injunctive sentence.
An explanatory statement (*arthavādavākya*) is: "Longevity, luster, strength, happiness, and eloquence are established in food. A restatement (*anuvāda*) is: the repetition "Cook!
Cook!", or "Let it be cooked quickly," or "Indeed, let it be cooked."
[The particle *eva*] is for the purpose of requesting (*adhyeṣaṇārtha*) and for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇārtha*), namely "let it be cooked indeed.

Just as in worldly sentences there is validity because the meaning is grasped through division [of words], so too in the case of Vedic sentences, validity ought to exist because the meaning is grasped through division. // 65 //
There is no distinction between a restatement (*anuvāda*) and a tautology (*punarukta*), because both result in the repetition of words.

"The distinction that ‘repetition (punarukta) is incorrect, whereas restatement (anuvāda) is correct’ is not tenable. Why? Because in both cases, a word whose meaning has already been understood is repeated. Since a word whose purpose has already been fulfilled is being repeated, both are equally incorrect. // 66 //
As in the instruction to move more quickly, there is no lack of distinction due to repeated practice.
There is no lack of distinction between restatement (anuvāda) and tautology (punarukta).
Why? Because repetition that possesses meaning constitutes restatement;

whereas when the repetition is identical [but meaningless], it is tautology. Meaningful repetition is restatement—just as in the instruction for moving more quickly, "Go faster and faster," the excellence of the action is expressed by the repetition itself.
This is given as an illustration;
likewise, other types of repetition include: "He cooks, he cooks" (*pacati pacati*), which denotes the non-cessation of an action;
and "Every village is beautiful" (*grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ*), which denotes pervasion (*vyāpti*).
"Paripari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ" (The god has rained all around the Trigartas) indicates exclusion;
"adhyadhimaṇḍaṃ niṣaṇṇam" (Seated right upon the maṇḍala) indicates proximity.
The phrase "bitter, bitter" is an example of this mode;

thus, it has been established that such a restatement serves the purpose of indicating a qualification in cases of praise, censure, and all injunctions, as well as the purpose of referring to what immediately precedes. // 67 //
But is the validity of the word established merely by the removal of the reasons for its negation? No; and for this reason:
"Its validity is like the validity of the Mantras and Ayurveda, because of the validity of the authoritative person (āpta). (Nyāyasūtra 2.1.68)
Furthermore, what is the authority of Āyurveda?

It is the fact that when that which is taught by Āyurveda— namely, "by doing this one attains the desired, and by avoiding this one abandons the undesired"— is put into practice, it occurs exactly as stated.

Truthfulness is non-erroneousness; it is the fact that when mantra words intended for the purpose of warding off poison or thunderbolts are employed, their effect occurs exactly as intended. This is authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*).
What is the cause of this? It is caused by the authority of the trustworthy ones (āpta).
But what, then, is the authority of the trustworthy ones?
[The definition of an authoritative person (*āpta*) consists of: the direct realization of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), genuine compassion, and the desire to explain things as they truly are.

Indeed, those who have directly realized the nature of reality feel genuine compassion for living beings, thinking: "This is to be abandoned; this is the cause of its abandonment. This is to be attained; this is the cause of its attainment.
For these living beings, who do not understand by themselves, there is no cause for understanding other than instruction from such [authoritative persons].
Furthermore, there can be no striving for or avoidance of what is not understood;
nor is there a state of well-being without having acted;
nor does anything else exist that could be of benefit to it.

"Come now, let us teach them according to our vision and as it truly is; having heard this and practicing accordingly, they will abandon what is to be abandoned and attain that which is to be attained. Such is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*). When embraced by these three kinds of reliability of the authoritative person and put into practice, it becomes the means of accomplishing the goal. Thus, the instruction of a reliable person is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, authoritative persons are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By means of the portion of the Veda concerning perceptible matters—namely, the authoritative instruction of Ayurveda—the portion of the Veda concerning imperceptible matters should be inferred to be a means of valid cognition; for the reason, namely the authority of the authoritative person, is the same.
And a part of this [Veda] also—
One should infer that [the injunction] beginning with "one who desires a village should sacrifice" has a visible purpose;
furthermore, in the world, most worldly practice relies upon such instruction.

Even in the case of a worldly instructor, authority arises from their knowledge of the subject matter to be taught, their desire to favor others, and their wish to communicate the reality of things as they truly are; because of the acceptance of such a person, the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta-upadeśa*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, it is an inference based on the identity of the seers and the speakers: those very same reliable persons who were the seers and speakers of the meanings of the Vedas are also the [seers and] speakers of the *Āyurveda* and so forth; thus, just as the authority of *Āyurveda* is established, the authority of the Veda should be inferred.
If the Vedic sentences possess authority simply by virtue of being eternal, then the statement "their authority derives from the authority of the reliable persons" would be incorrect.
The status of sound as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the comprehension of meaning arises from its capacity to denote;
for if it were eternal, since everything would be expressed by every [sound], the fixed relationship between word and meaning would be untenable.
If it is argued that there can be no denotative power if [sound] is non-eternal?
No—because we observe that worldly things have purposes.

If it is argued that those [worldly things] are also eternal, we say no; for if they were eternal, it would be impossible for there to be a discrepancy between the teaching of an unreliable person and the actual state of affairs, since a word would then be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of its eternity.
If it is argued that "it is impermanent," this is a statement lacking qualification. One must state the reason why a worldly instruction from an unreliable person is not eternal.

The authority of words used as names in the world arises from their conveying meaning according to convention (*niyoga*). Their authority does not result from eternality (*nityatva*); rather, when a word used as a name is applied to a certain object in the world, it becomes a signifier of that object through the power of convention, not through eternality. Furthermore, the eternality of the Vedas consists in the uninterrupted continuity of tradition, study, and usage throughout past and future *manvantaras* and *yugas*. Moreover, their authority derives from the authority of the trustworthy person (*āpta*).
This is the same in the case of worldly words as well. // 68 //
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second daily lesson (āhnika) of the second chapter of the Nyāyabhāṣya.
Thinking that the enumeration of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is incorrect, he says:

"There are not four [means of valid cognition], because tradition (*aitihya*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), probability (*saṃbhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are also means of valid cognition. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.1)
There are not only four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What then? Tradition (*aitihya*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), probability (*saṃbhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*)—these too are means of valid cognition. Why were they not mentioned?
"Tradition" (*aitihya*) is a succession of reports whose original speaker has not been specified, in the form "so they say."

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the implication of a meaning. *Āpatti* means attainment, reaching, or logical consequence; it is that other meaning which necessarily follows when a certain meaning is being stated. For example: "When clouds are absent, rain does not occur."
What follows from this?
"That [other] exists.

What is called "possibility" (sambhava) is the apprehension of the existence of another thing based on the apprehension of the existence of a thing that is invariably concomitant with it; for example, from the apprehension of the existence of a *droṇa* measure, there is the apprehension of the existence of an *āḍhaka* measure, and from the [apprehension of the existence of an] *āḍhaka*, [the apprehension of the existence of a *prastha*].

Non-existence (abhāva) is the opposite; it is the non-existent that is the counter-agent of the existent. The non-existent activity of raining establishes the existence of the conjunction between wind and clouds—for when the conjunction of wind and clouds acts as a restrainer, the activity of falling does not occur for water due to its weight. // 1 //

It is true that these are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but they are not distinct means of valid cognition. Since you maintain that there are other means of valid cognition, you state this refutation:

"There is no refutation [of our position] because oral tradition (*aitihya*) is not different from verbal testimony (*śabda*), and because presumption (*arthāpatti*), possibility (*saṃbhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are not different from inference (*anumāna*). (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.2).

The prohibition [of *aitihya*] is untenable. How so? Because "verbal testimony (*śabda*) is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*)," and the definition of verbal testimony does not exclude tradition (*aitihya*). Thus, this particular [tradition] is included within the general category. Inference (*anumāna*) is the apprehension of an imperceptible object connected to a perceptible one; likewise, presumption (*arthāpatti*), probability (*saṃbhava*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) [are forms of inference].

The apprehension of a meaning not explicitly stated through the comprehension of the sense of a sentence—due to its being in a relationship of direct opposition—is presumption (*arthāpatti*), which is indeed nothing but inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, the apprehension of one member of a whole by means of the whole, between two related entities that exist in a state of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), is possibility (*saṃbhava*), and that too is indeed inference. When a contradiction is established in the form "this being present, that is not possible," an obstructing factor of the cause is inferred from the non-arising of the effect.

Thus, this enumeration of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is indeed accurate; it has been stated that "these are the [only] means of valid cognition, and there are no other means of valid cognition. // 2 //

In this regard, the admission that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is a means of valid cognition is not tenable; for it is as follows: NyS 2.2.3: Presumptive testimony is not a means of valid cognition because of its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*).

From the fact that "there is no rain when clouds are absent," it follows by implication that "it occurs when they are present. Yet, even when they are present, at times there is no rain. Thus, this presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). // 3 //

There is no inconclusiveness regarding presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), because there is a misconception of presumptive testimony where there is actually no presumptive testimony. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.4)

From the statement, "In the absence of a cause, an effect does not arise," the contrary meaning—namely, "When a cause exists, an effect arises"—is established by implication. For existence is the opposite of non-existence. Thus, this arising of an effect, being established by implication when a cause exists, does not deviate from the existence of the cause; indeed, it does not occur when the cause is absent.
Therefore, the effect arises from that [cause], so it is not inconclusive.

As for the claim that "the effect does not arise even when the cause exists due to an obstruction of the causal conditions," this is a property of the cause itself and is not an object of inference by presumption (*arthāpatti*).
What, then, is its object of cognition?
It is this: when a cause exists, the effect arises.
That arising of the effect, which does not deviate from the existence of the cause, is its object of cognition.
This being the case, since there is no [logical] necessity for the negation, the negation is stated based on a misconception of necessity;
furthermore, the property of the cause, as it is observed, cannot be rejected.
Nyāyasūtra 2.2.5: And the invalidity of the negation is due to its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).

The statement, "Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)," is a negation. By this [statement], the validity of presumption is negated, but not its existence; thus, it remains inconclusive. Because it is inconclusive, no object whatsoever is negated by this which is not a valid means of cognition. // 5 //
If you think that there is deviation [of inference] regarding objects within its own restricted domain, and that the existence of a negation is not its object—then, in that case:
"Or, if that [negation] is a valid means of knowledge, then there is no invalidity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (NyS 2.2.6)

Now, even in the case of a deficient cause (*vaikalya*), the subject matter is the non-deviation of the existence of the cause from the production of the effect; nor is it the case that the property of being a cause consists in the non-production of the effect due to an obstruction of the instrumental conditions. // 6 //
In that case, the admission of non-existence as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not tenable. Why? Because the object of knowledge (prameya) is not established.
(Nyāyasūtra 2.2.7) Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition because its object of knowledge is not established.
Since the non-existence of an object is established in the world as a vast field of cognition, [the opponent] speaks out of sheer audacity:
"Non-existence is not a means of valid cognition, because its object of cognition is not established. (7)
Now, because this subject matter is extensive, only a portion of it is illustrated:

NyS 2.2.8: "The establishment of those [objects] not yet characterized as objects of knowledge follows from the fact that those which have been characterized are characterized by the absence of characterization."

The object of cognition (prameya) consisting in that non-existence is established. How so? Because among the garments that have been examined and are to be rejected, those that are to be accepted are characterized by the absence of characteristics—that is, they are characterized by the non-existence of [defining] characteristics.

When both [the primary meaning and the secondary] are present, one who is commanded, "Bring the garments that are unmarked," understands those garments among which there are no marks by means of the absence of marks; having understood them, he brings them; and the cause of this understanding is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). // 8 //
If it is argued that non-existence cannot occur in the absence of an object, we say no, because its definition is established through something else.

Where something, having existed, no longer exists, there its non-existence is established. However, in the case of unstained garments, it is not that the stains, having existed, no longer exist. Therefore, the non-existence of stains in those [garments] is untenable—no, rather, it is because another characteristic has arisen.

Just as one perceives the presence of stains on other garments, one does not perceive them thus in the unstained ones; seeing this absence of stains, one understands the object through its non-existence. // 9 //
Because that [non-existence] is established, it is not a reason [for proving non-existence] in the case of things that have not been characterized.
Success is achieved when those marks are observed;
for those [marks] which exist, there is no absence of their characteristics.

Furthermore, the claim that those characteristics which are present in the marked objects are absent in the unmarked is not a valid reason—for the non-existence of things that actually exist is a contradiction. 10.
Not so, because the establishment [of the object] depends on that which is established as abiding according to its characteristic.

We do not say that there is an absence of those characteristics which actually exist; rather, some characteristics are established in certain things, while in others they are not established. One who, upon investigation, does not perceive the existence of characteristics in certain things, is afflicted by the non-existence of those characteristics. // 11 //
