And because non-existence prior to production is logically established.
Indeed, there are two kinds of non-existence (abhāva): first, non-existence prior to origination; and second, the non-existence of an entity that has arisen due to its destruction.
Among these, in the case of unmarked garments, it is the absence of characteristics characterized by non-existence prior to origination that is intended, and not the other kind. // 12 //

By stating the qualification regarding its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in the aphorism, "Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (1.1.7), it is made known that "verbal testimony is of various kinds. Regarding that, there is an inquiry in general terms: "Is it eternal or non-eternal?
And when the cause for such deliberation is questioned, doubt arises due to conflicting views (vipratipatti).
"Some maintain that sound is a quality of space, all-pervading, eternal, and characterized by manifestation;
others hold that it resides within substances in association with odor and other qualities, remaining therein like odor and the rest, and being characterized by manifestation;
still others maintain that sound is a quality of space, possessing the characteristics of origination and cessation, just like cognition."

"Others [hold] that sound is produced from the agitation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), is independent, and possesses the nature of arising and the nature of cessation. From this, a doubt arises: "What is the truth in this matter?
The answer is: "Sound is impermanent.
How so?
Because it has a beginning, because it is perceptible by the senses, and because it is treated as something produced.

"Ādi" means origin, "yoni" means source, and "kāraṇa" means that from which something is derived (ādīyate). That which possesses a cause is observed to be non-eternal. Furthermore, sound is produced by conjunction and disjunction; therefore, because it possesses a cause, it is non-eternal. What, then, is the meaning of this expression "because it possesses a cause"? It means that sound is non-eternal because its nature is to arise—that is, having come into being, it ceases to be; it is subject to destruction.

This is a matter of doubt: are conjunction and disjunction the causes of the production of sound, or rather the causes of its manifestation? To this, he says: "Because it is perceptible by the senses."
That which is perceivable through the proximity of the sense organ is "sensory" (*aindriyaka*).
Is this [sound] manifested by the manifestor as being in the same location [as it], like color and so forth?
Or, when a series of sounds arises from a sound produced by conjunction, is it perceived because it has reached the proximity of the auditory organ?
Thus—since sound is perceived even when the conjunction has ceased, it is not the case that what is manifested is perceived only when it occupies the same location as the manifestor.

When wood is being split, sound is perceived by one standing at a distance once the conjunction between the wood and the axe has ceased. Furthermore, the manifestation of a manifested object does not occur in the absence of the manifestor; therefore, conjunction is not the manifestor.

Rather, when conjunction acts as the producer, a series of sounds arises from the sound produced by that conjunction, and the perception of that which is proximate to the ear occurs. Thus, it is logical that sound is perceived even upon the cessation of the conjunction.

Furthermore, sound is produced and not manifested—because it is treated as something created, for "loud" and "soft" are applied to what is created, just as one says, "intense pleasure," "mild pleasure," "intense pain," or "mild pain. And it is likewise treated [metaphorically] as:
"a loud sound," "a soft sound."

If it is argued that the intensity or dullness of the perception [of sound] is due to the corresponding state of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), just as [the intensity of the perception of] color [is due to the light],
we say no— because suppression (*abhibhava*) is logically possible.

Through the intensity or dullness of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which acts as the manifestor, there occurs the intensity or dullness of the perception of the sound, but the sound itself does not differ, just as the perception of color [varies] through the intensity or dullness of the light.
But that is not so, because suppression is logically possible: a loud sound of a drum suppresses a faint sound of a lute, but a faint sound does not;
and it is not the perception of the sound that acts as the suppressor, for the sound itself is not different [in both cases].
However, when the sound is indeed different, suppression is appropriate. Therefore, sound is produced, it is not manifested.

Furthermore, the impossibility of suppression [of one sound by another] follows: for if manifestation occurs when [the manifester] occupies the same location as [the manifested], there is no contact [between them].
On the view that "sound is manifested by a manifester occupying the same location," suppression is not possible; for the sound of a lute string is not reached by the sound of a drum.
If it is argued that suppression occurs even without contact?

If one were to think that "overpowering occurs even when there is no contact," then just as the sound of a drum overpowers a certain sound of a lute string, it would likewise overpower the sounds of lute strings located far away, just like those located nearby— since there is no difference in the absence of contact. In that case, [overpowering] would occur only in some instances...
When a drum is sounded, the sounds of lute strings throughout all worlds would not be heard at the same time.
Since there exist various successions of sounds, it is logical that one sound—whether intense or weak—should overpower another due to its proximity to the ear.
But what, then, is this so-called "overpowering"?

Overpowering (*abhibhava*) is the non-apprehension [of one thing] caused by the apprehension of another belonging to the same class as the object to be apprehended; for example, the light of a torch, though fit to be apprehended, is not apprehended because of the light of the sun. // 13 //

NyS 2.2.14: [The term "non-existent" does not apply to space, etc.,] because the non-existence of a jar is a generality (sāmānya) and is eternal, and because of the metaphorical application of the term "non-eternal" even to eternal things.
Sound is certainly not impermanent because it has a beginning.
Why? Because of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*): for the non-existence of a jar, which indeed has a beginning, permanence is observed.
How does it have a beginning?
For a jar does not arise from the disjunctions of its causes;
how, then, could it be eternal?
That which does not arise from the disjunctions of its causes—its non-existence can never be brought about by means of an existing thing.
As for the argument "because it is perceptible by the senses," that too is inconclusive, since the universal (*sāmānya*) is both perceptible and eternal.

As for the argument "because of its being metaphorically treated as something produced," this too is inconclusive, for metaphorical treatment as if it were non-eternal is observed even in the case of eternal things, as for example:
For it occurs thus: "a portion of a tree," "a portion of a blanket"—in the same way, it occurs that "there is a portion of space" and "a portion of the self. // 14 //
NyS 2.2.15: There is no deviation [from the definition] because of the distinction between that which possesses the essence and that which participates in it.

Regarding the term "eternal" (*nitya*), what is its true nature? Eternality is the impossibility of the destruction of that which is of a different nature from [the object] and is characterized by non-arising; this is not possible in the case of a non-existence (*abhāva*). However, it is used figuratively: that which has abandoned its own self, having once existed, does not exist again—it never comes into being again. In that context, the non-existence of a jar is "eternal" in the sense that it is like something eternal; such is the meaning of the term.
In this regard, no effect whatsoever is observed to be eternal in the same manner as its cause; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule]. // 15 //

As for the statement "because the universal is eternal": that which is graspable through sensory proximity is "sensory" (aindriyaka)—[this is so] because of the qualification [implied] by the inference of a continuum (santāna). (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.16)
The subject under discussion is "non-deviation regarding eternal things.
It is not because of the capacity for apprehension by the senses that sound is non-eternal.
What then? Because it is apprehended through proximity to the senses, there is an inference of a continuum; by means of that, its non-eternality [is established]. // 16 //
As for the claim that "there is a figurative application [of the term] to eternal things as if they were non-eternal," this is not so;
because the word "part" (*pradeśa*) denotes a constituent substance (*kāraṇadravya*), there is no deviation [from the definition] even in the case of eternal things. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.17)
"Thus, a space-point is a self-point. Here, no causal substance of space and the self is being denoted, as is the case with something produced.
For how can that which does not exist be denoted?
And its non-existence is established through its non-apprehension by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What, then, is stated in that regard?

It is the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of conjunction; the conjunction of space itself with a delimited substance does not pervade space—it exists without pervading it. This is its similarity to a produced substance, for the conjunction of two *āmalaka* fruits does not pervade the locus of that conjunction.
And there is devotion based on generality, as in "a portion of space"; by this, a portion of the self is explained.
And like conjunction, sound, cognition, and so forth, possess non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*).
And since the intensity or mildness [of a sound] has been examined, it follows that the true nature of sound (*śabdatattva*) is not produced by its manifestation (*bhakti*).
Why, then, is no sūtra heard from the author of the sūtras regarding this point?
This is because it is the habit of the Blessed One, the author of the sūtras, not to establish two opposing positions in many instances.
In this regard, it is considered that the determination of reality ought to be understood from the established tenets of the treatise;
for the established tenet of the treatise is inference, which is designated as "reasoning" (nyāya), is accepted [as valid], and has many branches. // 17 //
Furthermore, how is it to be understood that "this exists" and "this does not exist"?
It is through the apprehension and non-apprehension [respectively] by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In that case, the word (*śabda*) would be non-existent—
NyS 2.2.18: Because it is not perceived prior to its utterance, and because no obstruction or other such cause for non-perception is perceived.
Before its utterance, the sound does not exist.
Why? Because it is not perceived.
That the non-perception of an existing thing is due to obstructions and so forth is not tenable in this case.

Why? Because the causes of non-perception, such as obstruction and the like, are not apprehended—that is to say, no cause of non-perception is grasped, such as "this sound is not perceived because it is obstructed," or "it is not perceived because it is not in contact with the sense organ due to an intervening barrier.
Therefore, this [sound] which has not been uttered does not exist.
"Utterance is its manifestor; because of its absence, there is non-perception prior to utterance.
What, then, is this so-called "utterance"?
It is the manifestation of phonemes resulting from the impact of the abdominal air, impelled by an effort born of the desire to speak, against the throat, palate, and other points of articulation.

A specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*) is indeed what constitutes the obstruction; and the capacity of conjunction to manifest [the sound] has been refuted. Therefore, the non-perception [of the sound] is not due to the absence of a manifester, but rather due to its very non-existence. Thus, when it is being uttered, it is heard; and while being heard, it is inferred that it comes into existence after having not existed.
Furthermore, after the utterance, it is no longer heard; having existed, it ceases to exist—it is not heard because of its non-existence.
How so? It has been stated that "because no obstruction and so forth are perceived," therefore sound possesses the nature of arising and disappearing. // 18 //
This being the case, while scattering it as if with dust, he states this:
NyS 2.2.19: "Because that [object] is not perceived due to its non-perception, the existence of an obstruction is established."

If there is no obscuration because it is not perceived, then the non-perception of the obscuration must also not exist because it is not perceived. Since that [non-perception] is absent, the obscuration is unrefuted.
But how do you know that the non-perception of the obscuration is not perceived?
What is to be known here? Because it is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedanīya*).

It is common [to all]: indeed, one who does not perceive an obstruction personally realizes for oneself, "I do not perceive an obstruction," just as one who is obstructed by a wall perceives the obstruction and personally realizes it for oneself.

Thus, this non-apprehension of an obstruction is itself to be experienced just like the apprehension of an obstruction; and this being the case, there exists a subsequent statement whose object has been removed [by the preceding argument]. // 19 //
Indeed, it is stated by the proponent of the theory of birth (jātivādin) as a mere concession:

"Just as the existence of non-perception [is established] despite its own non-perception, so too there is no logical impossibility of an obstruction simply because it is not perceived. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.20)

Just as the non-perception of an obstruction exists even though it is not being perceived, so too the obstruction exists even though it is not being perceived. If you concede— saying, "The non-perception of an obstruction does not exist when [the object] is not being perceived"— and yet state, "The obstruction does not exist because it is not perceived," then even in this doctrine of concession (*abhyanujñāvāda*), there is a restriction on understanding.
It is not tenable. // 20 //
NyS 2.2.21: Because non-apprehension consists in the nature of non-perception, it is not a valid reason.

That which is perceived exists; that which is not perceived does not exist. Thus, it is established that non-existence is characterized by non-perception, and non-perception is the absence of perception.

Since this [absence] is of the nature of non-existence, it is not perceived. Furthermore, an obscuration must indeed be perceived if it were to exist, yet it is not perceived; therefore, it does not exist.
Consequently, what was stated—that "the impossibility of an obscuration does not follow from its non-perception"—is incorrect. // 21 //
Now, for what reason does one who asserts the eternity of sound assert it?—[Nyāyasūtra 2.2.22:
Because it is intangible.
Just as space is seen to be eternal and intangible, so too is sound. // 22 //
Thus, this [reason] is inconclusive on both counts: an atom is seen to be tangible and yet eternal, while action is seen to be intangible and yet non-eternal.
Regarding the reason "because of being intangible," the example by way of similarity with the probandum is:
"not [so], because action is non-eternal" (NyS 2.2.23).
An example by dissimilarity with the probandum (sādhyavaidharmyeṇodāharaṇa): [Sound is eternal] because it is not non-eternal. (NyS 2.2.24)
In both examples, because of deviation [from the rule], it is not a valid reason. // 24 //
In that case, the reason is this:
"Because of tradition" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.25).
It is observed that sound remains while it is being imparted, and it is indeed imparted by the teacher to the pupil; therefore, it is permanent.
That is not a valid reason, because there is no perception of anything intervening between them.
By what mark is its existence perceived in the interval between that by which something is given and that to whom it is given?
For it is an unavoidable fact that while being given, it must persist as it departs from the giver and reaches the recipient. // 26 //
NyS 2.2.27: There is no prohibition [of inference] because of teaching.
Teaching is the indicative mark—because in the absence of a recipient, teaching would not be possible. // 27 //
NyS 2.2.28: There is no refutation [of the argument] because it is taught as one of the two alternative positions.
The teaching is the same for both positions, because doubt remains unresolved: Is this "teaching" that the word residing in the teacher passes over to the student?
Or rather, is teaching the imitation of what has been grasped, like the instruction in dancing? Thus, teaching is not a probans for the existence of a recipient (saṃpradāna). // 28 //
In that case, the reason is this:
"From practice" (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.29).
Practice is observed to consist of that which is stable being repeated: "He sees it five times" means that a form already established is seen again and again;
and there is also practice in the case of sound—as in "the hymn has been recited ten times" or "it has been recited twenty times.
Therefore, practice is the repeated utterance of what is already established. // 29 //
[The objection] does not apply even if there is difference, because of the figurative application of the term "repetition."

Even in cases where there is no fixed limit, the expression of repetition occurs—as in "May you dance twice, may you dance thrice," "He danced twice, he danced thrice," "He performs the Agnihotra twice," and "He eats twice.

Thus, because of the fallacy of deviation, the use of the word "other" (*anya*) in a refuted reason is prohibited: "If one thing were other than another because it is not non-other, then there would be an absence of otherness. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.31)
That which you consider to be "other" does not become other because it is non-different from its own self; thus, there is an absence of otherness.
In this regard, what was stated—that "even in the case of otherness, [the designation 'self'] occurs through habitual usage"—is incorrect. // 31 //
For one who denies the employment of a word, the employment of another word is also denied:
"In the absence of that [word], there is no non-difference between the two, because their establishment is mutually dependent. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.32)
Your Lordship establishes the distinctness of one thing from another, and having established it, you deny that other [distinctness];

yet you also admit the word "non-distinct" (*ananya*) and employ this compound term "non-distinct. This word "other" (*anya*) is compounded with a negation. If there were no subsequent member [of the compound] here, with what would this negation be compounded?

Therefore, between those two terms, "other" and "not other," the term "not other" is established only by depending upon its opposite, the term "other. Consequently, what was stated—that "there is an absence of otherness"—is incorrect.
Let it be, then, that sound is eternal:
NyS 2.2.33: Because no cause for destruction is perceived.
Whatever is impermanent, its destruction arises from a cause, as in the case of a clod of earth, whose destruction results from the disjunction of its constituent substances.
If sound were impermanent, the cause from which its destruction arises would be perceived; yet it is not perceived. Therefore, it is eternal. // 33 //
NyS 2.2.34: Since no cause for non-hearing is perceived, there would follow the consequence of constant hearing.

Just as there would be the consequence of non-destruction because no cause of destruction is perceived, so too there would be the consequence of constant hearing because no cause for not hearing is perceived.
If it is argued that there is no hearing due to the absence of a manifestor (*vyañjaka*),
[we reply] that a manifestor has already been refuted.
Now, [if it is argued] that there is no hearing of what exists because it lacks a cause, [we reply:
there is likewise a causeless destruction of what exists.
Furthermore, the contradiction with observed facts is the same in the case of destruction without a cause as it is in the case of the non-hearing [of sound]. // 34 //
And since non-apprehension is non-existent when there is apprehension, it is not a valid reason.

Furthermore, when the cause of a sound's destruction is apprehended through inference, the statement "because no cause of destruction is perceived—i.e., because it does not exist"—is not a valid reason (*anapadeśa*), just like saying "because it has horns, therefore it is a horse.
If one asks, "What is the inference? [the answer is: the logical possibility of a continuous series (*saṃtāna*).
The continuity of sound has been established—namely, that from a sound produced by conjunction or disjunction, another sound arises, from that yet another, and from that yet another;

in this process, the effect-sound obstructs the cause-sound. However, contact with a solid, resistant substance is the obstructer of the final sound, for it is observed that a sound is not heard by one standing nearby if there is a wall in between, whereas it is heard by one standing at a distance provided there is no obstruction.
When a bell is struck, a series of various sounds is heard without interruption, distinguished by differences in pitch—such as high, higher, low, or lower.

In that case, if sound were eternal, one must state whether the cause of its manifestation resides in the bell itself, in something else, or exists as a continuous process; for it is by this means that the continuity of hearing occurs.
Furthermore, since there is no difference in the sound itself, the difference in the auditory perception must be accounted for.

But if sound is impermanent, then there exists within the bell another instrumental cause, consisting of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), which operates as a continuous series and functions in conjunction with the contact [of the striker];

through its persistence, the series of sounds persists, and from its state of being intense or weak, the sound itself is intense or weak. And it is this [impression] that produces the difference in audition. // 35 //

It is not the case that a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra) is perceived without another cause; because it is not perceived, it does not exist—[this is incorrect], for there is no non-perception [of sound] due to the cessation of contact with the hand as its cause. (NyS 2.2.36)

Through the action of the hand, there occurs contact with the bell; and when that occurs, the series of sounds is no longer perceived, and thus the hearing [of the sound] becomes impossible. In this case, it is inferred that the conjunction with a resistant substance acts as another cause that obstructs the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Due to the obstruction of that [impression], the series of sounds is not produced, and because it is not produced, the hearing ceases.

Just as when the momentum (*saṃskāra*)—which is the cause of the motion of an arrow—is destroyed by contact with a resistant substance, there is an absence of movement; so too, the cessation of the series of vibrations perceptible by the sense of touch is the mark (*liṅga*) of the series of momentum in objects such as bronze vessels, due to contact with the hand.
Therefore, it is not the case that another cause, in the form of momentum, is unperceived. // 36 //
And because no cause for destruction is perceived, if [sound] were to persist, it would follow that it is eternal.

If that for which no cause of destruction is perceived remains, then by virtue of that persistence, its eternity follows as a consequence? In this way, regarding these very perceptions of sound which you consider to be manifestations of sound—for you, no cause of their destruction is established; because no such cause is established, they persist, and from their persistence, their eternity follows as a consequence.
If, on the other hand, it is not so, then sound is not eternal because it persists due to the non-perception of a cause for its destruction. // 37 //
Furthermore, the resonance (*anunāda*) which has the same substratum as the vibration ceases due to the cessation of its cause upon the contact with the hand;
for if they were in different loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), then because there would be no contact with a resisting substance, only that which has the same substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) would cease.
NyS 2.2.38: There is no refutation [of sound] because it is intangible (*asparśatva*).

As for this [proposition], "Sound is not a quality of space," it is refuted. This refutation is untenable—because the substratum of sound is intangible, and because a continuum of sound is possible even when its location is not perceived as being co-extensive with color and other qualities—it is known that sound has as its substratum a substance that is intangible and all-pervading, and not one that shares the same substratum as vibration. // 38 //

It is not tenable that sound, which exists together with color and the other qualities in each substance, is manifested as occupying the same location [as them]. Why? Because in the case of a compound, there arises the occurrence of different grammatical case-endings (NyS 2.2.39).
And the meaning of the phrase "because of the occurrence of a continuum" has already been explained.

If color-forms and so forth, as well as sound, are present in their entirety— that is, collectively— in each substance, then by means of the apprehension of that which is situated within that composite aggregate according to its specific nature, [one perceives it] as being of that very same nature.
Sound must exist [as a substance], just like color and other qualities;

for in that regard, there is this distinction: in a single substance, sounds of various forms are manifested as having different auditory perceptions and distinct properties, and there is another distinction where sounds are similar, having identical auditory perceptions and common properties, by virtue of their being intense or faint.
They are heard as distinct. Both of these [observations] are untenable: that this property belongs to multiple things arising [simultaneously], and not to a single thing being manifested.

Yet, this distinction and further differentiation do exist; therefore, because such differentiation is established, we conclude that sound is not manifested as something inherent within each substance along with [its other qualities like] color and so forth. // 39 //
And this sound is of two kinds: consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) and mere resonance (*dhvani*). Regarding that which consists of phonemes, first:
NyS 2.2.40: There is doubt because of the teaching of both modification (*vikāra*) and substitution (*ādeśa*).
Regarding the expression "dadhy atra," some consider it a *vikāra* (modification), thinking that the vowel *i* abandons its state as *i* and undergoes the state of *y*.
Others maintain that when the vowel *i* ceases to occupy its position due to the specific context of usage, they speak of the employment of *y* there;
that is, in the context of *saṃhitā*, the vowel *i* is not employed, and *y* is employed in its place—that is the *ādeśa* (substitute).
Both of these are taught therein, yet it is not known which one is the reality.

The reality is the instruction of the original material (ādeśa). For if there were an instruction regarding a modification (vikāra), the modification could not be inferred because the underlying continuity (anvaya) would not be perceived. If there were continuity, it would be possible to infer a modification on the grounds that "something ceases while something else arises"; however, no continuity is perceived. Therefore, there is no modification.
Furthermore, regarding two phonemes with distinct articulations, the occurrence of one in place of the other is logically justified.

The vowel *i* has an open articulation (*vivṛta-karaṇa*), whereas the semivowel *y* has a slightly contacted articulation (*īṣatspṛṣṭa-karaṇa*); these two must be pronounced using separate efforts known as "articulation" (*karaṇa*). Thus, when one of them is not employed, the employment of the other is established as valid.

And there is no distinction when there is no modification (avikāra). Where these two—the letter *i* and the letter *y*—are not subject to modification, as in "yatate," "cchati," "prāyaṃsta," and "ikāraḥ idam"; and where they are subject to modification, as in "dṛṣṭyā" and "dadhyāhara"—in both cases, the effort of the speaker is the same and the hearing of the listener is the same; thus the substitution (*ādeśa*) is established.

Indeed, it is not that the sound *i* is perceived as undergoing a transformation into the sound *y* when it is employed; rather, when the sound *i* is employed, the sound *y* is employed [in its place]. Therefore, there is no modification (*avikāra*).
And if there is no modification, there is no loss of the grammatical derivation of words;
for it is held that "phonemes do not undergo transformation.
Furthermore, under this view, there is no impossibility of the grammatical derivation of words such that we would have to accept the transformation of phonemes.
Indeed, one phoneme cannot be the effect of another phoneme—for instance, the letter *y* does not arise from the letter *i*, nor does the letter *i* arise from the letter *y*.
For these phonemes are produced by distinct places of articulation (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*); it is therefore logical that one is employed in the place of another.
And this [substitution] can only be either a transformation (*pariṇāma*) or a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Since neither of these two exists, there are no modifications of phonemes.

And just as the transformation of a collection of phonemes is untenable, so too is the transformation of individual phonemes. For instance, in rules such as "for *as*, *bhū*" and "for *brū*, *vac*," it is not the case that a different collection of phonemes undergoes a transformation in place of a collection of phonemes characterized as a verbal root (*dhātu*) in certain contexts; rather, one distinct word is employed in place of another distinct word.
Likewise, [there is] another color of a color. // 40 //
For this reason as well, modifications do not exist:
because when there is an increase in the primal nature (prakṛti), there is an increase in the modification (vikāra). (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.41)

In the case of transformations, conformity to the original material is observed; however, in the case of the letter *ya*, there is no conformity to shortness or length by which its status as a transformation could be inferred. // 41 //
The observation of modifications as being inferior, equal, or superior is not a valid reason [for the existence of a creator].
Substances and their modifications are perceived as being inferior, equal, or superior. Likewise, this modification might be inferior.

Since neither of these two types of reason exists, the example is not a proof—here there is no reason based on similarity to the example, nor one based on dissimilarity; and an example that is not connected by a reason is not a means of establishment.
Furthermore, in the case of a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), there would follow the consequence of non-restriction (*aniyama*).

Just as when a horse is employed in place of an ox to carry a load, it does not become a modification (*vikāra*) of that ox; so too, the letter *y* employed in place of the vowel *i* would not be its modification.
And in this matter, there is no reason for restriction—that a positive example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a proof while a counter-example is not. // 42 //
And an example of a modification of substance is as follows: NyS 2.2.43:
[The cause is not different from the effect], because there is a variety of modifications among things that do not have identical material causes.
In the case of incomparable substances (*dravya*), there is an original state (*prakṛti*) and a modification (*vikāra*) when conceptualized, and the modification conforms to the original state;
however, the letter *ya* does not conform to the letter *i*. Therefore, "modification of a substance" (*dravyavikāra*) is not a valid example. // 43 //
In the case of a modification of substance, there is an alternative [explanation] regarding the modification of color, similar to the case of inequality.

Just as there is a diversity of modifications from a primordial nature that is identical in terms of its substantial being, so too is there a variety of modifications from a primordial nature that is identical in terms of its qualitative being. // 44 //
NyS 2.2.45: No, because the properties of modification are not applicable [to space].

This is the nature of transformation: when a substance—whether clay or gold—which constitutes the essence of a generic category of substance, undergoes a persistence of that essence, its previous configuration ceases and another configuration arises.
However, in the case of a generic category of phonemes (*varṇasāmānya*), there is no persisting essence of sound that abandons the state of *i* and assumes the state of *ya*.
In this regard, just as when a substance exists, a horse is not a transformation of an ox because the properties of transformation are impossible [between them], so it is here.
In this way, the letter *ya* is not a modification (*vikāra*) of the letter *i*, because the properties of being a modification are untenable. // 45 //
For this reason as well, there are no modifications of phonemes:
because those that have undergone modification do not return to their original state. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.46)
Furthermore, a re-occurrence of the offense is untenable.
Why? Because there is no inference of a re-occurrence.
The letter *i* having attained the state of the letter *y*, it becomes the letter *i* again.
But is there not an inference here that the letter *y* is not used in place of this [letter *k*]? // 46 //
Furthermore, the recurrence of gold and other such substances is not a valid reason [for the non-eternality of sound].

"It is not because there is no inference"—for this is indeed an inference: gold, having abandoned the state of being an earring (*kuṇḍalatva*), attains the state of being a necklace (*rucakatva*); having abandoned the state of being a necklace, it again attains the state of being an earring.
In the same way, the vowel *i*, having attained the state of *y* (*yakāratva*) through *yaṇ*-substitution, becomes the vowel *i* once more. // 47 //
Because of deviation, there is no inference—just as milk that has reached the state of curd does not become milk again—is it the case that phonemes do not likewise undergo reversion?
Or is there reversion, as in the case of gold? And here follows the justification for the example of gold.
Not so, because the modifications are not distinct from the nature of the gold.

Gold remains constant as a substrate (dharmin) through its changing properties (dharma), such as being diminished or produced; however, no such essence of sound (śabdātman) is perceived as a substrate through its diminishing nature (itva) or its emerging nature (yatva). Therefore, the example of gold is not tenable. // 48 //
NyS 2.2.49: There is no refutation of the modification of phonemes, because they are not distinct from the nature of being a phoneme.
Even modifications of color do not deviate from the nature of being color, just as a modification of gold does not deviate from the nature of being gold. // 49 //
The connection with a property belongs to that which possesses a universal, not to the universal itself.
The two earrings and the necklace are properties of gold, not of "gold-ness. Likewise, of what nature of the phoneme (*varṇa*) are *i* and *y* the properties?

They cannot be properties of that universal (*sāmānya*) which is "phoneme-ness" (*varṇatva*). Furthermore, a property that ceases to exist cannot be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of that which is being produced; therefore, the *i*-sound, which ceases to exist, is not the material cause of the *y*-sound, which is being produced. // 50 //
For this reason as well, the transformation of phonemes is untenable:
because there would be no modification if they were eternal, and instability if they were non-eternal. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.51)
In the view that "phonemes are eternal," since both the phoneme *i* and the phoneme *y* are eternal, a modification is untenable;
for if they are eternal, being indestructible, what could be the modification of what?
Or is the position that "phonemes are non-eternal"?
Even so, there is instability of the phonemes.
What is this instability of the phonemes?
It is their arising and cessation.
When the sound *ikāra* has arisen and ceased, the sound *yakāra* arises; and when the sound *yakāra* has arisen and ceased, the sound *ikāra* arises.

Which one is the modification of which? This should be understood as applying when there is a pause (*avagraha*) followed by a combination (*saṃdhāna*), and when there is a combination followed by a pause. // 51 //
Regarding the position that [the phonemes] are eternal, the resolution is as follows:
NS 2.2.52: "Because eternal things are beyond the senses, and because of the diversity of their properties, there is no refutation of the modifications of the phonemes."
The contradiction is that "letters are eternal and do not undergo modification.

For instance, while they are eternal, some things are supersensible and some are perceptible by the senses; and letters are indeed perceptible by the senses. Thus, while being eternal, some things do not undergo modification, yet letters do undergo modification.
It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory: the distinction of its properties is that the eternal neither arises nor perishes;
that which has the nature of being devoid of arising and perishing is eternal, whereas the impermanent is characterized by arising and perishing.
Furthermore, no modification is possible without arising and passing away.
Therefore, if the phonemes (varṇas) were to undergo modification,
their eternity would be lost.
If they cease, then are they eternal?
If their nature of being subject to modification ceases, this is a contradictory fallacy of the reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*).
The conceptual construction of phenomena (dharmavikalpa). // 52 //
The argument for the position that sound is impermanent:
NyS 2.2.53: And because it is non-abiding, there is the perception of its modification, just as there is the perception of the phonemes themselves.
Just as there is the hearing of phonemes that do not persist, so too does their modification occur.
Because it lacks a connection, the perception of phonemes is incapable;
that is, the perception of phonemes which conveys meaning is not capable— due to the absence of a connection with modification—
of being apprehended in such a way as to infer a modification of the phonemes.
In this regard, it is as follows: just as the earth possesses the quality of fragrance, so too does it possess the qualities of sound, pleasure, and so forth. Such is the case here;
for there is no perception of a phoneme upon the cessation of one phoneme, because of the application of another phoneme.
The term *nirvartikā* refers to this employment of the phoneme *y* in place of the vowel *i*; that is,
if this [substitution] is brought about by the perception of the vowel *i*.
In that case, would it not be understood that the letter *i* perceived there undergoes the change into *y*?
Therefore, the perception of a letter is not the cause of the modification of a letter. // 53 //

NyS 2.2.54: There is no refutation [of the objection], because if there were the nature of being subject to modification, there would be an absence of permanence; and because modification is possible at another time.

The prohibition [of permanence] based on the argument "because of the conceptualization of its properties as subject to change" is not tenable; for indeed, nothing characterized by the property of modification is ever perceived to be permanent.

The refutation [of the objection] that "it is like the perception of color" is not tenable; for in the case of *avagraha*, after one has employed the expression "dadhi atra" and remained there for a long time, [one subsequently proceeds] to the *saṃhitā*.
One employs [the word] "dadhyatra. But when this letter *y* is employed after the letter *i* has long since ceased to exist, of what is it perceived to be the modification?
Since there is no cause, there can be no effect; thus, [the theory of modification] is untenable.
It follows [as a logical consequence]. // 54 //
For this reason as well, the transformation of phonemes is untenable:
because there is no fixed rule for the transformations of phonemes. (Nyāyasūtra 2.2.55)
In place of the letter *i*,
the letter *y* is heard; and indeed, in place of the letter *y*, the letter *i* is prescribed— as in the word "vidhyati" (he pierces).

If, then, there were a relationship of original material and modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) among the phonemes, there would be a restriction regarding that original material; for a restriction of the original material is observed when something possesses the nature of being a modification. // 55 //
NyS 2.2.56: Since there is a restriction regarding what is unrestricted, there is no lack of restriction.
This aforementioned lack of restriction regarding primordial nature (prakṛti) is actually restricted;
it is established according to its respective domain. Because it is restricted, it is called "restriction" (niyama).
This being so, there is no fixed rule regarding the primary causes (*prakṛti*). In that regard, it was said: "Because of the lack of restriction in the primary causes."
Thus, this is incorrect. // 56 //
There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because of the contradiction between restriction and non-restriction, and because there is restriction even in the case of non-restriction.

In the term "niyama" (restriction), there is the permission of an object; in "aniyama" (non-restriction), there is its prohibition. Because there is a contradiction between what is permitted and what is prohibited, they do not constitute the same thing.
Furthermore, "aniyama" is not "niyama" because of its lack of necessity.
In this case, the existence of the object as such is not being prohibited; rather, what is it?
Since an object of such a nature, when expressed by the word "restriction" (niyama), is indeed restricted, the word "restriction" itself is appropriate.
Thus, this negation does not apply to the case where there is non-restriction within a restriction. // 57 //
And this production of phonetic modification does not arise from transformation (*pariṇāma*) or from the relation of cause and effect; what then?

[Nyāyasūtra 2.2.58: But the modifications of phonemes result from the occurrence of another quality (*guṇāntarāpatti*), suppression (*upamarda*), decrease (*hrāsa*), increase (*vṛddhi*), diminution (*leśa*), and conjunction (*śleṣa*).

The meaning of the term "modification" (*vikāra*) consists in the employment [of a substitute] in place of that which is not employed due to the relationship between the original and the substitute; this is divided as follows: (1) the attainment of different qualities (*guṇāntarāpatti*), such as an acute vowel becoming grave, and so forth;
(2) "suppression" (*upamarda*), which is the emergence of another form upon the cessation of a single form, i.e., diminution (*hrāsa*).
The short vowel for a long one is *vṛddhi*;
the long vowel for a short one, or the protracted (*pluta*) vowel for both of those, is *leśa*.
*Lāghava* is a modification (*vikāra*) of the root *as*, meaning "it exists" (*astaḥ*); it is *śleṣa*.
The augment (āgama) belongs either to the base (prakṛti) or to the suffix (pratyaya);
these very [elements] are the specific modifications (vikāra), and these very [elements] are the substitutes (ādeśa). If these are indeed modifications...
Therefore, it follows that there are modifications of phonemes. // 58 //
Those [phonemes], ending in an inflectional suffix, constitute a word (pada).
According to their appearance, modified phonemes ending in case-terminations (vibhakti) receive the designation "word" (pada).
Case-termination is twofold: nominal and verbal; examples are "brāhmaṇaḥ" and "pacati."
In that case, prefixes and particles would not have the designation "pada," and another rule would have to be stated; yet, indeed,
the elision of the nominal case-ending after those two [prefixes and particles] following an indeclinable is taught.
"For the sake of the designation 'word'" means that the purpose is the comprehension of meaning through a word. // 59 //
An examination concerning the word as a name: "cow" is indeed a word. This is the example;
[now for] its referent.
Nyāyasūtra 2.2.60: There is doubt because of the figurative application [of a word] when the individual, the configuration, and the genus are present together.

Proximity (*saṃnidhi*) is the occurrence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); [the word] "cow" [is applied] to individuals, configurations, and universals that exist through inseparable connection.
In that case, it is applied, yet it is not known whether it refers to any one particular category of object or to all of them. // 60 //

The determination of the meaning of a word follows from the capacity of its usage; therefore—Nyāyasūtra 2.2.61: Because of the application [of terms] such as collection, abandonment, acceptance, number, increase, decrease, color, compound, and connection to the individual (vyakti), the individual is [the meaning].
The individual is the meaning of a word; why?
Because words such as "yā" (she) and others are applied metaphorically to the individual.
Metaphorical application (*upacāra*) is usage,
such as "the cow that stands" or "the cow that sits.
Surely this sentence does not denote the universal (*jāti*), because there is no difference [between the individual and the universal].
But because of differentiation, it denotes a substance;

for instance, in the expression "a collection of cows" (*gavāṃ samūhaḥ*), there is a denotation of a substance due to differentiation, not of a genus (*jāti*)—because there is no differentiation [in the genus].

In the case of "he gives a cow to the physician," it is the substance that is relinquished, not the genus—because the genus is formless (*amūrta*) and because neither succession nor non-succession is possible for it.

Possession (*parigraha*) is the connection with the status of ownership, as in "Kauṇḍinya’s cow" or "the Brāhmaṇa’s cow. Since the substance is denoted, there is a difference in the relationship due to the difference in the substances.
Thus it is established. As for the claim that "the genus (*jāti*) is indivisible," [it is argued that] number—such as "ten cows" or "twenty cows"—is applied to distinct substances;
it is not applied to the genus, because the genus is non-distinct. This is the point regarding increase (*vṛddhi*).
The accumulation of parts in a substance possessing causes is expressed as "the cow grew"; however, since a genus (jāti) is partless, by this [same principle], its diminution [is also excluded].
It has been explained that color— such as "the cow is white" or "the cow is tawny"—
is a connection with a quality (guṇa) of a substance (dravya), not of a universal (sāmānya).

The compound is: "beneficial for cattle" (*go-hita*) or "happiness for cattle" (*go-sukha*); this indicates that the connection with happiness and so forth belongs to the individual substance (*dravya*), not to the genus (*jāti*).
This is the *anubandha*.

The continuity of procreation with a similar form— such as "a cow produces a cow"— is appropriate in the case of a substance because it possesses the property of arising; it is not so in the case of a genus, for the opposite is true.
For substance and individuality are not different things. // 61 //
The refutation of this [position] is as follows:
NyS 2.2.62: No, because that would lead to an infinite regress.
The individual is not the word-meaning; why?
Because of the lack of finality, since it is that which is qualified by [words] such as "this" (*ayam*).

That which is the meaning of the word "cow"—as in "the cow that stands" or "the cow that sits"—is not denoted as a mere substance devoid of generality (*jāti*); what then? It is denoted as qualified by generality. Therefore, the individual (*vyakti*) is not the word-meaning.
In this same way, it should be understood regarding collections and so forth. // 62 //
If the individual is not the meaning of the word, how then is there a metaphorical application (upacāra) to the individual? [The answer is:
due to a cause, even when it is not that thing.
Indeed, such metaphorical usage is observed:

Nyāyasūtra 2.2.63: "Metaphorical usage occurs—despite the absence of the actual identity—with respect to a Brāhmaṇa, a bed, a mat, a king, barley-flour, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cart, food, and a man, due to association, location, purpose, function, measure, support, proximity, connection, instrumentality, and sovereignty."
"Even in the absence of that [nature], there is a metaphorical designation of it" means that a word not denoting that [object] is expressed by that very word due to association (*sahacaraṇāt*).
Just as in the expression "feed the staff," the term refers to the Brahmin who is associated with the staff,
so too [the meaning is understood] from position— as in "the platforms [are crying]."
Those staying on the bed are designated as "coughing" because they exist for that purpose—
just as when the *vīraṇa* grass intended for a mat is being arranged, one says, "he is making a mat."
From conduct— meaning it behaves in the same manner as [the statements] "Yama is king" or "Kubera is king";
from measurement— by means of an *āḍhaka*.
"Measured": as in "a measure of barley flour" (*āḍhakaṃ saktavaḥ*), because it is weighed; "held": as in "a *tulā* of sandalwood," because it is held by a scale;
"by proximity": as in "the cows are grazing on the Ganges."
A proximate object is denoted by way of association (*yoga*):
for example, a cart-yoke (*śākaṭa*) joined with black dye (*rāga*) is called "black" (*kṛṣṇa*).
It is denoted by way of being an instrument (*sādhana*): as in "food is life" (*annaṃ prāṇāḥ*).
By way of predominance—[it is said]: "This person belongs to this family," "This person belongs to this lineage.
In that regard, this...
A genus-word is applied to an individual either through association or through conjunction. // 63 //
If the individual is not the meaning of the word "cow," then let it be so:
NyS 2.2.64: The configuration (ākṛti) [is the meaning], because the establishment of the existence [of an individual] depends upon it.
The generic form (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of a word; why? Because the establishment of the existence of a substance is achieved through dependence upon the word.

The generic form is the fixed arrangement of the parts of a substance and their own constituent parts; when that [arrangement] is perceived, the establishment of the existence of the substance occurs.

It is established [in cognition] as "this is a cow" or "this is a horse. It is not [established] when [the universal] is not being apprehended. That from whose apprehension the determination of existence is established, that is what the word is capable of denoting;
that is its meaning.

This is not tenable: that which is connected with a genus (*jāti*) is designated here as "qualified by the genus," namely, "cow. Now, the connection with the genus does not belong to the mere arrangement of parts;
rather, it belongs to the substance (*dravya*) whose arrangement of parts is fixed.
Therefore, the generic form (ākṛti) is not the meaning of a word. // 64 //

Let it be, then, that the universal (jāti) is the meaning of a word—because, even though [the term] applies to both the individual and the configuration, sprinkling and other such rites would not [inappropriately] apply to a clay elephant; therefore, it is the universal.
The universal (jāti) is the meaning of the word; why?
Because [the word "cow" applies] even to a clay cow, which possesses neither individuality (vyakti) nor form (ākṛti).
"Because [actions] such as sprinkling would not apply"—that is to say, the commands "Sprinkle the cow," "Bring the cow," and "Give the cow" are not applied to a clay cow. Why?
Because of the absence of the universal (jāti).
For in that case there is both the individual (vyakti) and the form (ākṛti); that absence of which results in the lack of comprehension [of the object] is the meaning of the word (padārtha). // 65 //
NyS 2.2.66: No, because the manifestation of the universal depends upon the form and the individual.
The manifestation of the genus depends upon both the form and the individual;
for when neither the form nor the individual is perceived, the genus alone [is not perceived].
Therefore, only the pure [form] is apprehended; thus, the universal (jāti) is not the word-meaning. // 66 //
Indeed, it is not possible for there to be no category of object (padārtha). What, then, is this category of object?
But the individual, the configuration, and the genus are the referents of a word.

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of specification; what is specified? That the status of being a constituent element (*padārthatva*) belongs to the relationship between the primary and the subsidiary (*pradhānāṅgabhāva*) without restriction. For when there is a desire to express distinction and a comprehension of specific details, [this status applies].

In that case, the individual (vyakti) is primary, while the genus (jāti) and the configuration (ākṛti) are subordinate. But when the distinction is not intended to be expressed and there is a comprehension of the universal (sāmānya), then the genus is primary, while the individual and the configuration are subordinate; such is this [case].
It is predominant in the applications; however, the primary status of the generic form (ākṛti) is to be inferred. // 67 //
But how, then, is it known that there are distinct individuals (*vyakti*), forms (*ākṛti*), and universals (*jāti*)?
It is because of the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*);
in this regard, first of all—
Manifestation is a corporeal form that serves as the substratum for specific qualities.
It is called a "manifest" (*vyakti*) because it is manifested. It is that which is perceptible by the sense organs. Not every substance is a manifest;
rather, [it is that] in which there are specific qualities ending with touch, as well as gravity, density, fluidity, and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Matter (*mūrti*) is that substance which, as the case may be, is the substratum of non-pervasive dimension, because its constituent parts are congealed (*mūrchita*). // 68 //
The generic form (ākṛti) is that which expresses the genus (jāti) and its characteristic marks (liṅga).

One should understand that *ākṛti* (form) is that by which genus and the characteristics of genus are manifested; and it is nothing other than the fixed arrangement of the parts of a being and their constituent parts.
Indeed, the limbs of a living being, when arranged in their fixed configuration, constitute the mark of the genus; for one infers that it is a cow by means of its head or its foot.
And when the arrangement of the parts of a being is fixed, "cowness" (gotva) becomes manifest;
this refers to a universal that is not manifested by a configuration (ākṛti).
In cases such as "dead," "gold," and "silver," the generic form (ākṛti) ceases; that is, it loses its status as the primary meaning of the word. // 69 //
Genus (jāti) has as its nature the production of similar [cognitions].
That which produces a uniform cognition with respect to diverse substrates,
by virtue of which many things do not exclude one another— that object which is the cause for the recurrence of a single notion across multiple instances is the universal (sāmānya).
And that which effects non-difference for some things and difference for others is the universal-particular, which is the genus (jāti). // 70 //
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the second chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
And the second chapter is completed.

Now, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* with its commentary (*vṛtti*), the first section of the third chapter: The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have been examined; the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) are now to be examined. Since that [set of objects] begins with the self (*ātman*), the self is now being analyzed: Is the self merely an aggregate of body, sense organs, mind, intellect, and feelings, or is it something distinct from those?
Whence arises this doubt?
Because the designation [of agency] is established in two ways.

Designation is the expression of the relationship between the action and the instrument with the agent; it is of two kinds: that of a part [representing] the whole, as in "the tree stands by its roots" or "the palace is supported by its pillars."

There is the designation of one thing by means of another—as in "he cuts with an axe" or "he sees with a lamp"—and this designation exists here as well: "one sees with the eye," "one cognizes with the mind," "one deliberates with the intellect," and "one experiences pleasure and pain with the body.
In this regard, it is not determined whether [the action belongs] to the whole by means of its part.
Is it of the aggregate consisting of the body and so forth? Or is it of one thing by means of another distinct from it?
That is to say, of something other than that [aggregate]?
This designation of one thing by means of another—why is this so?
Because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.1)

Whatever object is grasped by sight is also grasped by touch—thinking, "This very thing which I saw with my eye, I now touch with my sense of touch," or "This which I touched with my sense of touch, I now see with my eye. These two cognitions, having the same object and the same agent, are unified; they do not have a composite [body] as their agent, nor do they have the sense organ alone as their agent.

Therefore, that entity which synthesizes two cognitions—each having a different cause, each produced by no other agent, and each having the same object—as the grasper of a single object through both the eye and the sense of touch, must be distinct from the objects themselves.
But how is it not produced by a single agent through the senses?

Indeed, a sense organ is capable of synthesizing its own respective grasping of an object when produced by no other agent, but it is not capable of synthesizing the grasping of an object belonging to another sense organ.

How is it that [cognition] is not produced by a composite? Indeed, this single person experiences two cognitions—each having a distinct cause and each having itself as its agent—conjoined together; it is not the composite that does so. Why?
Because within the composite, there is no conjunction of the individual apprehensions of different objects, just as there is none between different sense organs. // 1 //
NyS 3.1.2: No, because of the fixed determination of objects.
There is no conscious being other than the aggregate of the body and so forth; why?
Because of the fixed determination of objects.

The sense organs have fixed objects: when the eye is absent, form is not perceived, and when it is present, it is perceived. And that which does not occur when something else is absent, but [does occur] when it is present...
It is understood that "it belongs to him";
therefore, the apprehension of form is the function of the eye, such that "the eye sees the form," and the same applies to the nose and the other sense organs as well.
These sense organs are conscious because they grasp their respective objects; for the grasping of objects occurs in such a manner depending on the presence or absence of the senses.
This being so, what need is there for another conscious entity?
This is not a valid reason because it is doubtful.

As for this fact that the perception of objects occurs only when the sense organs exist and not when they do not: is this due to their being conscious, or rather because they are instruments of consciousness serving as the cause of perception?
Thus it is doubted;
for even though the sense organs are instruments of the conscious being, they ought to exist because they serve as the cause of perception. // 2 //
As for what was stated— "Because of the determination of objects" (NyS 3.1.3)—
there is no refutation [of the self] because the existence of the self is established precisely by that very determination.
If indeed a single sense organ were all-knowing, having an unrestricted range of objects and being the conscious perceiver of all objects, who could then infer any other conscious being? However,
since the sense organs have restricted ranges of objects, therefore there exists a conscious being, distinct from them, who is all-knowing.
The grasper of all objects, who transcends the fixed arrangement of objects, is inferred;

in this regard, this recognition—which cannot be denied—is cited as an instance of the activity of consciousness: indeed, one who perceives a form infers a previously perceived taste or smell, and one who discerns a smell infers a form or a taste. Thus...
The same should be stated regarding the remaining objects as well:

having seen a form, one smells a fragrance; and having smelled a fragrance, one sees a form. Thus, this apprehension of all objects, which occurs through an indefinite succession of moments, has a single conscious substrate as its locus and no other agent.
It synthesizes perception, inference, scripture, doubt, and various cognitions of diverse objects, attributing them to its own self as the agent; having synthesized them, it experiences them.

Furthermore, one encounters a treatise whose scope encompasses all objects. Having heard the phonemes—which do not constitute a single object for the ear—arising in succession, and having synthesized them into the state of words and sentences, one understands the established relationship between word and meaning. This collection of objects, which consists of many things that cannot be grasped by a single sense organ at once, constitutes the range of the omniscient one's knowledge;
it is impossible to traverse this systematic arrangement of the knowable step by step.
However, it was merely the form that was brought forward;
therefore, what was stated—namely, "If the senses themselves possess consciousness, what is the need for another conscious being?"—is incorrect. // 3 //
For this reason as well, the self is distinct from the body and so forth, and is not merely the aggregate of the body and its constituents:
because there is no sin when the body is burned. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.4)
By the term "taking up a body" (*śarīragrahaṇa*), a living being consisting of an aggregate of body, sense organs, intellect, and sensations is meant.

For one who burns a living body, the sin committed through the injury of a living being is called a transgression (*pātaka*). Its non-existence [is asserted] because the agent has no connection with its fruit, while the non-agent has a connection with it.
Indeed, within the continuum of body, sense organs, intellect, and sensations, one aggregate arises and another ceases.

The continuity consisting of the sequence of arising and ceasing does not contradict [the doctrine of] non-otherness, because it is the locus of otherness in the case of the aggregate of the body and so forth.
For this [continuity] is perceived as having otherness as its locus;

such being the case, that living being who performs an act of violence within the aggregate of the body and so forth is not connected with the fruit of that violence, and he who is connected with the fruit did not perform the violence.

Thus, if there were such a distinction of sentient beings, it would follow that there is the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done; and if there were the arising and cessation of sentient beings, the creation of beings would result in being without the cause of karma, in which case the practice of celibacy for the sake of liberation would be purposeless. Furthermore, if a "sentient being" were merely the aggregate of the body and so forth, there would be no sin in burning a corpse, and this is an undesirable consequence. Therefore, the self is eternal and distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth.
NyS 3.1.5: Its absence [is established] even when that which possesses a self is burned, because of its eternity.
Even for one whose body is burned while being possessed of a permanent self (*ātman*), there would be no sin of killing for the burner; why?
Because the self is permanent;
for no one can ever harm that which is permanent.
Now, if it is destroyed, its eternity does not exist; thus, in one case this violence is fruitless, while in the other it is untenable. // 5 //
Not so, because of the destruction of the effect, its substratum, and the agent.

We do not say that violence (*hiṃsā*) is the killing of an eternal sentient being; rather, for a sentient being whose nature is indestructible, violence is the injury, affliction, or impairment characterized by deficiency, or the destruction of the continuity—consisting of the body which is the locus of activity and the sense organs which are the agents of the perception of their respective objects.
This is what constitutes "killing" (*vadha*).
The effect, however, is the experience of pleasure and pain; its locus (*āyatana*) is its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The support (*āśraya*) is the body. [This refers to] the body, which is the support of the effect.
Furthermore, injury (hiṃsā) is the destruction of the sense organs, which are the agents of the perception of their respective objects, and not of the eternal self;
regarding this, it has been said:
“Their non-existence [follows] even when that which possesses a self is burned, because of its eternity”—
this is incorrect.
For one for whom violence is the destruction of the *sattva*, there is the fault of the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.

And this must be the extent of the matter: either violence is the destruction of a sentient being (*sattva*), or it is the killing of the agent who is the substratum of action for a sentient being whose nature is indestructible. There is no other possibility. Since the destruction of a sentient being is prohibited, what else remains there?
"According to reality" (yathābhūtam); or alternatively, [it refers to] "the destruction of the support of the effect and the agent," where "the support of the effect" (kāryāśraya) is [meant].
The aggregate of body, sense-faculties, and intellect belongs to the eternal self;
therein lies the experience of pleasure and pain, which is its locus and support.

That which is the basis of sensation is not other than that [the self]; thus, it is the self alone that is the agent—for the production of the experience of pleasure and pain has that as its cause, and does not occur without it.
Its "killing" is its injury.

For violence (*hiṃsā*) consists in causing pain or destruction, not in the annihilation of the eternal self (*ātman*); therefore, as for what was stated—"The absence [of that] occurs even when that which possesses a self is burned, because it is eternal"—that is not so. // 6 //
For this reason as well, the self is distinct from the body and so forth:
because of the recognition by one [eye] of what was seen by the other. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.7)

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the connecting cognition (*pratisaṃdhijñāna*) between two preceding and succeeding cognitions regarding the same object— for example: "I see now that very same thing which I previously knew," or "This object is that very same one."
Thus, because there is recognition by the other eye of what was seen with the left eye— namely, "I see now that very same thing which I saw"—
if the senses were conscious, one [sense] could not perceive what was seen by another.
Recognition occurs as "I recognize"; thus, recognition is established.
Indeed, this recognition exists; therefore, the conscious being is distinct from the sense organs. // 7 //
It is not so, because there is a misconception of duality regarding what is obstructed by the single nasal bone.
This eye is one, situated in the middle and separated by the bone of the nose; its two ends, when perceived,
give rise to the misconception of duality in that which is actually separated in the middle.
As if of something long. // 8 //
NyS 3.1.9: There is no oneness [of the two], because when one is destroyed, the second is not destroyed.
When one eye is impaired or removed, the second eye remains as the means for perceiving objects; therefore, it is impossible for one [eye] to be obstructed. // 9 //
Even when the parts have perished, the whole is still perceived; therefore, [the opponent's reason] is not a valid proof.
“The non-destruction of the second [moment] because of the destruction of the first” is not a valid reason; why?
For when some branches of a tree have been cut off, the tree is still indeed perceived. // 10 //
NyS 3.1.11: There is no refutation [of our position] because it contradicts the illustrative example.
When the constituent substance is divided, the effect-substance does not remain,
because that would entail the consequence of its being eternal; [this applies] to whichever [effect] among the many composite wholes.

Those things whose causes are divided undergo destruction, while those whose causes are not divided remain stable. Alternatively, there is a contradiction with observed facts and a contradiction with illustrative examples.

For in the skull of a dead person, two cavities are perceived distinctly in the location of the eyes, separated by the bone of the nose; and this is not possible if there were only one [cavity] separated by the bone of the nose.

Moreover, because the destruction of one [obscuration] is not necessarily concomitant with the other, these two objects are inferred to be distinct, as they constitute separate impairments of the obscurations;
this is also evident from the suppression of one.

Due to the difference in the contact between the ray of the eye and its object, a difference in the perceived object is apprehended as if it were real; this is contradicted by the fact that [the object] is one.
Furthermore, when the pressure is removed, there is a recognition of non-difference.
Therefore, it is impossible for a single entity to be obstructed. // 11 //
And this conscious being is inferred to be distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth— Nyāyasūtra 3.1.12: because of the transformation of another sense organ.

When the color or odor of a certain sour fruit, which has been previously grasped together with its taste, is perceived by some sense organ, there occurs a modification of another sense organ, namely the tongue,
which is prompted by the memory of the taste and the longing for that taste.
Since [the body] is composed of the dissolution of teeth and fluids, it is untenable for it to possess the consciousness of the senses—
for one person does not remember what was seen by another.
NyS 3.1.13: No, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered.
The dharma called memory arises from a sign; its object is that which is to be remembered, and the modification of another sense organ caused by it is not produced by a self. // 13 //
NyS 3.1.14: There is no refutation [of the self] because of the existence of its qualities within the self.
If it exists as a quality of the self, there is no refutation of the self:
if memory is indeed a quality of the self, then memory is logically established— since one person does not remember what was seen by another.
If the senses were sentient,
there would be no synthesis of the apprehensions of objects performed by various agents; or, if such synthesis did occur, the distinct determination of specific objects would be impossible.
But a single conscious being, perceiving multiple objects and possessing distinct causal conditions, remembers an object previously perceived;
this is because of the synthesis of perceptions by that single perceiver of multiple objects.
If memory were a quality of the self, it would exist [only when the self is present]; in the opposite case, its occurrence would be impossible;
for all living beings, every instance of memory has a basis.
These are the conventional usages.
The modification of another sense-organ is merely an example of the mark of the self. // 14 //
And because the object of memory cannot be enumerated.
And without enumerating [all] objects of memory, this is stated:
"No, because memory has as its object that which is to be remembered. (NS 4.2.36)
Thus, this memory which occurs when an object is no longer being perceived— namely, "I knew that object"— has as its object an object previously known as qualified by a knower and a cognition,
and not the mere object alone. [It is expressed as] "I have known that object."
"I have known this object" (3), and "I had knowledge regarding this object" (4). These four types of statements are equivalent in meaning, as they indicate knowledge whose object is memory.
Indeed, in all cases, the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge are apprehended. Now,
when there is a memory regarding a perceptible object, by means of that memory, three cognitions having a single agent are connected with respect to one and the same object.

They are neither produced by multiple agents nor are they without an agent; rather, they have a single agent. [The statement] "I saw that very object which I see now"—the word "saw" refers both to the act of seeing and to the consciousness of seeing.

Indeed, if the appearance of sweat were not perceived, there would be no thought, "I have seen it. These two are indeed cognitions; "I see this very thing now" is the third cognition. Thus, a single object is associated with three cognitions.
It is not without an agent, nor does it have multiple agents;
rather, it has a single agent. Thus, this object of memory is not being enumerated.
An object that exists and is known is being negated—namely, "there is no self"—on the grounds that "memory has as its object that which is to be remembered.
And this [memory] is not merely memory, nor does it have merely that which is to be remembered as its object; this...
Indeed, the reconnection of memory is like the reconnection of cognition;
because a single [subject] has all things as its object—this single knower, having all things as its object, reconnects its own cognitions: "I shall know this object," "this object..."

"I cognize" means "I have known this object"; having desired to know this object for a long time but not having known it, one determines—"I have known it. In this same way, one also [cognizes] memory as qualified by the three times.
And he connects [the memory] with that which is distinguished by the desire to remember.
If, however, a sentient being were merely a continuum of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), then as those formative forces arise again and again, they would vanish;
there would not be even a single formative force that is distinguished by the three times.
One would experience both knowledge and memory; and without such experience,
the synthesis of knowledge and memory— as well as the notions "I" and "mine"—
would not arise, just as they do not in the case of another body.
From this it is inferred: there exists a single [self] whose object is everything, which, in each body, possesses its own continuous stream of cognition.
And it reconnects the continuum of memory; for one whose activity does not persist in other bodies, such reconnection does not occur. // 15 //
Not so, because the reasons for establishing the self are present in the mind.
The self is not distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth; why?
Because the means for the cognition of the self reside in the mind.

"From the possibility [of such reasons]" means the possibility in the mind of those reasons that establish the self (*ātman*), such as: "Because one perceives a single object through both seeing and touching," and so forth; for the mind...
For [the self] has all things as its object;
therefore, there is no self distinct from the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect. // 16 //
NyS 3.1.17: Since the means of knowledge are established for the knower, there is merely a difference in terminology.
Indeed, instruments of knowledge are appropriate for a knower—
as in, "one sees with the eye," "one smells with the nose," and "with the sense of touch."
In this way, for one who thinks, there exists an instrument of cognition (*matisādhana*) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

which has all things as its object, by means of which he thinks; such being the case, while the designation "knower" (*jñātṛ*) for the self (*ātman*) is not accepted, the designation "mind" (*manaḥ*) is permitted.

And while the notion of "mind" (*manas*) regarding the mind is not tolerated, the notion of "means of cognition" (*matisādhana*) is tolerated; thus, this is merely a difference in terminology, and there is no dispute regarding the actual object.
Alternatively, if it were denied, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of all the sense faculties.
Or, if the means of cognition for an omniscient person—the one who knows all objects—is itself denied, saying "it does not exist," then [the following applies]. Thus:
Since even the means for apprehending form and so forth would not exist, it follows that there would be the total abolition of all the sense faculties. // 17 //
And restriction is without inferential proof.
This restriction which is asserted—
that while this [self] possesses the means for apprehending form and so forth, it lacks a means of cognition whose object is everything— is a restriction that is devoid of inference.
There is no inference here by which we might apprehend such a necessity;
furthermore, pleasure and the like are objects distinct from color-form and so forth, and thus there exists another instrument for their perception.
Just as smell is not perceived by the eye, and thus the nose is a distinct instrument, so too taste is not perceived by the eye or the nose, and thus the tongue is a distinct instrument.

The same applies to the remaining [senses]; likewise, since pleasure and so forth are not perceived by the eyes and other [senses], there must be another instrument for that [perception], and that is...
The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the inferential mark;
and that which is the instrument for the apprehension of pleasure and so forth is also the inferential mark for the non-simultaneity of cognitions.
