Because his sense-faculties are sometimes in proximity and sometimes not in proximity to their respective objects, cognitions do not arise simultaneously; regarding this, it has been said:
“The [objection] that ‘because the causes for the realization of a self are present in the mind’ (verse 16) is incorrect. (verse 18)
But is this [self] distinct from the aggregate of the body and so forth, and is it eternal? Or is it non-eternal?
Whence arises this doubt?
The doubt arises because it is observed in both ways.
That which exists is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal;
for even when the existence of the self has been established, doubt does not cease.
By the very same reasons that establish the existence of the self, its persistence prior to the differentiation of bodies is also proven.
Established: It persists even after the dissolution of the body.
Why?
Because of the continuity of memories practiced in a previous life, there is the manifestation of joy, fear, and grief in one who has been born [again]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.19)
Indeed, this prince was born in this life with joy, fear, and sorrow, even though the causes of joy, fear, and sorrow had not yet been grasped.
One proceeds by means of the inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the objects to be inferred;
and these arise from the continuity of memory, not otherwise. Furthermore, the continuity of memory does not exist without prior practice.

It does not exist [without a cause]. Furthermore, since prior practice occurs only when there was a previous birth and not otherwise, this is established: that this [consciousness] persists after [and before] the dissolution of the body. // 19 //
NyS 3.1.20: Its modification is like the modifications of opening and closing found in lotuses and other such things.
Just as in the case of lotuses and the like, which are impermanent, there occurs the transformation of opening and closing.
Thus, for an impermanent self, the occurrence of joy, fear, and sorrow would constitute a modification.
This is untenable due to the absence of a reason;
for by this reason, just as there are changes of opening and closing in lotuses and the like,
there would be the occurrence of joy and so forth in a non-eternal self.
In this case, there is no proof of the probandum through the similarity of the example,
nor is there any through dissimilarity,
because of the absence of a reason (hetu).
That which has an unconnected meaning is called "meaningless" (apārthaka).
Furthermore, from the example [of worldly experience], there is no cessation of the causes of joy and so forth;
and as for this [craving] regarding objects that have been indulged in...

The internal apprehension of joy and so forth, produced by the continuity of memory, is grasped by each individual; this is not negated by the analogy of the closing of the lotus and other flowers. And just as this [apprehension] is not negated, so too—
"Even for one just born":
the arising of action consists in the disjunction and conjunction of the petals [of the lotus] during its opening and closing; and the cause of that action is to be inferred from the action itself.
And this being so, what is being refuted by means of an example? // 20 //

Now, if it is held that just as there is the modification of opening and closing in lotuses and the like even without a [conscious] cause, so too is there the experience of joy and so forth for the self; and that—
NyS 3.1.21: [The earth] is not [composed of the five elements], because the modifications consisting of the five [elements] have as their causes the seasons characterized by heat, cold, and rain.

Since [the lotus and other plants] exist when heat and so forth are present and do not exist when they are absent, their transformations—namely, opening and closing—are caused by those [factors]; they are not produced by the favor of the five elements.
Thus, they are not without cause.
In this way, transformations such as joy and the like must arise from a cause and not without a cause;
and there is no other cause than the persistence of the memory of what was practiced in a previous life.
Nor can there be an inference regarding the causes of the soul's arising and cessation,
because no illustrative example exists;
for joy and the like do not arise without a cause.
Nor is there the assumption of another cause for joy and so forth, as there is for heat and the like; therefore, this [objection] is untenable. // 21 //
For this reason also the self is eternal:
because of the longing for breast-milk produced by the habituation to food after passing away [from a previous life]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.22)
In a newborn calf, a desire for breast milk is observed through the sign of its activity; and this cannot exist without a prior habituation to food.
By what reasoning?
For it is seen that among embodied beings who are afflicted by hunger, [the desire for food arises] from the habituation to food.
The desire for food arises from a continuous stream of memory;
and this is not possible for one who has just been born without the prior habituation of a previous body.
From this it is inferred that there was a previous body in which he practiced taking food; indeed,
this self, having departed from its former body, has entered another body.
Afflicted by hunger and recollecting food experienced in a previous life,
one longs for breast milk; therefore, the self does not cease with the dissolution of the body.
It is indeed split and rises upward after the dissolution of the body. // 22 //
Its movement toward that [object] is like the movement of iron toward a magnet.
Just as iron approaches a magnet without prior practice, so too does an infant desire breast milk without prior practice regarding food. // 23 //
Is this approach of iron toward the magnet without a cause,
or is it due to a cause?
First, it is without a cause—
NyS 3.1.24: No, because there would be an absence of activity elsewhere.
If it were without a cause,
even clods of earth and the like would approach the magnet;
for there is never any cause for such a restriction.
Now, if it is from a sign (*nimitta*), by what is that perceived? It is perceived through the mark of action (*kriyāliṅga*).
The cause of activity is the mark of the restriction of activity; it is the cause for the restriction of activity, by which there is an absence of engagement elsewhere.
Even in the case of a child, there is a restricted approach [to the mother].

An action is perceived; and the sign of the desire for milk is not established by an example as being caused by anything other than the continuity of memory produced by previous habituation to food. Nor does [the action] exist in the absence of a cause.
The arising of something for someone is not observed; an example does not subvert a perceived cause of desire,
therefore the movement of iron toward a magnet is not a valid example.
Furthermore, iron indeed does not move elsewhere;
iron never approaches a clod of earth. What is the cause of this?
What is this "restriction"?
If it is due to the restriction of causes, then that [restriction] has the restriction of actions as its mark.
In this way, even for an infant, a desire directed toward a specific object must arise from a restriction of its causes,
and that cause is the recollection of what has been previously experienced.
The phrase "on another occasion" (anyedyus) qualifies it by means of what is observed;
for it is observed that among embodied beings, the desire for food arises from the recollection of what was practiced [in the past]. // 24 //
For this reason as well, the self is eternal; why?
Because no birth is observed for one who is free from passion. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.25)
It follows by implication that one is born with passion;
this one being born is born permeated by passion. [This] is the recollection of objects previously experienced by passion.

The womb. Furthermore, the prior experience of objects would not be possible without a body in a previous birth. Thus, this self, recollecting the objects experienced in a previous body, [enters the womb].
One takes delight in various things. Thus, there is this linking of two births,
and likewise, the previous body with what preceded it.

By the statement "of a previous body by a more previous one," and so forth, it is established that the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless, and the persistence of attachment is also beginningless; thus, its permanence is proven. // 25 //

But how is it known that the passion of one who is born is produced by the recollection of previously experienced objects, and not— like the production of a substance with its qualities— the simultaneous production [of both the object and the passion]? NyS 3.1.26.

Just as the qualities of a substance subject to origination arise from a cause, so too does passion arise from something for a self subject to origination. Herein, this restatement of what has been said is for the purpose of illustration. // 26 //
NyS 3.1.27: No, because passion and the like have conceptualization as their cause.
Indeed, the arising of the self and of passion is not like the arising of a substance possessing qualities.
Why? Because passion and the other [afflictions] have conceptualization as their cause.

Indeed, this disease born of conceptual construction (saṃkalpa) is apprehended in living beings who indulge in sense objects. And conceptual construction has its source in the recollection of previously experienced objects; therefore, it is inferred as follows:
Even for one who has been born, passion arises from reflecting upon objects previously experienced; however,
since the self is the locus of its arising, the production of passion must be explained as occurring through volition when another cause of passion is present.
Like a product possessing substance and qualities,
the production of a self is not established, nor is there any cause for passion other than volition.
Therefore, it is incorrect to say:
"The production of those two is like the production of a substance possessing qualities.
Furthermore:
Even if one were to admit that, apart from volition, there is another cause for attachment— an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized as merit and demerit—
nevertheless, the connection with a previous body cannot be denied;
for its manifestation occurs therein, not in this present birth.
"Passion arises from being absorbed in that [object].
Indeed, this repeated practice regarding an object is the cause of cultivation; it is called "being absorbed in that."
And because there is a distinction in birth, there is a distinction in passion;
for indeed, it is karma that brings about this distinction in birth.
The designation [of desire] by that term is understood through identity;
therefore, it is untenable to say that there is a cause for passion other than volition. // 27 //

It has been stated that the connection of the conscious principle with a body is beginningless. Furthermore, its body—which is the locus of pleasure and pain—is caused by its own previously performed karma; that [body] is now examined:
is it composed of a single material cause, like the sense of smell and the other organs?
Or is it of diverse natures?
Why is there this doubt?
The doubt arises from conflicting views.
They assert that the elements, beginning with earth, through their various numerical combinations, constitute the nature of the body.
What, then, is the truth in this matter?
NyS 3.1.28: [Odor] belongs to earth, because other qualities are perceived [in it].
In this regard, the human body is composed of earth; why?
Because of the perception of a distinct quality: earth possesses smell, and the body likewise possesses smell, whereas water and the other elements are devoid of smell.

That [body] would be odorless by its very nature; however, this [body] is not produced from earth alone when it is uncombined with water and the other elements, but rather as the substratum for movement, the sense organs, and their objects.
It is thus conceived: when there is a conjunction of the five elements, the body comes into being;
for it is indeed the conjunction of the elements [that constitutes it].

It is not prohibited for these five to exist in mutual combination; thus, even in other worlds, there are bodies composed of water, fire, and air, and in those too, there is a conjunction of the elements.
Regarding the phrase "dependent on human effort":
even in the production of substances such as cloth and the like,
there is no doubt that production does not occur without the conjunction of [causes] such as threads.
"Consisting of earth, water, and fire—because its qualities are perceived"; "consisting of four elements—because inhalation and exhalation are perceived";
"consisting of five elements—because of fragrance, moisture, digestion, expansion, and the providing of space.
He disregarded these as fallacious reasons because they are doubtful.
The author of the Sūtras:
How are they doubtful?
[It is because] the state of being the base (prakṛtibhāva) exists.

The perception of the properties of the elements occurs when they are present, because there is no prohibition against their conjunction; for example, as in the case of water, fire, air, and space within a vessel.
Thus, this [object] has multiple elements as its constituent nature.

The body would be odorless, tasteless, formless, and intangible if it were to conform to its [material] nature; however, it is not of such a character, therefore it is earthen because other qualities [besides those of the elements] are perceived. // 28 //
And because of the authority of the sacred revelation (śruti).
In the mantra, “May your eye go to the sun,” the phrase “your body to the earth” is heard; this is the designation of the dissolution of the modification into its material cause.
In another mantra, “I preserve your eye for the sun,” the phrase “I preserve your body for the earth” is heard; this is the designation of the preservation of the modification by means of its cause.

Furthermore, since we observe that things of the same class (tulyajātīya) initiate a single effect in cases such as pots and the like, it is logically impossible for things of different classes (bhinnajātīya) to initiate a single effect. // 29 //
Now, the sense organs are investigated according to the sequence of the objects of knowledge: are they unevolved (avyaktika), or are they elemental (bhautika)?
How is doubt produced?
NS 3.1.30: Doubt arises because [the object] is perceived when the black pupil is present, and it is also perceived when [the pupil] is absent.
The black antelope skin is material; when it is unimpaired, there is perception of form, and when it is impaired, there is no perception.
However, an object situated apart from the black antelope skin is perceived, whereas one that has come into contact with the black antelope skin is not.
Furthermore, the sense organs do not function without reaching their objects.
This [object] is possible because it is non-material and all-pervading;
thus, due to the perception of these two contradictory properties, there is doubt. // 30 //
He says they are non-material;
why?
Because of the perception of both the large and the minute. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.31)
"Great" (mahat) means that which is perceived as larger or largest, such as a banyan tree, a mountain, and so forth. "Minute" (aṇu) means that which is grasped as smaller or smallest, such as...
The seed of a banyan tree and so forth—
both of these, being perceived, subvert the material nature of the eye; for whatever is material...
It pervades only to that extent; however, because it is non-material and all-pervasive by virtue of its omnipresence, it pervades everything. // 31 //
The non-materiality and omnipresence of the sense organs cannot be established merely by the grasping of large and small objects. Indeed, this is so:
"Because of a specific contact between the ray and the object, there is the perception of that [object]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.32)
The perception of those two large objects occurs due to a specific kind of contact between the ray of the eye and the object, just as it does for the ray of a lamp and its object;
and this contact between the ray and the object is indicated by the presence of an obstruction.
For the ray of the eye does not illuminate an object obstructed by walls and the like, just as the ray of a lamp [does not]. // 32 //
Since [the existence of an obstruction] would have to be inferred from that [non-perception], he says this:
"Because that is not perceived, it is not a valid reason" (NyS 3.1.33).
For fire, like color and touch,
would be perceived through direct perception— just like a lamp— if its visual ray were present, given that it possesses magnitude, consists of multiple substances, and possesses color.
It may be so. // 33 //
The non-perception by means of direct perception of that which is being inferred is not a valid reason for its non-existence.

The non-perception through direct observation of a ray of light— which is inferred by the mark of an obstruction intended to prevent its proximity— does not establish its non-existence, just as in the case of the far side of the moon or the lower part of the earth. // 34 //
And the difference in the means of apprehension arises from the distinction between the properties of substance and quality.

Indeed, this property of substance and this property of quality are distinct: a watery substance that is large, composed of many substances, and has detached parts is not perceived through direct perception, yet its cold touch is apprehended.
Due to the persistence of that substance, the winter and the cool season are brought about; likewise, a fiery substance of such a kind, with its form unmanifested,
is not perceived along with its color, yet its heat is perceived through touch.
Due to the persistence of that substance, summer and spring are established. // 35 //
But where this [perception] of them occurs—NyS 3.1.36:
The perception of color arises from its inherence in multiple substances and from a specific quality of color.
Where both form and substance, as well as its substratum, are perceived through direct perception,
yet the specific quality of form exists such that, due to its presence, form is perceived in some instances [and not others].
And because of the absence of which there is the non-perception of a substance in some cases, that property of form is designated as "manifested" (*udbhūta*);
and this [substance] possesses unmanifested form (*anudbhūtarūpa*).
The visual ray is not perceived through direct perception;
yet, a distinction in the properties of light is observed: light in which both form and touch are manifested is perceptible, as in the case of the rays of the sun.
Fire is perceptible when its color is manifest and its touch is unmanifest,
as in the case of the rays of a lamp.
That which has manifested touch but unmanifested color is imperceptible, such as fire in contact with water;
that which has unmanifested color and touch is imperceptible and invisible to the eye.
"Ray" (raśmi). // 36 //
The arrangement of the sense organs is brought about by karma and is dependent upon the purpose of the Puruṣa.
Just as the purpose of the conscious being is conceived as consisting in the perception of objects and the perception of pleasure and pain, so too are the sense organs arrayed.
Furthermore, there is the expansion of the visual ray for the purpose of reaching the object,
as well as the non-manifestation of its color and touch.
It exists for the purpose of establishing conventional usage;
and the occurrence of obstruction due to resistance against specific substances is likewise for the sake of conventional usage,
just as the manifold array of all substances is like that of the sense organs.
It is brought about by action and depends upon human effort;
for action, consisting of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), exists for the sake of the experience of the conscious being. // 37 //
And because it is non-deviant, the counter-argument is a property of material elements.

Furthermore, that resistance of a sense faculty toward a particular substance due to the perception of an obstruction is a property of derived matter (*bhautika-dharma*); it does not deviate from being elemental.
For nothing non-material has ever been observed to possess the property of resistance.
However, non-obstruction is inconclusive, because it is common to both material and immaterial things.
As for the view that the sense organs are material because they possess obstruction—

It follows that they are non-material because they are non-obstructive. Furthermore, non-obstruction is observed, since objects are perceived even when separated by glass, a layer of clouds, or crystal; therefore, that [position] is not tenable.
Why?
For even that which is material is not obstructed— such as the rays of a lamp when its light is separated by glass, a layer of clouds, or crystal.
There is no obstruction of the digestive fire within vessels and the like. // 38 //
And non-apprehension is possible due to a difference in causes:
like the non-apprehension of the light of a meteor at midday, there is its (the sound's) non-apprehension. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.39)

Just as perception occurs due to inherence in multiple substances and due to a specific quality of color, yet when the causes for perception are present, the light of a torch at midday is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun, so too [is the case here].
Since perception occurs due to the possession of many constituent substances and a specific quality of color,
when the causes for perception are present, the visual ray is not perceived because of some other cause.
And that has been explained: there is no perception by means of direct observation of a substance whose color and touch are unmanifest;
moreover, absolute non-perception is the cause of [the cognition of] absence. // 39 //
For one who says,
"The light of the clod of earth is not perceived at midday because it is overwhelmed by the light of the sun," this [objection] might apply to him:
Not so, because [the object] is not perceived even at night.
"Also [it is established] by means of inference from non-perception":
because of its absolute non-perception, the light of a clod of earth does not exist, but such is not the case for the visual ray. // 40 //
And this [non-perception] is logically consistent:
NS 3.1.41: Because the apprehension of an object occurs through the assistance of external light, there is non-apprehension due to its non-manifestation.
The eye, assisted by external light, is the grasper of its object;
in the absence of that [light], there is no perception, but when there is the assistance of light, [perception occurs].
And when there is the perception of color and touch, the substance which is their substratum is apprehended by the eye,
because the color is not manifest.
This non-perception of the substance that is the substratum of form is observed due to the non-manifestation of its form;
regarding this, what was stated— “Therefore, its non-perception is not a valid reason [for its non-existence]”— is refuted.
This is incorrect. // 41 //
Why, then,
is overpowering (*abhibhava*) not stated to be a cause for the non-perception of the visual ray?
And because [the sound] is overwhelmed when there is manifestation.
The word "and" (ca) signifies that [the object] is independent of the assistance of external light; that form which is manifested (*abhivyakta*),
emergent (*udbhūta*), and does not require the assistance of external light— that is the object of suppression (*abhibhava*).
In the opposite case, because there is no overpowering and because its form is unmanifest, it is not perceived; however, when aided by external light, it is perceived and thus is not overpowered.
Therefore, it is logically established that the visual ray exists. 42.
And because the rays from the eyes of nocturnal creatures are observed.
For the rays of the eyes of nocturnal wanderers, such as cats and the like, are indeed seen at night; therefore, there is an inference regarding the remaining [beings].
If it is argued that there is a difference in the sense organs just as there is a difference in species?
Furthermore, a mere differentiation of dharmas is untenable, because we observe that an obscuration has the purpose of negating attainment. // 43 //
The impossibility of the contact between the sense organ and its object being the cause of cognition; why?
Because there is perception of things separated by glass, clouds, films, or crystal, which occurs without [the sense organ] reaching [the object]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.44)
A substance such as grass that is moving is seen when obstructed by glass or a layer of clouds; it is perceived as if in close proximity, despite being separated [by the obstruction].
Indeed, perception is obstructed by an intervention; for if the contact between the ray and the object were the cause of apprehension,
then there would be no apprehension of what is screened, because there is no contact with that which is obstructed.
Furthermore, there is this perception of objects obstructed by glass, mica, or crystal; this will demonstrate that the sense organs function without reaching their objects (*aprāpyakārīṇi*).
For this very reason, they are non-material (*abhautikāni*); for functioning by reaching the object is indeed a property of material things.
Thus [ends verse] 44.
Nyāyasūtrabhāṣya 3.1.45: There is no refutation [of the argument] because of the non-perception of things obstructed by a wall.
If the sense organs functioned without reaching their objects, there would be no non-perception of an object obstructed by a wall. // 45 //
But even if [the sense organ] functions by reaching [its object],
how could there be the perception of things separated by glass, a layer of clouds, or crystal?
Because there is no resistance, the occurrence of contact is possible.
Neither glass nor a layer of clouds obstructs the visual ray;
being unimpeded, it approaches its object.
And as for the one who thinks that there is no non-obstruction of the elemental [fire], that is not so;
for the rays of the sun are not obstructed even when the combustible object is separated by a crystal (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.47).

Because of the phrase "due to the non-obstruction of the sun's rays," "because there is no obstruction even when [the object] is behind a crystal," and "because there is no obstruction in the combustible [object]," there is a division of the sentence due to the connection with the word "non-obstruction" (avighātāt) in each case.
Thus, according to the statement, there is a distinction in meaning:
the ray of the sun is not obstructed by jars and the like; because it is unimpeded, it [reveals] the water contained within the jar.
It shines; for when there is contact, there is the perception of the quality of another substance, namely heat, and by that, the suppression of the sensation of cold.
Even when the object to be illuminated is separated by crystal, there is no obstruction of the lamp’s rays;
because there is no obstruction, that which has reached [the object] is perceived. This applies to [objects] situated within a frying pan or similar vessels.

And a substance is burned by fiery heat; since there is no obstruction in that case, there must be contact, and only upon contact does burning occur—for fire does not act without reaching its object. 3.
And the word "non-obstruction" (*avighātāt*) alone is employed; what is this non-obstruction?
What is it? It is the non-expansion of a substance on all sides due to a substance that does not have its parts rearranged and which acts as an obstructer;
it is the non-obstruction of the cause of action.

Regarding the statement "there is no prohibition of [perception through] contact," it is observed that water adhering to a jar is perceived externally by its cold touch; yet this does not occur for that which is not in contact with the sense organ.
There is the perception of the touch of a substance,
as well as trembling and oozing upon sight;
this is because the visual ray encounters no resistance from such things as glass or clouds.
Because of the proximity with the object, its apprehension is established through differentiation. // 47 //
Not so, because it would entail the mutual transfer of their respective properties.
Otherwise, it would follow that there is no obstruction by walls and the like, just as there is none by glass or clouds;
or conversely, that there is obstruction by glass, clouds, and the like, just as there is by walls and the like.
The reason for this restriction must be stated. // 48 //
Just as there is the perception of form due to the inherent clarity of a mirror or water, so too is there the perception of that [self].
The clarity of mirrors and water is their own specific property (svadharma), because it is observed as a rule; or rather, the perception of form is the own property of clarity.

Just as when the ray of the eye, having struck against a mirror and been reflected back, comes into contact with one's own face, there occurs the perception of one's own face— known as the apprehension of a reflection— due to the assistance provided by the form of the mirror.
That serves as the cause [for the perception], because in the case of damage to the form of the mirror, that [perception] is absent.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a reflection does not occur on walls and such;
likewise, there is no obstruction of the visual ray by glass, clouds, veils, and the like.
And there is obstruction by walls and so forth—due to the restriction of the inherent nature of substances. // 49 //
NyS 3.1.50: There is no possibility of injunctions or prohibitions regarding things that are either perceived or inferred.

Because the means of valid cognition has reality as its object, indeed, O sir, objects that have been seen or inferred by one who is investigating cannot be arbitrarily constrained [by him] with the words, "It must be thus."
Nor can it be denied by saying,
"It does not exist in this way," for it is not logically tenable to say, "Let odor also be visible like color," or "Let color be visible like odor."
lest it be so; [and lest one think] that "just as there is the cognition of fire through smoke, let there also be the cognition of water through smoke."
"Or else, let there be no cognition of fire by means of smoke either, just as there is no cognition of water [by means of it].
What is the reason?
Indeed, things exist just as they do;
that which is their own intrinsic nature.

"One's own dharma" means that such persons understand it through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for valid cognition has as its object that which is as-it-is (*tathābhūta*). Indeed, these two— prescription (*niyoga*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)— have been taught by you.

Or let there be no obstruction by walls and the like, just as there is none by glass, clouds, and the like; or let there not be no obstruction by glass, clouds, and the like, just as there is none by walls and the like— this is not so, for these [atoms] are indeed perceived through direct observation and inference.
These are the properties of substances.
For it is the perception or non-perception of resistance and non-resistance that establishes them; thus, by the non-perception of what is obstructed, [resistance] is inferred.
Resistance by walls and the like is inferred from the perception of what is obstructed; however, there is no resistance by glass, clouds, thin veils, and so forth. // 50 //
Now, moreover, is there indeed one sense-faculty,
or are there many sense-faculties?
From what does this doubt arise?
There is doubt because there is multiplicity when the locations are different, and because the whole occupies multiple locations.

Many substances are seen to occupy various locations, yet they constitute a single composite whole (*avayavin*) despite being in different places. Therefore, there is doubt regarding the sense organs because they occupy distinct locations. // 51 //
There is one sense organ—because the skin is not distinct [from it]. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.52)
He says, "The skin is a single sense-faculty.
Why?
Because there is no distinction [among its parts].
There is no location of any sense organ that is not reached by the skin; nor does the apprehension of any object occur when the skin is absent—
that [skin] by which all the seats of the senses are pervaded, in which...
And since the apprehension of objects occurs when that [wind] is present, that skin is a single sense-faculty. // 52 //
Not so, because other objects of the senses are not perceived;
for when the skin is being grasped, there is the perception of touch as its characteristic mark.

When touch is perceived by the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*), other objects of the senses such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are not apprehended by those who are blind and the like. Therefore, there is no separate sense faculty distinct from the one that perceives touch.
If it were a single sense organ consisting of the skin, then color and other objects would be perceived by the blind and others through touch; yet they are not so perceived.
Therefore, the skin is not the sole sense organ.
The perception of that [the sense organ] occurs through a specific part of the skin, just like the perception of smoke;
for example, there is a specific part of the skin.

Just as a certain [person] who is in close proximity to the eye perceives the touch of smoke and no other does, so too there are specific parts of the skin that perceive color and other qualities; because these are impaired, color and the rest are not perceived by the blind and others.
It is not a valid reason because it is contradicted [by experience].
Having stated, "There is only one sense-faculty because there is no distinction from the skin," [the opponent replies:
"The perception of color and so forth occurs through a specific part of the skin, just like the perception of smoke."
Thus it is said. And this being so, the perceivers of objects are manifold—because of the determination of objects;
for when they exist, there is the perception of objects, and when they are impaired, [there is none].
And because [the latter] does not exist, the preceding argument is thus contradicted by the subsequent argument.
Furthermore, the negative concomitance (avyatireka) is doubtful;
for even by the elements such as earth and the rest, the seats of the sense organs are pervaded, yet when those [elements] are absent, there is no apprehension of objects.
Thus it is said. Therefore, neither the skin nor any other single sense organ has all objects as its domain. // 52 //
NyS 3.1.53: No, because objects are not perceived simultaneously.
The self is connected with the mind, the mind with the sense organ,
and the sense organ is in contact with all objects; thus, from the contacts of the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects,
there would be simultaneous perceptions, yet color-form and the other [sensory qualities] are not perceived simultaneously.
Therefore, it is perceived that there is no single sense organ that has all objects as its domain;
and because the apprehensions of objects do not occur simultaneously, there is no single sense organ.
It pertains to all objects;
for if it were based on association, there would be no possibility of blindness and so forth when grasping objects. // 53 //
And because of contradiction, the skin is not one.

Indeed, the skin is not a single sense-organ, because that would lead to a contradiction: if it were to function without contact (*aprāpyakāritva*), as in the case where visible forms (*rūpa*) are perceived by the skin without being reached, then the same consequence would follow for tactile sensations (*sparśa*) and the rest as well.

And since there is the apprehension of tangible objects and so forth when they have come into contact, it follows that there must also be the apprehension of visible forms and so forth when they have come into contact.
If it is argued that there is the functioning [of the senses] both by reaching [the object] and without reaching it, [we reply:

because an obstruction would be impossible, there would be the apprehension of the mere object. Or, if it should be thought: "Tangible objects such as touch are apprehended by the skin when they have reached it, whereas visible forms are apprehended without having reached it."
This being so, there is no obscuration.
And because obscuration is untenable, there would be the apprehension of mere form, whether it be obstructed or unobstructed.
Furthermore, there would be no conformity to distance or proximity regarding the perception or non-perception of form;
for if form were grasped by the skin without being reached, then there would be no non-grasping of form at a distance, nor [specific grasping] when it is near.
And thus, this [notion] that there is "grasping" would not exist. // 54 //
And since plurality is established by the negation of unity,
the reason "because of the fivefold nature of the sense organs and their objects" (NyS 3.1.55) is also adduced as a supporting argument.
The "purpose" (artha) is the objective; that is fivefold for the sense faculties.
When there is the grasping of touch by means of the sense faculty of touch, form is not grasped by that very same [faculty]; thus, the purpose is the grasping of form.
The eye is inferred;
and since odor is not perceived by those two [the eye and the body] when touch and visible form are being grasped, the nose is inferred as the means for the perception of odor.
In the apprehension of three [objects], the sense-organ of taste is inferred for the purpose of apprehending taste, since taste is not apprehended by those [other organs] alone;
likewise, in the apprehension of four [objects], the sense-organ of hearing is inferred, since sound is not heard by those [other organs] alone.
The auditory organ is inferred from the purpose of perceiving sound;
likewise, because the purposes of the sense organs cannot be accomplished by one another's means, there are exactly five sense organs. // 55 //
Not so, because there is a multiplicity of objects.
Indeed, it is not established that "there are five sense faculties because there are five types of sense objects," for what reason? Because those sense objects are many;
indeed, these sense objects of the faculties are numerous.
Tangibles (*sparśa*) are, first of all, cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold.
Visible forms (*rūpa*) are white, green, and so forth. Odors (*gandha*) are desirable, undesirable, and indifferent.
Tastes (*rasa*) are pungent and so forth.
Sounds consist of phonemes and are distinct from mere noise; thus, for one who holds that there are five sense organs because there are five types of sense objects,
there would be many sense organs because there are many types of sense objects.
They follow as logical consequences. // 56 //
There is no negation of odors and so forth, because they are not distinct from the nature of odor-ness and so forth.

The perceptions of odors and so forth— which have been established as distinct by their own respective general properties such as "odor-ness" (*gandhatva*)— do not necessitate other perceivers, because they are to be accomplished by means that do not share the same instrument (*asamānasādhanasādhyatvāt*). Thus, the collection of objects has been described as inference (*anumāna*).
It is not a single part of the object;
yet, relying upon a single part of the object, you deny the mere fivefold nature of the objects. Therefore, this denial is illogical.
But how, then, are odors and so forth established by their own general properties such as "odor-ness" (gandhatva) and the like? It is indeed touch [that serves as the basis].
It is threefold— cold, hot, and neither-hot-nor-cold— and is subsumed under its own general property of tangibility;
and when cold tangibility is being perceived...
The perception of a touch that is neither hot nor cold does not necessitate another perceiving organ— since different types of touch are accomplished by a single instrument;
for by the very same [organ] by which a cold touch is perceived, the other two are also perceived.
In this way, [the arguments apply] to odors by virtue of their being odors, to forms by virtue of their being forms,
to tastes by virtue of their being tastes, and to sounds by virtue of their being sounds. Furthermore,
the apprehensions of odor and so forth do not belong to other perceivers, because they are to be accomplished by means that are not common [to those others].
They are the motivators; therefore, it is logical that there are five sense-faculties because there are five objects of the senses. // 57 //
If the universal (*sāmānya*) is the unifier, then it follows that the sense organs are one, because they do not differ in their status as objects (*viṣayatva*). (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.58)
For odors and the rest are subsumed under the general category of "object-ness" (viṣayatva). // 58 //
NyS 3.1.59: [The soul is not one] because of the fivefold distinctions of cognition, characteristics, substrata, movement, form, and genus.
Indeed, objects established as such by way of their general status as objects are not independent of other apprehending factors;
they are inferred as being apprehended by a single means of cognition, and thus the five [objects] are inferred.

Odors and the rest are established as distinct by their own respective universals, such as "odor-ness" (gandhatva), and are thus apprehended by different sense organs. Therefore, this [objection] is irrelevant; and it is precisely this point that is restated in the phrase: "because of the fivefold nature characterized by cognition."
The faculties themselves are the characteristics— since the senses have the apprehension of objects as their indicative mark—
as stated in this [sūtra]: "Because of the fivefold nature of the senses and their objects" (55).
It is explained in the Sūtra that there are five sense organs because the characteristics of the intellect (buddhi) are fivefold;
indeed, the seats of the sense organs are also five.
The skin, which has the entire body as its locus, is the means of perceiving touch; the eye, which has the black pupil as its locus and extends outward,
is the means of perceiving form.
The nose has the nose as its basis; the tongue has the tongue as its basis;
[the ear] has the ear-cavity as its basis.
The ear [is distinct] because it has as its mark the apprehension of smell, taste, color, touch, and sound.

Furthermore, there is a distinction among the sense organs due to a difference in their mode of operation: the eye, being attached to the black pupil, goes outward and reaches the substances that are the substrata of color.
[The object] is reached; however, the sense organs such as touch approach their objects only by moving toward the substrate [of the object],
whereas sound approaches the ear through the process of a continuous series (*santāna*).

Form (ākṛti) is indeed dimension (parimāṇa); it consists of a specific quantity (iyattā) and is fivefold: the nose, tongue, and skin have their own respective locations as their measure; they do not pervade their objects and are to be inferred [by their functions].
The eye has its locus in the black pupil (kṛṣṇasāra) and, having extended outward, pervades the object;
the ear is nothing other than space (ākāśa).

And that [universal] is all-pervasive; it is to be inferred from the experience of the mere sound, and by means of the assistance of the person's mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it manifests the sound according to the restriction of its substratum.
They call the "genus" (*jāti*) the "source" (*yoni*).

Indeed, the five elements, beginning with earth, are the sources of the five sense organs; therefore, it is established that there are five sense organs because of the fivefold nature of the primary constituents (prakṛti). // 59 //
How, then, is it known that the sense organs have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*) and not the unmanifest (*avyakta*) as their material cause? [The answer is:
Because of the perception of specific qualities of the elements, there is identity with them. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.60)
For a rule regarding the manifestation of specific qualities in the elements, such as air and the rest, is observed:
air is the manifester of touch, water is the manifester of taste,
fire is the manifester of color, and certain substances belonging to earth [are the manifesters of odor].

There exists a specific rule regarding the perception of the particular qualities of the elements, which serves as the manifestor of the [latent] seeds of certain substances; and since there is this restriction on the perception of the particular qualities of the elements by the sense organs, we conclude that the sense organs have the elements as their material cause (*prakṛti*), and not the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) as their material cause. // 60 //
Now, for the analysis of the meaning: it was stated that smell and the other [qualities] are the qualities of earth and the other [elements].
This statement [concerns] whether earth and the others possess a single quality or multiple qualities.
To this he says:
"Of smell, taste, color, touch, and sound, those ending with touch belong to earth. (NyS 3.1.61)
Having successively excluded earth, water, fire, and air, the subsequent [property] belongs to space.
Regarding the phrase "of those ending with tangibility," there is a change of case-ending;
the word *uttara* (following) from *ākāśasya* (of space) is construed as *sparśaparyantebhyaḥ* (from those ending with tangibility).
How, then,
is the designation of "independence" (tarap) explained? By virtue of the capacity for independent application.

From this, it is understood that the word "subsequent" (uttara) signifies denotation for the sake of another; for in the *uddeśa-sūtra*, sound is subsequent to [the elements] ending with touch, or alternatively, it is the primary topic (*tantra*) because touch is intended to be expressed.
When [the elements] ending with tangibility have been assigned [their respective qualities], that which is other than those and subsequent to them is sound. // 62 //
NyS 3.1.63: No, because not all qualities are perceived.
This application of qualities is not correct; why?
Because not all the qualities of a given element are perceived by a sense organ composed of that same element.
For by means of the earthy sense-faculty (ghrāṇa), everything up to touch is not apprehended;
only odor is apprehended.
The same applies to the remaining [faculties] as well. // 63 //
How, then, are these qualities to be applied? [To this, it is said:
"Because each subsequent quality exists within each preceding one, the subsequent ones are not perceived therein. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.64)
Each one among the [qualities] beginning with odor is, respectively,
the specific quality of each one among the [substances] beginning with earth; therefore,
there is the non-perception of those, of those two, and of that.
By means of the nose, [one does not know] tastes, forms, or tangibles; by means of the tongue, forms or tangibles; and by means of the eye, tangibles. // 64 //
How, then, are the elements perceived as possessing multiple qualities? [Answer:
Because of their conjunction, there is the perception of multiple qualities. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.65)
And because of contact with water and the other elements, taste and the other qualities are perceived in earth; the same applies to the remaining elements as well. // 65 //
In that case, the restriction would not obtain,
because there is no restriction regarding their association: "earth has four qualities," "water has three qualities," "fire has two qualities," and "air has one quality."
Thus, the restriction is also established; how so?
For that which is lower is pervaded by that which is higher. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.66)

Since earth and the other elements are each pervaded by the subsequent ones in succession, there is no fixed rule regarding their combination; and this should be understood as pertaining to the original creation of the elements, not to the present state. // 66 //
NyS 3.1.67: It is not so, because both the earthen and the watery [substances] are perceptible.
"No"—thus he rejects the three-sūtra argument; why?
Because this substance, being composed of earth, is also perceptible.
Perception occurs due to largeness, being composed of multiple substances, and color; therefore,
only a substance consisting of fire (taijasa) would be perceptible, and not an earthy or watery one— due to the absence of color [in the latter].
Just as in the case of the luminous [element], since the earthy and watery [elements] are perceptible, it is not due to their conjunction that multiple qualities are perceived in the elements.
Furthermore, for one who asserts that the perceptibility of the earthy and watery [elements] is caused by the form of another element, it would follow that air is also perceptible.
Or rather, let the reason for the restriction be stated:
because the tastes of both the earthy and the watery [substances] are perceptible, the earthy taste is of six kinds while the watery is only sweet; and this cannot be due to a mixture [of the two].
Or rather, because the two colors—those of the earthy and the watery—are perceptible;

for when they are in contact with the color assisted by fire (tejas), the color is merely a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and not something to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*). And because the two colors of the earthy and the watery are perceived as being of both single and manifold kinds.

The color of earth is of many kinds, such as green, red, yellow, and so forth; that of water, however, is white and non-luminous. Furthermore, this [variety] is not perceived when there is a mere conjunction of single qualities.
This is merely an illustration; hereafter follows the detailed exposition—namely, regarding the two types of touch, those of earth and fire.

Because it is perceptible. Earth possesses a touch that is neither hot nor cold, whereas fire possesses a hot touch which is perceptible. And this [perceptibility] would not be possible through the contact of substances possessing only a single quality with air, which has a touch that is neither hot nor cold.

Alternatively, because the substances earth and water, which possess fixed qualities, are perceptible— namely, that the earthly substance possesses four qualities and the watery substance possesses three qualities— it is inferred that their cause is likewise of such a nature.
The effect of that [substance] is indicated by the verbal suffix *liṅ*— for the state of being an effect follows from the state of being a cause.
Thus, because the two substances consisting of fire and air are perceptible,
the determination of their qualities allows for the inference of that determination regarding the substance which is their cause.
And separation is observed— because the earthy and the watery [substances] are perceptible;

an earthy substance is perceived by direct perception as separated from water and so forth, and the watery [substance] is [perceived] as separated from the other two, and the fiery [substance] from air.
And it is not that each individual quality is perceived; for this would be without inference, as it has been said:
"For the lower is pervaded by the higher. (66)
Regarding the phrase "it is thus":
no indicative mark (*liṅga*) that could lead to an inference is apprehended here, by which we might understand this to be so.
And as for what was said—"For the lower is pervaded by the higher; this should be understood as pertaining to the creation of the elements, not to the present"—[that too is incorrect].
This is untenable because there is no restrictive cause;
moreover, it is observed in the present that "the lower is pervaded by the higher."
And "fire is pervaded by air" means pervasion;
this is conjunction, and that is common to both, as well as [the conjunction] with air.
Because fire possesses touch due to being pervaded [by earth],
but there is no restrictive reason why air should possess color simply because it is pervaded by fire.
And it is observed that the tactile quality of air is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the tactile quality of fire; yet, a thing cannot be overwhelmed by its own very nature. // 67 //
Thus, having refuted that claim which is contrary to logic, the objection raised in [sūtra] 63— "because not all qualities are perceived"— is now resolved.
NyS 3.1.68: Because of the progressive excellence of each preceding quality, each [subsequent element] is predominant in its respective quality.
Therefore, there is no perception of all qualities by the olfactory organ and the others.
Each preceding organ is predominant because of the excellence of its respective quality, such as odor.
What constitutes this predominance?
The capacity to grasp objects;
what is the excellence of the quality? It is the capacity for manifestation.
Just as external substances— terrestrial, aqueous, and fiery— which possess four, three, and two qualities respectively, do not manifest all qualities,
but rather manifest smell, taste, and form respectively due to the predominance of those specific qualities; so it is here.

Thus, the nose, tongue, and eye—which possess four, three, and two qualities respectively—do not perceive all qualities; rather, due to the predominance of odor, taste, and color, they perceive odor, taste, and color respectively. Therefore, [perception] does not occur through the nose and the other [senses].
It is the apprehension of all qualities.
However, he who asserts: "Because smell is its quality, the nose is the perceiver of smell alone," and so forth...
"In the case of the tongue and so forth as well"—
this means that it would follow that the apprehension of qualities by the nose and other organs occurs according to their respective connection with those qualities. // 68 //
But by what is this distinction established— that some sense-faculties are composed of earth and not all,
while some sense-faculties are composed of water, fire, or air and not all?
But its determination [is made] on account of the majority.
The "abundance" (*bhūyastva*) is the combination of distinct substances capable of accomplishing a purpose, brought about by the refinement of the person;
for the word "abundance" is seen to denote excellence— just as an object that is excellent is called "abundant."

Just as substances such as poison, medicine, and gems— which are capable of performing distinct purposeful actions— are produced through the power of human refinement so that not everything serves every purpose, in the same way, [the sense organs] are capable of apprehending distinct objects.
The olfactory and other faculties are produced, yet they are not capable of grasping all objects. // 69 //
The sense organs do not perceive their own qualities; if it is asked why this is so, [the answer is]:
because the sense organs exist only when accompanied by their respective qualities. (Nyāyasūtra 3.1.70)
The olfactory and other sense organs do not perceive their own odors and so forth.
If one asks for what reason,
it is because the olfactory and other organs function as sense faculties only in conjunction with their own respective qualities.

The nose perceives an external odor together with its own odor, which performs the same function; however, the perception of that [nose's] own odor does not occur due to the absence of a cooperative cause. Thus...
And also for the remaining [elements]. // 70 //

If, moreover, odor were both a concomitant cause of the sense of smell and its object, [it would indeed be perceived]; therefore, he says: "And because that [odor] is not perceived by that [same sense]. (NyS 3.1.71)
There is no perception of the qualities of the sense organs.
He who says: "Just as an external substance is perceived by the eye, so too that very same [substance] by that very same eye..."
"Let the eye be grasped"—this is similar [to the previous case], for in both instances there is an absence of a cause for comprehension. // 71 //
Not so, because sound is perceived as a quality.
It is not the case that the sense organs do not perceive their own qualities; for indeed, the quality of sound is perceived by the ear. // 72 //
Its perception [is established] through the mutual difference in properties between substance and quality.
Space does not become a sense-faculty by virtue of possessing the quality of sound; nor is sound the manifester of sound;
and the perception of their own respective qualities by the olfactory and other faculties does not occur.
Nor is it inferred; rather,
it is inferred that sound is perceived by the auditory faculty, which is space, and that space possesses the quality of sound.
And the remainder should be understood as inference: first of all, the self is the hearer, not the instrument,
given that the mind is the sense of hearing.
The absence of deafness;
and the capacity of earth and the other elements to function as the olfactory organ and so forth when they exist as the auditory organ.
And [the other elements] lack that capacity;
yet this auditory faculty exists, and since space remains as the only residue, by the method of elimination, space is the auditory faculty. // 73 //
Thus ends the first Āhnika of the third Adhyāya in the Nyāyabhāṣya composed by Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second Āhnika of the third Adhyāya of the Nyāyabhāṣya.
The sense organs and their objects have been examined;
now follows the sequence for the examination of the intellect (*buddhi*): Is it non-eternal or eternal?
From what source does this doubt arise?
NyS 3.2.1: Doubt arises because of the similarity between action and space.

The property of being intangible is perceived in the intellect as a common characteristic shared by those two [the body and the self]. Furthermore, the specific characteristics—namely, possessing the properties of arising and passing away in one case, and their opposite, eternity, in the other—are not perceived in that intellect according to their respective natures. Therefore, there is doubt.

This doubt is indeed untenable—for all embodied beings, the intellect (*buddhi*) is personally experienced as impermanent, just like pleasure and other such states. Furthermore, there is the cognition: "I shall know," "I know," and "I knew.

And since the manifestation of the three times [past, present, and future] does not occur without arising and passing away, it is established by this manifestation of the three times that "the intellect is impermanent.
This is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and it is also stated in the Śāstra:
“[Cognition] produced from the contact of a sense faculty with its object” (NS 1.1.4);
“The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind” (NS 1.1.16),
and so forth.

Therefore, the process of doubt is untenable; rather, this treatise is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of various views. For it is thus that the Sāṃkhyas, holding such a view, proclaim: "The intellect (buddhi) is eternal and constitutes the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of the person (puruṣa). // 1 //
And they state the proof:
"Because there is recognition of the object. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.2)
What, then, is this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)? It is the synthesizing cognition (*pratisandhijñāna*) regarding a common object in the form "I knew this object previously; I know it now.

This is possible only if the intellect (*buddhi*) is permanent. If, however, there were multiplicity—meaning if cognitions were distinct entities that arise and perish—then recognition would be impossible.
One person does not recognize what has been known by another. // 2 //
NyS 3.2.3: It is not a valid reason because it is equal to that which is to be proven.
Just as the permanence of the intellect (*buddhi*) is to be established, so too is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
What is the reason?

Because it is impossible for the property of a conscious being to reside in an instrument—this [recognition], namely knowledge, vision, apprehension, and awareness, is indeed a property of the person (*puruṣa*).
"Recognition is determination"—for it is the conscious being who recognizes an object previously known;
therefore, for this reason, its eternity is logical.

But if consciousness is admitted to belong to the instrument (the sense organ), then the nature of the conscious being must be stated; for it is impossible to establish the existence of another self whose specific nature has not been defined.

If knowledge is admitted to belong to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then what is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of this conscious being (*cetana*) now, what is its property (*dharma*), and what is its reality (*tattva*);
and furthermore, what does this conscious being do with knowledge residing in the intellect?
If you say, "He intends"?
This is not a statement of something different from knowledge.

[The claim that] "the person intends" and "the intellect knows" does not express something distinct from knowledge; for "he intends," "he knows," "he sees," and "he perceives" all have one and the same meaning.

If it is argued that "the intellect (buddhi) makes [the self] know"?—certainly, the person knows; it is true that "the intellect makes [him] know. But if this is accepted, it follows that ignorance belongs to the person, not to the intellect, which is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
And regarding the thesis that there is a distinct word for each individual person,
the statement of the reason for the refutation is as follows:
whoever asserts that "one person wills, another perceives, another apprehends, and another sees"— these are indeed different persons.
Regarding the statement that "the conscious one, the knower, the perceiver, the seer" does not belong to a single [self] but rather to the phenomena (dharmas),
what here is the reason for this negation?
If you argue that there is no difference in meaning, the same [objection] applies.
If you think that because these words have non-different meanings, the established distinction [between them] is untenable,
then the same [point] holds true.

In the expressions "the person intends" (*puruṣaś cetayate*) and "the intellect knows" (*buddhir jānīte*), the meaning does not differ; for in that case, since both possess consciousness (*cetanatva*), one or the other would be redundant. Furthermore, if "intellect" (*buddhi*) is defined as that by which one perceives—that is, cognition—and this is said to be the mind (*manas*) itself, then is that [mind] eternal?

Let it be so; however, the permanence of the mind does not follow from the recognition of objects. For it is observed that recognition occurs despite a difference in instruments, because the knower is one—just as in the case of the eye, where there is recognition by the other [eye] of what was seen by the left, and just as in the case of a lamp, where there is recognition by another lamp of what was seen by a previous lamp.
Therefore, this is the reason for the permanence of the knower. //3//

And as for what he thinks—that while the intellect (*buddhi*) remains stable, cognitions (*jñāna*) emerge as its modifications (*vṛtti*) according to their respective objects, and that the modification is not different from that which possesses the modification—that too is incorrect. NyS 3.2.4:
Because there is no simultaneous apprehension.

If there were non-difference between the modification and that which possesses the modification, then because the possessor of the modifications persists, the modifications themselves would persist; thus, those perceptions of objects would remain constant, and it would follow that there is a simultaneous apprehension of all objects. // 4 //
And if there is no recognition, it follows that [the object] must perish.
Furthermore, if recognition were directed toward the past, then even that which possesses activity would be past, which entails the destruction of the internal organ;
otherwise, there would be no plurality [of cognitions]. // 5 //
And the non-omnipresent internal organ (manas) connects with the sense organs successively; thus, because its operation is sequential, there is no simultaneous apprehension.
— Nyāyasūtra 3.2.6: "Because of its successive functioning, there is no simultaneous perception."

There is a distinction between the functioning and that which functions in the case of the sense organs and their objects; and if there were identity [between them], there would be an absence of manifestation and disappearance. // 6 //
And there is a lack of recognition due to the engagement with another object.

Non-recognition is non-apprehension. And the non-apprehension of some object occurs when the mind is occupied with another object—because of the difference between the function and that which possesses the function; for if there were identity, such occupation would be purposeless. // 7 //
Regarding the pervasiveness of the internal organ, its successive conjunction with the sense organs [is not possible] because there is no motion. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.8)

Since the sense organs have been reached by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is an absence of "going" in the sense of reaching; therefore, because of the absence of sequential activity therein, simultaneous perception would be impossible. Furthermore, since movement is absent, the non-simultaneous grasping of objects—which was previously denied for the all-pervading internal organ—is not inferred by any other mark (*liṅga*).
This is just as the movement of the eye is denied, because objects both near and far are perceived at the same time.
It is inferred from the obstruction [of light] caused by the intervention of the hand or the moon;
thus, there is no dispute regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), nor regarding its eternity— for it is established that the mind (*manas*) is the internal organ and that it is eternal.
Where, then, is the dispute?
It concerns its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*). And that [pervasiveness], being unperceived through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is refuted.

Furthermore, while the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is one, these modifications (*vṛtti*) consisting of cognitions are manifold—such as visual cognition (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and olfactory cognition (*ghrāṇavijñāna*).
There is visual consciousness and olfactory consciousness. And this [distinction] is untenable if the activity and the agent of activity were one and the same.
Thus, it is established that the Puruṣa knows, not the internal organ;
by this, the objection regarding attachment to other objects is refuted.
The attachment to another object, characterized by the apprehension of that other object, belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) and not to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
However, this attachment—consisting in proximity to one sense-organ and non-proximity to another—is admitted to belong to the mind (*manas*). // 8 //
Regarding the claim that there is a single internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) despite the diversity of its functions, this is stated [in response] even though the distinction between functions is real:
"The misconception of their difference is like the misconception of the difference in a crystal. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.9)

In that state, there is the conceit of diversity, just as there is the conceit of otherness—such as "it is not blue" or "it is red"—in a crystal when it is overlaid by another substance; so too [is it] due to the overlaying of different objects.
No—because there is no reason.

There is no reason why this misconception of multiplicity regarding cognitions is secondary (gauṇa), like the misconception of difference in a crystal, and not rather like the misconception of difference in odor and so forth; thus, due to the absence of a reason, [your position] is untenable.
If it is argued that the absence of a reason is the same [for both sides]?

No; for we observe that cognitions arise and perish in succession, since it is seen that cognitions regarding sensory objects arise and perish in a sequential order. Therefore, this misconception of multiplicity regarding cognitions is like the misconception of difference regarding odors and the like. // 9 //
Not tolerating the statement, "like the misconception of difference in a crystal," the proponent of momentariness (kṣaṇikavādin) says:
"Even in the case of a crystal, because of the production of successive [moments], and because individual manifestations are momentary, [the example] is not a valid reason. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.10)
"The misconception of multiplicity arises from the difference in the adjuncts (upadhāna) of a crystal that exists without differentiation"—this position is one whose reason is non-existent. Why?
Because even in the case of the crystal, there is the arising of successive [moments].
Even in the case of rock crystal, other manifestations arise and others cease;
how so? Because manifestations are momentary, and a moment is exceedingly brief.
Time consists of moments; [entities] that exist for a moment are momentary.
But how is it known that individual manifestations are momentary?
It is because we observe a continuous process of increase and decrease.
In the body and other [tissues],
there is a continuous process of accumulation and depletion of the nutrient essence (*āhārarasa*), which has been transformed through digestion, as it becomes blood and so forth within the body.

From accumulation arises the production of manifest entities, and from depletion comes the cessation of manifest entities; and this being so, growth of the body is perceived over time through the differentiation of the transformation of its constituent parts.
Thus, this property of a particular individual is to be understood as belonging to the individual in general.
NyS 3.2.11: Since there is no cause for restriction, everything is permitted as it is observed.
The rule that in all individual entities there is a continuous process of increase and decrease, as in the case of a body, is not a universal necessity;
why? Because of the absence of a reason—that is, because there exists neither perception nor inference to establish this.
Therefore, there is an admission according to what is observed:
wherever a continuous process of increase and decrease is seen,
there the production of successive individuals is admitted on the basis of observing that continuous process of increase and decrease.
Just as in the case of the body and so forth; wherever it is not observed, there it is denied, as in the case of stones and the like;
even in the crystal, there is a continuous process of increase and decrease.

Therefore, it is unreasonable to claim that "even in a crystal there is the production of successive [moments]," for this would be like the bitterness of a *arka* plant imparting bitterness to all other substances. // 11 //

And for one who maintains that momentariness consists in the non-sequential arising of what was previously non-existent through the total cessation [of the preceding], within the continuum of substance— this [is the case]:
NyS 3.2.12: [Sound is non-eternal] because the causes of its production and destruction are perceived.
First, a cause of origination is observed— the accumulation of parts in the case of anthills and the like. And a cause of destruction is also observed—
the disjunction of parts in the case of jars and the like.

But for one [who holds] that what has its parts unimpaired ceases and what has its parts unaccumulated arises, no cause is perceived in either case— neither when there is cessation without remainder nor when there is the arising of something unprecedented. // 12 //
The establishment of that [soul] is like the non-perception of a cause during the destruction of milk, and like the production of curd.

Just as the cause of the destruction of milk and the cause of the production of curd are admitted even though they are not perceived, so too are the causes of destruction and production [admitted] in the case of a crystal with respect to its successive individual manifestations.
And it must also be permitted. // 13 //
Non-apprehension is not [the cause], because [the object] is apprehended through its mark (liṅga).

The signs of the destruction of milk and the causes of the destruction of milk, as well as the signs of the production of curd and the causes of the production of curd, are perceived; therefore, there is no non-apprehension [of change].
However, in the case of substances such as crystal, there is no sign for successive productions [of new entities]; thus, there is only persistence [of identity]. // 14 //
Regarding this, someone offers a rebuttal:
"No, because of the appearance of different qualities resulting from the transformation of the milk. (NyS 3.2.15)
"One person says: 'There is transformation of milk, not its destruction.
And transformation is the arising of another property upon the cessation of a previous property of a persisting substance."
Another says: "It is the manifestation of another quality.
That is to say, when the previous quality of an existing substance ceases, another quality arises.
Thus, it is indeed like the state of being a single wing. // 15 //

But here is the rebuttal: *Nyāyasūtra* 3.2.16: "The observation of the production of a different substance from a rearrangement [of parts] is an inference for the cessation of the previous substance."

When a distinct substance, curd, is perceived to have arisen from the re-arrangement of parts characterized by coagulation (*saṃmūrchana*), it is inferred that the previous substance, milk, has ceased to exist due to the disjunction of its parts,
just as [the cessation of the substance clay is inferred] from the parts of clay.
When another substance has arisen in the pot from a different configuration, the previous substance— the lump of clay— ceases to exist due to the disjunction of its constituent parts.
And the continuity of parts is like that between milk and curd;
for if there were a cessation without remainder, the arising of a different substance as a non-continuous [succession] would not be possible. // 16 //
Having granted that there is no destruction of milk without a cause, the objection is raised that the production of curd [likewise] cannot be denied—NyS 3.2.17:
[This is not so,] because the non-perception of a cause for destruction occurs in some cases, while its perception occurs in others; thus, [your argument] is inconclusive.
The claim that the destruction and arising of individual crystals are causeless, like [the transformation of] milk into curd, is not an absolute rule.
Why? Because there is no logical reason;
for there is no reason here [to establish] that destruction and arising are causeless.

The manifestation of crystals and the like is like that of milk and curd; it is not, however, as in the case of a jar, where destruction occurs due to the presence of a cause of destruction and production occurs due to the presence of a cause of production—
such that the manifestation of crystals and the like would involve destruction and production through the presence of causes for destruction and production.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the statement of the example is without a basis;
for this example would have a substratum only if destruction and arising were perceived occurring simultaneously in things such as crystals.
It is like the non-perception of the cause for the destruction of milk, and like the non-perception of the cause for the production of curd.
Since those two causes are not perceived, this illustration is without a basis.

And having admitted the production and destruction of crystal, that which proves them is thereby admitted; thus there is no refutation [of our position]. Like a jar, destruction and production are not without cause.
This example of crystal and so forth must be accepted, because it is impossible to refute; however,
like milk and curd, they are without a cause.
This [notion] that there is destruction and origination can be refuted—
because destruction and origination are observed to arise from causes,
as in the case of the destruction of milk and the origination of curd.
Observing that, its cause must be inferred—for the cause is indeed known through the mark of the effect; thus it is established that cognition is non-eternal. // 17 //

But this is now considered: whose cognition is this, that "the quality [of cognition] belongs to the self, the senses, the mind, and the objects"? For although this matter is indeed well-known, it remains to be examined.
"I am setting it in motion"— thus it is formulated;
this is a doubt arising from the occurrence of contact with the intellect, due to the non-apprehension of the specific characteristic.
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
[NS 3.2.18] It is not [the case that cognition belongs to the sense organ or the object], because even when those two perish, cognition persists.
Knowledge is not a quality of either the sense organs or their objects, because knowledge persists even when they have perished; indeed,
this [knowledge] exists even in the absence of the sense organ and the object.

When [the knower] has perished, there is the cognition "I saw. Furthermore, it is not possible for cognition to exist when the knower has perished; indeed, [cognition] is something other [than the knower].
That cognition which does not occur when the sense organ and the object have perished is indeed born from the contact of the sense organ and the object;
this other [type of cognition] is born from the contact of the self and the mind.
The notion that "this state belongs to him" is indeed a recollection, namely "I saw," which has as its object something previously seen;
and there can be no recollection of a prior perception if the knower has perished.
This is logical: one person does not remember what was seen by another,
and when the mind is accepted as the knower, it is impossible for the sense organ or the object to be the knower.
In order to establish [this]. // 18 //
Let it be, then, that cognition is a quality of the mind; [this is not so], because objects of knowledge are not perceived simultaneously by the mind. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.19)

The non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge is the mark of the internal organ; in that regard, the cognition which is inferred by means of the non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge does not belong as a quality to that internal organ.
To whom, then?
To the Knower—because of his mastery; the Knower is the master, and the instrument is that which is mastered.
Or, if [the sense organ] were of the nature of knowledge,
there would be an absence of its status as an instrument (karaṇa) for the means such as the nose.

And from the existence of the cognition of smell and so forth by the knower, it is inferred that there is the cognition of pleasure and so forth, as well as memory, which have the internal organ as their instrument;
therein, that which is the quality of cognition—

The mind is that self. As for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is the means for the perception of pleasure and so forth, it is called "mind" (*manas*); this is merely a difference in designation, not a difference in substance. Furthermore, because objects of knowledge are not perceived simultaneously by one who is not a yogi.
