And this is the meaning: when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) has arisen, the yogi, possessing the nature of transformation, creates other bodies provided with sense faculties, and through them simultaneously perceives various objects of knowledge; and this is as follows.
It is established that cognition occurs in an all-pervading knower, not in an atomic mind. Or, if the mind were all-pervading, there would be no refutation of cognition being a quality of the self—
since the mind is all-pervading and constitutes the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), it [could] [simultaneously engage] with all the sense organs.
Because of [the soul's] conjunction [with the sense organs], cognitions would arise simultaneously. // 19 //
Even if it were a quality of the self, the same [objection] would apply.
If the self were all-pervasive and conjoined with all the sense organs, it would follow that cognitions would arise simultaneously. // 20 //
NyS 3.2.21: Due to the absence of contact between the sense organs and the mind, there is no production of that [cognition].

Just as the contact between the sense organ and its object is the cause for the perception of odor and so forth, so too is the contact between the sense organ and the mind the cause; and this [contact] is not simultaneous—because the mind is atomic, there is no simultaneous production of cognitions, even though they are qualities of the self. // 21 //
If, however, the cognition of odor and so forth arises merely from the contact of the self, the sense organ, and the object— NyS 3.2.22: No, because no cause for its production has been specified.

The cognition of odor and so forth arises merely from the contact between the self and the sense organ; therefore, no cause for its production is specified here by which we might understand this [matter]. // 22 //
And because no cause of destruction is perceived, if [the entity] were to persist, it would follow that it is eternal.
The phrase "this is the same even if it were a quality of the self" (20) is conjoined with this [point],
for there are indeed two kinds of causes for the destruction of a quality:
The absence of a substratum for qualities and a quality that is contradictory [to them] are [the two reasons];

the former is untenable because the self is eternal, and a quality of the intellect that is contradictory [to it] is not perceived. Therefore, [if these were qualities], they would have to be qualities of the self.
If it exists, it would follow that the Buddha is eternal. // 23 //
Because cognition is grasped as impermanent, it is destroyed by a subsequent cognition, just like sound.
That cognition is impermanent is something to be personally realized by every embodied being. Furthermore, since a continuum of cognitions is perceived therein,
it is inferred that one cognition is a contradictory quality (guṇa) with respect to another cognition.
Just as in the continuum of sound, one sound is the contradictory of another sound. // 24 //

When there exist innumerable conditioned factors produced by cognition that serve as causes for memory and are inherent in the self, and when the contact between the self and the mind— which is likewise a cause of memory— is equally present, there is no lack of simultaneity among these causes.
If memory were to arise simultaneously [if cognition were a quality of the self], then someone, wishing to establish that there is no simultaneity of contact, says:
"Because memory arises from the mind's contact with those parts of the self in which cognition is inherent, there is no simultaneous production. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.25)

The refinement (*saṃskāra*) which is the means for knowledge is called "knowledge. By means of the regions of the self (*ātmapradeśa*) refined by knowledge, the mind (*manas*) comes into contact with them in succession. From the contact between the self and the mind, even memories arise in succession. // 25 //
NyS 3.2.26: No, because the mind functions within the body.
The conjunction of the embodied self with the mind,
accompanied by the ripening latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), is held to be life;
in that state, it exists within the body prior to death.
It is not possible for there to be a conjunction of the mind with those regions of the self that are conditioned by external cognition, apart from the body. // 26 //
NyS 3.2.27: It is not a valid reason because it is itself that which is to be proven.
Life is merely the ripening of the latent impressions of karma; this being the case, it follows that the mind exists within the body. // 27 //
Because the maintenance of the body is possible for one who remembers, there is no refutation [of the existence of the self].

Indeed, when one applies the mind with the desire to remember, one eventually recalls some object; and for one who is remembering, the maintenance of the body is observed. Furthermore, the effort born from the contact between the self and the mind is of two kinds—
It is both the sustainer and the impeller;
and when the mind has issued forth outside the body,
it falls due to its weight because of the absence of the sustainer's effort.
It might be that the body possesses a self. // 28 //
That is not so, because the mind possesses the quality of rapid movement.
The mind’s swift movement consists of its contact with an external object through a portion of itself refined by cognition, and once it has returned, the production of a sustaining effort;
both of these are logical. Or, having produced a sustaining effort, [it remains].
Since the mind issues forth from the body, it is therefore appropriate that concentration (dhāraṇā) occurs there [within the body]. // 29 //
NyS 3.2.30: No, because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of recollection.
Some [objects] are remembered quickly, while others are remembered after a long time.

When it is after a long time, then— while a continuous stream of reflection (*cintā-prabandha*) is being maintained in the mind through the desire to remember (*susmūrṣā*)— there arises [the recollection of] some object that serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Cognition, when cultivated, becomes the cause of memory; however, this is not possible in the case of a mind that has long since departed. Furthermore, the conjunction of the self and the mind does not depend upon its conjunction with the body.

It is not the cause of memory—because the body is the locus of experience. For the knower, the person, the body is the locus of experience; therefore, the mere conjunction of the mind—which has departed from it—with the self is not sufficient for the production of cognition, pleasure, and so forth, unless such a capacity is postulated. Alternatively, [if it were sufficient], [memory would arise even without the body].
"The body would be purposeless," thus [ends the verse]. // 30 //
Nor is there a specific conjunction [of the self with the mind] due to the self's impulsion, chance, or ignorance.
Either by the impulse of the self, or by chance, there would be a particular conjunction of the mind with something external to the body;
this would occur either through the mind's spontaneity or its capacity for cognition.
In every respect, [the existence of a self] is untenable.
How so? Because it would have to be an object of memory, and because it is impossible for one who desires [to remember] to possess a cognition of memory [of that self].
For if the self were the cause of the memory of such-and-such an object—

When [the soul] impels the mind, thinking, "Let the mental faculty (manas) be conjoined with that impression (saṃskāra) which is inherent in this particular part of the self," then that object becomes something already remembered, not something yet to be remembered. It is not...
Neither a region of the self nor a mental impression (saṃskāra) is directly perceived by the self; therefore, cognition [of them] through direct perception of the self is untenable.
Furthermore, when one directs the mind with the desire to remember, even after a long time—
One does not remember any object without a cause;
furthermore, the mind lacks the capacity for cognition, because cognition has been denied to it. // 31 //
And this is the same as [the case of] the pain in the foot of one whose mind is distracted, due to a particular kind of contact. — Nyāyasūtra 3.2.32.
Indeed, when this person, whose mind is distracted elsewhere, experiences a piercing of the foot by a pebble or a thorn in a certain place,
then a specific conjunction between the self and the mind must be postulated.
For it is observed that "suffering" and "the sensation of suffering" are distinct; in this regard, the refutation is the same for both,
yet there is no distinction made by mere whim.
Action is not without cause, nor is conjunction without cause.
If it is argued that unseen karma (adṛṣṭa) is the cause of action for the sake of experience, [the response is] the same.
If unperceived karma resides in the person as the cause of activity in the mind for the sake of the person's experience,
then suffering and the perception of suffering would not be established.
If you think thus, then it is the same regarding the cause of memory: a specific conjunction ought to exist there. As for what was said—
"The specific conjunction [of the self with the intellect] does not arise from self-impulsion, chance, or ignorance;
thus, this is not a refutation," whereas the former was indeed a refutation.
“Because the mind functions within the body, [the self] is not [perceived by it].
What, indeed, is now the cause for the non-recollection of [all things] simultaneously, even when the simultaneity of their causes exists?
NyS 3.2.33: Because cognitions of the sign of a resolution and so forth do not occur simultaneously, there is no simultaneous recollection.

Just as the contact between the self and the mind and the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) are the causes of memory, so too are the formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*) and the cognitions of the inferential marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
And these do not occur simultaneously; therefore, the memories produced by them [do not arise at once].
Non-arising simultaneously. // 33 //

But in the case of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*), which does not depend on mental application (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth, there would follow the consequence of simultaneity with respect to memory (*smārta*).

Indeed, regarding this memory that arises at times as if it were intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*), independent of application of the mind (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth— the consequence would be its simultaneous production,
because there is no cause [to restrict its timing].

Because the cause of memory is not perceived, there is the misconception that it is intuition (*pratibhā*). When there is a continuous stream of thought concerning many objects, only one particular object becomes the cause of memory for someone;
through the contemplation of that [object], the memory of it arises, and not [of others].
Furthermore, this rememberer does not perceive any cause for the memory, such as thinking, "In this way my memory has arisen"; because of this lack of perception,
one considers this memory to be intuitive (prātibha),
yet there is no memory that exists independent of attention (praṇidhāna) and other factors.
If it is asked how this is so regarding intuitive cognition (*prātibha*),
[the answer is: there is a restriction, just as in the case of experience, due to a specific quality of human karma.
Why does intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) not arise simultaneously now?
Just as karma intended for experience [does not produce] simultaneous experience.
In this way, a specific human effort does not act as the cause for intuitive insight; it does not produce multiple intuitive cognitions simultaneously.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because of the absence of a cause, we say no;
for the instrument possesses efficacy in the sequence of conditions.
If you think that there is an example for the rule "like enjoyment," but no logical reason (hetu), [then consider this:]
No— for because of the capacity of the instrument (karaṇa) in the succession of cognitions,
multiple cognitions do not arise simultaneously regarding a single object of knowledge, nor regarding multiple objects; this is so.
The capacity of the instrument is to be inferred from the observed sequence of cognitions as being of such a nature; it does not belong to the knower, for the knower—
whose nature is devoid of instruments— is not subject to multiplicity of bodies due to the simultaneity of cognitions.
And this is the second refutation: for one whose body is fixed,
because of the inherence of multiple cognitions [in a single locus], there would be the simultaneous recollection of multiple objects in a single location— somewhere.
For a knower whose body is situated in a particular location, cognition produced by the continuous contact of the sense organs with their objects inheres in a single region of the self. Therefore...

When the mind is conjoined [with the soul], then the simultaneous recollection of many previously known objects would follow as a logical consequence— because there is no succession in the conjunction with a single location.

Since the spatial points of the self are not distinct substances, there is no difference in their inherence in a single object; consequently, the refutation of the simultaneity of memory would be untenable.
This applies to the series of sounds as well.

However, just as sound is heard due to the proximity of the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) to its substrate, memory arises in the mind due to the proximity of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*); thus, there is no consequence of simultaneous production.
But the refutation has already been stated: "Because multiple cognitions do not co-inhere [in a single soul], there is no consequence of simultaneous recollection in a single location. (34)
As for the view held by some that "knowledge is an attribute of the self (puruṣadharma),
whereas desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)," that is [as follows].
It is refuted [as follows]:
"Because the commencement and cessation of activity are caused by the desire and aversion of one who possesses knowledge. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.35)
Indeed, this person first understands: "This is a means to my happiness;
this is a means to my suffering. Having understood what is a means to his own happiness, he desires to obtain it, and [avoids] the means to suffering.
He desires to abandon [it]. For one joined with the desire to attain, the specific effort for the sake of obtaining the means to happiness is "undertaking" (ārambha);
for one joined with the desire to abandon, it is the avoidance of the means to suffering.
Cessation [of activity] occurs in this way: there is a connection with a single entity for knowledge, desire, effort, aversion, pleasure, and pain.
This constitutes having a single agent and having a common substratum for knowledge, desire, and activity.
Therefore—
Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are attributes of the knower,
not of the insentient;
and [these] belong to the inner self (pratyagātman) in relation to the commencement and cessation [of activity].
Because it has been seen [in this case], it should be understood that there is inference regarding another [case]. // 35 //

On this point, the proponent of the doctrine that consciousness belongs to the elements (bhūtacaitanika) says: "Because desire and aversion have those [elements] as their mark, there is no denial [of consciousness] in earth and the other elements. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.36)
"Desire and aversion are the marks of undertaking and desisting.
It follows that for whom there are undertaking and desisting, for him there are desire and aversion,
and for him there is knowledge— [this applies] to those consisting of earth, water, fire, and air.
Consciousness is the conjunction [of the self] with desire, aversion, and knowledge, because the commencement and cessation of bodies are observed [to result from them]. // 36 //
NyS 3.2.37: Because the commencement and cessation [of action] are observed in the case of axes and similar tools.
The cessation of consciousness in the body [is established].
It follows that there is a conjunction with desire, aversion, and knowledge, because we observe the cessation of activity in the case of axes and the like.
Consciousness [belongs to the body] because we observe the initiation and cessation of activity in the instrument [of action].
Now, if it is argued that the connection of the body with desire and so forth is inconsistent, since such initiation and cessation of activity are absent in instruments like an axe, [we reply: no.
In that case, this is the reason: "The connection with desire, aversion, and cognition is established because we observe the commencement and cessation of earthy, watery, fiery, and airy bodies.
In that case, this is another meaning:
"Because desire and aversion have those as their marks, there is no denial [of them] in earth and the other [elements]" (VS 4.1.36).
To begin with, the origination of the elements, such as earth and so forth, [is as follows]:
In the bodies of mobile and stationary beings,
there is a specific activity characterized by the arrangement of their constituent parts;
this is because such a characteristic is absent in clods of earth and the like, and thus they lack that specific activity.
Cessation [is the mark].

Since desire and aversion are indicated by the commencement and cessation [of activity], and these are observed in the atoms of earth and the other elements, it is established that consciousness belongs to the elements because of their connection with those [desires and aversions] through the conjunction with cognition; thus, the sentience of the elements is proven.
NyS 3.2.38: [The argument] based on non-perception in jars and the like is not a valid reason.
The specific activity characterized by the arrangement of the constituent parts of clay, such as those of a jar, is "origination" (ārambha);

the absence of such specific activity in sand and the like is "cessation" (nivṛtti). Furthermore, clay and sand do not possess a connection with desire, aversion, effort, or cognition, merely because origination and cessation are observed in them.
Therefore,
the argument "because they have that as their mark" [regarding desire and aversion] is not a valid reason. // 38 //
But restriction and non-restriction are qualifiers of that [cause].
Of these two,
desire and aversion, restriction and non-restriction are the differentiators;
they are the factors that distinguish them, for the activity and cessation of the knower are caused by desire and aversion.
Not in its own substratum; rather, in the substratum of that which is employed. In that case, activity and cessation occur with respect to the elements being employed.
The justification for the lack of restriction is that [these qualities] do not exist in all [beings];
however, for one who possesses knowledge, [the states of] desire and aversion toward beings arise as their cause.
There would be no restriction of its commencement and cessation to its own substratum,
just as the activity of the elements is caused by other qualities.
Furthermore, because of the obstruction of qualities (*guṇa*), cessation occurs necessarily only in the primary elements (*bhūta*).
If activity and cessation were caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion, they would occur in their own substratum (the self) and not in the primary elements;
however, this is not the case. Therefore, knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort reside in the instigator (*prayojaka*), whereas activity and cessation reside in the instigated (*prayojya*).
This is established:
the multiplicity of knowers in a single body is without inferential support.
For one who maintains that consciousness consists of the primary elements (*bhūta-caitanyavādin*), there are many primary elements in a single body.

If one asserts that [the self possesses] the qualities of knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort, it follows that there is a plurality of knowers; for one who says "yes" [to this], there is no proof [for a single self], just as there are multiple knowers in different bodies due to the distinctness of their cognitions.
In this way, even with respect to a single body, there would be an inference for the plurality of knowers based on the arrangement of cognitions.
And since a specific activity of beings is observed to be caused by another quality, this serves as an inference for other cases as well.

It is observed that in the case of elements characterized as instruments, such as axes and the like, and those characterized as materials, such as clay and the like, there is a specific activity caused by the quality of another; this serves as an inference for other cases as well.
Thus, the specific activity of the elements within the bodies of mobile and immobile beings, which is evidenced by the particular arrangement of their parts, is caused by the quality of another.

And that quality, which has the same substratum as effort, is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) designated as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); it serves all purposes and, like effort, is the motivator for living beings toward the attainment of the goals of human life.
This is established by the reasons for the existence of the self and the reasons for the permanence of the self.
The refutation of the view that consciousness is an emergent property of the elements (*bhūta*) should be understood as having been established.

Furthermore, the refutation is equally applicable [to the views that consciousness resides] in the sense organs or their objects, because consciousness persists even when those [organs and objects] have perished. (18)
Intending that "commencement" and "cessation" refer merely to action and the mere cessation of action, it was stated:
"Because they are the marks of those [actions], there is no denial of desire and aversion in earth and the other elements. (VS 4.1.3)
(Thus it is said). Otherwise, however, these two—commencement and cessation—are expressed [by verbal roots].
And such [commencement and cessation] are not observed in the case of earth and the other [elements]; therefore, [the objection] is untenable.
"Because they possess those same marks, there is no denial [of desire and aversion] in the case of kings and others.
The same refutation applies to the elements, the sense organs, and the mind; however, the mind is mentioned merely as an illustration.
(Nyāyasūtra 3.2.40): [The mind is not eternal] because of the reasons already stated, because of its dependence on another, and because of the arrival of the results of actions not performed by it.

From the point beginning with "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks of the self" (NS 1.1.10), that which has been stated is summarized; by this, the sentience of the elements, the sense organs, and the mind is refuted.
Due to their dependence on another, the elements, the senses, and the mind are subordinate in the acts of sustaining, impelling, and arranging.

[The elements] proceed by the force of effort; however, if they were conscious, they would be independent. Furthermore, [this is so] because of the arrival of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). And: "Activity is the initiation of speech, mind, and body" (NS 1.1.17).
If the elements, the senses, and the mind were conscious, it would follow that the person experiences the fruit of actions performed by another; however, since they are unconscious,
the experience of the fruit of one's own performed actions belongs to the means [of action] themselves.
Thus, it is appropriate [to say] "of the person. // 40 //
Now, this is the summary of the established conclusion:
NyS 3.2.41: Because of the method of elimination (pariśeṣa) and because the previously stated reasons are applicable.
"Knowledge is a quality of the self"— this is the subject under discussion.

"Elimination by remainder" (pariśeṣa) means that when something has been excluded after its possibility was established, and because it cannot belong elsewhere, there arises a conviction regarding what remains.
When the elements, the sense organs, and the mind are negated, no other substance is implicated; the self alone remains, and it is known that knowledge is its quality.

"And because the reasons as stated are established"— that is, because there is no refutation of the reasons for establishing the self, such as [Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.1]: "Because one and the same object is apprehended by both seeing and touching," and so forth.

The statement of the proof for the reason as it has been stated is for the purpose of making known the remainder and for the purpose of making known the establishment of the subject (*prakṛta*) and so forth;
or alternatively, [it serves another purpose].
“And because of rebirth”—
this is indeed another reason: this self is certainly eternal, because, having practiced dharma in one body, [it experiences the results].
"Upon the dissolution of the body, one is reborn among the gods in heaven; having practiced unrighteousness,
upon the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in the hells"— this is rebirth (*upapatti*).
Characterized by the attainment of another body, that [consciousness] would have a basis only if a permanent self existed; however,
it exists merely as a continuum of cognition.
However, in the absence of a self, [transmigration] would be baseless and thus untenable.

Furthermore, it is tenable that *saṃsāra* consists in the connection of multiple bodies based upon a single sentient being. Moreover, it is tenable that liberation (*apavarga*) or release is the cessation of the continuity of the body.
If there were merely a continuum of consciousness, then since a single sentient being would be impossible,
no one would traverse the long course [of existence],
and no one would be liberated from the succession of bodies; thus, both saṃsāra and liberation would be untenable.
Moreover, if there were merely a continuum of consciousness, then because of the distinction between individual beings,
this entire collection of worldly transactions involving living creatures would be disconnected, uncoordinated, and incomplete,
due to the absence of recollection.
"One who has seen does not remember it as another," for memory indeed consists in the grasping by a cognizer identical [to the one] who previously knew.
"I have known this object to be known"—
this single knower grasps the object previously known, and that grasping of his is recollection. Thus, it pertains merely to the continuity of cognition.
It is not tenable in the case of that which is without self. // 41 //
Memory, however, belongs to the self because of its nature as a knower.
"It is established" means that the recollection belongs to the self alone, and not to the mere continuum of the intellect;
the word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis.
How so?
Because its nature is that of a knower (*jñasvābhāvyāt*); "knower" is its own inherent property—this [Self] indeed will know.
He is connected with manifold cognitions pertaining to the three periods of time, such as "he knows" and "he has known. And this cognition of his, which has the three periods of time as its object,
is to be personally experienced— namely, "I shall know."

The expressions "I know" and "I have known" are used [in this sense]. Therefore, memory belongs to that which has this as its own nature; it does not belong to a mere continuum of cognition that is devoid of a self. // 42 //
It has been stated that there is no simultaneous recollection because the causes of memory do not occur simultaneously;
now, from what does memory arise?
Memory, indeed—

NyS 3.2.43: *Praṇidhāna* (volition) is the fixing of the mind by means of a cause for remembering— such as a vow, a bond, repetition, a mark, a characteristic, similarity, possession, that which is supported, that which supports, a connection, immediate succession, separation, a single effect, opposition, excellence, attainment, intervention, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, fear, purposefulness, action, passion, merit, or demerit— and it consists in reflecting upon the mark of that which one wishes to remember.
And it is the cause for the recollection of meaning. 1.
Binding (nibandha) indeed consists in the gathering of meanings into a single composition;
for meanings gathered into a single composition [are easily remembered].
They exist either in a sequential order or otherwise as causes for mutual recollection,
or they are produced by the treatises on mnemonic retention (dhāraṇā).
2. *Nibandha* (connection) is the placing together of things to be remembered among objects already known.

3. *Abhyāsa* (repetition), however, is the recurrence of cognitions regarding the same object; the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by repetition, which is a quality of the self, is designated by the term *abhyāsa*, and it is a cause of memory because it is common [to the objects].
4. Furthermore, *liṅga* (the inferential mark) is that which is related by conjunction (*saṃyogin*), inherent (*samavāyin*), or inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*).
And "contradictory" [is another type]:
the conjoined (saṃyogi), such as smoke [in relation] to fire, a horn [in relation] to a cow, a hand [in relation] to a foot, or color [in relation to its substrate].
Regarding contact, [the phrase] "of the non-existent and of the existent" (4) refers to the characteristic residing in the five limbs,
which is the cause for the recollection of the lineage— this belongs to the learned.
5. "This belongs to the Gargas," and 6. similarity, such as a portrait or a likeness of Devadatta depicted in a painting, and so forth.

7. From possession (*parigraha*): one remembers the owner by means of his property, or the property by means of its owner. 8. From the locus (*āśraya*): one remembers that which is subordinate to it by means of the village headman. 9. From the dependent (*āśrita*):...
"By one dependent on him, [one says] 'the village headman'" (9)—
this is due to a relationship; for example, one remembers the teacher as being joined with the pupil, or the sacrificer as being joined with the officiating priest.
10. Because of immediacy—regarding those matters that ought to be done; 11.
Because of separation—he intensely remembers that by which he is separated, experiencing the sensation of that separation; 12.
From a common purpose— recollection of another agent arises from seeing a different agent (13); from opposition— the perception of one of two contending parties leads to the inference of the other.
It is recorded [in the scriptures]: (14) due to excellence—that by which an excellence has been produced;
(15) due to attainment—that one frequently remembers him from whom something has been obtained or is to be obtained. (16)
Due to intervention— swords and the like are remembered [only] through sheaths and such;
likewise, [the self is not perceived] due to pleasure and pain.
Its cause is memory (19);
through desire and aversion, one remembers that which one desires and that which one hates (21).

From fear—from that of which one is afraid (22); from desire—for that by which one desires, such as food or clothing (23); and through action—a chariot-maker remembers [his work] by means of a chariot (24).
From passion— when one is attached to a woman,
one remembers her repeatedly (25); from dharma,
there is the recollection of other births in this world.

From unrighteousness (*adharma*), one remembers the means of suffering previously experienced (27); and since simultaneous cognitions do not arise with respect to these causes, there is no simultaneous recollection.
And this is merely an illustration of the causes of mindfulness, not an exhaustive enumeration. // 43 //

And since cognition is impermanent, there arises a doubt regarding things that are impermanent— due to their perishing as soon as they arise and because of their persistence for a period of time— is cognition like sound, perishing as soon as it arises, or rather is it like a jar, persisting for a period of time?
The position is adopted that [the soul] possesses origination and cessation;
why?
Because action is perceived as non-durable (NyS 3.2.44).
"Because of the perception of action as non-abiding"—
that is, a continuum of activity is perceived from the moment a discharged arrow is released until it falls, and because cognitions are restricted to their respective objects.
The occurrence of a continuum of cognition is like a continuum of action;

furthermore, when an object is perceived as persisting, direct perception ceases for that which is being interrupted. And when a jar is perceived as persisting, it is indeed by means of a continuum [of cognitions].
Cognition functions prior to the intervention [of an object]. Therefore,
when [an object] is intervened by that [time], perceptual knowledge ceases,
provided it persists for another duration of time.
But even when there is an intervention by the object of perception, cognition would still remain perceptible;
furthermore, memory is not a valid inferential mark for the persistence of cognition, because memory is caused by a latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by that cognition.
And as for one who might think— "The intellect persists"— for memory is observed regarding an object of the intellect, and that [memory] would not exist if the intellect were impermanent.
The claim that "it would not exist due to the absence of a cause" is not a valid logical mark (*aliṅga*).
Why? Because a mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is born of cognition (*buddhi*).
A different quality is the cause of memory, not cognition.
If it is argued that this is incorrect because of the absence of a cause, [we reply:
since it exists as a state of cognition, there is no absence of memory when it is perceptual.
As long as the cognition persists, so long is the object to be cognized perceptual; and since memory is untenable regarding that which is being perceived, [the object] must be past. // 44 //
The non-apprehension of the unmanifest [sound] is due to its instability, like the non-apprehension of form during a flash of lightning.
If the cognition belongs to the class of those that have arisen,
it follows that the apprehension of the object to be known would be indistinct;
just as, for example, during a flash of lightning, the light of the lightning is indistinct because of its instability.
Regarding the phrase "the grasping of form": since the grasping of substances is actually manifest, this [position] is therefore incorrect. // 45 //
NyS 3.2.46: By the employment of a reason, there is the admission of that which is to be negated.
The view that "cognition perishes as soon as it has arisen" must be refuted;
rather, that very [view] is accepted [in the following manner]:
"like the perception of an indistinct form during a flash of lightning."
Thus [ends verse] 46.
Where there is an indistinct apprehension,
there the cognition arises and ceases;
the variation in apprehension results from a variation in the cause of apprehension, not from a variation in the cognition itself.

That is to say, this conceptualization— which consists of grasping that is indistinct in some respects and distinct in others— is not established anywhere because it arises from the conceptualization that serves as the cause for grasping.
In that context, the unmanifest is the cause of apprehension, while the manifest is where [the object] is situated; it is not, however, due to the mind's (buddhi) abiding or non-abiding.
Why? Because the apprehension of the object is indeed the mind.

That apprehension of an object, whether unmanifest or manifest, is what constitutes the intellect (*buddhi*); and therein, the apprehension of a generality when specific qualities are not apprehended is the unmanifest apprehension.
The non-arising of another cognition regarding a different object is due to the absence of a cause.

Where a substratum (dharmin) is perceived as endowed with both general properties (sāmānyadharma) and specific properties (viśeṣadharma), that is a clear perception; however, in that case, if the specific property is not being perceived—
The mere apprehension of the universal is that indistinct apprehension; and due to the connection with specific attributes, the connection with particular attributes constitutes a different object.
In this regard, that there is no apprehension [of the object] is due to the absence of the cause for apprehension, and not because of a non-cessation of the intellect;
moreover, apprehension is clearly manifest according to its respective objects, because it is restricted to each particular object.
The apprehension of cognitions has a universal as its object, while the apprehension directed toward its own specific object is clearly characterized by a particular as its object.
It is manifest with respect to its own object— for cognitions are restricted to their respective objects— this is what is taught as the apprehension of the unmanifest.
In what respect could there be a lack of stability of the cognition?
Rather, the establishment of that [cognition] occurs through the presence or absence of a plurality of cognitions regarding the differences in the attributes (dharmas) of the substratum (dharmin).
For indeed, the object which is the substratum has both common and...

And those properties are distinct and restricted to their respective objects; if those various cognitions—both [the universal and the particular]—subsist in the substratum, then the apprehension is clearly intended with respect to that substratum. But when...

The apprehension of that which consists merely of the universal is then the unmanifest apprehension. Thus, with reference to the substratum (*dharmin*), the occurrence of both manifest and unmanifest apprehensions is established; it is not [otherwise].
And this unmanifest perception of either the intellect or the object of cognition is possible because of their non-static nature.
For this is stated in Nyāyasūtra 3.2.47: "The apprehension of that [object] is not like the apprehension of what is manifested by the continuity of a lamp's flame."
Even though cognition is non-durable,
the apprehension of those substances must be understood as being manifest.
How so?

Just as in the case of the perception of a lamp-flame made manifest by its continuity, there is a non-abiding of the grasping and a non-abiding of the object to be grasped, because the lamp-flames exist as a continuous succession.
Alternatively, because cognitions are restricted to their respective objects, there are as many cognitions as there are flames of a lamp;
and this is clearly observed in this case.
The apprehension of the flames of a lamp. // 47 //
Volition is a quality of the body, because it exists when the body exists and is absent when the body is absent.
(Nyāyasūtra 3.2.48): There is doubt [regarding whether volition belongs to the body] because qualities belonging both to itself and to others are perceived in a substance.
The state of being doubtful is as follows: in water, its own quality, fluidity, is perceived, as well as the quality of another, namely heat.
Therefore, this doubt arises: is consciousness a quality of the body?
Is it perceived as a quality of the body itself, or is it a quality of some other substance? // 48 //
Consciousness is not a quality of the body;
why?
Because qualities such as color and so forth persist only as long as the body exists. (NyS 3.2.49)
A body devoid of form and so forth is not perceived, whereas one devoid of consciousness is perceived—just as water devoid of heat [is perceived];
therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body.
If it is argued that [the self] is like the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), we say no— because there is no cessation of its cause.
Is it the case that the cessation [of mental activity] occurs in relation to the very same kind of substance as that in which the impression (saṃskāra) resides? No;
for in that case, due to the destruction of the cause, there is an absolute non-arising of impressions.

Just as consciousness is perceived in a body of a certain kind, so too is the absolute cessation of consciousness perceived in that very same kind of body. Therefore, the argument "like conditioned phenomena" (saṃskāravat) is not analogous.
Concentration.
Furthermore, if the cause for the arising of consciousness were to reside in the body, or in some other substance, or in both, that is not the case—
Because there is no cause for restriction, there is no reason for the restriction that consciousness sometimes arises while residing in the body and sometimes does not.

Furthermore, there is no restrictive cause for why consciousness arises only in the body when residing in another substance, and not in clods of earth and so forth; for [consciousness] resides in both.

If [consciousness] were caused by a substance of the same genus as the body, there would be no reason for the restriction that consciousness does not arise in other substances of that same genus as the body, but arises only in the body itself. // 49 //

And as for the thought that— just as when a substance possessing qualities such as blackness is present, the cessation of that blackness and so forth is indeed observed, so too might there be a cessation of consciousness— it is not so.
No, because of the production of another quality arising from baking.
"An absolute cessation of form" means that when the dark color of a substance has ceased, another quality produced by heating— namely, a red color—
arises; however, in the case of the body...
The complete cessation of mere volition. // 50 //
Moreover: "Because [the existence of] things produced by baking is established by their opposites, there is no refutation [of our position]. (NyS 3.2.51)

In as many substances as there is the establishment of qualities contrary to those previously present, in that many is the production of qualities born of heating (*pākaja*) observed— because the coexistence of qualities born of heating with the previous qualities is not perceived. And this is not the case in the body.
If another quality, which is the opposite of consciousness and cannot coexist with it, were apprehended, then by that [apprehension] the contradiction of consciousness would be inferred.
Therefore, if consciousness were unobstructed, it would persist as long as the body exists; however, it does not so persist.
Consequently, consciousness is not a quality of the body. // 51 //
For this reason as well, consciousness is not a quality of the body:
because it pervades the entire body. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.52)

Since both the body and all its parts are pervaded by the arising of consciousness, there is no place where consciousness does not arise. Consequently, it follows that just as there is a body, so too are its parts conscious; thus, a multiplicity of conscious entities results.

In that case, just as the distribution of pleasure, pain, and cognition serves as a mark for the multiplicity of conscious beings in respect to each individual body, so too would it be within a single body; but this is not so.
But it does not [occur]. Therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body. // 52 //
As for what was said—
that there is no place among the parts of the body where consciousness does not arise— that is not so.
NyS 3.2.53: [The objection that] it is not [so] because of the non-perception [of the soul] in hair, nails, and so forth.
Since consciousness does not arise in the hair, nails, and so forth, its pervasiveness throughout the body is untenable. // 53 //
NyS 3.2.54: Because the body extends only as far as the skin, there is no [logical] application [of the definition of the body] to the hair, nails, and so forth.
The defining characteristic of the body is that it is the substratum of the sense faculties.
The body is that which extends to the skin and serves as the locus for the experience of life, mind, pleasure, and pain; therefore, consciousness does not arise in hair and the like.
However, the attachment of the body to the hair and so forth is for the sake of performing a function. // 54 //
For this reason as well, consciousness is not a quality of the body—because it possesses characteristics contrary to those of the qualities of the body. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.55)

The quality of the body is twofold: that which is imperceptible, namely gravity, and that which is perceivable by the senses, such as color and so forth; however, consciousness is of a different category altogether.

It is not imperceptible, because it is an object of cognition; nor is it graspable by the [external] sense organs, because its domain is the mind. Therefore, it is a quality belonging to a distinct substance. // 55 //
NyS 3.2.56: No, because color and the other [sensory objects] possess mutual dissimilarity.

Just as form and the other [sensory objects], though possessing mutually distinct properties, do not forfeit their status as qualities of the body, so too consciousness, despite its dissimilarity to form and the rest, will not forfeit its status as a quality of the body. // 56 //
NyS 3.2.57: There is no refutation [of the existence] of form and so forth, because they are supersensuous.
And because it is not perceptible;

for just as color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], which possess mutually distinct characteristics, do not transcend the two-fold classification, so too [the self] does not, due to its being of a different nature from color-form and the rest.
Volition would not transcend duality if it were a quality of the body; however,
it does transcend it, and therefore it is not a quality of the body.

Since the negation of knowledge regarding the elements (bhūta), the sense organs (indriya), and the mind (manas) has already been established, this new undertaking is for the purpose of making known a specific distinction:
that reality (tattva), when examined in many ways, becomes even more firmly ascertained. // 57 //
The intellect has been examined;
now follows the sequence for examining the mind. In this regard, we investigate whether it is one or many in each body.
NyS 3.2.58: Because cognitions do not occur simultaneously, the mind is one.
Indeed, there is a non-simultaneity of cognitions;
for each individual sense organ has the capacity to produce only a single cognition with respect to its respective object.

That [simultaneity of cognitions] is not a mark for the oneness of the mind. Rather, the fact that there is no simultaneity of cognitions regarding different objects by the various sense organs is indeed the mark.
Why? Because it is possible for there to be many minds.
If there were simultaneity in the conjunction of the sense-faculties and the mind, there would be simultaneity of cognitions; however, this does not occur.
Therefore, because cognitions of objects arise in succession, the mind is one.
Thus it is said. // 58 //
Not so, because multiple actions are perceived simultaneously.
Indeed, this teacher studies, walks, carries his water-pot,
looks at the path, hears the sounds produced by forest creatures, fears them, and desires to know the signs of wild beasts.

Furthermore, because one remembers that "what is to be gone to" and "the place where one stands" [simultaneously], and since no sequence is perceived, it follows that these actions occur at once; thus, the multiplicity of the mind is established. // 59 //
The perception of that [succession] occurs due to rapid movement, like the sight of a whirling firebrand.
Due to the rapid movement of a whirling firebrand,
its existing sequence is not perceived;
because the sequence is not perceived, there arises the cognition of continuity.
The intellect functions like a wheel; thus, due to the rapid succession of cognitions and actions, it appears as if existing [simultaneously].
The sequence is not perceived. Because the sequence is not perceived, there arises the misconception that the action occurs simultaneously.
But why is this so?
Is it because the sequence is not perceived that there is the misconception of simultaneity?
Or is it that the perception of multiple actions as simultaneous occurs precisely because they exist simultaneously?
In this regard, no reason for the apprehension of such a distinction is stated.
It has been stated:
"Cognitions of the various sense organs arise with respect to their respective objects in succession."
And that [simultaneity] cannot be denied, because it is directly perceived by oneself.
Furthermore, one should infer from this that when a person reflects on objects seen or heard, cognitions arise in succession and not simultaneously.
Because the cognitions of phonemes, words, and sentences, as well as the cognitions of their meanings, occur with such rapidity, the sequence is not perceived.
How so? Indeed, in the case of those [cognitions] residing in a sentence...
While the phonemes are being articulated, there is first of all the hearing of each individual phoneme.
Having heard one or more phonemes, one synthesizes them into the form of a word. Having synthesized them, one determines the word. By means of this determination of the word...
Through memory, one apprehends the meaning of the words, and by synthesizing the collection of words, one determines the sentence.
Having grasped the related word-meanings, [one apprehends] the sentence-meaning.
It proceeds [in this way],

yet because these cognitions occur in succession with such rapidity, their sequence is not perceived; thus, this is the inference [that proves] that the impression of simultaneity regarding the activity of cognitions occurs elsewhere [than in reality].
Furthermore, there is no doubt-free simultaneous arising of cognitions by which one might infer a multiplicity of minds within a single body. Thus [ends verse 60].
And because it possesses the aforementioned cause, it is atomic.
The atom and the mind are each one; this is a conjunction of properties— because knowledge is not simultaneous,
whereas if the mind were large, there would be simultaneous contact with all the sense organs.
There would be the apprehension of an object. // 61 //
Indeed, sir, the mind together with the senses attains its function within the body and nowhere else than in the body;
and for the knowing Puruṣa, the body is his abode.
Cognition and the like, the enjoyment of objects, the avoidance of what is to be shunned, the attainment of what is desired, and all worldly activities whatsoever are dependent upon the body.
In this regard,
due to conflicting views, there arises a doubt: Is this creation of the body caused by human action?
Or rather, is it caused by the mere elements and not by karma?
Indeed, a disagreement is heard regarding this point;
herein lies the truth:
Its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of actions performed in the past.

The activity in a previous body—characterized by the initiation of speech, intellect, and the physical body—is called "previously performed karma" (*pūrvakṛta-karma*); its fruit consists of the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) produced thereby. The "consequence" (*anubandha*) of that fruit is its continued persistence as something inherent in the self (*ātma-samaveta*). From those [causes] impelled by that [consequence],...
The production of that body is not from independent elements; rather,
it is that which serves as the locus for this self, which, conceiving "I am this," is engaged in [action] and possesses a thirst for experience therein.
Not perceiving sense objects, it forms merit and demerit;
that is its body. By means of that formation characterized by merit and demerit, together with the primary elements, when this [body] has fallen—
Another body is produced within the [original] body;
and once it has been produced, its performance of purposeful action for the person is like that of the previous body, and the person’s [relation to] the previous body is likewise.

The activity of speech and so forth is possible when the production of a body occurs from the elements dependent upon karma; for it is observed that [activity] arises from the elements impelled by effort, which is a quality of the person (puruṣa).

The production of substances such as chariots and the like, which are capable of performing purposeful actions for a person, must be inferred by that [analogy]: "The body also, being produced, is capable of performing purposeful actions for a person."
"The [body] of a person arises from the elements which depend upon other qualities. // 62 //
On this point, the nihilist says:
"The appropriation of that [body] occurs from the elements, just as the appropriation of form [occurs]. (NyS 3.2.63)
Just as forms such as sand, gravel, stones, red chalk, collyrium, and so forth— which are produced from elements independent of karma—
are appropriated because they serve the purposes of human beings, so too [is this case].
The body is produced from elements that are independent of karma; it is appropriated because it serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha). // 63 //
No, because it is equivalent to the probandum.
Just as the production of a body is to be proven as being without the cause of karma,

so too the creation of sand, gravel, stones, red ochre, collyrium, and so forth must be proven as being without the cause of karma; since it is equivalent to what is yet to be proven, it does not constitute a valid proof— just as [the argument] "like the taking up of forms from the elements."
And this is what must be proven by him. // 64 //
NyS 3.2.65: [The self is not produced] because the mother and father are merely the cause of its birth.
Moreover, this presentation is inconsistent;
why? Because these forms arise without a seed, whereas the production of a body is preceded by a seed.
By the term "mother and father," the blood and semen which constitute the seed are understood; therein,
there is the karma of the sentient being to be experienced as dwelling in the womb, and that of the parents to be experienced as having a son.
Since the two karmas cause the production of the body from the elements within the mother’s womb, it is logically established that there is conformity with the seed. // 65 //
Likewise, [the same applies] to nutriment.
The subject under discussion is "because it is the cause of production";
[this refers to] food that has been eaten or drunk.
The substance of nutrient essence (*rasadravya*) produced by digestion accumulates in the mother's body;
while the seed resides in the womb, it grows in proportion to the seed’s own maturation and increases in measure as long as the seed [remains].

"Accumulation" (saṃcaya) refers to that which is capable of formation (vyūha). Once accumulated, it is formed through the stages of the *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, *kaṇḍara*, head, hands, and so forth—by way of a formation consisting of the differentiation of the seats of the sense faculties (*indriyādhiṣṭhāna*).
And during this formation, the substance of nutritive essence (*rasadravya*) brought down by the umbilical cord of the embryo is further augmented.
As long as it is capable of producing [results],
this [food] is not fit for consumption when it has entered into a vessel or similar container;
for this reason, it is characterized by its causal nature as karma.
It is understood as belonging to the body. // 66 //
And because there is no restriction regarding attainment.
Not every union of husband and wife is observed to be the cause of conception.
In this regard, since [conception] does not occur when the [specific] action is absent and it does occur when that action is present, the absence of a universal rule is established.

If the elements that cause the production of the body were independent of karma, there would be a fixed necessity; for in this case, there would be no absence of a cause [for such a necessity]. // 67 //
Moreover:
"Action is the cause of the production of conjunction, just as it is the cause of the production of the body. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.68)

Just as this body consists of channels that carry the bodily constituents and the vital breaths, as well as the constituents ending with semen, and of sinews, skin, bones, vessels, muscles, the embryo, and tendons,
as well as the head, arms, abdomen, and thighs.
The wind, bile, and phlegm residing within the visceral cavities, as well as the mouth, throat, heart, stomach, large intestine, and the lower channels,
are situated in an arrangement that produces extreme suffering.
Since it is impossible for the earth and other elements to produce [the body] when independent of karma,
the arising of the body has karma as its cause.
It is understood that,
because there is no such individual-specific cause and because they are connected with unsurpassed selves, the [bodies] produced by all selves from earth and the other elements are not identical.

Furthermore, since there is no cause for restriction regarding that which resides in the earth and other elements, it follows that the body— the means for all selves to experience pleasure and pain— would be common to all.
As for that which is established individually for each person,
it is understood that karma, which is the cause for the arising of the body, is the factor of determination therein.

For the latent impression of karma (*karmāśaya*), which is determined for each individual and is undergoing ripening, produces a body as the locus of experience for that very self in which it resides.
Thus, it is established that action is the cause of conjunction, just as it is the cause for the production of the body; this is how it is understood.
However, we maintain that the individual determination [of experience] is the conjunction of the body with the self. // 68 //
By this, the restriction (niyama) has been refuted.
This which is called "restriction" (niyama) when the production of the body occurs without the cause of karma is as follows:
"Like the cause for the production of the body..."
This has been answered by the statement: "Action is the cause for the production of conjunction" (68).
What, then, is this restriction?
The rule is that as the body belongs to one self, so it belongs to all;
otherwise, it would be different for another.
"Of one thing in another way" means there is no fixed rule;
"difference" (bheda) is a specific exclusion (vyāvṛtti).
Thus, the exclusion of birth is observed— namely, as being of high birth or low birth, praiseworthy or censurable,
full of disease or free from disease.
"Complete or incomplete," "abounding in suffering or abounding in happiness," "endowed with the marks of a superior person or the opposite," and "possessing praiseworthy marks or censurable marks."
There are those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties; moreover, the subtle distinctions are immeasurable.
This differentiation of births arises from the differentiation of karma, which is determined for each individual.

In the absence of a distinction in karma determined for each individual, because selves are without excellence and because earth and the other elements are uniform, [there would be no distinction] regarding that which resides in earth and the other elements.
Due to the absence of a cause for restriction, everything would follow as being of the nature of everything else; however,
this is not the case.
Therefore, birth is not caused by a lack of action; thus, the production of the body does not have non-action as its cause. // 69 //
And the separation from that [bondage] is established, because the exhaustion of karma is established.

Since the production of the body is caused by karma, the separation of the self from that body is logically established. Why? Because the exhaustion of karma is established; indeed, the exhaustion of karma is established through right vision (*samyagdarśana*).
When delusion has been exhausted, one who is free from passion performs no karma that causes rebirth through body, speech, or mind; thus, there is no further accumulation of future existence.
There is exhaustion through the experience of the maturation of what was previously accumulated;
thus, due to the absence of a cause for further production, there is no re-linking because another body does not arise again once this body has fallen away.
But if the production of the body were caused by karma, then because the destruction of the elements would be impossible, their separation from the body would also be impossible. // 70 //
If it is argued that this is caused by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then that same consequence would follow even at the time of final liberation (*apavarga*).
Indeed, non-perception is called "the unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*).
The production of the body from the elements is caused by the unseen.
For as long as the body has not been produced, the seer cannot exist without a locus.
He perceives the visible. And this visible object of his is twofold:
the objective field and the diversity between the unmanifest and the self; for that purpose, the creation of the body occurs.
When that [process] has ceased, the elements, having accomplished their purpose, do not produce a body; thus, the dissociation from the body is established. In this way...
If you think that,
then the consequence is that liberation would entail the production of a body once again. That is, the recurrence of bodily birth would follow.
The non-arising of perception when the body has not yet arisen, which is considered non-perception,
and the non-arising of perception upon liberation when the body has ceased, which constitutes non-perception—
there is no difference whatsoever between these two forms of non-perception; thus, there would be no cessation of non-perception even in liberation.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the body arising again.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in the fact that [the agent] has already achieved his purpose, we say no; for we observe the commencement of both doing and not doing.
If it is argued that the specific distinction is that the elements, having achieved their purpose, do not initiate another body because they terminate with the final vision [of truth],
we say: no.

Because the commencement [of a body] is observed both through the performance and the non-performance [of actions]: for the elements, once their purpose has been fulfilled, are seen to repeatedly initiate a body in order to perform the apprehension of objects;
whereas [the reverse is true] because of the non-performance of the discernment of the difference between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

The repeated undertaking of a body is seen to be purposeless. Therefore, since the creation of the elements is not caused by karma, it is not logical that the production of a body is for the sake of perception. Rather, it is logical [that it serves another purpose].
In a creation caused by karma, the production of a body is for the purpose of seeing;
"seeing" is the experience of the fruition of karma,
and it is the view of some that this is brought about by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
The so-called *adṛṣṭa* is a specific quality of atoms that serves as the cause of action; impelled by it, the atoms coalesce and produce the body, which the mind then enters.
Impelled by its own unperceived quality (adṛṣṭa), the perception of the seer occurs within the body endowed with the internal organ (samanaska).
This is indeed the view in this system.
Furthermore, because the qualities [of the atoms] are not destroyed, that same consequence follows:
in every instance of liberation, the production of a body would occur, since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is a quality of the atoms, is indestructible. // 71 //
And because mental action is the cause [of contact], there is no cessation of conjunction.
If the mind were permeated by an unseen mental quality (*adṛṣṭa*),
there would be no severance of the conjunction [between the mind and the self]. In that case, what would cause the mind's departure from the body?
But when the latent deposit of karma is exhausted, it is possible for [the soul] to withdraw from another latent deposit of karma that is currently maturing.

If it is argued that the departure [of the soul] is due to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone, we say no; for that same unseen force which is the cause of the soul's approach to the body cannot also be the cause of its departure.
Because it is logically untenable for a single [unseen force] to be the cause of both living and departing;
this being the case, it follows that a single unseen force (adṛṣṭa) must be the cause of both living and departing.
This is not tenable. // 72 //
And there would follow the consequence of eternality, because death would be impossible.
Death is the falling away of the body upon the exhaustion of the accumulation of karma through the experience of its fruition. From another accumulation of karma, there is rebirth.
But if the production of the body were to occur from the mere elements alone, independent of karma, then upon whose exhaustion would the body fall away?
Regarding "departure" (*prāyaṇa*):
indeed, we understand that because departure is impossible, there would follow the consequence of [the self] being eternal.
But if death were accidental, the distinction between different types of death would be untenable. // 73 //
"Furthermore, there would be the recurrence of that [fault] in the case of liberation (apavarga).
Desiring to establish this, he says:
"This might be like the non-eternality of the blackness of atoms. (Nyāyasūtra 3.2.74)

Just as the blackness of an atom, though eternal, does not arise again when it is obstructed by contact with fire, so too the body produced by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) does not arise again upon liberation (apavarga). // 74 //
Not so, because it would entail the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed.
This is not a valid analogy; why?
Because it would entail the consequence of obtaining what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). It is "not done."
Its acquisition is not established by means of valid cognition;
"acquisition" (abhyupagama) means acceptance (abhyupapatti), which is to say, admission (abhyupāya).
One who has faith in this should consider it to be logically untenable as a valid means of knowledge;
therefore, this is not a valid example— namely, that "nothing is said [to be established] through perception or inference."
This is stated to be the "equality of the example with the probandum" (*sādhyasamatva*).
Alternatively: [The view that the body arises without a cause] is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of experiencing the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅga*);
for by the example of the blackness of atoms (*aṇuśyāmatā*), one would imply that the production of the body is not caused by karma.
For one who maintains [the self as permanent], there follows the consequence of the arrival of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅga*).
It would follow that pleasure and pain arrive for a person even when the karma that is the cause of pleasure and pain has not been performed.
For one who asserts "om," there is contradiction with perception, inference, and scripture.
First, there is contradiction with perception: this pleasure and pain are distinct, because they are perceived by each individual self; this is directly perceived by all embodied beings.
What is the distinction? It is the differentiation such as intense or mild, long-lasting or brief, manifold or uniform, and so forth;
yet there is no [distinction] fixed for each individual soul.
There is a distinction between the causes of pleasure and pain, and no distinction in the effect is observed when there is no distinction in the cause; however,
regarding the connection with pleasure and pain caused by karma, [it is due to] the karmas.

The distinction between pleasure and pain is established through the occurrence of intensity and mildness, the existence of increase and decrease in the accumulation of karmas, and the fact that karmas are both manifold and uniform.
Thus, because there would be no difference in the cause, this observed distinction between pleasure and pain would not exist; this constitutes a contradiction with direct perception.
Likewise, there is a contradiction with inference: for it is observed that the distribution of pleasure and pain results from the distribution of human qualities;
indeed, whoever is conscious [acts] toward what is to be accomplished by means.
Having understood pleasure and desiring it, one strives to obtain its means; such a person is joined with happiness, and not one who acts otherwise.
And likewise, having understood that suffering is to be brought about by its own causes...
One who desires to abandon that [suffering] strives for the avoidance of its causes;
such a person is abandoned by suffering, but not one who acts otherwise. Furthermore, this establishment of pleasure and pain for sentient beings does not occur without effort.
There must also be an inference that this [experience] is produced by the establishment of a distinct quality of volition (*cetanā*);
however, this contradicts the position that the connection with pleasure and pain is not caused by karma.
Furthermore, that other quality (dharma/adharma) is unperceived because it is not an object of consciousness, and it is indeterminate because there is no fixed rule for the time of its fruition;
the intellect and the other [evolutes], however, are both perceivable and subject to cessation.
Now, there is a contradiction with scripture: "Indeed,
I have heard much from the sages regarding the collection of their instructions concerning what is to be practiced and what is to be avoided,
as well as the fruit of those instructions for embodied beings."
Activity characterized by performance according to the divisions of caste and stage of life is *pravṛtti*, while that characterized by avoidance is *nivṛtti*.
According to this view, neither of these two exists; there is no such thing as well-performed action.
Or, [the claim] that "the connection of men with pleasure and pain is caused by their own past actions (karma)" would be contradicted; this [view] belongs to the most wicked.
False view (mithyādṛṣṭi) is the belief that "the creation of the body is not caused by karma, and the connection with pleasure and pain is not caused by karma. // 75 //
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the third chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya of Vātsyāyana.
And the third chapter is completed.
Now begins the first section of the fourth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya with its commentary (Saṭīka).
The activity following immediately after the mind is to be examined;
indeed, everything that has been examined up to this point—such as the body which is the substratum of merit and demerit—is the examination of activity.
Thus it is said: "Activity is as previously described. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.1)
Thus it has been examined. // 1 //
"In that case, let the defects immediately following activity be examined"; to this he says:
"In the same way, the defects [are to be examined]. (NyS 4.1.2)
They have been examined as follows:

because they reside in the same substratum as the intellect (*buddhi*), they are qualities of the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, because they are the cause of activity and possess the capacity for the reconnection of rebirth, they are the causes of *saṃsāra*. Since *saṃsāra* is beginningless, it proceeds through a beginningless continuum;

the cessation of false knowledge occurs through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and upon that cessation, when the continuity of passion and aversion is severed, there is liberation (*apavarga*).
Thus it has been stated regarding the defects that they possess the nature of appearing and disappearing, and so forth. // 2 //
It was stated [in NS 1.1.18] that "faults (doṣas) have the characteristic of causing [the cycle of existence] to proceed.
In that case, why are these—namely, pride, envy, malice, doubt, avarice, and so forth—not included? To this he says: NS 4.1.3:
"That [threefold division] consists of three groups because they are distinct from passion, hatred, and delusion."
These faults consist of three groups or three categories:
the category of attachment—namely, lust, envy, longing, craving, and greed; the category of aversion—namely, anger, jealousy, malice, hostility, and resentment;
and the category of delusion—namely, false knowledge, doubt, pride, and negligence. Because they fall into these three groups, they are not enumerated separately.

If it is argued that, because their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is non-different, their threefold nature is untenable—this is not untenable, because passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*) have distinct meanings. Passion is characterized by attachment; hatred is characterized by intolerance; and delusion is characterized by false cognition.
This is to be personally experienced by all embodied beings:

this embodied being recognizes a desire that has arisen, thinking, "There is the quality of passion within me," and he recognizes the absence of passion, thinking, "There is no quality of passion within me. The same applies to the other two [feelings].
But pride, envy, malice, and so forth, because they fall within the three categories [of the previously mentioned faults], are not enumerated separately. // 3 //
Not so, because there is no state of being a single counter-argument.
Attachment and the other afflictions are not distinct entities; why?
Because they have a single adversary, which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Right understanding, noble wisdom, and full awakening— this is the triad of opposites to those three. // 4 //
Because of deviation, it is not a valid reason.

On earth, substances such as black [iron] and others have a single counter-positive (ekapratyanīka) through their conjunction with a single fire; and those produced by baking (pākaja) have a single origin (ekayoni). // 5 //
And since they exist as distinct entities:
"Among these, delusion (moha) is the worst, because the others do not arise in one who is not deluded. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.6)
Delusion is either a sin or a greater sin; this was said with reference to two [other sins]. Why?
Because the other two do not arise in one who is not deluded:
passion and hatred do not arise in one who is free from delusion.
For the deluded person, however, birth occurs according to their volitions (*saṃkalpa*).

Among objects, volitions that are provocative of passion are the cause of attachment (*rāga*); volitions that are provocative of anger are the cause of aversion (*dveṣa*). And both types of volitions are not distinct from delusion (*moha*), because they are characterized by wrong practice;
thus, these two—attachment and aversion—have their origin in delusion.
Furthermore, when delusion ceases through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), passion and aversion do not arise; thus, there is the logical establishment of their being mutual opposites.

And having established this, [the Sūtra states]: "From the knowledge of reality, upon the successive disappearance of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and finally false knowledge, from the disappearance of each preceding member, there follows the disappearance of the one immediately following it, which is liberation" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.2).
Thus it has been explained. // 6 //
In that case, it follows:
[Nyāyasūtra 4.1.7] Because of the relationship between cause and effect, there is a state of being a different entity from the defects.
For the cause (nimitta) is one thing and the effect of that cause (naimittaka) is another; therefore, because delusion (moha) has faults as its cause, it is not itself a fault. // 7 //
[Reply: No, because delusion is included within the definition of a fault.
By this definition of a defect, namely, "A defect has the characteristic of causing [the mind] to function" (NS 1.1.18), delusion (*moha*) is included among the defects. // 8 //
And because of the occurrence of the cause and its effect, there is no refutation of those things belonging to the same class.
It is observed that among substances or qualities of the same class, there exists a relationship between cause and effect characterized by manifold varieties. // 9 //
Following the defects [of the soul], there is the state after death (*pretyabhāva*); its non-establishment follows from the eternity of the self (*ātman*).
Indeed, nothing that is eternal is ever born or dies. Since birth and death are impossible for an eternal self, and yet both constitute the state after death, [the latter] is not established.
In this regard, the restatement of what has been established is as follows:
NyS 4.1.10: Given the eternity of the self, the existence after death is established.
This eternal self departs;
it leaves the previous body and dies. And having departed, it...
Having abandoned the previous body, it comes into being; it is born;
it takes up another body. And this consists of both [of these].
Rebirth is "existence after death" (*pretyabhāva*). And this is possible only if [the self] is eternal.

However, for one who holds that existence after death consists in the arising of a sentient being and the cessation of a sentient being, there is the fault of the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*);
furthermore, in a doctrine that asserts annihilation as the cause, the instructions of the Seers (*ṛṣi*) would be rendered meaningless. // 10 //
If it is asked, "How does origination occur?
[the answer is: From the manifest, the manifest [originate], because perception is the means of valid knowledge.
In what manner and from what cause does the manifest body arise? It arises from the manifest—
from that which is designated as the elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and so forth, which are supremely subtle and eternal— from the manifest,
the known substance consisting of the support for the body, the senses, and the objects of experience, arises.
Indeed, that which is perceptible by the senses is manifest; because of this commonality, the cause as well must be manifest.
What is the commonality?
It is the possession of qualities such as form and so forth.

From eternal earth and other elements endowed with qualities such as color, bodies and other effects endowed with those same qualities are produced—this is because perception is a valid means of knowledge.

For it is observed that from substances such as clay, which possess qualities like color, there arises a substance of a similar nature; and by this, the existence of the unobserved [cause] is inferred.
Since the persistence of color and other qualities is seen in both the material cause and its modification, the causal status of eternal, supersensuous entities such as earth is inferred. (11)
NyS 4.1.12: No, because a jar is not produced from a jar.

This too is a matter of direct perception: indeed, it is never observed that a manifest pot is produced from a manifest [pot]. Since it is seen that the manifest does not arise from the manifest, the manifest is not the cause.
Nyāyasūtra 4.1.13: There is no refutation [of our position] because a jar is produced from a manifest cause.

We do not say that everything is the cause of everything; rather, whatever manifest substance (*vyakta-dravya*) arises, it arises from that which is of the same nature.
