And that manifest clay-substance designated as "potsherds" from which a jar arises—no one who denies this can ever obtain acceptance [of their view]. This is the truth. 13.
Hereafter, the views of the various teachers are presented:
"The arising of an entity from non-existence [is not possible], because nothing manifests without having destroyed [its cause]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.14)
The position that "the existent arises from the non-existent" is held because of manifestation following destruction;
for the sprout arises having destroyed the seed, not without having destroyed it.
If the destruction of the seed is not the cause of the sprout, then the sprout would have to arise even when the seed is not destroyed. // 14 //
To this it is replied: "There is no application [of that reason] because of contradiction" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.15).
The formulation "because of appearing after having destroyed" is incorrect due to contradiction.

That which destroys cannot appear after having been destroyed, because it already exists. And that which appears cannot be a destruction by means of what has not yet appeared—that is, by means of what is non-existent. // 15 //
Not so, because the term "agent" (kāraka) is applied to both the past and the future.

Even when the past and the future do not exist, the term "agent" (kāraka) is employed: "A son will be born," "He rejoices in the son who is about to be born," "He gives a name to the son who is about to be born," "The jar existed," "He grieves over the broken jar," and "The shards of the broken jar."
The expressions "unborn sons cause their father distress" and so forth are frequently seen as figurative usages (*bhākta*). What, then, is this figurative usage?
It is immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
The meaning is that [the seed] manifests after having destroyed [the fruit] due to the efficacy of the immediate succession (*ānantarya*).
Since the sprout, while about to manifest, destroys [the fruit], its status as an agent is figurative (*bhākta*). // 16 //
Not from those that have perished, because [the effect] does not arise [from them].
Since a sprout does not arise from a seed that has perished, it follows that an entity does not originate from non-existence. // 17 //
NyS 4.1.18: There is no refutation [of the opponent's position] because of the indication of a sequence.

Sequence is the fixed rule of priority and posteriority between destruction and manifestation; indeed, it is pointed out as the cause for the arising of existence from non-existence, and that [sequence] is not denied.
In the case of parts arranged in a specific configuration, when the previous configuration ceases, the substance is produced from a subsequent configuration, not from non-existence.

The parts of the seed, having manifested activity due to some cause, abandon the previous configuration and assume another configuration; from this subsequent configuration, the sprout arises. Indeed, the parts and their conjunctions are observed to be the causes for the production of the sprout.

Furthermore, as long as the previous arrangement has not ceased, it is impossible for the parts of the seed to assume another arrangement; thus, the sequence is the fixed order of priority between the destruction [of the cause] and the manifestation [of the effect]. Therefore, an entity does not arise from non-existence, nor is it tenable that there is any cause for the production of the sprout other than the parts of the seed; hence, the restriction regarding the material cause (upādāna) of the seed is established. // 18 //
Then another says:
"God is the cause, because human actions are seen to be fruitless. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.19)

This person, though striving, does not necessarily obtain the fruit of his effort; therefore it is inferred that the attainment of the fruit of action by a person is dependent on another. That upon which it depends is the Lord (Īśvara); therefore, the Lord is the cause. // 19 //
NyS 4.1.20: No, because the fruit is not produced in the absence of human action.
If the production of results were dependent solely on God, then results would be produced even without human effort. // 20 //
That is not a valid reason, because it is brought about by that very [cause].
The Lord favors human effort;

He brings about the fruit for the person who strives for it. When He does not bring it about, then the human action becomes fruitless. Therefore, because it is caused by the Lord, [human effort] is not the cause—[as stated in the Sūtra]:
"Because the fruit is not produced in the absence of human action."
The Lord (Īśvara) is another self distinguished by [auspicious] qualities; because he is like a self, the postulation of another self for him is untenable,
due to his abandonment of demerit, false knowledge, and negligence.
And by means of the perfection of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) on the knowledge of *dharma*, the Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct self;
and his fruit, which is the result of that *dharma* and *samādhi*, is the eightfold sovereignty beginning with atomization (*aṇimā*),
while his *dharma* conforms to his will and operates within each individual soul.
It sets in motion the accumulation of merit and demerit as well as the primary elements such as earth,
and thus, it does not involve the loss of the results of one's own actions.
The manifestation of the Lord’s power should be understood as the fruit of his own performed karma;
and he is like a trustworthy authority, for just as a father is to his children, so the Lord is the father of all beings, and no other authority is possible apart from one who is like himself.
First of all, no property capable of serving as a logical mark (*liṅga*) can be established for him apart from his cognition; and according to scripture, God is the seer, the knower,
and the omniscient one.

Who, being attached [to worldly gain], would attempt to establish an indefinable Lord— who transcends the objects of perception, inference, and scripture— by means of the marks of the self such as cognition and so forth?
Furthermore, for one who proceeds by thus disregarding the consequences of his own actions:
As for what was stated—that the entire collection of prohibitions regarding the creation of the body when there is no cause for action would follow as a consequence—all that [applies here]. // 21 //
Now another says:
"The production of entities occurs without a cause, as seen in the case of the sharpness of thorns and so forth. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.22)

The production of bodies and so forth is without a [specific] cause—this is known from the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like; for instance, the sharpness of a thorn, the variegated nature of mountain minerals, and the smoothness of stones. Furthermore, a material cause is observed to be without a [further] cause.
In the same way, the creation of the body also [is not for the sake of the Self]. // 22 //
Because it has the signless as its sign, it is not [established] through signlessness.
It is said that "the arising of entities occurs from the signless" (*animittataḥ*). That from which something arises is the "sign" (*nimitta*);
since what is signless cannot function as a sign, the arising of entities does not occur from the signless. // 23 //
NyS 4.1.24: There is no refutation [of our position], because there is a difference in meaning between the "causal" (nimitta) and the "non-causal" (animitta).
For the sign is one thing, and the negation of the sign is another.

Furthermore, the negation itself cannot be the object of negation; just as in the case of "the water-pot is without water," the prohibition of water does not mean that the water itself becomes the pot.

Indeed, this doctrine—that the creation of the body and so forth has no cause other than karma—is not distinct from the previously mentioned [view]; therefore, being non-different, it should be understood as refuted by the very refutation of that [prior view]. // 24 //
But others think:
"Everything is impermanent, because it possesses the nature of arising and perishing. (NyS 4.1.25)

What is called "impermanent"? That which exists at some time is impermanent; that is to say, there is nothing possessing the nature of arising that has not arisen, and there is nothing possessing the nature of destruction that has not perished.

What more is there to say? All things, both those composed of the elements, such as the body, and those not composed of the elements, such as the intellect, are known to possess the properties of origination and destruction; therefore, all of that is impermanent.
(NS 4.1.26) [Objection: No, because impermanence itself is permanent.

If, first of all, the impermanence of everything is permanent, then because of its permanence, not everything is impermanent. Or, if it is impermanent, then in its absence, everything would be permanent. // 26 //
That impermanence [of fire] is like the destruction of fire following the destruction of what is to be burned.
Even that impermanence is itself impermanent.
How so? Just as fire, having destroyed what is to be burned, perishes along with it, so too does the impermanence of everything perish after having destroyed everything. // 27 //
NyS 4.1.28: There is no rejection of the eternal, because its existence is established according to how it is perceived.
Indeed, this doctrine constantly refutes [the existence of] the eternal, yet the refutation of the eternal is untenable.
Why? Because its status is established according to how it is perceived;
for that which is perceived as having the nature of arising and perishing [is not eternal].

That which is perceived through a means of valid cognition is non-eternal. That which is not so perceived is its opposite; however, this does not apply to the most subtle elements—space, time, direction, self, and mind—nor to some of their qualities, nor to generality, particularity, and inherence.
Since their nature of arising and perishing is perceived through valid means of cognition, therefore these [elements] are eternal. // 28 //
Furthermore, there is this other extreme view: "Everything is eternal, because the five elements are eternal. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.29)
All this is merely the elements; and those elements are eternal, because the destruction of the elements is impossible. // 29 //
NyS 4.1.30: [Sound is non-eternal] because the causes of its production and destruction are perceived.
Furthermore, both a cause of origination and a cause of destruction are perceived;
these would be contradicted if everything were eternal. // 30 //
There is no refutation [of our position], because it is included within that definition.

That which you think has its causes of arising and destruction perceived is not apprehended as a distinct entity devoid of the characteristics of the primary elements (bhūta). Because it is encompassed by the characteristics of the primary elements, this is merely the primary elements themselves.
Thus, this negation is improper. // 31 //
NyS 4.1.32: [The self exists] because its production and its causes are perceived.
The production of an effect possessing qualities identical to those of its cause is observed, and that cause is also perceived;
yet neither of these two facts pertains to eternal objects, nor is there any perception of production or its cause in the case of the eternal.
It can be denied [that there is no object]; for no perception is without an object.
By the power of perception, it is inferred that an effect arises with qualities similar to those of its cause; indeed, that is the object of perception.
Thus, in this way, there is the logical establishment of its inclusion within that definition;
for the effort of a cognizer who is impelled by the causes of production and destruction is observed,
and the composite whole (avayavin) is well-known to possess those properties.
Furthermore, it is established that the whole (avayavin) possesses the properties of arising and perishing;

moreover, there is non-pervasion [of the definition] regarding sound, action, cognition, and so forth, because the five elements are eternal and because this contradicts their defining characteristics. By this [it is shown].
Sound, action, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are not pervaded [by the soul]; therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive.
If it is argued that this is a false perception, like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream,
[we reply] that the same applies to the perception of the elements.

Just as there is the conceit of objects in a dream, so too is there the conceit of causes of production; and this being the case, it applies equally to the perception of the elements, for the perception of earth and the other elements would likewise result in being like the conceit of objects in a dream.
If it is argued that "in the absence of earth and the other elements, all worldly transactions would cease," that is equally true in the other case as well.

If there were an absence even of that object which is the locus for perceiving the causes of arising and destruction, then all worldly transactions would collapse. Therefore, because eternal things are beyond the senses and thus not objects [of perception], the argument "like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream" is not a valid reason for [the non-existence of] arising and destruction. // 32 //
While the substratum (*upādāna*) remains constant, a mere phenomenon (*dharma-mātra*) ceases and a mere phenomenon arises; this indeed is the domain of arising and destruction.
Furthermore, that which arises exists even prior to its arising.
And that which ceases exists even when it has ceased; thus, everything would be eternal—[this is not so], because the established order [of things] would be untenable. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.33)
The distinction that "this is origination" and "this is cessation" is not tenable— because both origination and cessation would [simultaneously] exist;
this is the property.
Because there is no difference in its actual existence, the distinction that "this has arisen" or "this has ceased" would be untenable; furthermore,
the temporal distinction that "the arising and ceasing occur now, not at other times" is not possible, because it exists at all times.
The establishment [of temporal distinctions] is untenable because there is no arising or ceasing of this dharma; for there is no distinction between the two.
Furthermore, the temporal establishment of "future" and "past" is untenable.
Because the present is characterized by existence;
for "origination" is the acquisition of self-nature by that which was non-existent, and "cessation" is the loss of self-nature by that which was existent— this being the case.
Since these faults do not apply, therefore that which was stated— “it exists even prior to its production, and having ceased, it still exists”— is correct.
Therefore, that is incorrect. // 33 //
Furthermore, this is another exclusive position:
"Everything is distinct, because the characteristics of entities are distinct. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.34)
Everything is manifold; not a single entity exists. Why?
Because the characteristics of entities are distinct.
The characteristic and the designation of an entity:
that word by which an entity is characterized is its technical name (samākhyā-śabda).
Because their objects are distinct:
the word "all" (*sarva*), which is a term denoting existence, expresses a collection;
whereas the designation "jar" (*kumbha*) refers to a collection of odor, taste, color, and touch.
And it also exists in a collection such as the thighs, sides, neck, and so forth;
this is merely an illustration. // 34 //
NyS 4.1.35: [The objection that there is no universal] is not [valid], because a single entity is produced through multiple characteristics.

The term "anekavidhalakṣaṇaiḥ" is a compound with the middle member elided (madhyamapadalopī samāsa); thus, a single entity is produced as connected with qualities such as odor and so forth, and with parts such as the base and so forth.
Furthermore, substance is distinct from its qualities, and the whole is distinct from its parts;
both of these cases follow the same logical principle. // 35 //
Moreover, there is no refutation [of our position] precisely because of the established definition [of the categories].
"The negation that 'no single entity exists at all' is improper;
why? Precisely because of the establishment of defining characteristics.
Whatever here constitutes the defining characteristic of an entity—that is, its designation as a word—exists in a single [entity]."

It is established: "I touch that very jar which I saw," and "I see that very thing which I touched. A collection of atoms is not perceived; and since a collection of atoms is not being perceived, that which...
That which is grasped is indeed one alone.
Moreover, this has been stated: "There is no single entity from which a collection could arise;
since a single unit is untenable, a composite whole does not exist at all."
There is not a single entity because the application of the word "entity" occurs only in a collection; and since a single [entity] is untenable,
a collection is not tenable— for a collection is indeed a unification of ones.

Regarding the term "aggregate" (*samūha*), it is untenable because it is contradictory— namely, the claim that "no single entity exists," for which a negation is being asserted by one who states the reason:
"because the word 'entity' is applied to an aggregate."
That very point is authorized: for a collection is indeed a single aggregate;
this is because the term denoting an entity (*bhāvaśabda*) is applied to the aggregate as a whole.
And by relying on the collection, there is the negation of each individual within that collection—
namely, "there is no single entity"—
and thus this [argument] is from both sides.
Because it involves contradiction, it is a mere babble. // 36 //
This is another extreme view:
"Everything is non-existent, because the existence of things is established through their mutual non-existence. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.37)
Whatever collection of entities exists, all that is non-existence. Why?

Because among entities, mutual non-existence is established: "The cow is non-existent in the form of a horse," "The cow is not a horse," "The horse is non-existent in the form of a cow," and "The horse is not a cow"—such is the cognition of non-existence, which is a negation.
And because of its grammatical coreferentiality with the word "existence" (bhāva), everything is non-existence.
It is improper because there is a contradiction between the two words in the proposition-statement, as well as between the proposition and the reason.
The meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) is the state of being without remainder of that which is manifold;

the meaning of the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is the negation of existence. The former is characterized by designation (*sopākhyam*), while the latter is devoid of designation (*nirupākhyam*). Among these, that which is being designated...
"How could that which is indefinable be non-existence?"— it is never possible to assert that non-existence is indefinable in its manifoldness or in its entirety;
all of this is non-existence.
If you say this?
If you think that "all this" which you consider to be such is indeed its very nature (*tadbhāva*), then the contradiction remains unresolved— namely, that it is both manifold and without remainder.
It is not possible for this to exist by means of the condition of non-existence; yet this condition "all" does exist. Therefore, it is not non-existent.
And [this applies] to both the proposition and the reason.

Contradiction (*vyāghāta*): "Everything is non-existent" is the thesis (*pratijñā*), which is a negation of existence. "Because the mutual non-existence of entities is established" is the reason (*hetu*). [This is stated] having admitted the mutual non-existence of entities.
If it is argued that everything is non-existence because mutual non-existence is established by depending [on things], then if everything were non-existence,
how could mutual non-existence be established among existing things?

Thus, it is not tenable. If, on the other hand, the establishment of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is among existing things (*bhāva*), then the claim that "everything is non-existent" (*sarvam abhāvaḥ*) is not tenable. // 37 //
And the connection with the Sūtra is as follows:
"No, because things are established by their own nature" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.38).
Not everything is non-existent; why?
Because things exist by way of their own being. It is asserted that things come into existence by means of their own specific characteristics.

And what is the intrinsic nature (*svadharma*) of entities? It is the universal (*sāmānya*), such as "existence" (*sat*) and so forth, for substances, qualities, and actions; and it is the particular (*viśeṣa*), such as "possessing action" and so forth, for substances.
And [it is said that] "the qualities ending with touch belong to earth," and furthermore,
there is an infinite variety for each [element], as well as for generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya).
Distinguished dharmas are apprehended;
however, because non-existence (abhāva) is indefinable (nirupākhya), this differentiation of meaning does not convey [a distinct object].
It might be so. However, since this [emptiness] exists, it is not the case that everything is non-existent.
Or alternatively:
"Because things are established by way of their own-being (svabhāva)."
Thus, because its own nature is established: when the word "cow" (gaur) is employed, a substance qualified by a universal (jāti) is apprehended, not mere non-existence.
And if everything were non-existence, then "cow" would be understood as non-existence.
If non-existence were expressed by the word "cow," it would be improper because, when the word "cow" is employed, a specific substance is perceived and not non-existence.
Alternatively:
[the phrase] "because it is not established by way of intrinsic nature" refers to [the case where] "the cow is non-existent as the essence of a horse," [but exists] as the essence of a cow.
Why is it not stated? Because it is not so stated, the establishment of intrinsic nature— that "the cow exists as the essence of a cow"— is [implied].
Why is it not said that "a horse is a non-horse" or "a cow is a non-cow"?
Because of its own non-utterance.
The existence of a substance is understood through its form;
furthermore, when the non-distinction [of one thing from another] is negated, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the notion of non-existence regarding entities.

A relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth is "separation" (*vyatireka*); here, "non-separation" (*avyatireka*) refers to the relation called non-difference (*abheda*). And when that [separation] is negated, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the suffix of non-existence (*asat*), as in: "there are no jujube fruits in the bowl," or "it is non-existent."
By the statement "the cow is not non-cow by way of its own nature as a horse," the non-distinction between the cow and the horse is negated;
that is, the oneness of the cow and the horse does not exist. When that [oneness] is being negated...
There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cow and the notion of non-existence in the form:
"The cow does not exist as a horse. This is just as when one says, "There are no jujube fruits in the bowl," whereby the conjunction of the jujube fruits with the bowl is being negated.
The wise maintain that there is grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between the non-existent and its cause. // 38 //
There is no establishment of intrinsic nature because of its relativity.
That which is produced through dependence is relative:
length is produced in dependence on shortness, and shortness is produced in dependence on length. Nothing exists by way of its own intrinsic nature.
Why?
Because of the efficacy of dependence. Therefore, there is no establishment of things by way of intrinsic nature. // 39 //
It is improper because it is self-contradictory.
If "long" is produced in dependence upon "short," then in relation to what is "short" now apprehended? Or if it is produced in dependence upon "long"?
The short is not dependent on the long, and likewise the long is not dependent on the short;

thus, since there would be the absence of one in the absence of the other among these two mutually dependent entities, the absence of both would follow, and therefore the establishment of dependence is untenable.
If intrinsic establishment (*svabhāvasiddhi*) does not exist, why would length and shortness—which are relative—fail to occur in two substances that are equal or circular?
Whether there is dependence or non-dependence, there is no difference between the two substances;
for as much as the substance is when being depended upon, it is exactly that much when not being depended upon, and there is no distinction in either case.
If, however, [the distinction] were merely relative, then a specific quality would have to arise in one of the two.
If it is asked, "What is the efficacy of this relativity?"— it is the possibility of perceiving intensity when both are perceived.
Perceiving two substances, one perceives the excellence existing in one of them and determines "this is long," while perceiving that which is inferior.
"One determines that it is short"—this is the power of relative dependence. // 40 //
Now, the monistic positions regarding number: "Everything is one, because of the lack of distinction in existence"; "Everything is twofold."
Due to the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal, everything is threefold— namely, the knower, the means of knowledge,
and the object of knowledge; and everything is fourfold— namely, the subject, the means of knowledge, [the object, and the result].
The object of cognition (*prameya*) and valid cognition (*pramiti*); in this manner, others also [are to be understood] according to their respective possibilities.
Regarding that, the examination (*parīkṣā*) is as follows:
NyS 4.1.41: The absolute determination of number is not established, because of both the impossibility and the possibility of a cause.
If there is a difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), then an absolute [conclusion] is not established because of their distinction;
or, if there is no difference between the probandum and the probans?
Even so, absolute certainty is not established—due to the absence of proof;
for without that [proof], nothing whatsoever can be established. // 41 //
Not so, because it exists as a constituent part of its cause.
There is no non-establishment of the absolute positions regarding number; why?

Because the cause exists as a constituent part (*avayava*). That is to say, since some constituent part serves as the means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no exclusion [of that position]. The same applies to dualism and the others. // 42 //
Because it is partless, [the reason] is not a valid reason.
The argument "because the cause exists as a constituent part" is not a valid reason; why?
Because [the claim] "everything is one" does not allow for any exclusion.
Having made a proposition, if unity is asserted of something, then in that case a distinct constituent part serving as a means of proof is not possible;
the same applies to duality and so forth.
Indeed, if these proponents of absolute number proceed by rejecting the expansion of distinct objects produced by specific causes,
they contradict perception, inference, and scripture.
They become speakers of falsehood;
or else, they proceed by means of authorization?
The acquisition of wealth is brought about by common characteristics, and the differentiation of wealth is brought about by specific characteristics.
Thus, they abandon exclusivity; indeed,
these exclusivities have been examined for the sake of discerning the knowledge of reality.
Thus [ends verse] 43.
After the state of rebirth (pretyabhāva) follows the fruit (phala).
Regarding that—NyS 4.1.44: there is doubt because the production of the fruit occurs both immediately and after an interval of time.
In the cases "he cooks" and "he milks," the results— rice and milk— are immediate;
whereas in the cases "he plows" and "he sows," [the results occur] at a later time.
The fruit is the attainment of the harvest;
and there exists this action: "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice."
Thus, there is doubt regarding the fruit of this [action]. // 44 //
Not so, because it is to be enjoyed at a later time.
Heaven is heard of as the fruit; and since that arises from a different body once this one has perished, it does not occur immediately.
Desires for villages and the like, however, are the fruits of the initial undertaking. // 45 //
NyS 4.1.46: There is no production at a later time because of the destruction of the cause.
When the process of manifestation has been destroyed, the fruit of that manifestation cannot arise without a cause—
for indeed, nothing whatsoever is produced from a cause that has perished. // 46 //
Prior to its production, it would exist like a fruit on a tree.

Just as one seeking fruit performs preparatory work such as watering at the root of a tree, and when that [root] has perished, the earth element— sustained by the water element and ripened by internal heat— produces the substance of the sap.

Just as that substantial sap, following the tree, distinguished by its transformation through maturation and being arranged by a specific configuration, brings about leaves and so forth up to the fruit; in this way, ritual actions such as sprinkling water and the like are purposeful.
Nor is the production of a fruit from that which has perished; rather,
through such activity,
a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized as merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*) is produced, and once it has been produced—
Supported by other causal factors (*nimitta*), it produces its fruit at a later time. And this has been stated:
"Its production [occurs] due to the connection with the fruits of previous actions" (3.2.62).
Thus [ends the verse]. 47.
This very [effect], while being produced prior to its actual production—
NyS_4,1.48: is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the mutual exclusion between existence and non-existence.
Prior to its production, that which possesses the nature of being produced is not non-existent— because of the restriction of material causes;
for something specific is to be taken as the material cause for the arising of a particular thing, not everything.

Regarding the phrase "of everything," a restriction [on its existence] is not tenable if it were non-existent; nor is it existent—for the arising of that which already exists prior to its production is untenable; nor is it both existent and non-existent—because of the mutual incompatibility (*vaidharmya*) between the existent and the non-existent. "Existent" implies the admission of an object's reality, while "non-existent" implies the negation of such an object.
The contradiction between these two is their dissimilarity; because of this contradiction, the non-existence of the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is untenable. // 48 //
NyS 4.1.49: It is certain that what possesses the property of arising is non-existent prior to its production;
why? Because we observe both arising and passing away.
Furthermore, as for what was stated:
"Prior to its production, the effect is not non-existent, because of the restriction regarding the material cause. // 49 //
But that which is established by mere cognition is non-existent.

"This [cause] alone is capable of producing this [effect], not everything"— thus, prior to its production, the effect is established by the intellect as having a restricted cause, because a restriction regarding production is observed.
Therefore, the restriction of the material cause is established;
for if the effect already exists, there is no production at all prior to its arising. // 50 //
"Because of the difference in their substrata, like the production of fruit from a tree; therefore, this is not a valid reason."

The cultivation such as watering the roots and the fruit both depend upon the tree. Since action occurs here in the body while the fruit occurs there [in the next life], they do not share a common substratum; therefore, [the example] is not a valid reason. // 51 //
NyS 4.1.52: There is no refutation [of the self] because pleasure has the self as its locus.

Since pleasure is directly perceived by the self, it has the self as its locus; likewise, action designated as *dharma* has that very same [self] as its locus—because *dharma* is a quality of the self.
Therefore, a separation from the locus is impossible. // 52 //
NyS 4.1.53: [The Veda is not non-authoritative] because it points toward fruits such as sons, cattle, women, household goods, gold, food, and so forth.

The fruit [of sacrifice] is specified as sons and so forth, not as pleasure—as in the injunctions, "One desiring a village should sacrifice" and "One desiring a son should sacrifice. Therefore, what was stated—that "pleasure is the fruit"—is incorrect. // 53 //
Because the fruit is produced through connection with that [action], there is a metaphorical designation of "fruit" applied to those [auxiliaries].

Because a fruit characterized by joy arises from the relationship with sons and so forth, there is a metaphorical designation of "fruit" applied to sons and others, just as the word "life-breath" (prāṇa) is used for food.
"Food, indeed, is the vital breaths. // 54 //
Immediately after [the discussion on] the fruit, suffering was indicated and stated:
"Suffering is characterized by affliction" (NS 1.1.21).
Is this [suffering] something to be personally experienced by each individual?
Is there a rejection of pleasure that is perceptible to all living beings, or is there another alternative? He says it is another; how so?
Indeed, it is not possible to deny happiness that is witnessed by the entire world.

However, for one who is weary of the suffering caused by the experience of the continuous succession of birth and death, and who desires to abandon that suffering, this instruction on the cultivation of the perception of suffering is for the purpose of eliminating suffering.
By what reasoning?
Indeed, all classes of sentient beings, all places of birth, and every form of renewed existence are accompanied by affliction because they are associated with suffering;
for it has been stated: "Suffering is characterized by affliction" (1.1.21). Therefore, the sages teach the cultivation of the perception of suffering.
And here a reason is adduced:
"The arising of birth is indeed suffering because it is associated with manifold afflictions. (NyS 4.1.55)
Birth (*janma*):
that which is born (*jāyate*) consists of the body, the sense faculties, and the intellect;
[this refers to] the body and so forth.
Manifestation is the appearance of things characterized by specific configurations;
and affliction is of various kinds—inferior, middling, and superior. Superior affliction belongs to those in the hells; middling affliction belongs to animals.

They are inferior to humans and even more inferior to the gods and those free from passion; thus, for one who perceives every place of rebirth as being beset by various afflictions, [there is no attachment] toward pleasure, nor toward the means of attaining it, nor toward the body, the senses, or the intellect.

The perception of suffering becomes established. From the establishment of the perception of suffering, there arises the perception of non-delight in all worlds. For one who dwells in the perception of non-delight, craving for the objects of all worlds is severed. Through the abandonment of craving—

"One is liberated from all suffering," as when one who understands that milk is poisonous due to its contact with poison does not take it; by not taking it, one does not incur the suffering of death. // 55 //
The enumeration of suffering is not a denial of pleasure; why?
Because pleasure also arises during the intervals [between sufferings]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.56)
Indeed, this enumeration of suffering is a rejection of pleasure;
why? Because pleasure arises in the intervals [between sufferings].
For pleasure, which is to be personally experienced, certainly arises within the intervals of affliction.
For embodied beings, that [pleasure] cannot be denied. // 46 //
Moreover—NyS 4.1.57:
There is no refutation [of the existence of the self], because for one who experiences [pleasure and pain], there is the fault of seeking [their causes] due to the non-cessation of affliction.
"By means of the designation of suffering for [the sake of] happiness" refers, according to the context, to seeking and longing.
The thirst for acquiring sense objects. The fault of seeking is this:
while experiencing [sensation], one craves; yet that which is craved by him either does not come to pass, or having come to pass, it perishes, or it comes to pass in a deficient manner.
Or it results in many adversaries. From this fault of seeking, various kinds of mental distress arise.
Thus, for one who experiences [feeling], there is affliction due to the fault of seeking.
There is no return. The cultivation of the perception of suffering is intended for the sake of ceasing affliction.
For this reason, birth is suffering, not because of the absence of pleasure.
Furthermore, this has been stated as follows:
“When the desire of one who longs for pleasure is fulfilled, another desire quickly overcomes him.

Even if he should obtain the earth on all sides, bounded by the ocean, together with its cattle and horses, that seeker of wealth is not satisfied by that riches; what happiness, then, can there be for one who craves wealth?”
Thus [ends verse] 57.
And because of the misconception of pleasure within the variety of suffering.
The instruction for the cultivation of the perception of suffering is given because this person, being established in the experience of pleasure,
considers pleasure to be the supreme human goal— nothing other than pleasure.

There is the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). When happiness is attained, one has fulfilled one's purpose and accomplished what was to be done. Through false resolve, one becomes attached to happiness and to the objects that serve as its means. Being thus attached, for the sake of happiness...

It occurs. For one who is thus engaged, there arises manifold suffering caused by birth, old age, disease, death, union with the unpleasant, separation from the beloved, and the failure to obtain what is desired; yet he mistakenly conceives this variety of suffering to be pleasure.
Suffering is a constituent part of pleasure—for it is not possible to attain pleasure without encountering suffering.

In order to attain happiness; because it is for that purpose, one whose wisdom is impaired by the notion of "this is indeed happiness" does not transcend saṃsāra—thinking, "Be born, die, and come together. This is due to that notion of happiness.
The antidote is taught as the cultivation of the perception of suffering. Birth is suffering because it is accompanied by suffering, not because of an absence of pleasure.
If this is so, why is it not simply stated that "birth is suffering"? This [is] thus...
Regarding what was stated [by us],
namely: "Birth is indeed suffering" (55), by that he makes known the absence of happiness.
Indeed, this word "eva" (only) is intended for the purpose of excluding birth; how so?
Birth is not suffering.

However, it is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) that [birth] is [called] suffering in its own nature; likewise, pleasure is also [so designated]. This very point is what is being refuted here, and not the claim that birth is merely suffering. // 58 //
Immediately after the teaching on suffering, liberation (apavarga) is refuted:
"There is no liberation because of the continuous succession of debts, afflictions, and worldly activity" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.59).

"There is no liberation due to the connection with debts": "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, being born, is born burdened with three debts—to the sages by means of studentship, to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny.
These are the debts; their connection is the "connection with debts."
The connection with one's own actions follows from the statement regarding the connection with action:
"This sacrificial session, namely the Agnihotra and the New and Full Moon sacrifices, lasts until old age and death; for by old age one is released from that session, and indeed by death."
Thus, because of the persistence of debt, there is no time for the practice of liberation; hence, there is an absence of liberation.
Because of the persistence of afflictions, there is no liberation.
This person dies still bound by afflictions, and [is born] again bound by afflictions.
The severance of the continuity of his afflictions is not perceived;
because of the continuity of worldly activity, there is no liberation.
From birth until death, he remains unliberated from the undertaking of speech, cognition, and the body.

In this regard, that which was stated— "Upon the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge, there follows the removal of each preceding one, resulting in liberation" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.2)—
is untenable. // 59 //
To this it is replied: as for the argument that "because of the connection with debts" (*ṛṇānubandhāt*), [the word *ṛṇaiḥ*] means "as if by debts" (*ṛṇairiva ṛṇaiḥ*).

This is because the primary meaning of the word is untenable; rather, it is a figurative reference (*anuvāda*) using a secondary term, which is appropriate for either censure or praise. (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.60)
Regarding the word "debts" (*ṛṇaiḥ*), this is not a primary term; for it applies only where one person gives what is to be repaid and another receives what is to be returned.

Because it is observed [in common usage], the word "debt" (ṛṇa) refers to the primary sense. However, this is not appropriate here because the primary sense is untenable; therefore, this is a figurative restatement using a secondary term—namely, "as if by debts, as if by debts."
And this is an illustration by application (*prayuktôpamam*), as in:
"The boy is fire. This word *ṛṇa*, having been observed elsewhere, is employed here.
Just as the word "fire" [is applied] to a young brahmin.

How is there a restatement by means of a word denoting a quality? Because censure and praise are applicable: when there is an omission of ritual action, one is censured like a debtor for failing to repay a debt.

And in the performance of ritual action, he is praised like a debtor after the repayment of a debt; this alone is the meaning of the simile. The word "being born" (*jāyamāna*) is a term denoting a specific quality—because there is no entitlement [to the rites] in the opposite case—as in: "Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa is being born... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.2.1).
And the word "thus" refers to the householder;
when he is being born— that is, when this householder is born— he is then qualified for ritual actions through his duties.
Because one who is being born from the mother lacks qualification;

for when a boy is born from the mother, he is not at that time qualified for ritual acts— since qualification belongs to one who is both desirous and capable— and because qualification for ritual acts belongs to the desirous, as there is a traditional teaching (smṛti) regarding the connection with desire in the injunctions for ritual acts.
“For one desiring heaven, one should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice,” and so forth; for it is possible for a capable person to engage in such action.
One who is incapable has no entitlement to ritual acts—because activity is impossible for him; indeed, only one who is capable engages in prescribed action, not another.
However, there is an absence of both [capacity and entitlement] in the case of the primary meaning of the word [Brahman].
When a boy is born from his mother, both [the factors of] desire and capacity do not exist; thus,
it does not differ from the worldly [case].
From one sentence [of scripture], another Vedic sentence [is inferred]—because it was composed by a person who acts with foresight.

In that regard, even an ordinary worldly person, though lacking critical investigation, would not say to a newborn child: "Study! Sacrifice! Practice the life of a student! [Rather, he would say this: "Study! Sacrifice! Practice the life of a student..."
"Go! From what [source] does this seer, who speaks what is appropriate and faultless, being impelled by the purpose of instruction, teach?
Indeed, it is not [from himself].
A dancer does not perform for the deaf, nor does a singer sing for those who are hard of hearing;
furthermore, the object of instruction is the comprehension of the meaning taught,
and instruction is directed toward one who understands the meaning that has been taught.
And this [performance] is not done in the case of a newborn infant;
furthermore, the ritual acts prescribed in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas signify the marks of the householder's life.
And those ritual acts prescribed in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas [are performed] through the connection with a wife and so forth.
Since he is endowed with the marks of a householder, therefore this person, upon being born, is designated as a "householder."
Furthermore, the statement regarding "old age and death" is established on the basis of the non-alteration of one's purpose;
for as long as one possesses the purpose for its fruit, [so long does that purpose persist].
It does not undergo transformation,
nor does it cease; rather, it persists as long as this karma must be performed— thus,
with reference to that [karma], the teaching that "one dies when one has grown old" (jarāmarya) is established.
The statement beginning with "Indeed, by old age" refers to the fourth part of the life-span— that which is connected to the life of a wandering mendicant.
"By old age, indeed, he is released from this"— that is, the fourth part of the lifespan, which is associated with the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), is called "old age. In that regard:
For renunciation is prescribed for one who is joined with extreme old age, as in the passage: "Indeed,
by old age..."
Thus, this is meaningless;
even the statement "one who is powerless is liberated" is not tenable— for one who is himself powerless, [the text] speaks of an external power.
“Either a resident pupil should offer the oblation, for he has been purchased by means of the Veda; or one who offers milk should offer it, for he has been purchased by means of wealth.
Thus, would that which is already prescribed be merely restated? Or is there a purpose based on desire?
Would it be imagined that the recitation of what has been prescribed is proper?
For like one who owes a debt, the householder, lacking independence, engages in ritual acts.
Thus, the capacity of the statement is established.
For the means of accomplishing a result are the objects of effort, not the result itself; when these [means] are perfected, they conduce to the result.
And that which is being produced is enjoined, and that which is being produced is prescribed; therefore, he who is connected with it [is the one enjoined].
If it is argued that this [statement], "he who is being born," lacks the status of a direct perception (pratyakṣa), we say no— because a negation likewise lacks the status of a direct perception.

The householder's stage is prescribed directly by the Brāhmaṇa; if there were another stage of life, that too would have been prescribed directly. Since there is no direct prescription for it, there is no other stage of life.
No—for even a prohibition is not established through direct perception; indeed, no prohibition is directly enjoined by a Brahmin such as, "There are no other stages of life (āśramas);
there is only the householder stage. Since no such prohibition is heard directly, this [objection] is untenable.
And because of the specific qualification, there is a separate injunction, as in the case of other sciences.

Just as other treatises are directly prescriptive within their own respective domains because there is no other purpose for them, so too this Brāhmaṇa, which is a treatise on the householder's life, is directly [prescriptive] within its own domain.
"It is not a prescriptive injunction for other stages of life because they do not exist.
Furthermore, the *Ṛgveda* and the *Brāhmaṇas* are declared to be expressive of liberation;
both the *Ṛks* and the *Brāhmaṇas* proclaim liberation.
And indeed, the Ṛgveda says:
"The seers, possessing progeny and desiring wealth, settled upon death through ritual acts; then other wise seers attained immortality beyond ritual acts."
"Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality;
beyond the heavens, that which is placed in the secret cave shines forth, which the ascetics enter.
"I know this Great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness."
"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey.
Then the Brāhmaṇas [say]:
"There are three pillars of dharma: sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity..."
Thus, the second [type of student] is the one who lives as a religious student in the teacher's family;
the third is the one who completely devotes himself to living in the teacher's family.
All these indeed attain worlds of merit, but he who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality.
“It is for the sake of this very world that those who have gone forth [as mendicants] go forth,” they say;
and moreover, they say: “This person consists entirely of desire.
As is his desire, so is his resolve.”

Having stated that transmigration occurs through actions— namely, "As one's resolve is, so is one's action; whatever action one performs, that one attains"— they teach another matter related to the subject at hand:

"Thus indeed for one who desires; but then for one who does not desire—he who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desire is attained—for him the vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right here into Brahman alone."
Regarding the statement, "The virtuous man attains Brahman," that which was previously asserted— namely, "there is an absence of liberation due to the bondage of debts"—
is incorrect.

Furthermore, because of the scriptural mention of the four stages of life (*cātu-āśramya*) in the passage, "The four paths that lead to the gods," the doctrine of a single stage of life (*aikāśramya*) is untenable;
moreover, this Brāhmaṇa text is intended for one who seeks the fruits [of religious action].
“This Agnihotra and the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed a sacrificial session (sattra) that ends with old age and death. // 60 //
How so?—NyS 4.1.61: There is no prohibition [of the self] because of its superimposition upon the self.

It is heard in scripture: "Having performed the *prājāpatya* sacrifice, having offered all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) in it, and having internalized the fires within oneself (*ātmani agnīn samāropya*), a Brahmin should go forth. From this we understand that the internalization of the fires occurs for one who has turned away from the desires for offspring, wealth, and worlds, and whose seeking of fruits has ceased.
It is thus prescribed; and so the Brāhmaṇas state:
"Now Yājñavalkya, being about to undertake another vow, said to Maitreyī: '..."
"Or rather, Maitreyī, I am about to depart from this state; come, let me make an end [of my life] together with this Kātyāyanī.
"But you have already been instructed, Maitreyī; this much, indeed, is [the teaching], my dear."
"Indeed, immortality is this," having said this, Yājñavalkya departed. // 61 //
And because the final accumulation of the sacrificial vessels is impossible, there is an absence of fruit.
And if ritual action were prescribed without distinction as lasting until old age and death, it would follow that the rites for everyone must end with the piling of the funeral pyre;
in that case, the departure from desire would not be heard of in scripture.
“Indeed, in this regard, the ancient Brahmins who were learned and wise did not desire offspring, saying: ‘What shall we do with offspring, for us this self is the world? They, indeed...”
"Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then lead the life of mendicancy";
and for one who has risen above these desires, [the stages] ending with the collection of alms-bowls [are prescribed].
Actions do not arise [without distinction]; thus, the fruit does not belong to the instigator of the agent indiscriminately.

Furthermore, because of the prescription of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras, the existence of only a single stage of life (*aikāśramya*) is untenable.
If it is argued that this is not authoritative, we say no; for its authority is acknowledged by means of a valid source of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Indeed, by means of a *pramāṇa*, the Brāhmaṇa [acknowledges] the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.
Its authority is acknowledged:
"Indeed, these Atharvāṅgirases recited this Itihāsa-Purāṇa;
the Itihāsa-Purāṇa is the fifth Veda among the Vedas."
Thus, it is incorrect to say that [the Dharmaśāstra] lacks authority. Furthermore,
if the Dharmaśāstra were without authority, there would follow the consequence of the destruction of the world, because the worldly transactions of living beings would come to an end.

Furthermore, non-authoritativeness is untenable because the seers and proclaimers are the same: those very individuals who were the seers and proclaimers of the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas were indeed the seers and proclaimers of the Itihāsas,
Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras.

And because of the determination of their respective domains, authority is established according to the domain: the domain of the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* is one thing, while that of the *itihāsa*, *purāṇa*, and *dharmaśāstra* is another.
Sacrifice is the domain of the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa*; worldly conduct is the domain of the *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*;
and the establishment of worldly transactions is the domain of the *dharmaśāstra*.

Regarding the object: since everything is not established by a single means, these means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) function according to their respective objects, just like the sense organs and so forth. // 62 //
Furthermore, regarding the statement "because the connection with the afflictions (*kleśa*) is not severed" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.63):
for one who is in deep sleep and sees no dreams, there is liberation (*apavarga*) due to the absence of afflictions.
Just as for one who is in deep sleep, when no dreams are seen, the attachment to passion and the attachment to pleasure and pain are severed, so it is also in the state of liberation (apavarga).
And this is cited as the form of the liberated self by those who know Brahman. // 63 //
As for the argument that "because of the persistence of activity" (Nyāyasūtra 4.1.64): activity does not lead to rebirth for one whose afflictions have been destroyed.
When passion, hatred, and delusion have been exhausted,
there is no activity for the sake of rebirth;
yet rebirth occurs upon the cessation of the previous birth.
Rebirth is caused by that unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); when that is abandoned, there is no further birth,
which is non-relinking (*apratisaṃdhāna*).
If it is argued that this leads to the consequence of the fruitlessness of karma, we say no;
for the experience of the ripening of karma is not denied.
It is said that when previous births have ceased, rebirth no longer occurs; however, the experience of the maturation of karma is not denied,
for all previous karmas indeed ripen in the final birth.
Thus [ends verse] 64.
It is not so, because the continuum of afflictions is inherent by its very nature.
The severance of the continuity of the afflictions is not possible;
why? Because the continuum of the afflictions is inherent—this continuum of afflictions is beginningless, and that which is beginningless cannot be eradicated. // 65 //
Regarding this, someone offers a rebuttal:
"Just as there is non-eternality due to non-existence prior to origination, so too is there non-eternality even when [the property] is inherent. (NyS 4.1.66)
Just as the beginningless non-existence prior to arising is brought to an end by an arisen entity, so too the natural continuity of afflictions is impermanent. // 66 //
It is like the impermanence of the blackness of an atom.
Another says: Just as the blackness of an atom is beginningless and yet impermanent due to contact with fire, so too is the continuum of afflictions. // 67 //
Indeed, for an existent entity, the reality is both permanence and impermanence; these are figurative [designations] with respect to its presence and absence.
"The blackness of an atom is beginningless."
Thus, because there is no reason [for this], it is incorrect;
for there is no reason here that "that which has the nature of non-arising is impermanent."
But this is the [correct] concentration:
because passion and the other afflictions have conceptualization as their cause. (NyS 4.1.68)
The phrase "because they have karma as their cause and because they are mutually causal" is a conjunction;
[this refers to] from false conceptualizations that are provocative of passion, provocation of anger, and delusion.
Attachment, aversion, and delusion arise; and karma, which brings about a particular class of beings, produces the regularized forms of attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Because of the observation of a fixed rule;
for it is observed that some class of beings has an abundance of passion, some an abundance of hatred, and some [an abundance of delusion].
"One who is full of delusion," and the arising of passion and the other afflictions occurs through mutual causation.
One who is undeluded does not become attached; one who is deluded becomes angry. When attached, one becomes deluded;
when angry, one becomes deluded.
[This is the root] of all false conceptualizations.
Because there is no arising from the knowledge of reality, and because an effect does not arise when its cause does not arise, there is the absolute non-arising of passion and the other afflictions.
Thus, the claim that "the continuum of afflictions is beginningless" is incorrect; for indeed, all these internal [phenomena]...
Entities such as the body and so forth proceed in a beginningless continuum;
herein, nothing that has never previously arisen ever arises for the first time, except through the knowledge of reality.
And this being so, nothing that is of the nature of non-arising is asserted to be of the nature of decay;
for karma, which brings about the classes of sentient beings, [is overcome] by the knowledge of reality.
Because false conceptualizations are frustrated, they do not become the cause for the arising of passion and so forth;
rather, they result in the experience of pleasure and pain. // 68 //
Thus ends the first section of the fourth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya composed by Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second section of the fourth chapter of the Nyāyabhāṣya: "Now, indeed, sir, does the knowledge of reality arise with respect to each and every one of as many objects as there are?"
Now, does it arise in some particular place?
And what is the distinction here? It is certainly not in each individual case.

It arises with respect to as many objects as there are—since the objects of knowledge are infinite—and yet it does not arise with respect to any [object] whatsoever; for if it did not arise with respect to that [particular object], it would follow that there remains a residue of delusion (*moha*) because delusion has not ceased there. Furthermore, delusion regarding one object cannot be negated by knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) regarding a different object. Indeed, delusion is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), not merely the non-arising of knowledge of reality; and that false knowledge, when operating upon a certain object, becomes the seed of *saṃsāra*—that object must be known in its true nature.
Regarding the term "to be known":
what, then, is that false knowledge?
It is the grasping of a self in what is not-self.
The delusion "I am" is the conceit of "I. Indeed, the view of one who perceives what is not-self as "I am" is the conceit of "I.
Furthermore, what is that collection of objects which is the domain of the conceit of "I"?
It is the body, the sense faculties, the mind, feelings, and cognitions.

How does the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) directed toward that [body and so forth] become the seed of saṃsāra? Indeed, this [ego-sense], having resolved that "I am" with respect to the collection of objects such as the body, and imagining the destruction of the self upon the destruction of those [objects], being overwhelmed by the thirst for non-destruction, repeatedly grasps them; and grasping them, it strives for birth and death.

Because one is not separated from that [suffering], one is not completely liberated from suffering. However, he who perceives that suffering, the basis of suffering, and even pleasure that is conjoined with suffering—all this is suffering—thoroughly understands suffering; and suffering, once thoroughly understood, becomes abandoned through non-clinging, like food mixed with poison.
Thus, he perceives that the faults (*doṣa*) and karma are the causes of suffering.

He realizes that as long as the faults have not been abandoned, it is impossible to sever the continuity of suffering; therefore, he abandons the faults. It has been stated that when the faults are abandoned, there is no further activity for the sake of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhāna*);
thus, he establishes the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), which are the sufferings of existence after death and their fruits, as well as karma and the faults as things to be abandoned.

Liberation is that which is to be attained; the means for its attainment is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Thus, for one who cultivates, practices, and contemplates the objects of knowledge as divided into these four categories, right vision (*samyagdarśana*) arises.
Through the realization of things as they truly are,
the knowledge of reality arises.
And thus:
"From the knowledge of reality regarding those things caused by defects, there is the cessation of the ego-sense. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.1)

The objects of knowledge (prameya), beginning with the body and ending with suffering, are caused by defects (doṣa), because false cognition (mithyājñāna) has them as its object. Therefore, this true cognition (tattvajñāna), when produced regarding those same objects, removes the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), because there is a contradiction between the two when they share the same object. Thus, from true cognition, according to the sūtra: “Upon the successive disappearance of false cognition, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the absence of that which immediately precedes it, which is liberation” (NS 1.1.2).
Thus, this summary of the meaning of the treatise is restated; it is not being prescribed as something previously unknown. // 1 //
But indeed, according to the sequence of higher discernment (prasamkhyāna):
"The objects such as form and so forth, which are the causes of defects, are produced by conceptualization (saṃkalpa). — Nyāyasūtra 4.2.2.

The objects of desire are the sense-objects, which are called form and so forth. When these are falsely conceptualized, they give rise to passion, hatred, and delusion; therefore, one should first examine them.
For one who examines them, false conceptualization regarding the objects such as form ceases. Upon that cessation, one should examine the internal body and so forth.

Through the discernment of that [reality], the ego-sense whose object is the internal self ceases. One who thus dwells with a mind detached both internally and externally is said to be liberated. // 2 //
Beyond this, it is taught that some designations are to be abandoned while others are to be cultivated;
this is not for the purpose of rejecting objects or accepting objects. How so? [Nyāyasūtra 4.2.3: "But the misconception of a whole (avayavin) is caused by that."
The cause of those faults, however, is the conceit of a whole;
and that indeed consists of the notion of "woman" together with its equipment for a man, and the notion of "man" for a woman.
And the requisite:
the perception of signs and the perception of secondary characteristics;
this is the perception of signs.
The tongue, the ears, the teeth, the lips, the eyes, and the nose are the perception of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). [One perceives them thus:
"the teeth are like this," "the lips are like this."
This perception (saṃjñā) increases desire as well as the faults associated with it, which are to be avoided.
The avoidance of this [perception] occurs through the perception of its individual components;
the perception of hair, body hair, flesh, blood, bone, sinew, veins, phlegm, bile, excrement, and so forth—this they call the "perception of the foul" (aśubha-saṃjñā).

For one who cultivates that [perception], sensual desire is abandoned. Even when the two kinds of objects are present, it is taught that some perception should be cultivated and some should be avoided; just as, in the case of food mixed with poison, the perception of "food" is to be maintained while the perception of "poison" is to be abandoned. // 3 //
Now, in order to refute the [existence of] an object, the following is established regarding the whole (avayavin):
NyS 4.2.4: Doubt arises because of the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance.

Knowledge is twofold because of the perception of both the existent and the non-existent. Nescience is also twofold because of the non-perception of both the existent and the non-existent. Since the whole (*avayavin*) is being perceived, there is doubt due to the twofold nature of knowledge; and since it is not being perceived, there is doubt due to the twofold nature of nescience. Thus, whether this whole is perceived or even if it is not perceived, one is in no way released from doubt. // 4 //
There is no doubt regarding that, because it has been established by the previous reason.
In that regard, doubt is not appropriate; why?
Because the previously stated reasons have not been refuted, it follows that there is the commencement of another substance. // 5 //
Furthermore, because the occurrence [of doubt] is untenable, there can be no doubt.
In that case, doubt is also untenable because its occurrence is impossible—namely, [the doubt] "Does the whole not exist? // 6 //
He analyzes that [point]:
"Because parts do not subsist either wholly or partially [in the whole], the whole does not exist. (NyS 4.2.7)

Each individual part does not first produce the whole in its entirety—because of the difference in their dimensions and because it would follow that there could be no connection with other parts; nor does it produce it in a single part [of the whole], for there are no other parts of this [whole] that exist as mere parts. // 7 //
Now, does the whole reside in its parts?—NyS 4.2.8: Because it does not reside in them, the whole does not exist.
To begin with, it does not subsist in each individual part, because of the difference in their dimensions and because it would follow that the substance consists of only a single substance.
Nor does it subsist in a single portion [of the parts], because there would be an absence of other parts in all [other portions].
Thus, such a doubt is not logical: that "the whole does not exist. // 8 //
And because it does not exist separately from its parts.
And [the argument] that it is not perceived as separate from its parts—that is, from the substrata—is the same [as the previous one]. // 9 //
Nor are the parts the whole.
NyS 4.2.11: Since there is no differentiation within a single entity, the application of words denoting differentiation is untenable; therefore, the question is invalid.
The question—whether the whole composite exists in each part entirely or by way of a single portion—is untenable. Why?

Because since there is no division within a single entity, the employment of words implying division is impossible. "Entirely" (*kṛtsnam*) denotes the totality of what is manifold; "a single portion" (*ekadeśaḥ*) denotes a particularity within a state of multiplicity.

These two words, "part" (kṛtsna) and "one part" (ekadeśa), which have difference as their object, are not applicable to a single composite whole—because of the absence of difference [within it]. // 11 //
"It does not exist in part because there is no other constituent part"—this is not a valid reason;
for even if there were another constituent part, [the object] would still not subsist [in that part]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.12)
Regarding the statement "because of the absence of another part":
even if one part were to become another part, the other part would reside in that part rather than in the whole—that is, in something other than the whole.
Since it does not reside [in the whole] even when there is another part, the argument—"the whole does not reside in a single part because of the absence of another part"—is not a valid reason.
If it is asked, "How is there subsistence (vṛtti)?"—
it is the attainment characterized by the relationship between a substratum and that which is supported within one [entity] existing in many places.
If it is asked, "How is there the state of being a substratum and that which is supported?"— [the answer follows].

That from which something else cannot obtain its own existence is its substratum (*āśraya*). An effect-substance does not obtain its own existence apart from the causal substances; however, the reverse is the case regarding the causal substances themselves.
If it is asked, "How is this so in the case of eternal [substances]?
[the answer is: It is established because it is observed in the case of non-eternal [substances].
If it is asked, "How can there be a relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) in eternal substances?
[the answer is: Since the relationship of substratum and superstratum is observed in non-eternal substances and qualities, its existence in eternal ones is established.

Therefore, for one who desires the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the misconception of a "whole" (*avayavin*) is refuted, not the whole itself—just as, regarding color and so forth, the false conceptualization that they are the "self" is negated, though color and so forth themselves are not denied. // 12 //
Even when opposed by the argument, "There is no perception of anything at all because the whole (avayavin) is not established" (NS 2.1.34), he says this:
"The perception of that [the whole] is like the perception of a mass of hair by one with ophthalmia. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.13).

Just as a single hair is not perceived by one with cataracts, whereas a mass of hairs is perceived, so too a single atom is not perceived, whereas a collection of atoms is perceived; thus, this apprehension has the aggregate of atoms as its object. // 13 //

NyS 4.2.14: Due to the sharpness or dullness of the sense organ, the apprehension of the object occurs accordingly without overstepping its own specific domain; it does not function with respect to what is not its object.
The clarity or dullness of the apprehension of objects occurs according to the clarity or dullness of the sense faculties with respect to their respective domains.
Indeed, even when the eye is heightened, it does not perceive an odor, which is not its domain; and when it is diminished, it does not deviate from its own domain.

Thus, a certain person afflicted with cataracts (taimirika) does not perceive a single hair, which is the object of the eye, yet perceives a mass of hairs. For both [the hair and the mass] are perceived by an eye free from cataracts.

Atoms, however, are beyond the senses; they are not objects of any sense-organ individually, yet they are perceived when aggregated. Thus, it would follow that the sense-organ functions upon what is not its proper object—namely, that no entity distinct from the atoms is ever perceived. Indeed, these very atoms exist in a state of aggregation.
If they are being perceived, they abandon their state of being beyond the senses; yet if they are separated and not being perceived, they do not attain the status of being objects of the senses.
Thus, if no distinct substance were produced, there would be this very great contradiction; therefore, it is established that there must be a distinct substance which is the object of perception.
If it is argued that the object is merely an accumulation?
No; this is incorrect because accumulation (*saṃcaya*) consists in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and since that [conjunction] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it cannot be perceived.

Indeed, accumulation is the conjunction of many things, and it is perceived only when its substratum is perceived, not when its substratum is beyond the senses. For one perceives: "This is conjoined with that. Therefore, this [argument] is incorrect. Furthermore, for an object being perceived by a sense organ, causes of non-perception such as obstruction are observed; therefore, the non-perception of atoms is not due to the weakness of the sense organs, just as the non-perception of odors and so forth by the eye is not due to the weakness of the sense organ.
And in this way, there would follow an infinite regress of parts and sub-parts until the dissolution of the world.

Indeed, that non-existence which follows from the negation of the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) in its parts (*avayava*), when applied to a part existing in its own parts, would either result in the dissolution of everything or lead to the exclusion of the partless. In both cases, there is the non-existence of the object of perception;
and due to that non-existence, there is the non-existence of perception itself.
Furthermore, this negation of mental modifications has perception as its substratum; thus, by destroying that substratum, it leads to self-destruction. // 15 //
Moreover: "There is no dissolution [of the world], because atoms exist. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.16)
Since the negation of existence based on the division of parts results in non-existence, this [non-existence] is excluded from the partless atom; it does not apply to the dissolution of all things.
Indeed, the partlessness of the atom is established because there is no possibility of further reduction through divisions, since nothing smaller than that can exist.

Indeed, when a clod of earth is divided into its constituent parts, it becomes increasingly smaller and smaller; and this process of becoming smaller reaches its limit because there is nothing smaller than that.
That which is the ultimate minimum is where the process ceases. Since there is nothing smaller than that, we designate it as the *paramāṇu* (atom). // 16 //
Or else, [the atom] is beyond the point of division.
Because the division of parts is not infinite and because substances are innumerable, there is no cessation of the state of being an atom (*truṭi*). // 17 //
Now, the proponent of non-apprehension (anupalambhika), thinking that everything does not exist, says:
"That [non-existence] is untenable because of the interpenetration with space. (NyS 4.2.18)
The existence of such an atom—partless and eternal—is untenable. Why?
Because it is permeated by space;
the atom is pervaded by space both internally and externally.
Because it is interpenetrated due to being intermixed, it possesses parts; because it possesses parts, it is impermanent. // 18 //
Or else, space would not be omnipresent.
Now, if it is not accepted that there is no space within the atom, it follows as a logical consequence that [the atom] would not be omnipresent. // 19 //
NyS 4.2.20: Since internal and external [space] are stated to be the causes of other substances that are effects, it follows that it does not exist in that which is not an effect.

The term "internal" (*antaḥ*) refers to a cause that is concealed by other causes, while "external" (*bahiḥ*) refers to a cause that is either intervening or non-intervening. This [distinction] is possible for a substance that is an effect; it is not possible for an atom, because it is not an effect.
For in an atom, which is not an effect, there is an absence of "internal" and "external."
And that in which its existence consists as a subtle effect is not an atom, for an atom is that than which nothing smaller exists. // 20 //
And because conjunction and sound are all-pervasive, [ether] is omnipresent.

Wherever sounds arise, they manifest in space; they have space as their substratum. Conjunctions occur in space between minds, atoms, and their effects. No corporeal substance is perceived that is not conjoined with space; therefore, it is not non-omnipresent. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.22): Non-displacement, non-obstruction, and omnipresence are the properties of space.
Just as water is not obstructed by a solid, resistant substance such as wood— why?
because it is partless— likewise, a solid, resistant substance does not block [the movement of] that which possesses parts.
It does not obstruct the quality that is the cause of its action; why?
Because it is intangible (*asparśatva*). For obstruction is observed in the opposite case;
one ought not to suspect a property observed in a composite, tangible substance to apply to its contrary.
Because it would follow that the minute part would be even more minute than the atom, the existence of the atom as an effect is refuted.
Furthermore, if the atom were composed of parts, it would follow that the part of the atom must be even smaller than the atom itself. Why?
Because a difference in magnitude is observed between a causal substance and its effect. Therefore, the part of the atom must be subtler;
thus, that which is composed of parts is the effect of the atom. Consequently, this [atom] is denied to be an effect of another atom.
Furthermore, the impermanence of an effect results from the disjunction of its causes, not from its penetration by space;
the impermanence of a clod of earth results from the disjunction of its constituent parts, not from its occupation by space. // 22 //
And because the configuration of corporeal things is possible, there exists the reality of constituent parts.

For among those things that are delimited and possess touch, it is possible for there to be configurations such as triangular, square, even, and circular; since that which constitutes a configuration is an arrangement of parts, and atoms are circular, they must therefore possess parts. // 23 //
And because conjunction is possible.

An atom situated in the middle, when conjoined with two atoms—one preceding and one following—creates a separation between them. By virtue of this separation, it is inferred that it is conjoined with the preceding atom by its front part and conjoined with the following atom by its rear part. Those two parts, the front and the rear, are its constituent parts (*avayava*). Thus, for that which is conjoined on all sides, there are constituent parts corresponding to its parts on every side. // 24 //
