As for the statement: "The existence of parts [is established] because of the occurrence of configuration in things possessing form" (VS 4.1.6),
this has already been addressed.
What has been said? "Because there is no further reduction of the degree of division beyond that point where it becomes minimal, [division] ceases there; [this applies to] the part of an atom."
"Because it would follow that [the atom] is even more minute, the existence of an atomic effect is denied.
Furthermore, as for this [argument]:
"And because conjunction is possible..."
[If one asks] why [it is not perceived], it is because there is an obstruction due to its possessing tangibility.

Furthermore, because the substratum does not pervade [the whole], there is a partiality of division. And it has been stated in this regard: "An atom possessing tangibility acts as an obstructor due to the resistance between two atoms that possess tangibility."
It is not so, because [the atom] has parts and possesses tangibility; thus, when there is an intervening space, the conjunction of atoms does not pervade its substratum.

There arises a division into parts, as in the thought "this one possesses a portion"; it has been stated here that [such a division] leads to the undesirable consequence of becoming increasingly minute.
Because there is no smaller [magnitude] for it to abide within; and because it would follow that its constituent part must be even more minute, the existence of atoms as effects is refuted.
And because of the occurrence of spatial configuration and the occurrence of conjunction in those things possessing form, the atoms must possess parts— on account of these two reasons.
There is no refutation [of our position] because [the opponent's argument] would lead to an infinite regress, and an infinite regress is untenable.
"Whatever has form and whatever is joined, all that is composed of parts"—these two reasons bring about an infinite regress (anavasthā).
Yet such an infinite regress is not tenable;
for only if the infinite regress were real would these two reasons be valid.
Therefore, this [argument] does not constitute a refutation of partlessness.
Furthermore, division is not possible because it entails the destruction of that which is being divided; consequently, the state of having dissolution as its end is not tenable.
Moreover, in the case of infinite regress, there would be an infinity of substance-parts for every substratum.
The non-perception of differences in magnitude and of weight, as well as the equality of magnitude between the part and the whole, occurs after the division of the parts of the atom. // 25 //

That you, relying on the intellect (*buddhi*), think that "objects of the intellect exist," is a false cognition; for if these were cognitions of reality, they would persist even when analyzed by the intellect.
If the true nature of objects of cognition were perceived while they were being analyzed—[it would not be so].

However, because the true nature of entities is not perceived through the analysis performed by the intellect, that [nature] is not perceived; just as the existence of a cloth is not perceived when the threads are pulled away. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.26)

Just as when each individual thread is being analyzed— thinking "this is a thread, this is a thread"— no distinct entity whatsoever is perceived that could be the object of the cognition of a cloth, because its true nature is not apprehended.
When a cognition of a cloth arises in the absence of an object, it is a false cognition;
so it is in all cases. // 26 //
NyS 4.2.27: It is not a valid reason because it is contradictory.
If there is an analytical discernment of phenomena by means of the intellect,
it does not follow that the true nature of all phenomena is unapprehended.
Now, is it that the true nature of all entities is not perceived?
It is not; for the analytical investigation of entities by means of the intellect and the non-perception of their true nature through such investigation are contradictory. As it has been said:
“And thus there would be the consequence of an infinite regress of parts and sub-parts until the dissolution [of the world]. (15) // 27 //
Because it has that as its substratum, there is no separate apprehension.
An effect-substance (kāryadravya) rests upon its cause-substances (kāraṇadravya) and is not perceived separately from those causes. In the opposite case, because it is perceived separately,
wherever the relationship of support and supported does not exist, there [the two] are separate.
Regarding "grasping":
through the discernment by the intellect, there is the grasping of entities as distinct from one another.
Regarding atoms which are beyond the senses, that which is perceived by a sense organ, when analyzed by this intellect, is [determined to be] something else. // 28 //
And because the understanding of the meaning [of the Veda] arises from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The realization of the true nature of entities through analytical investigation by the intellect—
namely, what exists and how it exists, and what does not exist and how it does not exist— is established entirely through the apprehension of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And that which is apprehension by means of valid cognition is the analytical discernment of entities by the intellect; through that, all treatises,
all actions, and all embodied beings [are established].

Empirical transactions are pervaded [by this]: for one who investigates determines through the intellect, "this exists" or "this does not exist. And in that regard, there is no impossibility of all entities existing. // 29 //
NyS 4.2.30: [The non-existence of the self is established] by the non-establishment and establishment of the means of valid cognition.
And this being the case, the claim that "everything does not exist" is not tenable;
why? Because of the non-establishment or establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If the statement "everything does not exist" were established by a means of valid cognition, then [everything would exist].
If it is argued that "it does not exist" is contradicted because no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is possible,
then how can the proof of the claim "everything does not exist" be established?
Now, if establishment occurs without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), how is it that the claim "everything exists" is not established? // 30 //
NyS 4.2.31: This conceit regarding the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition is like the conceit regarding objects in a dream.

Just as in a dream objects do not exist and yet there is a conceit [of their existence], so too the means of valid cognition and the objects of valid cognition do not exist, and yet there is a conceit of means of valid cognition and objects of valid cognition. // 31 //
Or rather, it is like an illusion, a city of Gandharvas, or a mirage.
NyS 4.2.33: There is no proof because of the absence of a reason.

"There is no reason for the claim that 'the conceit regarding the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge exists at the end of a dream like the conceit regarding objects [in a dream], but not at the end of waking like the perception of objects [in the waking state]'; due to the absence of a reason, this [claim] is unestablished."
Furthermore, regarding the claim that non-existent objects are perceived at the end of a dream, there too is a lack of evidence.
If it is argued that [the objects of dream] do not exist because they are not perceived upon waking, we reply:
there is no such negation, because objects are indeed perceived within the scope of waking consciousness. If, on account of their non-perception upon waking, the objects in a dream do not exist...
If they exist, then these objects which are perceived by one who has awakened must exist because they are perceived.
For the causal efficacy of a reason lies in its contrapositive:
when there is an absence of perception, non-existence is established by that very non-perception;
however, when non-existence is established in both ways, it is not through non-perception.
There is efficacy. Just as, for example, due to the absence of a lamp there is no seeing of form, in that case the absence is established by means of the presence;
and this statement of a reason applies to the conceptualization within a dream.
By stating "like the conceit regarding the objects of a dream," the cause for the diversity within dreams must be explained:
some dreams are accompanied by fear, while others are accompanied by joy.
Someone might be the opposite of both [cases], never even seeing a dream; however,
this refers to the conceit regarding dream objects which possesses a causal basis.
From the conceptualization of signs, the arising of conceptualization occurs. // 33 //
And the conceit regarding the objects of a dream is like memory and mental construction.
It has as its object that which was previously perceived;
for example, memory and intention have as their objects what was previously perceived, and they do not serve to deny it.

It is conceptualized thus: just as the apprehension of objects in a dream is not a denial of those objects previously perceived, so too the end of the dream state is [not distinct from] the end of the waking state with respect to the objects seen.

He who, while asleep, sees a dream, is the very same person who, upon waking, connects those dream-visions with the thought, "I saw this. In that state, by virtue of the waking state's cognitive function, there arises the determination that the conceit regarding the objects of the dream was false.

And when one reconnects [with waking consciousness], the determination that "the mental state of one who is awake is false, being a conceit regarding dream objects" occurs by virtue of that [waking] cognition.
However, if there were no distinction between the two states, the means of proof would be purposeless.
For one for whom there is no distinction between the state of dreaming and the state of waking,
the proof that "it is like the conceit regarding objects in a dream" is useless, because its very basis has been refuted.
Furthermore, the determination that "this is that" when it is not that is based on the primary [cause];
for example, the determination that "this is a person" with respect to a post that is not a person.
That [cognition] has the primary object as its basis— for indeed, when a person is not perceived, there can be no determination that "this is a person" regarding one who is not a person;
likewise, the determination of an object in a dream is such as "I saw an elephant."
The statement "I saw the mountain" ought to have its primary locus in the self. // 34 //
And this being so:
"The destruction of false perception results from the knowledge of reality, just as the disappearance of the conceit regarding the objects of a dream occurs upon waking. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.35)

The determination "this is a person" with respect to a post is a false perception; it is a cognition of something as what it is not. The determination "this is a post" with respect to a post is knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
And by the knowledge of reality, false perception is sublated— not the object characterized as a common feature of both a post and a person,
as in the case of waking from sleep.
By that function of knowledge, the conceit regarding the objects of a dream is sublated— not the object characterized as a mere generality,
but likewise [the conceit] regarding illusions, cities of the Gandharvas, and mirages.

Those cognitions which consist of the determination "this is that" even in that case, by this very method, there is the destruction of the perception of "me" through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
It is not a negation of the object.

And just as in the case of grasping [an object], there is false cognition regarding illusions and the like. Having taken up a substance that resembles the thing to be made known, the possessor of the means produces a false determination in another.

That is illusion (māyā): for instance, when the city-like configuration of Nīhāraprabhā and others is perceived from a distance, the cognition of a "city" arises; yet in the absence of that [distance], it does not occur. Likewise, in the rays of the sun, due to terrestrial heat...

When things are mixed and moving, the cognition of water arises due to the apprehension of common characteristics; for one standing nearby, this cognition is absent when those conditions are reversed.
Since false cognition occurs at some time, in some place, and for someone, it is not without a cause.
Furthermore, a duality of cognitions is observed in the case of a magician and another person situated at a distance or nearby, regarding such things as a city of Gandharvas or a mirage.

And [the distinction] between one who is asleep and one who has awakened regarding the object of a dream is not tenable if all this were non-existent, if it were indefinable, or if it were devoid of self-nature. // 35 //
And it is the same for cognition, because the existence of its cause is perceived.
And there is no negation of [the existence of] false cognition as something possessing an object; why?
Because its cause is perceived and its actual existence is perceived.
Both the cause of false cognition and the false cognition itself are perceived.
It is apprehended as having arisen within each individual self because it is an object of experience;
therefore, even a false cognition exists. // 36 //
And because of the distinction between the real and the primary, the twofold nature of false cognition is established.

The reality is "it is a post," or "it is the primary matter (pradhāna), it is the person (puruṣa)," because there is no loss of the reality or the primary matter. Due to this difference, the false cognition arises that "there is a person in the post."
Because of the apprehension of a commonality;
thus, for example, one says "crane" for a banner and "pigeon" for a clod of earth.
However, there is no coexistence of false cognitions regarding dissimilar objects,
because of the fixed determination of the apprehension of the universal.

But for one for whom everything is selfless (*nirātmaka*) and devoid of designation (*nirupākhya*), the consequence follows that there would be a total immersion [of consciousness] therein; furthermore,
regarding objects of cognition such as odor and so forth, cognitions of odor and so forth are considered false from the perspectives of both reality (*tattva*) and the primary [element].
And because there is no apprehension of a universal (sāmānya), these are indeed cognitions of reality; therefore, it is incorrect to say that "cognitions of objects of knowledge are false. // 37 //
It has been stated: “The cessation of egoism [occurs] through the knowledge of reality regarding the causes of defects” (4.2.1). Now, how does this knowledge of reality arise?—[The answer is:
“From the practice of a specific form of meditative concentration” (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.38).

But that [concentration], when the mind has been withdrawn from the objects of the senses and is being held by an effort that sustains it, is a conjunction with the self characterized by the desire to know reality (tattva-bubhutsā), provided that...
For indeed, when cognitions do not arise toward the objects of the senses, the cognition of reality arises through the power of that practice. // 38 //
NyS 4.2.39: It is not so, because of the predominance of a specific object.
This is not tenable because cognition arises even against one’s will;
why? Because of the intensity of a particular object, the arising of cognition is observed even for one who does not desire to know it, as in the case of the sound of thunder and the like.
In that case, a distinction between concentrations is not tenable. // 39 //
And because [the self] is impelled by hunger and other such states.
Because cognitions arise even against one's will due to hunger and thirst, cold and heat, and diseases, therefore one-pointedness of mind is impossible. // 40 //
Let this be the cause for emergence from meditative absorption and that which is antagonistic to absorption. However, even when this exists—NyS_4.2.41:
its arising occurs due to the connection with the fruits of previously performed [actions].
That which was performed previously,
accumulated in another birth, and serves as the cause for the knowledge of reality is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapraviveka*). It is that which is followed by its fruit.
There is the capacity for the practice of yoga; for if practice were fruitless, people would not respect it.
Indeed, the efficacy of practice is observed in worldly activities. (41)
And for the purpose of avoiding obstacles:
NyS 4.2.42: Instruction on the practice of yoga in forests, caves, sandy banks, and similar locations.
The dharma produced by the practice of yoga persists even in another birth;

when that dharma, which is the cause of the knowledge of reality, reaches the pinnacle of accumulation through the cultivation of intense meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the knowledge of reality arises.
And the suppression of a particular object by the intensity [of another] is observed through meditative concentration;
for a worldly person says: "I did not hear this, I did not know this—my mind was elsewhere. // 42 //
If it is granted that cognition arises even against one's will due to the intensity of a particular object, then the same consequence would follow regarding liberation as well. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.43)
Even for one who is liberated, cognitions might arise due to the power of external objects. // 43 //
NyS_4.2.44: No, because that which has already been established necessarily occurs.

When the body— which is the locus of movement, the sense organs, and their objects— is produced by the power of karma, the arising of cognitions necessarily occurs because [the body] serves as their instrumental cause;
and yet, even though it is powerful, the external object [is not the cause].
The self becomes capable of producing cognition; for it is observed that its capacity to produce cognition arises from its conjunction with a sense organ. // 44 //
And the absence of that [suffering] occurs in liberation (apavarga).

In the state of liberation (apavarga), there is an absence of that body and sense organs which serve as the substratum for the causes of cognition, due to the absence of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma).
Regarding this, it has been said:
"The same undesirable consequence would apply even to liberation (apavarga)"—
this is incorrect;
therefore, apavarga is the release from all suffering.
Since the seed of all suffering and the locus of all suffering are severed in liberation (apavarga), therefore liberation is freedom from all suffering; it is not without seed and without locus.
And suffering arises. // 45 //
For that purpose, there is the refinement of the self through restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), and through yoga by means of the methods prescribed for internal discipline.
For the attainment of that liberation, there is the purification of the self through restraint (yama) and observance (niyama); [first] restraint.
The means for accomplishing dharma are common to those in all stages of life (āśrama),
but the observance (niyama) is distinguished; furthermore, it consists of the purification of the self, the destruction of demerit (adharma), and the accumulation of merit (dharma).

Furthermore, the method for the higher self (adhyātma-vidhi) is to be understood from the Yogaśāstra; that [method] consists of austerity (tapas), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), and concentration (dhāraṇā).
The practice of discernment regarding the objects of the senses is for the purpose of abandoning attachment and aversion;
the means, however, is the application of the rules of yoga practice. // 36 //
The practice of grasping knowledge and engaging in discussion with those who possess that same knowledge.
The phrase "for that purpose" refers to the subject at hand.

"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which something is known; it is the scripture of self-knowledge (*ātmavidyā*). Its "acquisition" (*grahaṇa*) consists of its study and retention, as well as its repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), which is constant application.
Study, hearing, and reflection,
as well as discussion with those who possess that knowledge, are for the sake of maturing wisdom.

Maturation (paripāka), however, consists of the cutting off of doubt, the awakening to an unknown object, and the confirmation of what has been determined; it is a concordant agreement accompanied by the removal of objections. // 47 //
The statement, "And a discussion with those who possess that knowledge," whose meaning was not yet fully analyzed, is now being analyzed:
NS 4.2.48: One should approach such a person [for discussion] along with disciples, teachers, fellow students, and those seeking the highest good, provided they are free from malice.
This very statement establishes that it is of definitive meaning (nītārtha). // 48 //
If one should think: "The adoption of a position and its counter-position is unfavorable to the opponent"—then [the answer is]:
"Or, even if it lacks a counter-position, it may be employed for the sake of a specific purpose, provided there is a desire [to engage]. (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.49)
The phrase "one should approach him" carries over [from the previous context];
this refers to one who, desiring to acquire wisdom from another, approaches by manifesting a desire to know reality.
Without establishing his own position, he should purify his own philosophical system. // 49 //
Furthermore, the philosophical views of various teachers are mutually contradictory, and some overstep the bounds of logic due to attachment to their own positions. Regarding this:
NyS 4.2.50: "Wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth, just as one uses a covering of thorny branches to protect the growth of seeds."
This is for those who have not yet produced the knowledge of reality, whose defects are not yet abandoned, and who are striving for that purpose. // 50 //
And for one who is being treated with contempt by another due to [the latter's] learning, disillusionment, and so forth—NyS 4.2.51:
"Engaging in debate after having been provoked by those two."

"Having engaged in debate" means with the desire for victory, not with the desire to know the truth; thus, this is for the sake of protecting one's learning, not for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. // 51 //
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya composed by the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Now, in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* with its commentary (*Ṭīkā*), the first section (*āhnika*) of the fifth chapter begins.

It was stated briefly that "the multiplicity of *jātis* arises from the various ways of counter-arguing by means of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*"); that [point] is now analyzed in detail:
these *jātis*, indeed, constitute twenty-four refutations when a reason for establishing a position (*sthāpanāhetu*) has been employed.

NyS 5.1.1: *Sādharmyasama*, *vaidharmyasama*, *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, *sādhyasama*, *prāptisama*, *aprāptisama*, *prasaṅgasama*, *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*, *anutpattisama*, *saṃśayasama*, *prakaraṇasama*, *ahetusama*, *arthāpattisama*, *aviśeṣasama*, *upapattisama*, *upalabdhisama*, *anupalabdhisama*, *nityasama*, *anityasama*, and *kāryasama*—these are [fallacies] consisting of counter-objections based on similarity (*sādharmya*).
Since they are not distinguished from the original probative reason (*sthāpanāhetu*), they are called *sādharmyasama*.
I shall provide examples of these various types in their respective places.
In this same manner, the *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the heterogeneity) and other such sophisms are also to be explained.
The definition, however, is as follows:

NyS 5.1.2: When a conclusion is drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the two sophistries known as *sādharmya-sama* (balancing the similarity) and *vaidharmya-sama* (balancing the dissimilarity) arise from the possibility of proving the opposite of that property.

When an objection is raised through similarity (*sādharmya*) such that the opposite of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is established, the counter-argument (*pratyavasthāna*) made through that very same similarity—which is not distinguished from the original reason for establishing the thesis—is the "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmyasama*) refutation.

An example is as follows: "The self possesses action (*kriyāvān*), because it is a substance endowed with qualities that are causes of action. A clod of earth is a substance endowed with qualities that are causes of action and it possesses action; likewise, the self is so [endowed], therefore it possesses action."

When [the argument] has been thus presented, the opponent objects on the basis of similarity alone: "The self is inactive, because an all-pervading substance is inactive. Space is all-pervading and inactive, and the self is likewise;
therefore, it is inactive.

Furthermore, there is no specific reason [to prefer one conclusion over the other]: that by virtue of similarity with something possessing action, it must be active, rather than by virtue of similarity with something inactive, it must be inactive.
Because there is no specific reason [to distinguish between them], the refutation based on similarity (*sādharmyasama*) occurs.

Now, as for the refutation based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*): "A clod of earth is seen to be limited because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action; the self (*ātman*) is not like that, therefore it does not possess action like the clod. [To this we reply: There is no specific reason [for such a conclusion]; by virtue of its similarity to that which possesses action, [the self] ought to be one that possesses action.

"Furthermore, [the soul] is not [active] because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action. This is the "balancing by dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*) due to the absence of a specific reason (*viśeṣahetu*).

And when there is a conclusion based on dissimilarity—namely, "The self is inactive because of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*); for a substance possessing action is seen to be non-omnipresent, like a clod of earth, whereas the self is not so; therefore, it is inactive"—there is an opposition based on dissimilarity as follows: "A substance devoid of action is seen to be space (*ākāśa*), which is devoid of qualities that cause action."

"The self is not like that; therefore, it is not inactive. Nor is there a specific reason [to prefer one conclusion over another]: that because of its dissimilarity to that which possesses action, it must be inactive, and not, conversely, because of its dissimilarity to that which lacks action, it must possess action. Due to the absence of a specific reason, this is "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*). Now, as for "balancing the similarity" (*sādharmyasama*): "A clod of earth is seen to possess action and to be endowed with qualities that are the causes of action; likewise [the self]..."

"And therefore the self must likewise possess action. But there is no specific reason [to establish this]—namely, that because it is dissimilar to that which possesses action it is devoid of action, yet because it is similar to that which possesses action it must possess action. Due to the absence of a specific reason, this is the "balancing the similarity" (sādharmyasama) fallacy. // 2 //
The answer to these two is:
"Its establishment is like the establishment of 'cowness' as a cow. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.3)

If the proof of the probandum were asserted merely through similarity or merely through dissimilarity, there would be an infinite regress; however, that [regress] does not apply when there is a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*).

A cow is established as a cow because of its similarity to other cows—namely, because of "cowness" (*gotva*), which is a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*)—and not because of its connection with the dewlap and so forth. A cow is established as a cow precisely because of its dissimilarity to horses and the like—namely, because of "cowness"—and not because of differences in qualities (*guṇa*) and so on.
This point has already been explained in the section on the members of the syllogism (*avayava-prakaraṇa*).

Furthermore, because the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are interconnected, they function toward a single object in common within a sentence; thus, this lack of systematic order is indeed based on fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa). // 3 //

NyS 5.1.4: Because of the variation in properties between the subject and the example, and because both may be unestablished, there are the fallacies of *utkarṣasama*, *apakarṣasama*, *varṇyasama*, *avarṇyasama*, *vikalpasama*, and *sādhyasama*.

*Utkarṣasama* (balancing by addition) occurs when one attributes a property of the example to the subject of the thesis: "If the self possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action, like a clod of earth, then it follows that it must also possess touch, just like the clod of earth. Alternatively, if it does not possess touch, then it cannot possess action either, like the clod of earth;
or else, some distinction [between the two cases] must be stated."

*Apakarṣasama* (the equalization by subtraction) occurs when one seeks to establish the absence of a property in the subject (*sādhya*) based on the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance: "A clod of earth is indeed seen to possess action and to be non-omnipresent; well then, let the self (*ātman*) also possess action and be non-omnipresent. Or, [if the opponent objects,] one must state the distinction in the opposite case. The *khyāpanīya* (to be explained) is the *varṇya* (the subject to be described), while the opposite is the *avarṇya* (not to be described). These two—*varṇyasama* and *avarṇyasama*—arise from reversing the properties of the subject and the example. Specifically, *varṇyasama* consists in treating the example as if it were the subject, and *avarṇyasama* consists in treating the subject as if it were not the subject. Thus, these two involve the inversion of the properties belonging to the subject and the example.

*Vikalpasama* (the equalization by alternative) occurs when, based on an alternative regarding another property in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) which is endowed with the probans (*sādhanadharma*), one implies an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). For instance: "Just as some things endowed with the qualities of action and gravity are heavy, such as a clod of earth, while others are light, such as air; likewise, some things endowed with the quality of being a cause of action might possess action, like a clod of earth, while others might be inactive, like the self. Or else, a distinction must be stated.

The *sādhyasama* (equal to the probandum) is a property connected with the capacity of the reason (*hetu*) and other members of the syllogism which, when applied to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), results in the probandum itself being [treated as] the example. For instance, if it is argued, "As is a clod of earth, so is the self," then it follows that "as is the self, so is the clod of earth. Since this self is the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*)—namely, that it possesses action—it would follow that the clod of earth must also be something to be proven;
yet, if this is not accepted, then the fallacy remains.
In that case, [the statement] "as is a clod of earth, so is the self" is not [correct]. // 4 //
The reply to these is as follows:
"Because the establishment of the conclusion [of the inference] occurs through some similarity, there is no refutation on the basis of dissimilarity. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.5)
The concealment of what has been established is inadmissible;
and an analogy is something established through some commonality—as in "as is a cow, so is a gavaya.
In that case, it is not possible to raise an objection regarding a variation in the properties of the cow and the gavaya.

Thus, when the property to be proven (sādhya) is established in the subject (dharmin) through the power of examples and so forth, it is not possible to state a refutation on the grounds of a difference in properties between the subject and the example, because of their dissimilarity (vaidharmya). // 5 //
And because the example is established through the extension of the property to be proven.

Where there is a consensus of intellect among worldly investigators, by that means an unerring object is extended [by analogy] for the purpose of making it known. Thus, when the extension of the probandum (*sādhyātideśa*) is applicable to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the status of being the probandum is untenable.

(Nyāyasūtra 5.1.7): Because a reason (*hetu*) is indistinguishable whether it reaches the probandum or does not reach it—since it cannot establish it if it does not reach it, and since it is no different [in its incapacity] even if it reaches it—the two [objections] are "balancing the reaching" (*prāptisama*) and "balancing the non-reaching" (*aprāptisama*).

Does the cause establish the probandum by reaching it or without reaching it? First, it cannot be by reaching it; for if there is no distinction upon reaching, it is not an establisher. When both [cause and effect] already exist and have reached one another, which of the two is the establisher and which is the established?
It does not establish without reaching it either—for a lamp does not illuminate what it has not reached.
Objection based on attainment is "attainment-parity" (prāptisama);
objection based on non-attainment is "non-attainment-parity" (aprāptisama). // 7 //

NyS 5.1.8: There is no prohibition [of the production of sound] because we observe the production of jars and other things, and because there is the practice of sorcery (*abhicāra*) involving crushing.

Indeed, the negation is untenable in both ways: [it is seen that] the agent, the instrument, and the locus produce an effect such as a jar from clay after having reached it; and furthermore, in the case of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), when there is affliction, it is observed that they are effective even without reaching [the object]. // 8 //

NyS 5.1.9: Because no reason is stated for the example, and because of the counter-objection by means of a counter-example, there are the two [fallacies] known as "the consequence" (prasaṅgasama) and "the counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama).

The "balancing the consequence" (prasaṅgasama) refutation is an objection based on the consequence that the means of proof itself must have a further means of proof: [the opponent argues] that while it is stated as a reason that "a clod of earth possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action," no such reason is specified for the clod itself, and there can be no establishment of a point without a reason. The "balancing the counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) is an objection based on a counter-example: when it is said, "The self possesses action because it is endowed with the quality that is the cause of action, like a clod of earth," a counter-example is adduced: "Space is also endowed with the quality that is the cause of action..."
"It is observed to be devoid of action.
But what quality of space serves as the cause for action?
It is conjunction with air, dependent upon a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), just like the conjunction between air and a tree. // 9 //
The answer to our two [objections] is as follows: "Just as there is a cessation of the requirement for the fuel of a lamp, so too is there a cessation of that [requirement]. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.10)
First, when asked this, he ought to say: "Who takes up a lamp, and for what purpose?
[The answer would be: "Those desiring to see, for the purpose of seeing the visible object.
Now, why do those desiring to see the lamp not take up another lamp?
Even without another lamp, a lamp is seen; therefore, the employment of a lamp for the purpose of seeing that lamp is useless.
Now, for what purpose is this example stated?
It is for the purpose of making known that which is not yet understood.

Now, for what purpose is the statement of the cause sought in the case of an example? If it is for the sake of making it known, then that example is already known—according to the definition: “An example is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts” (NS 1.1.25). Therefore, the statement of the cause for the sake of making it known is redundant.
Thus is the response to the *prasaṅgasama* [balancing-the-consequence] fallacy. // 10 //
Now, the reply to the "balancing by a counter-example" (pratidṛṣṭāntasama) fallacy: NyS 5.1.11: And when a counter-example functions as a reason, the [original] example is not a non-reason.

By one who states a counter-example (pratidṛṣṭānta), no specific reason is indicated—namely, that "in this manner the counter-example is the prover, whereas the example is not. Thus, if the counter-example functions as the reason, it follows that the example is not a reason. And how could that [counter-example] not be a reason, if it were an unrefuted prover? // 11 //
NyS 5.1.12: The "balancing the non-arising" (anutpattisama) [fallacy] occurs because of the absence of a cause prior to the arising [of the effect].

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," another person says: "Prior to its production, while the sound has not yet arisen, the quality of following immediately upon effort—which is the cause of impermanence—does not exist; in the absence of that [cause], permanence would follow, and for that which is permanent, there is no production."
The "balancing by non-arising" (anutpattisama) is an opposition based on non-arising. // 12 //
The answer to this is: Because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, the cause is established; therefore, there is no negation of the cause. (NyS 5.1.13)

"Because it exists as such once produced"—for it is indeed the case that "this sound has been produced. Prior to its production, the sound itself does not exist; [only] because the sound exists once produced, it is logical that the fact of being produced immediately following effort is the cause of the sound's impermanence.
Since this cause is established, this objection is untenable.
“Because of the absence of a cause prior to origination. // 13 //

NyS 5.1.14: Since the general property and the example are equally perceptible by the senses, [the fallacy] "balancing the doubt" (saṃśayasama) arises because of the commonality of both permanence and impermanence.

When the reason "sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar" has been stated, one objects by means of doubt: "Even if it follows immediately upon effort, it still possesses a commonality with the eternal [category], namely, being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*); and it also possesses this same quality with the impermanent jar. Therefore, because of this commonality with both the eternal and the impermanent, the doubt is not removed. (14)
The answer to this is:

*Nyāyasūtra* 5.1.15: "When doubt arises from similarity (*sādharmya*), there is no doubt from dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to an infinite regress of doubt; furthermore, since the universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted to be eternal, [the opponent's position] is not a valid refutation.

When an object is determined through its specific dissimilarities (*viśeṣa-vaidharmya*) as being 'not a person,' then doubt based on the similarity between a post and a person finds no room to arise."

Thus, when the impermanence of sound is ascertained through its specific dissimilarity—namely, its being produced immediately after an effort—doubt based on the similarity of both permanent and impermanent things finds no room. If it were to find such room, then doubt would be perpetual due to the non-cessation of the similarity between a post and a person;

for when a specific feature is perceived, the similarity with the permanent is not accepted as a cause of doubt—just as, when the specific features of a person are perceived, the similarity between a post and a person does not become a cause of doubt.
The "equal to the point at issue" (prakaraṇasama) [fallacy] occurs because the establishment of the process [of proof] results from the similarity to both sides.
The process (*prakriyā*) consists in the engagement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) due to their similarity through both the eternal and the non-eternal.

One person advances a thesis, saying: "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar. The second [person] does so by means of similarity with the eternal. This being the case, the reason "because it follows immediately upon effort," when stated by way of similarity with the non-eternal—
It does not transcend the state of indecision (*prakaraṇa*). Because it does not transcend the state of indecision, it does not bring about a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*);
and this is the same when the reason is stated by way of similarity with the eternal (*nitya-sādharmya*).
Thus, this opposition based on the non-transcendence of the state of indecision is *prakaraṇasama*.

This is the same even in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); because the establishment of the process occurs through the dissimilarity to both, it is called "the equal-to-the-issue" (*prakaraṇasama*). // 16 //
The answer to this is:
"Because the subject matter is established by means of a counter-position, the negation is untenable, since the counter-position is itself tenable. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.17)
By one who asserts the establishment of a process through the similarity of both sides, the establishment of a counter-position is effectively stated;

for if there is similarity between both, then one of them is a counter-position, and thus the counter-position becomes logically established. Since the counter-position is established, the refutation is untenable—because the establishment of a counter-position and the establishment of a refutation are mutually contradictory.

And the establishment of the treatise occurs through the ascertainment of reality; for if it were otherwise, the treatise would end in error. Indeed, when reality is ascertained, the treatise reaches its conclusion. // 17 //
NyS 5.1.18: Because the reason is not established in any of the three times, there is the "equalization by the non-reason" (ahetusama).
The cause is the means of proof; it must exist either before, after, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven (*sādhya*). If the means of proof exists first?
If the thing to be proven does not yet exist, for what is there a means of proof?
Or if it exists later?
If the means of proof (*sādhana*) does not exist, of what would this be the object to be proven (*sādhya*)?

Or, if the object to be proven and the means of proof were to exist simultaneously, then between two things that already exist, which would be the means of proof for which, and which would be the object to be proven for which? Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is no different from a non-reason (*ahetu*).
The "balancing by the non-reason" (ahetusama) is an objection based on the similarity [of the reason] with what is not a reason. // 18 //
The answer to this is:
"Because the probandum is established through the reason, there is no failure of proof across the three times. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.19)
There is no failure to establish [the existence of things] across the three times; why?
Because the probandum is established from the reason (*hetu*).

The accomplishment of that which is to be accomplished and the cognition of that which is to be known—both are seen to arise from a cause. This is a great instance of perceptible experience (*pratyakṣa-viṣaya*).
As for what was indeed said—"If the probandum does not exist, of what is there a proof?"—it is of that which is brought into being and that which is made known. // 19 //
And because the negation itself is untenable, there is no negation of that which is to be negated.
"Whether [the negation occurs] before, after, or simultaneously," such a negation is not tenable. Since the negation is untenable, the reason for the establishment [of the thesis] is proven. // 20 //
NyS 5.1.21: Arthāpattisama (the equalizing by implication) occurs when the opponent's position is established through an implication.

When the thesis has been established as "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the *arthāpattisama* (balancing the implication) occurs for one who establishes a counter-thesis by means of an implication (*arthāpatti*). [The opponent argues: "If sound is impermanent because of its similarity to impermanent things in that it follows immediately upon effort, then it follows by implication that it must be permanent because of its similarity to permanent things."
However, it possesses a commonality with the eternal: namely, intangibility. // 21 //
The answer to this is:

NyS 5.1.22: The occurrence of the defeat of one's own position (*pakṣahāni*) does not follow from the implication (*arthāpatti*) of what has not been stated, because that which has not been stated is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the nature of such implication.

For one who asserts that "even without explicitly stating the capacity [of the reason], it follows by implication," there is the possibility of the loss of the thesis—because it was not stated. That is to say, when the thesis of impermanence is established, it follows by implication that the thesis of permanence is subject to inconclusiveness (*anekāntika*). Furthermore, this implication applies equally to both sides: if sound is permanent because it shares the property of being intangible like space, then it follows by implication that it is impermanent because it shares the property of arising immediately after an effort.

Nor does this constitute an absolute presumption (arthāpatti) based merely on the opposite; for it is certainly not the case that from the fact that "a stone falls" one must presume as a matter of course that "there is no falling of liquid water. // 22 //

NyS 5.1.23: "The equalization based on existence" (sadbhāvopapatty-aviśeṣasama) occurs because, when there is no distinction due to the occurrence of a single property, it would follow that everything is without distinction, since [the property of] existence occurs [in all things].

A single property, namely "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), is applicable to both sound and a jar; thus, when there is no distinction between the two regarding their non-eternality, it follows that everything would be indistinguishable.
How so? Because existence is applicable: a single property, namely "existence," is applicable to everything.

Since this leads to the undesirable consequence of the non-distinction of all things due to the applicability of existence, the counter-argument is called "balancing the non-distinction" (*aviśeṣasama*). //23//
The answer to this is:
"Because in some cases a property is impossible, while in other cases it is possible, there is no [valid] negation. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.24)

Just as, because the single property of being produced immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is established for both the subject (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the other property of impermanence (*anityatva*) constitutes a non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*); it is not so in the case of all entities (*sarvabhāva*), for there is no other property that serves as the cause for the establishment of their existence by virtue of which they would be non-distinct.
Now, if it is thought: "Could impermanence itself be that other property serving as the cause for the establishment of the existence of entities everywhere? [the answer follows].
If this is indeed how it is conceived—"All things are impermanent because their existence is established"—then the following position results:

in that case, there is no example other than the very meaning of the proposition itself. And since there is no reason (hetu) without an example, it is untenable for a portion of the proposition to serve as the example; for that which is yet to be proven cannot itself be the example.

Since that which exists possesses both the states of being eternal and non-eternal, non-eternality is untenable; therefore, because the existence of "being" (sat) is established, the consequence is that there is no distinction between all things. Thus, this statement [of yours] is devoid of meaning.
By asserting that "all entities are non-eternal because their existence is established," you have admitted the non-eternality of sound; consequently, your negation of it is untenable. // 24 //
NyS 5.1.25: Equivalence through justification (upapattisama) occurs because the reasons for both [sides] are equally applicable.
If the cause for the non-eternality of sound is established, then sound is non-eternal;
however, the cause for its eternality is also established, namely its intangibility, and thus eternality is also established.
The counter-argument based on the establishment of the causes for both—non-eternality and eternality—is the "balancing of the proof" (*upapattisama*). // 25 //
The answer to this is:
"There is no refutation, because the reason for the proof is admitted. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.26)
By stating, "Because both causes are established," impermanence is not being denied on the grounds that the cause of impermanence is established;
for if it were denied,
there would be no establishment of both causes.
By stating that both types of causes are applicable, the applicability of the cause for impermanence is admitted; since this is admitted, the refutation is untenable.
If you argue that the refutation is valid because of a contradiction, then the contradiction is equal [in both cases].
If it is argued that a refutation has been stated by one who asserts the contradictory consequence of both permanence and impermanence for a single entity, [we reply:
the contradiction is equal for both one's own position and the opponent's position, and it does not establish either one. // 26 //
NyS 5.1.27: The "equal to apprehension" (upalabdhisama) occurs because [the probandum] is apprehended even in the absence of the stated cause.

Even in the absence of the stated cause of impermanence—namely, being produced immediately after an effort—the impermanence of sound arising from the snapping of a tree branch due to the impact of wind is observed.
Objection based on the perception of the property to be proven (the *sādhya*) even in the absence of the stated probans (*sādhana*) is the "equal to perception" (*upalabdhisama*) sophistry. // 27 //
The answer to this is:
"There is no refutation [of our position], because that property can also arise from another cause. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.28)

By stating "because it follows immediately after an effort," the production [of sound] from a cause is being asserted. However, this does not establish a necessary restriction of the effect to that specific cause;
and since sound can also arise from other causes, its impermanence remains established.
What is it that is being negated here? // 28 //
It is not the case that a sound which exists prior to its utterance is unperceived; why?

Because no such thing as an obstruction is perceived. Just as there is no perception of existing objects like water due to an obstruction and so forth, it is not the case that the non-perception of sound is due to an obstruction or similar cause for its non-apprehension. Furthermore, this cause for its non-apprehension would have to be perceived [if it existed], just as in the case of water and other such things;
yet it is not.
"Therefore, sound is apprehended as being contrary to water and so forth, because it is not perceived"—this is the "balancing of non-perception" (*anupalabdhisama*).
For when the non-existence [of something] is established through the non-perception of that [non-perception], its opposite is thereby rendered possible. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.29)
The non-apprehension of those [factors] such as the veil (āvaraṇa) is not itself apprehended; because it is not apprehended, its non-existence is established.

Since there is no evidence for the establishment of its non-existence, the opposite—namely, the existence of the veil and so forth—is determined. Because this opposite is proven, that which was asserted—that "there is no non-apprehension of the sound existing prior to its utterance"—is not established.

This is the reason: "because of the non-perception of obscuration and so forth. When one objects by means of an equal non-perception regarding both the obscuration and the like, as well as the non-perception of the obscuration and the like, it becomes the "equal to non-perception" (anupalabdhisama) fallacy. // 29 //
The answer to this is:
"Because non-apprehension is of the nature of non-perception, it is not a valid reason. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.30)

"The non-perception of an obstruction and so forth does not exist because of its non-perception"—this is not a valid reason. Why? Because non-perception consists in non-perception; that is, because non-perception is merely the absence of perception. That which exists is the object of perception—that is, by means of perception, it is asserted that "it exists. That which does not exist is the object of non-perception.
It is asserted that what is not perceived does not exist;
yet this non-perception of the non-perception of obstructions and so forth—which operates within its own domain—does not negate its own object.
And since the non-perception of obstructions and so forth remains unnegated, it is considered fit to serve as a logical reason (*hetu*).

Obstacles and the like, however, being existent, are objects of perception; there ought to be their perception. Since they are not perceived, that is understood from the non-perception—which is the absence of perception that would establish its own object—as follows: "Obstacles and the like do not exist as causes for the non-apprehension of sound."
Non-apprehension is established through non-perception; that [non-perception] has the [object] as its domain. // 30 //
And because one internally experiences the presence and absence of various cognitions and conceptual constructions.
The term "non-reason" (ahetu) carries over from the previous context.

Within the body, the existence and non-existence of the various cognitions of embodied beings are to be experienced through direct awareness—such as, "I have a cognition of doubt," or "I do not have a cognition of doubt. This applies likewise to perceptions, inferences, scriptural cognitions, and memories.
This very [awareness] constitutes the non-apprehension of obscuration and so forth.

The non-existence of perception is self-evident—[as in the thought] "I have no perception of an obstruction or the like of sound," meaning "the causes of sound's non-apprehension, such as obstructions and so forth, are not perceived.
In this regard, that which was stated—"the establishment of non-existence [of the cause] follows from the non-perception of its [i.e., the effect's] non-perception"—is not tenable. // 31 //

NyS 5.1.32: Anityasama (the equalization by the non-eternal) occurs because, through similarity, when a common property is established, it leads to the undesirable consequence that everything must be non-eternal.

For one who says, "Sound is impermanent because of its similarity to an impermanent jar," it follows that all things are impermanent— since there is a similarity between the impermanent jar and all entities—
and thus the impermanence of everything results, which is undesirable.
This is called "balancing the impermanent" (*anityasama*) because it is a counter-argument based on impermanence. // 32 //
The answer to this is:
"Because [the probans] is unestablished due to similarity, the negation is unestablished, owing to its similarity with that which is to be negated. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.33)
A "refutation" (pratiṣedha) is a statement consisting of members such as the proposition that negates the thesis and is characterized by a counter-position;
its similarity to the thesis—which is the object of negation—consists in its connection with the proposition and other members.
If, on account of this similarity to the impermanent, there is no establishment of impermanence?
Because similarity [with the subject] is unestablished, the negation is also unestablished—on account of its similarity with that which is to be negated. // 33 //

And since, in the example, the property known through the relationship of the probandum and the probans serves as the logical reason (*hetu*), and since that [property] exists in both ways [in the subject and in the example], there is no lack of distinction.

In an example, that property which is known through the relationship of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is designated as the "reason" (*hetu*). And that [property] exists in two ways: it is similar in some respects and distinct in others. From similarity comes similarity (*sādharmya*), and from distinction comes dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). A reason is a specific instance of similarity, not mere similarity in general, nor mere dissimilarity.

Alternatively, he states [these] positions by relying merely on similarity (*sādharmya*) and merely on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*): "The 'equalization through non-eternality' (*anityasama*) occurs because of the consequence that everything would be non-eternal due to the occurrence of a common property by virtue of similarity" (NS 5.1.32). This is incorrect.
And that which was stated regarding the refutation of the [fallacy] of "non-distinction" (aviśeṣasama) should also be understood here. // 34 //

The "balancing of the eternal" (nityasama) occurs when, because of the existence of the eternal in the non-eternal, the eternity [of the subject] is established; thus, it is a balancing of the eternal.
It is proposed that "sound is impermanent. Is that impermanence permanent in sound, or is it impermanent?
If, first of all, it exists at all times...

Because the property (dharma) exists at all times, the substratum (dharmī) must also exist at all times; thus, "sound is eternal. Alternatively, if it does not exist at all times, then because the property of impermanence is absent, sound is eternal.
Thus, because it is countered on the grounds of permanence, it is the "balancing of permanence" (nityasama). // 35 //

The answer to this is: NyS 5.1.36: Since the impermanent exists eternally within that which is to be negated, and since impermanence is established in the impermanent, there is no negation [of impermanence].

If it is stated, "Because of the existence of non-eternality in the sound which is to be negated," then the non-eternality of sound is admitted. And if, because non-eternality is established, the negation "Sound is not non-eternal" is not accepted, then the reason "because of the existence of non-eternality in the eternal" does not hold; and due to the absence of a reason, the negation is untenable.

Because of the cessation of what has arisen, there is the non-existence of sound; this is its impermanence. In that regard, the following inquiry is inappropriate: "Does this impermanence exist in sound at all times, or not?"
This is untenable. Why?

Because impermanence consists in the non-existence of a sound due to the cessation of that which has arisen. This being the case, there is no distinction between the locus and the contained because of contradiction.
Furthermore, permanence and impermanence are contradictory; thus, it is a contradiction for both permanence and impermanence to be attributes of a single substratum.
This is not possible;
therefore, as for what was stated there—namely, "Because non-eternality exists eternally, it is indeed eternal"—that was said with reference to something that does not actually exist. // 36 //
NyS 5.1.37: "The 'balancing the effect' (kāryasama) [fallacy occurs] because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort."
"Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort.

That which acquires its own existence immediately after effort is indeed something that comes into being after having not existed, such as an effect like a jar. And "impermanent" is understood to mean "having come into being, it ceases to be";
this being the case:
The refutation is stated as: "Because the effects of effort are manifold.

For instance, the acquisition of their own nature immediately following effort is observed in the case of jars and the like; and for concealed objects, there is manifestation through the removal of obstructions.
In that case, is the acquisition of its own nature by the sound subsequent to effort,
or is it its manifestation?
There is no distinction between these two.
The "equal to the effect" (kāryasama) fallacy consists in an objection raised on the basis of the non-distinction of the effect. // 37 //
The answer to this is:
"If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be its cause, because the reasons for non-perception are applicable. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.38)

If there were a difference between the effect [of sound] and [its manifestation], then since no cause for non-perception would be possible, effort would not be the cause for the manifestation of sound.

Where manifestation occurs immediately after effort, an obstruction is logically possible as the cause of non-perception; and by the removal of that obstruction, there occurs the manifestation characterized by the perception of the object that exists immediately following the effort. However, there is no such cause for the non-perception of sound.
It is possible that for some [thing], following an effort, there occurs a manifestation characterized by perception through the removal [of obstacles].
Therefore, sound is produced; it is not manifested. // 38 //

If it is argued that the reason is shown to be inconclusive— on the grounds that "because it is inconclusive, it is non-probative"— and if, moreover, its non-probativeness is due to its inconclusiveness,
then the same fault applies even to the refutation. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.39)
The negation is also inconclusive—meaning it negates some things but not others. Because it is inconclusive, it is not a proof.

Alternatively, regarding the position that sound is impermanent, there is an absence of a specific reason [to distinguish] that its appearance immediately after effort is production rather than manifestation; likewise, regarding the position that it is permanent, there is an absence of a specific reason [to distinguish] that its appearance immediately after effort is manifestation rather than production.
Since this absence of a specific reason is equal for both sides, both [arguments] are inconclusive. // 39 //
In all cases, it is thus.
In all these refuting reasons beginning with "similarity" (*sādharmya*), wherever no distinction is observed, an equal [fallacy] applies to both sides. // 40 //
Nyāyasūtra 5.1.41: In the counter-refutation of a refutation, there is a defect corresponding to the defect in the original refutation.

This very same fault of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) which is leveled even against the negation is equally applicable to the negation of that negation as well. Thus, the first position is the proponent’s formal argument (*sthāpanā*): "Sound is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort. This is [refuted by] the "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*) fallacy, based on the diversity of effects produced by effort. (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.37)
Thus, for those who argue with refutation, the second position is that [the opponent's argument] is negated by a reason of negation (*pratiṣedhahetu*), and this is called "negation" (*pratiṣedha*);
the third position is that even in the negation of this [second position], the same fault applies, and this is called "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*).
In this refutation of the refutation as well, the same fault applies; moreover, the fourth position is inconclusive. // 4 //
NyS 5.1.42: Having accepted that the refutation is faulty, to then apply the same fault to the counter-refutation is the fallacy of "admission of one's own position" (matānujñā).
Having accepted the second position as faulty, and having failed to state its refutation, one merely permits it when there is a counter-refutation of that prohibition.

In the third position, the fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) remains the same; thus, for the opponent who applies the same refutation, the charge of "admitting the opponent's view" (*matānujñā*) follows—this is the fifth position. // 42 //

NyS 5.1.43: When the reason is stated in the conclusion of an argument supported by evidence that depends on the definition of one's own position, the same fault applies because one would be admitting the fault of the opponent's position.

Regarding the requirement of establishing [the reason], the fault stated as "because the effect of effort is manifold" becomes a characteristic of the proponent's own position (svapakṣa) for the one who asserts the probans of negation; why? Because it arises from within his own position.
Thus, disregarding the fault characterized by his own position and failing to extract it,
and having tacitly admitted it, he attributes the applicable fault to the opponent's position, saying: "The same fault applies even to the refutation" (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.39).

Thus, he points out that the negation is inconclusive (anaikāntika) by indicating the reason; for when there is both the attribution of a fault that arises in relation to the definition of one's own position and the indication of a reason, the opponent's position becomes accepted [by implication]. How so?

Without having removed the fault of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) that was stated by the opponent through the argument beginning with “because the effects of effort are manifold” (prayatnakāryānekatvāt),
[the opponent says]: “The same fault applies even in the case of the negation” (pratiṣedhe 'pi samo doṣaḥ).

Thus he says: having accepted that the establishment [of one's own position] is faulty, the same fault attaches even to the refutation, because one accepts the opponent's position; therefore, the fault becomes equal. Just as for the opponent, having accepted that the refutation is faulty, the consequence of the same fault attaching even to the counter-refutation results in the admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), so too for this [proponent], having accepted that the establishment is faulty...
If one attributes the same fault to the opponent even when he is engaged in a refutation, the fallacy of "admitting the opponent's position" (*matānujñā*) follows;
this indeed constitutes the sixth position.
Among those, the first, third, and fifth positions belong to the proponent who maintains the establishing reason (*sthāpanāhetu*).
The second, fourth, and sixth positions belong to those who propound a reason for negation;
when their validity or invalidity is being examined, since there is no distinction between the fourth and sixth positions, the fault of tautology would follow.
In the case of the fourth position, it is stated that the opponent shares the same defect.
Regarding the statement, “In the refutation of a refutation, the fault is like the fault in the original refutation” (Nyāyasūtra 5.1.41),

even in the sixth book it is stated that “the fault is the same because one has accepted the opponent’s position,” thus expressing only the equality of the fault; there is no specific difference in meaning whatsoever.
In the third and fifth [alternatives], there is the consequence of the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*).

Even in the third alternative, equality is accepted in the statement: "Even in the negation, the fault is the same" (39). In the fifth alternative as well, it is accepted that the consequence of the same fault applies to the counter-negation (*pratiṣedha-vipratiṣedha*), and no specific distinction in meaning is stated.
In that regard, because there is no difference in meaning between the fifth and sixth positions, there is the fault of redundancy;
between the third and fourth, there is the concession of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*);
and between the first and second, there is an absence of a distinguishing reason (*viśeṣahetu*). Thus, in this sixfold set of positions, neither [proponent] achieves success.
When is there a "six-winged" (ṣaṭpakṣī) debate?
When [the opponent] proceeds by saying, "Even in the case of a negation, the same fault applies," then there is a failure to establish either of the two positions; but when...

By the statement, “If there were a difference in the effect, effort would not be the cause, because the conditions for non-perception are present” (38), the third position is joined; since a specific reason has been stated, it is established that the first position—that sound acquires its beginning immediately after effort and is not merely manifested—is proven, and thus the "sixfold cycle" (*ṣaṭpakṣī*) does not proceed. // 43 //
Thus ends the first daily lesson of the fifth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya composed by Vātsyāyana.
Now begins the second daily lesson of the fifth chapter of the Nyāya-bhāṣya.

It was stated in brief that "the multiplicity of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) arises from the various combinations of misconception and non-comprehension"; this [topic] shall now be analyzed in detail.

Indeed, the points of defeat are grounds for loss, bases of transgression, which generally depend upon the members of the argument such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, and they apply to both the proponent of truth (*tattvavādin*) and the proponent of untruth (*atattvavādin*).

Their classification is as follows: [NS 5.2.1] Loss of the proposition (pratijñāhāni), shifting the proposition (pratijñāntara), contradiction of the proposition (pratijñāvirodha), abandoning the proposition (pratijñāsaṃnyāsa), shifting the reason (hetvantara),

the irrelevant (arthāntara), the meaningless (nirarthaka), the unintelligible (avijñātārtha), the incoherent (apārthaka), the mistimed (aprāptakāla), the deficient (nyūna), the redundant (adhika), the repetitive (punarukta), and failure to restate (ananubhāṣaṇa).

Ignorance, inability to respond, distraction, admission of the opponent's position, overlooking what requires censure, censuring what does not require censure, a tenet that deviates from one's own school, and fallacious reasons are the points of defeat.
These are characterized by being divided into twenty-two types. // 1 //
NyS 5.2.2: Abandonment of one's own proposition occurs when one admits the property of the counter-example into one's own example.

*Pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition) occurs when, an opposing property being set forth by means of a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), one admits the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*). For example: when it has been stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," another says, "Since perceptibility is observed in the universal (*sāmānya*), which is eternal, why is sound not likewise [eternal]? [Thus ends the section.]
When [the opponent] has thus countered, he says: "If the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses and yet eternal, then let the jar also be eternal.

Indeed, this person, by attributing eternality to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of the proponent, abandons the very thesis (*pakṣa*) up to its conclusion. One who abandons the thesis is said to abandon the proposition (*pratijñā*), because the thesis is the locus of the proposition.
"Of the side" (pakṣasya). // 2 //
NyS 5.2.3: When the meaning of the proposition has been refuted, the statement of another meaning by means of a modification of the property is "shifting the proposition" (pratijñāntara).
The meaning of the proposition (*pratijñātārtha*) is as follows: when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," there is a refutation of this.

The deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) occurs through a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), such as: "A universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses and yet eternal. And regarding that refutation of the meaning of the proposition, [the rejoinder is made] "due to the difference in properties" (*dharmavikalpāt*); that is, due to the difference in properties between the example and the counter-example, even though they share a commonality.

The universal (*sāmānya*) is perceptible by the senses and all-pervading (*sarvagata*), whereas the pot, which is perceptible by the senses, is not all-pervading; this is due to the differentiation of their properties (*dharmavikalpa*). The statement "for the sake of that" means for the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*). How so? Just as the pot is not all-pervading, so too is sound not all-pervading, and like the pot, it is impermanent (*anitya*).
In this context, "Sound is impermanent" is the first proposition (*pratijñā*); "not all-pervading" is the second proposition, which constitutes a "shifting of the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*).

How, then, is this a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? A further proposition (*pratijñāntara*) is not the means of proving the original proposition; rather, the means of proving the proposition are the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, this is the employment of what is not a means of proof, and is thus useless. It is a point of defeat because of its uselessness. // 3 //
NyS 5.2.4: Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is "contradiction of the proposition" (pratijñāvirodha).

"The substance is distinct from its qualities" is the proposition (*pratijñā*). "Because no object other than color and so forth is perceived" is the reason (*hetu*). This is a contradiction between the proposition and the reason.
How so? If the substance is distinct from its qualities, then [the reason] "because no object other than color and so forth is perceived" [is contradicted].
This is not tenable;
for if it is argued that no entity distinct from color and the other qualities is perceived, [then how can one maintain] that substance is distinct from its qualities?
This is untenable;
furthermore, it contradicts and is subverted by the principle that substance is distinct from its qualities, since no object other than [those such as] form and so forth is perceived.
It is not possible. // 4 //
NyS 5.2.5: When the thesis is refuted, the withdrawal of the matter asserted in the proposition is "renunciation of the proposition" (pratijñāsaṃnyāsa).

When it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," the opponent might say: "The universal (sāmānya) is perceptible by the senses and yet not impermanent; likewise, sound is perceptible by the senses and yet not impermanent. When the thesis has thus been refuted, if he should say: "Who, moreover, says that sound is impermanent?"
"Thus, this denial of the matter previously asserted is called *pratijñā-saṃnyāsa* (renunciation of the proposition). // 5 //
NyS 5.2.6: When a reason has been rejected because it was stated without qualification, the proponent's desire for a qualification constitutes "shifting the reason" (hetvantara).
The illustration: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature" is the proposition (*pratijñā*). For what reason?

"Because there is a finite measure (*parimāṇa*) of modifications that have a single primordial nature. It is observed that for objects such as bowls and the like which are preceded by clay, there is a finite measure:

"To whatever extent the configuration of the primordial nature exists, to that same extent is the modification. And a finite measure is observed in each individual modification. This [measure] exists.
This magnitude is observed in each individual manifestation;
therefore, because of the magnitude of these transformations, we see that this manifest world has a single primordial cause.
An objection is raised against this by way of deviation: it is observed that both transformations with diverse primordial causes and those with a single primordial cause possess magnitude.

When this has been established, he says: "Because, when there is a conjunction with a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), a limited dimension is observed in the modifications (*vikāra*) such as the clay bowl.

For this manifest world (*vyakta*), being endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, is perceived as finite. In that case, since there is an absence of conjunction with the form of any other primordial nature, it follows that there is a single primordial nature."
When a reason has been stated without qualification and that reason has been refuted, for one who then states a qualification, it becomes a "different reason" (*hetvantara*).
And when there is the presence of a different reason, because the previous reason lacks proving power, it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
If, upon stating a different reason, an example is adduced to illustrate the meaning of the reason?
This manifest [world] cannot be of a single nature, because it is derived from other constituent causes;

or, if it were not so derived, then since the probans (hetu) would not have been demonstrated in the example, its capacity to prove [the thesis] would be impossible, and the probans would be rendered useless. Thus, the point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) called "non-cessation" (anivṛtta) remains. // 6 //
NS 5.2.7: A point that is irrelevant to the subject under discussion is the fallacy of "irrelevance" (arthāntara).

When the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the reason (*hetu*) is the subject at hand—within the adoption of a thesis (*pakṣa*) and its counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) characterized as previously described—one might say:
"Sound is eternal, because it is intangible; this is the reason. Now, a "reason" (*hetu*) is a nominal word (*kṛdanta-pada*) derived from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*.
And a "word" (*pada*) consists of nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*).
A noun (*nāman*) is a word whose form is qualified by its connection with another action;

it is a collection of actions and factors of action (*kāraka*). A verb (*ākhyāta*) denotes the connection of an action—qualified by number and factors of action—with time. An indeclinable (*nipāta*) is the mere meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*), qualified by the expression of time, which in usage does not differ in form from its underlying sense.
"Prefixes are those which, when attached, indicate an action," and so forth; thus, their distinct meaning should be understood. // 7 //
NS 5.2.8: That which is meaningless is like the mere specification of the order of phonemes.
For example: "Sound is impermanent because *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* belong to the class of *ja-ba-ga-ḍa-da-śa*, like *jha-bha-ña-gha-ḍha-dha-ṣa*.
