This kind of argument is meaningless (*nirarthaka*), because when the relationship between signifier and signified is not established, there is no comprehension of meaning; it is merely the letters being pointed out in succession. (8)
NyS 5.2.9: That which is stated three times to both the assembly and the opponent yet remains uncomprehended is "the unintelligible" (avijñātārtha).

A statement that, even when uttered three times by the proponent before the assembly and the opponent, is not understood due to reasons such as the use of ambiguous words, the employment of unfamiliar terminology, or being spoken too rapidly—this is "the meaning not understood" (*avijñātārtha*). Since it is employed to conceal one's own incapacity, it is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). // 9 //
NyS 5.2.10: That which has no connected meaning due to the lack of proper sequence between earlier and later parts is "meaningless" (apārthaka).

When there is no syntactic connection between multiple words or sentences due to their sequence, such that an incoherent meaning is perceived, it is called *apārthaka* (meaningless), because the intended collective sense has been lost. For example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a pot, a goat-skin, a ball of minced meat; this is the lower garment of a maiden; her father is not present. (10)
NyS 5.2.11: A statement in which the members [of the syllogism] are inverted is "untimely" (aprāptakāla).

The sequence of the members [of a syllogism], such as the proposition and so forth, follows their respective definitions according to the requirements of the meaning. In that context, speaking by reversing the order of these members constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "speaking out of order" (*aprāptakāla*), because it renders the meaning incoherent. // 11 //
NyS 5.2.12: That which lacks even one of its members is deficient.

The *nyūna* (deficient) ground for defeat occurs when even one of the constituent members, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, is lacking; for in the absence of the means of proof, the object to be proven cannot be established. // 12 //
NyS 5.2.13: That which contains more than the [required] reason and example is "superfluous" (adhika).
"Because it is performed by one [of the two], the other would be useless"—this [objection] is to be understood as applying only when a restrictive rule (niyama) is accepted. // 13 //
NyS 5.2.14: Repetition of words or their meanings is "redundancy" (punarukta), except in the case of a restatement (anuvāda).

Except in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), there is either verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*) or semantic tautology (*arthapunarukta*). Verbal tautology is, for example: "Sound is eternal; sound is eternal. Semantic tautology is, for example: "Sound is non-eternal; it is a resonance characterized by cessation. However, in the case of a restatement, there is no tautology, because a specific meaning is established through the repetition of the words, as for example:
“Nigamana is the restatement of the proposition (pratijñā) following the presentation of the reason (hetu),” [Nyāyasūtra 1.1.39]. // 14 //
NyS 5.2.15: The restatement, by its own word, of that which has already been established through the force of the meaning.

"Redundancy" (punarukta) is the subject under discussion; the illustration is as follows: having stated "it is impermanent because its nature is to arise," there is a word that expresses what is already established by implication.

If one were to state by its own word, "that which has the property of non-arising is eternal," that should be understood as a tautology; for when a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, if that meaning is already established, it is understood through presumptive implication (arthāpatti). // 15 //
NyS 5.2.16: Non-reproduction is the failure to repeat what has been understood and stated three times by the assembly.

When the meaning of a statement has been understood by the assembly and has been uttered three times by the proponent, the failure to restate it is the point of defeat called "non-reproduction" (ananubhāṣaṇa).
Without repeating [the opponent's position], on what basis could one state the refutation of the opposing view? // 6 //
And ignorance is that which is not cognized.
When a matter has been understood by the assembly and stated three times by the opponent, that failure to understand it constitutes the ground for defeat called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*); indeed,
this occurs when one does not understand.
Of what would one speak as a negation? // 7 //
Non-rejoinder (apratibhā) is the failure to provide a response to the opponent's argument.
When one does not provide an answer that consists of the refutation of the opponent's position, then one is defeated. // 18 //
NyS 5.2.19: *Vikṣepa* (evasion) is the interruption of the discussion due to preoccupation with other business.
When one interrupts a discourse that ought to be carried out continuously by saying,
"I have this duty to attend to; once it is finished, I shall speak afterward"— this is the point of defeat called *vikṣepa* (evasion).
In a debate that is destined to end in a single defeat, he himself shifts to another subject of discussion. // 19 //
NyS 5.2.20: Matānujñā (conceding the opponent's position) is the attribution of a fault to the opponent's position by accepting that same fault for one's own position.
He who, having admitted a fault pointed out by another in his own position,
fails to remove it and instead says, "The same fault applies to your position as well," [commits the fallacy] because he admits a fault in his own position regarding the opponent's position.
By attributing a fault [to oneself] while conceding the opponent's position, one falls into the point of defeat known as "conceding the position" (matānujñā). // 20 //
NyS_5.2.21: Neglecting to censure one who has reached a point of defeat is "overlooking the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa).

"One who is to be questioned" (paryanuyojya) means one who should be urged [to respond] because a ground for defeat (nigrahasthāna) has occurred. "Neglecting him" (tasyopekṣaṇam) is the failure to urge him by saying, "You have reached a ground for defeat.
And this occurs when the assembly does not declare, "Whose defeat is it? [and thus fails to act].
It must be said: one who has incurred defeat should certainly not expose his own private parts. // 21 //
NyS 5.2.22: To charge someone with a point of defeat when it is not a point of defeat is "objection against one who does not deserve objection" (niranuyojyānuyoga).
Due to a false determination regarding the definition of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
one who addresses another as "you are defeated" when there is no point of defeat should be understood as being himself defeated because of his "irrelevant questioning" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).
Thus [ends verse 22].

NyS 5.2.23: Having accepted a tenet, the failure to maintain consistency [in its application] leading to an unintended consequence in the discussion is called *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of a tenet).

Having asserted the existence of some object in a certain way, one should be understood as having committed the fallacy of *apasiddhānta* (deviation from a tenet) if, by reversing the asserted meaning, one introduces an argument characterized by lack of restriction— as for example: "An existent entity does not abandon its own nature."
Having accepted the established doctrine that "there is no destruction of the existent" and "the non-existent does not acquire its own nature"— that is, "the non-existent is not produced"—
he establishes his own position: "This manifest world has a single primordial nature."
Because we observe the persistence of a common nature among modifications. Just as it is observed that bowls and other such objects, which are permeated by clay, possess a single material cause,
so too this diversity of manifest entities is seen to be permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Therefore, because of the observation of homogeneity with pleasure and so forth, it is said that this universe has a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having spoken thus, he is questioned: "Now, how are 'primordial nature' and 'modification' (*vikāra*) to be defined?"
Thus, that which remains constant while one property ceases and another property arises is the *prakṛti* (primordial matter); and that other property which arises is the *vikāra* (modification).
Thus, because he contradicts the meaning of his own proposition and because there is no fixed rule, he brings about a logical impasse in the discussion;
for he has indeed asserted: "The non-existent does not manifest, nor..."
"It becomes concealed" means that without the concealment and manifestation of the existent and the non-existent,
there can be no engagement in action nor any cessation of action for anyone.

When the clay has indeed been established [as the material cause], there occurs the process [of cognition] that "there will be another entity characterized as a bowl and so forth," and the cessation of that process occurs with the thought "it was. This same [principle] applies to the properties of the clay as well.
It would not be so, if one who has thus countered [the argument] accepts the loss of the self-nature of what exists and the acquisition of the self-nature of what does not exist;
in that case, this constitutes the point of defeat known as "departure from a tenet" (apasiddhānta).
Or, if he does not accept it?
Its proof is not established. // 23 //
And the fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa) are as previously described.

And fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). But do fallacious reasons become points of defeat by virtue of possessing a different characteristic, just as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [become] objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)?
To this he says: "as previously stated.
The status of being a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs precisely through the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
These aforementioned categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), have thus been enumerated.
They are characterized and examined. // 24 //
Vātsyāyana has composed this collection of commentaries on that Nyāya system which revealed itself to the sage Akṣapāda, the best among speakers.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Nyāyabhāṣya composed by Vātsyāyana, the best among the learned.
And thus the Nyāyadarśana is completed.
